0.title: Luke: The Gospel of the Saviour of the World
0.overview:
Luke is the longest book in the New Testament. It is also, in the judgment of many, the most beautiful — a Gospel written by a physician who was also a literary artist, a historian who was also a theologian, a Gentile who understood the Jewish roots of everything he was describing better than most of his contemporaries. When Luke sets out to write an orderly account of the things that have been accomplished among us, he produces something that is at once a careful historical document, a theological masterpiece, and a pastoral letter addressed to a world hungry for good news.

The author never names himself, but the ancient tradition is unanimous: this is Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), the companion of Paul (2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 24), the man who stayed with Paul when everyone else had left. He was almost certainly a Gentile — the only Gentile author in the New Testament — and this shapes everything he writes. He sees in Jesus the fulfilment not just of Israel's hopes but of the deepest longings of the whole human race. His Gospel is addressed to Theophilus, probably a Roman official of some standing, and through him to the entire Gentile world. Luke wants the world to know that what happened in Judea was not a local religious event. It was the turning point of all of history.

Luke writes in two volumes: the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Together they tell the story of what Jesus began to do (the Gospel) and what he continued to do through his Spirit in the church (Acts). The Gospel ends where Acts begins — with the ascension and the promise of the Spirit. This two-volume structure matters for reading Luke: his Gospel is not a self-contained biography but the first act of a larger drama, the story of how the good news of the kingdom moved from a manger in Bethlehem to the centre of the Roman world. The Gospel is movement toward Jerusalem; Acts is movement from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Luke's great themes are the themes of the kingdom come in unexpected ways. He gives more space than any other evangelist to women, to the poor, to Samaritans, to Gentiles, to tax collectors and sinners — the people whom polite religious society had written off as beyond the reach of God's grace. He is the Gospel of the outsider welcomed in. He shows Jesus praying at every major turning point of his ministry. He is the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, who appears from the first chapter to the last. And above all, he is the Gospel of joy, because at the centre of everything is the announcement that the Saviour has come, and his name is Jesus.

1.title: The Announcement of the King
1.overview:
Chapter 1 of Luke is one of the most carefully constructed passages in all of Scripture. Before a single miracle is performed, before a single sermon is preached, before Jesus has spoken a word in public — Luke gives us seven scenes of annunciation, visitation, and praise that set the theological coordinates for everything that follows. He is telling us, from the very first verse, what kind of Gospel this is going to be: historically grounded, theologically rich, and written to produce the certainty of faith in a world that desperately needs it.

The chapter opens with a prologue that is unlike anything else in the New Testament — a formal literary preface, modelled on the prefaces of great Hellenistic historians like Thucydides and Polybius, establishing Luke's credentials as a careful historian and his purpose as a pastoral one. He has investigated everything carefully; he writes in orderly sequence; his goal is that Theophilus may have certainty about the things he has been taught. This is not mythology. This is history — specific, datable, verifiable history — and Luke wants his reader to know it.

From the prologue, the chapter moves into a world saturated with Old Testament atmosphere. Zechariah and Elizabeth are introduced in language that echoes Abraham and Sarah; the angel Gabriel appears as he did to Daniel; Mary's Magnificat is the New Testament's Psalter. Luke is making the claim that the long story of Israel — the story of promise and longing and waiting — has reached its culmination. The God who made promises in Eden, who called Abraham, who spoke through the prophets, is now fulfilling everything he said. The silence of four hundred years is over. The angel's voice breaks into a world that thought God had gone quiet, and nothing will ever be the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The prologue of Luke is the one place in the Gospels where the author steps out before the story begins and speaks in his own voice about how he wrote it. What he says in four verses establishes the whole intellectual and pastoral framework of what follows. He is writing history — but history in the service of faith. He has predecessors; he has done his own research; he has a named recipient; and he has a stated goal.

The word in v. 1 for what the many compiled is diēgēsis, a narrative that leads a reader through events from end to end. The “orderly” of v. 3 is a different word, kathexēs, meaning in sequence, each thing in its proper place. That need not mean a rigid diary order; Luke sometimes gathers material by theme rather than by date. What he promises is an account with a shape you can follow and trust.

The “many” who had already attempted this were not writing fraudulently, and Luke names their work without a sneer. But he has something to add: his own careful investigation, traced back to the source, from the eyewitnesses themselves. The word in v. 2 is autoptes — those who saw with their own eyes. Luke's history is not rumour at several removes. It is testimony from the people who were there.

Theophilus is greeted as “most excellent,” a formal Roman honorific used of senior officials (cf. Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). He may be a patron who funded the research, an official investigating the Christian movement, or a recent convert who needs the foundations confirmed. The goal Luke states in v. 4 is asphaleia — the firm ground that comes of knowing that what you believe is true. For Luke, faith is grounded in history or it is not Christian faith at all.

Which raises the question a thoughtful reader feels at once: if Luke sifted sources like any careful historian, in what sense is this God's word rather than Luke's book? Scripture's answer is that it is both. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there — guiding the questions, the witnesses, the material kept and the order set (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21). God did not bypass Luke's mind; he used it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The prologue's insistence on eyewitness testimony and careful investigation is the New Testament's answer to every form of Christianity that treats the historical details of the gospel as negotiable. Luke does not begin with timeless spiritual principles. He begins with what happened. The things accomplished among us are events — specific, dateable, observable events — and his first act as a historian is to establish their factual grounding.

This rules out from the start any reading of the Gospel as mythology, allegory or spiritual symbol. The incarnation, the miracles, the death, the resurrection: these are things that took place, in a named reign, in a known country, in front of people who could be questioned about them.

The goal of certainty (asphaleia) is the pastoral heart of the prologue. Luke is not writing to entertain, nor primarily to persuade the uncommitted. He is writing to confirm the faith of someone already taught the Christian story who needs to know that what he has been taught is true. That is the function of historically grounded preaching in every generation — not to introduce people to a religious experience but to settle them in a historical faith.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prologue models what responsible handling of the gospel looks like for any teacher or preacher: go back to the sources, investigate carefully, present the findings in order, and do it all in the service of the hearer's certainty. The person in the pew wrestling with doubt does not need vague spiritual reassurance. He needs the kind of careful, ordered account Luke is about to provide.

The best pastoral response to doubt is rarely “just trust.” It is nearer to “let me show you why trust is reasonable” — which is precisely what the next twenty-three chapters do.

And asphaleia is a gift the gospel gives to those who receive it on its own terms: not the brittle certainty of someone who has never been challenged, but the settled certainty of someone who has looked at the evidence and found it solid. Theophilus is meant to close this Gospel knowing not only that Jesus is Lord but why that claim can be trusted — and equipped to give the reason to anybody who asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke writes in the tradition of earlier accounts, drawing on what eyewitnesses and ministers of the word handed down.

A historian’s preface. One long, polished Greek sentence (vv. 1–4), in the style of ancient historians. Luke wants to be read as history.

Accomplished among us. Literally “fulfilled”: these events complete God’s promises.

Eyewitnesses and ministers. The apostles who saw Jesus and passed on what they saw (Acts 1:21–22).

Where Christians differ: Luke’s sources. Scholars debate whether Luke used Mark and another source. Verdict: Luke says plainly that he used earlier accounts and eyewitness testimony. Using sources does not lessen inspiration; the Spirit guided his research and writing (2 Timothy 3:16).

On a Tuesday. Your faith rests on testimony to real events, not on feelings.
verseByVerse.note: Luke did not claim to be an eyewitness himself; he gathered the testimony of those who were.

parallels.desc: Luke’s second volume, also to Theophilus
what we have seen and heard

verseByVerse.quote: it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke has investigated everything carefully from the start and writes an orderly account for Theophilus.

Followed all things closely. Research, perhaps during Paul’s two years in custody at Caesarea (Acts 24:27), with access to people like Mary and James.

Orderly. Well arranged, not necessarily in strict time order.

Theophilus. “Friend of God”. “Most excellent” suggests an official of rank (Acts 23:26), probably a real person, perhaps Luke’s patron.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not afraid of careful investigation.
verseByVerse.note: Theophilus means “friend of God.” “Most excellent” was a title used for Roman officials, which suggests a man of rank.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of the things he has been taught.

Certainty. Asphaleia: firm ground. The Gospel is written to give assurance.

Taught. The word gives us “catechism”. Theophilus had been instructed already, and Luke confirms it.

On a Tuesday. If you are unsure, read Luke from start to finish. It was written for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–25 — Birth of John the Baptist Foretold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With v. 5 Luke moves from the historian's prologue to the historian's narrative, and the contrast could hardly be sharper. From a formal Hellenistic preface he plunges into a world saturated with the Old Testament. Zechariah is a priest; Elizabeth is a daughter of Aaron; and they are described in language almost identical to the description of Abraham and Sarah — both righteous, both blameless, and she barren.

A reader steeped in the Hebrew Scriptures recognises the pattern at once. God is about to do something only God can do. He did it with Sarah, with Rebekah, with Rachel, with Hannah. Now he does it a last time, because the child born of this barren womb will prepare the way for the one who needs no human preparation to be born.

The setting of the announcement is itself a sermon. Zechariah is at work, in his division's week of service, chosen by lot for the incense offering — the one duty most priests never received and no priest received twice (vv. 8-10). The whole multitude is praying outside at the hour of incense. God breaks four hundred years of silence not at a moment of revival but in the middle of an ordinary rota.

Gabriel has not appeared in Scripture since the book of Daniel, and the detail is deliberate. Daniel received angelic revelation about the end of the exile and the coming of an Anointed One; Gabriel's reappearance signals that what Daniel waited for is arriving.

The announcement about John is a mosaic of Old Testament promise: the prohibition on wine and strong drink (echoing the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6 and the birth of Samson), the filling with the Spirit from the womb (echoing Jer. 1:5 and Isa. 49:1), and the ministry in the spirit and power of Elijah (fulfilling Mal. 4:5-6). Every detail is a fulfilment of something Israel had been promised and had been waiting for.

Zechariah's response is entirely understandable and entirely insufficient. He asks how he can know — and then supplies his evidence, which is his age. He is asking for proof while the proof stands in front of him. The muteness that follows is as much mercy as discipline: nine months in which he can speak nothing except what God has spoken, and a limit written into the sentence (“until the day that these things take place”).

The chapter does not hurry past what that cost him publicly. The crowd waiting outside expected the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 and did not receive it; a man came out of the Holy Place making signs, and there was no benediction that day (vv. 21-23). And he stayed to the end of his rota, serving out his days in silence.

Elizabeth's response, by contrast, is hidden joy. Her first recorded words are not about the child but about God: the Lord has done this for me, and he has looked on me to take away my reproach among people. She understands what Zechariah will need months to grasp — that this is grace, and grace needs no explanation.
verseByVerse.theology:
The barrenness of Elizabeth, like that of Sarah and Hannah before her, is the Old Testament's persistent symbol of human inability and divine sufficiency. The child of promise is always the child who could not have been born by human power alone. That is not incidental; it is the pattern of grace. God works precisely where human capacity has run out.

The child born to a barren womb, the nation born out of an enslaved people, the Messiah born of a virgin — the pattern holds in every case, and the point is the same in every case: salvation is of the LORD, and not of man.

Gabriel's description of John's ministry — that he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah — identifies John as the fulfilment of Malachi 4:5-6, the last prophecy of the Old Testament. Israel's canonical story ends with the promise of Elijah. It begins again here, with his arrival.

And the four hundred years of silence end not with a king or an army but with a priest's speechless vision in the temple. God's timing is consistently unexpected, and his entry points are consistently the last places power would have chosen.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's request for a sign is the response of a man whose theology was correct and whose faith, in the moment, was smaller than his knowledge. He knew the God who opens barren wombs. He had read the stories and offered the prayers. But when the answer stood in front of him he asked for evidence.

The gap between what we confess and what we trust in the moment is one of the most honest things the Bible shows about the life of faith. And Gabriel's response is not contempt but the gift of silence: a season of enforced dependence on what God has said rather than on what Zechariah can say.

Elizabeth's instinct to remain in seclusion for five months (v. 24) is the instinct of someone who knows that a gift this size needs to be received before it is announced. A soul that has received extraordinary grace sometimes needs to be quiet with it before it can speak of it.

The rush to publicise every experience of God's goodness can short-circuit the deeper work the grace was given to do. Elizabeth sits with the miracle, lets it form her, and waits.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Herod’s reign lived a priest, Zechariah, and his wife Elizabeth, both righteous and blameless before God.

Herod. Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC. Jesus was born before then.

The division of Abijah. One of twenty-four priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:10).

Righteous and blameless. Not sinless (v. 20), but sincerely obedient, walking in God’s ways and using his provisions for sin.

From Israel’s faithful. The story of Jesus begins in the temple, among godly, ordinary Israelites.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC. The priests were organised in twenty-four divisions, each serving in the temple for a week at a time; Abijah’s was the eighth.

verseByVerse.quote: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren and both were old.

Barren. Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah. God often begins his great works where human hope ends.

What it does not mean. Childlessness was often seen as a sign of God’s displeasure. Luke has just called them righteous. It was not punishment.

On a Tuesday. Childlessness and unanswered longing are not proof that God has rejected you.
verseByVerse.note: Barrenness was a deep sorrow and often a social shame. Scripture’s great births often begin with a barren woman.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah was chosen by lot to burn incense in the temple, while the people prayed outside.

By lot. With thousands of priests, this was a once-in-a-lifetime honour. The lot is in God’s hand (Proverbs 16:33).

The hour of incense. Morning or evening; the people praying outside.

On a Tuesday. God meets people in the ordinary round of faithful duty.
verseByVerse.note: With so many priests, the honour of offering incense in the holy place came to few, perhaps once in a lifetime. It was offered morning and evening while the people prayed outside.

parallels.desc: let my prayer be counted as incense

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel of the Lord appeared beside the altar, and Zechariah was terrified.

The right side. The place of favour.

Fear. The usual response to an angel in Scripture. Holiness overwhelms.

The silence breaks. No prophet had spoken in Israel for around four hundred years. Now heaven speaks.
verseByVerse.note: The altar of incense stood just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to him, 'Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel tells Zechariah not to fear: his prayer has been heard, and Elizabeth will bear a son, to be named John.

Your prayer. Probably for a son, long since given up, or for Israel’s redemption. God answered both.

John. “The LORD is gracious”.

On a Tuesday. Prayers you have stopped praying may still be heard.
verseByVerse.note: John means “the LORD has been gracious.”

parallels.desc: Sarah will bear you a son

verseByVerse.quote: And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John will bring joy, be great before the Lord, abstain from wine, and be filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb.

Great before the Lord. Greatness in God’s sight, not the world’s (7:28).

No wine. Like a Nazirite (Numbers 6:3), set apart.

From his mother’s womb. The Spirit was at work in John before birth (v. 41).

What it does not mean. This was a unique calling, not the normal pattern for every child. Yet it shows that God can work in a person from the very beginning of life.
verseByVerse.note: No wine or strong drink was the rule for a Nazirite, someone set apart to God.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John will turn many in Israel to God, going before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah to prepare a people.

Malachi 4:5–6. The last Old Testament promise: Elijah will come before the day of the Lord.

Before him. Before the Lord God, and the next to come is Jesus. Jesus is the Lord.

Where Christians differ: was John Elijah? John denied being Elijah literally (John 1:21), yet Jesus said he was the Elijah to come (Matthew 11:14). Verdict: John came in Elijah’s spirit and power, fulfilling the role, not as Elijah returned.

Fathers to children. Repentance restores families.

On a Tuesday. Repentance shows itself at home first.

parallels.desc: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers to their children
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: And Zechariah said to the angel, 'How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah asks for a sign, because he and Elizabeth are old.

How shall I know? The question of Abraham (Genesis 15:8), but here from unbelief.

Contrast with Mary. Mary asks how (v. 34); Zechariah asks for proof. The angel hears the difference.

On a Tuesday. Even godly people struggle to believe God’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered him, 'I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel reveals himself as Gabriel, sent from God’s presence with good news, and because Zechariah did not believe, he will be mute until the promise comes true.

Gabriel. He spoke to Daniel of the Messiah’s coming (Daniel 8–9).

Good news. The first time Luke uses the verb euangelizō, “preach the gospel”.

Silent. Discipline, but also a sign. When he speaks again it will be in praise.

On a Tuesday. God’s discipline of his children is mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Gabriel appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah comes out unable to speak, and the people realise he has seen a vision.

No blessing. The priest should have pronounced the blessing (Numbers 6:24–26), but could not. The blessing Luke ends with is Jesus’ (24:50–51).

He went home. Faithfully finishing his service.
verseByVerse.note: The people waited for the priest to come out and pronounce the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, 'Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth conceives and hides herself for five months, praising God for taking away her disgrace.

The Lord has done this. She gives the credit to God.

Reproach. The shame of childlessness, lifted.

For worship. Thank God for the times he has looked on you with favour.

parallels.desc: Rachel: God has taken away my reproach

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six months after the annunciation to Zechariah, Gabriel is sent again — this time not to a priest in the temple but to a young woman in Galilee. The contrast is everything Luke is about. The gospel does not move from centre to periphery, from the established to the marginal, from the important to the overlooked. It moves the other way.

The temple in Jerusalem is where Gabriel went first; a village in Galilee, to a girl betrothed to a builder, is where he goes next. Nazareth was small and undistinguished — so undistinguished that Nathanael would later ask whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46). The answer, it turns out, is everything.

Gabriel's greeting is without precedent in Jewish literature. Nobody else in the Bible is greeted this way. Mary is “favoured” — the graced one, the one on whom divine favour has freely fallen.

Roman Catholic theology has developed from this greeting the doctrines of Mary's immaculate conception and sinlessness; the Reformed reading takes the word as referring to God's gracious choice of Mary for this specific task rather than to any inherent quality in her. The distinction matters, and Mary settles it herself at v. 47 when she calls God her Saviour. In Luke's account the wonder is never Mary's worthiness. It is God's freedom.

The announcement of Jesus's birth is the most theologically dense passage in the chapter. Gabriel says four things: he will be great; he will be called Son of the Most High; the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father; he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

These claims are simultaneously royal and divine. The throne of David identifies him as the Messiah of Israel's hope; the title Son of the Most High and the endless kingdom move beyond anything a merely human king could claim. Gabriel is announcing the fulfilment of 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and the inauguration of the kingdom of Daniel 7:14. The Messiah Israel expected and the Son of God the disciples would confess are one and the same person.

Mary's question is entirely different in character from Zechariah's request for a sign. She does not doubt; she asks for clarification. The mechanism puzzles her, not the possibility. And Gabriel's answer is the most direct statement of the incarnation in the Synoptic Gospels: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, the power of the Most High will overshadow her, and the child will be called holy, the Son of God.

The language of overshadowing recalls the cloud of divine presence that covered the tabernacle (Exod. 40:35) — the presence of God taking up residence. Mary is the new tabernacle, the place where God chooses to dwell. And her response, “Let it be to me according to your word,” is the finest answer to divine grace in the New Testament. Not resignation. Not reluctant compliance. Surrender that is also worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “Son of the Most High” places Jesus in direct relationship to the God of Israel's covenant. In Daniel 7:18-27 it is the saints of the Most High who receive the kingdom; here the kingdom is given to the Son of the Most High himself. Gabriel is announcing not merely that Jesus will be the greatest of Israel's kings but that he is the figure Daniel saw receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will not be destroyed.

The Davidic covenant and the everlasting kingdom of Daniel meet in this child — and a thousand years of promise, apparently stalled since the exile, resume in a single sentence spoken in a village house.

The Holy Spirit's role in the conception is the New Testament's clearest statement that the incarnation is a divine act and not a human achievement. Mary supplies the humanity; the Spirit supplies the initiative that makes this birth unlike every other.

The result is not a demigod — a being partly divine and partly human — but a fully human being who is at the same time the eternal Son of God. This is what the church has confessed from the beginning: two natures, one person, without confusion or mixture. Gabriel does not explain the mechanics of the mystery. He announces the reality.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary's “Let it be to me according to your word” is the model response to a divine call that exceeds comprehension. She does not understand how this will happen. She does not know what it will cost. She cannot see Simeon's sword or the hill called Golgotha. She says yes to a future she cannot see, on the strength of the word of a God she trusts.

That is what faith is — not the confident feeling that everything will be easy, but the willingness to place yourself in the hands of the One who has spoken.

The contrast between Gabriel's errand to the temple in Jerusalem and his errand to a house in Nazareth is Luke's first great declaration that the gospel is for everyone. The most important conversation in human history took place not in a palace or a sanctuary but in the home of an ordinary girl in a town nobody thought much of.

God's greatest gifts consistently arrive through the most unlikely channels — which means no person, no place and no circumstance is too small or too obscure to be the site of divine grace.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the sixth month Gabriel is sent to Nazareth to a virgin named Mary, engaged to Joseph, of David’s line.

Nazareth. An obscure village (John 1:46). From the temple to a village.

Betrothed. A binding engagement; breaking it required divorce.

A virgin. Luke says it twice in one verse.

House of David. Joseph’s line gives Jesus his legal claim to David’s throne.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hills of Galilee. Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; the couple did not yet live together.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to her and said, 'Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!' But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel greets Mary as favoured by God, and she is troubled.

Favoured one. Kecharitōmenē: one on whom grace has been bestowed.

Where Christians differ: “full of grace”? The Latin Vulgate’s “full of grace” has been used to support Mary as a source of grace and her sinlessness. Verdict: the word means she received grace (the same verb as Ephesians 1:6, of all believers). She is a recipient of grace, not a dispenser of it.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “Blessed are you among women”, from v. 42.

On a Tuesday. God’s favour can rest on the obscure and unimportant.

parallels.desc: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valour”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel tells Mary not to fear, for she will conceive and bear a son and name him Jesus.

Found favour. Grace, not merit.

Jesus. The Greek form of Joshua, meaning the LORD saves: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

Isaiah 7:14. The virgin will conceive and bear a son.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

verseByVerse.quote: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her son will be great, the Son of the Most High, and God will give him David’s throne, to reign over Jacob’s house for ever without end.

2 Samuel 7:12–16. God’s promise of a son of David whose kingdom will last for ever.

Son of the Most High. Divine sonship (v. 35).

Where Christians differ: David’s throne. Dispensationalists expect Christ to sit on a literal throne in Jerusalem in a future millennium. Verdict: Christ took David’s throne at his resurrection and ascension (Acts 2:30–36); he reigns now, and his kingdom will have no end.

For worship. Praise the King whose reign has no end.

parallels.desc: on the throne of David, no end
a kingdom that shall not be destroyed

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said to the angel, 'How will this be, since I am a virgin?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary asks how this can be, since she is a virgin.

How, not whether. A question of faith seeking understanding.

Where Christians differ: a vow of virginity? Some Roman Catholic interpreters read her words as a vow of lifelong virginity, supporting her perpetual virginity. Verdict: she is engaged to be married; her question means simply that she has not had relations with a man. The Gospels mention Jesus’ brothers and sisters (8:19–20; Mark 6:3), most naturally Mary’s later children.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered her, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the power of the Most High will overshadow her, so the child will be holy, the Son of God.

The Holy Spirit. The same Spirit who hovered over creation (Genesis 1:2).

Overshadow. The cloud of God’s presence over the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35).

Where Christians differ: the virgin birth. Liberal theology has denied it as a legend. Verdict: it is plainly taught by Luke and Matthew, and confessed by the creeds. It shows that salvation comes from God, and that the Son took true humanity without inheriting Adam’s guilt.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “of you” (“the holy one born of you”).

For worship. Worship the Son of God who became man.
verseByVerse.note: “Overshadow” recalls the cloud of God’s presence overshadowing the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: the cloud settled on the tent

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel tells Mary that her elderly relative Elizabeth has conceived, for nothing will be impossible with God.

A sign given. Unasked for: a kindness to Mary.

Nothing impossible. Genesis 18:14, said to Sarah. Literally “no word from God will be powerless.”

On a Tuesday. What are you calling impossible that God has promised?

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.' And the angel departed from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary answers, “I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.”

Servant. Literally “slave”: total surrender.

The cost. Misunderstanding, gossip and possibly losing Joseph.

The model of faith. Not Mary as an object of devotion, but Mary as a model of trusting obedience.

On a Tuesday. Pray Mary’s prayer about the thing God is asking of you.

For worship. Let it be to me according to your word.

parallels.desc: let your servant find favour in your eyes

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary leaves for the hill country of Judah “with haste” — the word suggests urgency, even a kind of breathless joy. She has just received the most overwhelming news in history, and the angel has told her that her elderly relative is also pregnant. She goes at once, not to tell the story but to be with somebody who might understand it: someone else visited by grace in a way that makes no human sense.

The moment Mary's greeting reaches Elizabeth, the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps. John recognises Jesus before either of them has been born. This is not sentimental detail; it is Luke's first testimony to what the Baptist's whole ministry will be. Jesus is the one who is coming, and John exists to point towards him. Even in the womb, before any conscious act of faith, John responds to the presence of the Lord.

The Holy Spirit fills Elizabeth in that moment and she speaks with prophetic clarity. Mary is blessed; the fruit of her womb is blessed; and Elizabeth marvels that “the mother of my Lord” should come to her. That exclamation is the first confession of Jesus's lordship in Luke's Gospel, and it comes from a woman who cannot know it by any natural means. The Spirit has revealed it.

Lord on Elizabeth's lips is the title Israel's Scriptures give to God himself. She is not saying “the mother of an important person.” She is saying “the mother of the one who is LORD.” The full theological weight of the title is present from the beginning.

And the section does not end with the confession. It ends with a beatitude, and the beatitude is about faith: “blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord” (v. 45). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, does not finally commend Mary's womb, her lineage or her purity. She commends her trust.

That is the section's real climax, and it sets Mary directly against Zechariah, who heard the same angel in the same six months and did not believe. Luke has framed his whole opening around a single question: the word of God has come — will it be received?
verseByVerse.theology:
John's leap at the sound of Mary's greeting is a pre-natal act of recognition that is also a pre-natal act of worship. The Reformed tradition reads this, alongside Jeremiah 1:5 and the Baptist's filling with the Spirit from the womb, as a sign that divine grace and knowledge precede human consciousness. The child does not decide to leap; the Spirit moves him.

This is the grace that goes before us — that calls and shapes and prepares before we are capable of any response. It is not an argument for conscious infant faith. It is a sign of the sovereign grace of God that precedes every human act.

Elizabeth's blessing of Mary — “blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” — applies the Old Testament's blessing language to the New Testament's supreme moment of grace. Mary stands in the line of those through whom God has worked unexpected deliverance.

But she surpasses them all, because the one she carries is not a deliverer of Israel only but the Saviour of the world. And v. 45 keeps even that from becoming a cult of the mother: what the Spirit singles out in her is not her body but her believing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary goes to Elizabeth with haste — not to process her experience alone, not to work things out in private, but to be with somebody who can understand. The instinct is exactly right. The grace of God is not meant to be received and kept in isolation.

The community of the gospel is the community of those who have all, in one way or another, been visited by unexpected grace, and who find in each other's company the confirmation and the joy that private reflection cannot produce. An isolated believer is a believer at risk.

Elizabeth's question — “Why is this granted to me?” — is the question of someone who has not lost the astonishment grace produces. She has been told by an angel that she will bear a child; she is herself six months into an impossible pregnancy; and when she hears Mary's greeting her first response is wonder at the privilege of the moment.

The soul still capable of asking “why me?” in the face of God's gifts is a soul grace is still shaping. The moment we begin to feel we have earned the visit, something essential has been lost. And notice what is entirely absent from Elizabeth: any trace of comparison with the younger woman whose portion is plainly larger than her own.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary hurries to visit Elizabeth, and at her greeting Elizabeth’s baby leaps in her womb and Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.

With haste. Eager to see the sign.

The baby leaped. John begins his work of pointing to Jesus before either is born.

Life before birth. Luke uses the same word, brephos, for the unborn John and the newborn Jesus (2:12). Scripture treats the unborn as persons (Psalm 139:13–16).

On a Tuesday. Defend and care for the unborn and their mothers.
verseByVerse.note: The hill country of Judea was the highland around Jerusalem, some 80 miles or more from Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: and she exclaimed with a loud cry, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth cries out that Mary is blessed among women, her child is blessed, and she is honoured that the mother of her Lord should visit her.

Blessed among women. Honoured above all women, like Jael (Judges 5:24).

My Lord. Elizabeth, by the Spirit, calls the unborn Jesus “Lord”.

Where Christians differ: Mary’s honour. Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions build devotion and prayer to Mary on these words. Verdict: Mary is rightly honoured as blessed, but never prayed to or worshipped. Her blessing lies in her son and in her faith (v. 45; 11:27–28).

parallels.desc: most blessed of women be Jael
how can the ark of the LORD come to me?

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth explains that the baby leaped for joy, and declares Mary blessed for believing the Lord’s word would be fulfilled.

Joy. A theme of Luke’s Gospel.

She who believed. The contrast with Zechariah is plain. Faith is Mary’s greatest blessing.

On a Tuesday. Believe what God has said, and you are blessed.

parallels.desc: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–56 — Mary's Song of Praise: The Magnificat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Magnificat — named from the first word of its Latin translation, “My soul magnifies the Lord” — is the New Testament's greatest hymn and one of the most theologically rich passages in Scripture. It is modelled so closely on Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2:1-10 that some have argued Luke originally assigned it to Elizabeth; but the text is clear, and the reasons for it belonging to Mary are overwhelming.

Mary is the New Testament's Hannah — the woman through whom God's greatest act of salvation is brought into the world. And like Hannah she responds not with private gratitude but with public theology: a proclamation of what God is like, what he has done, and what he always does.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 46-50) is personal. Mary sings of what God has done for her: he has looked on the humble estate of his servant; he has done great things for her; his mercy extends to those who fear him. The second (vv. 51-55) is cosmic and historical: God has scattered the proud, brought down the mighty, exalted the humble, filled the hungry, sent the rich away empty, and helped his servant Israel.

Those verbs are past tense — the Greek aorist, expressing completed action — even though none of it has yet visibly happened. Mary sings in the prophetic past: what God is going to do in Jesus is so certain that she sings it as already accomplished. This is the faith that sees the invisible reality and speaks it before it is seen.

The theology of the Magnificat is the theology of the great reversal — the consistent pattern in which God works through what the world considers weak, low, foolish and despised, to accomplish what power and wisdom cannot. The proud are scattered; the mighty brought down; the humble exalted; the hungry filled; the rich sent away empty.

This is not a manifesto for violent revolution — every verb has God as its subject — but the testimony of a God whose ways are not our ways, who chooses the foolish things of the world to shame the wise (1 Cor. 1:27). Mary has understood it because she has lived it: she is herself the lowly servant God has honoured beyond imagining.

And the song ends where the story began, with Abraham (vv. 54-55) — the reversals are not God changing his policy but God keeping an old appointment. Then, with no transition at all, Luke notes that Mary stayed three months and went home (v. 56). She walked back to Nazareth visibly pregnant, to a fiancé who would decide to divorce her. The extraordinary is set down in the middle of the ordinary, and the ordinary is where it has to be carried.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Magnificat's use of the past tense for events that have not yet occurred — he has scattered the proud, he has brought down the mighty — is the linguistic form of prophetic certainty. The prophets of Israel consistently spoke of future events in the past tense when the certainty of God's word made the outcome as sure as if it had already happened.

Isaiah 53 does exactly this, narrating the Servant's suffering and vindication in the past tense centuries before either occurred. Mary's song places her in that prophetic line — not as one who has received a vision of the future but as one who has received the seed of the future in her own body and understands what it means.

The “humble estate” of Mary is a condition of insignificance and social unimportance. God has looked upon it — deliberately noticed — not despite it but through it. This is the theology of election that runs from Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and David the youngest over his brothers, to Galilee over Jerusalem and Mary over every princess in Israel.

God's choices consistently invert the world's criteria. The reason is not that the lowly are inherently virtuous. It is that the glory of a grace which chooses them cannot possibly be confused with a favour granted on the basis of merit.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Magnificat has been sung in Christian worship since the earliest centuries — in the evening prayer of the church, in the liturgies of East and West, in the hymns of the Reformation — and set to music by composers from Monteverdi to Bach. It is not merely a beautiful poem. It is the church joining Mary's song, declaring that the God who did great things for her is doing great things still.

Every Christian who sings it stands in the line of Mary's witness: scattering the proud, filling the hungry, keeping covenant with his people, is what he is still doing.

It is also among the most politically subversive texts in the New Testament — not because it calls for revolution but because it announces a King whose reign will outlast every human empire, whose justice will overturn every human injustice, and whose mercy will outlive every human cruelty.

The church that sings this song is the community that knows how the story ends, and that knowledge shapes how it lives now: not grasping for power, not trusting in the mighty, not filling itself with the world's goods, but living in the pattern of the God who scatters the proud and exalts the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary’s song begins: her soul magnifies the Lord and her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour.

The Magnificat. From its first word in Latin. It echoes Hannah’s song (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and the Psalms.

Magnify. To make great: to declare God’s greatness.

God my Saviour. Mary needed a Saviour. Where Christians differ. Roman Catholic doctrine teaches that Mary was conceived without original sin. Verdict: Scripture says all have sinned (Romans 3:23), and Mary herself calls God her Saviour. She was saved by grace, as we are.

Textual note. A few Latin manuscripts attribute the song to Elizabeth. All Greek manuscripts give it to Mary.

For worship. Sing Mary’s song as your own.
verseByVerse.note: Mary’s song, known as the Magnificat, is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has looked on his humble servant, and all generations will call her blessed, for the Mighty One has done great things for her; holy is his name.

Humble estate. Her low position: poor, young, unknown.

All generations. Fulfilled. Christians rightly call her blessed.

Great things for me. The focus is on what God did, not on Mary herself.

Holy is his name. The reason behind everything.

parallels.desc: look on the affliction of your servant
holy and awesome is his name

verseByVerse.quote: And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s mercy is for those who fear him in every generation.

Psalm 103:17. God’s steadfast love from everlasting to everlasting.

Those who fear him. Reverent trust, not terror.

On a Tuesday. God’s mercy is not only for Mary, but for you.

parallels.desc: the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him

verseByVerse.quote: He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has shown his strength, scattering the proud, bringing down rulers, lifting up the humble, feeding the hungry and sending the rich away empty.

Past tense. What God will do is so certain that Mary sings of it as done.

The great reversal. A theme throughout Luke (6:20–26; 14:11; 16:19–31).

What it does not mean. Not a political programme, nor a blessing on poverty in itself. God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), whatever their wealth.

On a Tuesday. Where are you relying on status? Humble yourself.

parallels.desc: he brings low and he exalts

verseByVerse.quote: He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has helped his servant Israel, remembering his mercy as he promised Abraham and his offspring for ever.

Remembering. God keeps his covenant.

Abraham. Genesis 12:3; 22:18. The promise reaches its fulfilment in Jesus (Galatians 3:16).

For worship. Praise God that he keeps his promises.

parallels.desc: Israel, my servant, offspring of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months and then returns home.

Three months. Probably until John’s birth.

Fellowship. Two women sharing what God has done.

On a Tuesday. Find someone to share God’s work with you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–66 — The Birth of John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of John is narrated with characteristic Lukan brevity — one verse for the birth itself, and then immediate attention to what matters most, which is the naming. In Jewish custom the name was given at circumcision on the eighth day, and was normally taken from the father's family. The community assumes the child will be called Zechariah.

Elizabeth insists that he will be called John. The community is astonished — there is nobody in the family by that name — and they turn to Zechariah himself. He calls for a writing tablet and writes: his name is John. And immediately his mouth is opened, his tongue is loosed, and he speaks.

The sequence is telling. Zechariah does not begin to speak until he has first obeyed. The muteness that fell at his unbelief is lifted not when he privately makes up his mind but when he publicly and irrevocably acts on the word Gabriel gave him. The name John was not Zechariah's choice; it was God's command (v. 13).

By writing it without qualification he is doing what Mary did in a different register: surrendering his own preference and his family's expectation to the word of God. And the moment he does, the word God gave him is restored to his own mouth.

A small detail in v. 62 fills out the whole nine months. The family made signs to him, which suggests he could not hear either. He had been sealed inside his own head since the day at the altar, with nothing in there but Gabriel's sentence.

The neighbours and relatives are filled with fear, and they laid up all these things in their hearts — a phrase that will appear again of Mary after the shepherds' visit (2:19) and after the temple episode (2:51). Luke's Gospel is full of people who receive these events and hold them, turning them over, not fully understanding but refusing to let go.

That is the posture the gospel consistently produces: not an immediate confident grasp of everything, but the faithful keeping of what has been received, waiting for the understanding that comes in its own time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The crowd's question — what then will this child be, for the hand of the Lord was with him — is the question the rest of Luke-Acts will answer. John will be the voice crying in the wilderness, the preparer of the way, the greatest among those born of women (7:28).

He will baptise Jesus, proclaim the coming kingdom, confront Herod, and die in prison before Jesus's ministry reaches its climax. He is the last and greatest of the prophets, the hinge between the old covenant and the new. The hand of the LORD that the community perceives is the hand that has been shaping him for this purpose since before his birth.

The motif of a whole community sharing in the response to God's action — neighbours and relatives rejoicing, all who heard wondering, everyone laying these things up in their hearts — reflects Luke's consistent understanding that the gospel is not a private transaction between an individual and God. It is a public event that transforms communities.

The birth of John affects not only Zechariah and Elizabeth but the entire social network of their neighbourhood. The ripple of grace always extends further than the point of impact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's obedience at the naming — writing “his name is John” without qualification, against the family's expectation — is the delayed obedience of a man whom nine months of silence have changed. He came into the temple a man of correct theology and insufficient trust. He emerges from the silence a man who writes the word of God on a tablet before he says a word of his own.

The discipline has done its work. The man who needed a sign is now content to be one — the father who names his child what God chose, regardless of what the neighbours think.

The fear that falls on the community is the biblical response to the nearness of the holy. This is not terror but the awe that the presence of God in human history always produces. They sense that something larger than ordinary life is moving through the birth of this child, and they are right.

The instinct to hold that sense carefully — to lay it up in the heart — is exactly the right response to grace that exceeds our comprehension. Not analysis, not immediate explanation, but faithful keeping: holding what has been received until it is better understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth gives birth to a son, and her neighbours and relatives rejoice at the Lord’s great mercy to her.

Promise kept. Exactly as Gabriel said.

Rejoicing together. Joy shared (Romans 12:15).

parallels.desc: everyone who hears will laugh over me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered, 'No; he shall be called John.' And they said to her, 'None of your relatives is called by this name.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the circumcision on the eighth day, the relatives want to name the child Zechariah, but Elizabeth says, “No; he shall be called John.”

The eighth day. The covenant sign (Genesis 17:12).

His name is John. Elizabeth obeys God’s word over family custom.

On a Tuesday. Obey God even where it breaks with custom.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the name was often given then.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, 'His name is John.' And they all wondered. And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sign to Zechariah, who writes, “His name is John,” and at once his mouth is opened and he praises God.

Obedience restores. When he obeys, he speaks.

His first words. Praise. The silence of unbelief is broken by worship.

For worship. Let your restored voice be used to praise God.
verseByVerse.note: A writing tablet was a wooden board coated with wax.

verseByVerse.quote: And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, 'What then will this child be?' For the hand of the Lord was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear comes on the neighbours, the news spreads through the hill country, and people wonder what the child will be, for the Lord’s hand is with him.

Laid up in their hearts. Pondering (2:19).

The hand of the Lord. God’s power and favour on him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Zechariah's song — called the Benedictus from its first word in Latin, “Blessed” — is the longest prophecy in Luke's first chapter and in many ways its theological climax. Where Mary's Magnificat looked back at what God has done throughout Israel's history, the Benedictus looks forward to what God is now doing through the two children, and across the whole sweep of the covenant from Abraham to this moment.

It is the song of an old priest who has spent nine months in silence, and who opens his mouth for the first time not with relief or apology or explanation but with praise and prophecy.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 68-75) is about Jesus: the God of Israel has visited and redeemed his people, has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and has fulfilled the oath he swore to Abraham, so that his people might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness all their days.

The second (vv. 76-79) is about John: the child will be called the prophet of the Most High, will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, and will give knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins, because of the tender mercy of God by which the sunrise will visit them from on high. The two movements map exactly onto the two births — the greater to Jesus, the preparatory to John.

Verse 77 is the interpretive key to the whole song, and it answers the objection a modern reader raises at v. 71. Rome was never overthrown; Jerusalem fell within a lifetime. But the salvation Zechariah means is defined by Zechariah himself: knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins. The enemies in view are deeper than any empire.

The image of the sunrise from on high is among the most beautiful in Luke's Gospel. Zechariah the priest knows his prophets — the great light dawning on a people in darkness (Isa. 9:2), the sun of righteousness rising with healing (Mal. 4:2) — and the image he chooses reaches back through centuries of longing.

The Sunrise — the one who gives light to those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, and who guides their feet into the way of peace. Nine months of silence have filled this man's mouth with something far better than anything he said before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Benedictus is covenant theology at its most compact. Zechariah identifies the coming of Jesus as the fulfilment of three overlapping promises: the Davidic covenant (the horn of salvation in the house of David, vv. 69-70), the Abrahamic covenant (the oath sworn to Abraham, vv. 73-75), and the prophetic promise (the forerunner going before the Lord, vv. 76-77).

All three lines of God's covenant faithfulness converge in the two children born in this chapter. The God who made promises to Abraham two thousand years earlier is fulfilling them — not approximately, not symbolically, but specifically, in the births of two real children at a datable moment in history.

The purpose of that salvation is stated with remarkable precision in vv. 74-75: that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. Salvation is not merely rescue. It is freedom for a particular kind of life.

The one delivered from the enemy's hand is freed not for autonomous self-determination but for worship — for service before the face of God, in holiness and righteousness, without the crippling fear that guilt and condemnation produce. This is the goal of redemption: a people who serve God freely because they have been freely saved.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's first words after nine months of silence are praise and prophecy — not self-vindication, not explanation, not a word of reproach for the community that doubted him. The discipline of the long silence has produced a man who, when he opens his mouth, speaks entirely about God and about what God is doing.

That is the fruit of involuntary silence used well: what comes out at the end is not our own words. Preachers, teachers and parents forced into seasons of silence — made to listen rather than speak, to receive rather than give — often find that what finally emerges is purer and truer than anything they said before it.

The Benedictus ends with John: the child grew and became strong in spirit, and was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel. The wilderness is both his geographical home and his spiritual formation. He is being shaped in hiddenness for the public ministry that will announce the Coming One.

Every major figure in redemptive history has had a wilderness — Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul, and the Lord himself. The wilderness is not the failure of the plan. It is the formation of the messenger, and it cannot be hurried.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah, filled with the Spirit, prophesies and blesses God, for he has visited and redeemed his people.

The Benedictus. From its first word in Latin.

Visited. God has come in person (v. 78; 7:16).

Redeemed. Set free at a price, as from Egypt.

For worship. Bless the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited his people.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah’s song, known as the Benedictus, celebrates God’s faithfulness in terms of the Old Testament promises.

parallels.desc: blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel
he sent redemption to his people

verseByVerse.quote: and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has raised up a mighty saviour from David’s house, as the prophets promised, to save his people from their enemies.

A horn. Strength (Psalm 18:2; 132:17).

David’s house. Jesus, not John.

Enemies. Zechariah may have thought of Rome. Christ saves from deeper enemies: sin, death and Satan.
verseByVerse.note: A horn was a symbol of strength, like a bull’s horns.

parallels.desc: I will make a horn to sprout for David

verseByVerse.quote: to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God remembers his covenant oath to Abraham, to rescue his people so they may serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness all their days.

The oath. Genesis 22:16–18.

Saved to serve. Rescue leads to worship and holy living.

Without fear. Free from the fear of enemies and of condemnation.

On a Tuesday. You were saved to serve God today, without fear.

parallels.desc: the covenant he made with Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins,
verseByVerse.commentary:
John will be the prophet of the Most High, preparing the Lord’s way and giving knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins.

Prophet of the Most High. Jesus is the Son of the Most High (v. 32); John is his prophet.

Forgiveness. The heart of salvation.

Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 3:1. The forerunner.

parallels.desc: a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins

verseByVerse.quote: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of God’s tender mercy, the sunrise from on high will visit us, to give light to those in darkness and guide our feet into peace.

Tender mercy. Literally “the bowels of mercy”: deep compassion.

The sunrise. The Messiah as the dawn (Malachi 4:2; Isaiah 9:2).

The way of peace. Peace with God and among people.

Textual note. Manuscripts are divided between “shall visit” and “has visited”. The ESV follows “shall visit”.

For worship. Thank God that the dawn has come.

parallels.desc: the sun of righteousness shall rise
light on those in the land of deep darkness

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child grew strong in spirit and lived in the wilderness until he appeared publicly to Israel.

Grew. Like Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26) and Jesus (2:40).

The wilderness. The place of preparation, and of Israel’s new exodus (Isaiah 40:3).

On a Tuesday. Hidden years of preparation are not wasted.

For worship. Thank God for the quiet years he uses to prepare his servants.

parallels.desc: the word of God came to John in the wilderness

1.text: <sup>1</sup> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, <sup>2</sup> just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, <sup>3</sup> it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, <sup>4</sup> that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught. <sup>5</sup> In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. <sup>6</sup> And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. <sup>7</sup> But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years. <sup>8</sup> Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, <sup>9</sup> according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. <sup>10</sup> And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. <sup>11</sup> And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. <sup>12</sup> And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. <sup>13</sup> But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. <sup>14</sup> And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, <sup>15</sup> for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. <sup>16</sup> And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, <sup>17</sup> and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.” <sup>18</sup> And Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” <sup>19</sup> And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. <sup>20</sup> And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.” <sup>21</sup> And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. <sup>22</sup> And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. <sup>23</sup> And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. <sup>24</sup> After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, <sup>25</sup> “Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.” <sup>26</sup> In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, <sup>27</sup> to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary. <sup>28</sup> And he came to her and said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!” <sup>29</sup> But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. <sup>30</sup> And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. <sup>31</sup> And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, <sup>33</sup> and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” <sup>34</sup> And Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” <sup>35</sup> And the angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. <sup>36</sup> And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. <sup>37</sup> For nothing will be impossible with God.” <sup>38</sup> And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. <sup>39</sup> In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, <sup>40</sup> and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. <sup>41</sup> And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <sup>42</sup> and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! <sup>43</sup> And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <sup>44</sup> For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. <sup>45</sup> And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” <sup>46</sup> And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, <sup>47</sup> and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, <sup>48</sup> for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; <sup>49</sup> for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. <sup>50</sup> And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation. <sup>51</sup> He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; <sup>52</sup> he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; <sup>53</sup> he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. <sup>54</sup> He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, <sup>55</sup> as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” <sup>56</sup> And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home. <sup>57</sup> Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. <sup>58</sup> And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. <sup>59</sup> And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, <sup>60</sup> but his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.” <sup>61</sup> And they said to her, “None of your relatives is called by this name.” <sup>62</sup> And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. <sup>63</sup> And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered. <sup>64</sup> And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. <sup>65</sup> And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, <sup>66</sup> and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. <sup>67</sup> And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, <sup>68</sup> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people <sup>69</sup> and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, <sup>70</sup> as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, <sup>71</sup> that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; <sup>72</sup> to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, <sup>73</sup> the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us <sup>74</sup> that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, <sup>75</sup> in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. <sup>76</sup> And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, <sup>77</sup> to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, <sup>78</sup> because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high <sup>79</sup> to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” <sup>80</sup> And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

2.title: The Birth of the King
2.overview:
Chapter 2 of Luke is the world's most familiar story — and precisely because of that familiarity, it is the story most easily received without being heard. We have heard the angels and the manger and the shepherds so many times that the shocking strangeness of the events has been smoothed away by repetition. Luke is a careful historian, and he intends these details to be astonishing: the Emperor of Rome issues a decree, and the decree unwittingly fulfils a prophecy he knows nothing about. The Son of God is born not in a palace but in the place where animals feed. Heaven's armies appear not to priests or rulers but to shepherds — the lowest of the low in first-century Jewish society. The incarnation is not a dignified event. It is a scandal.

The chapter moves through four scenes: the birth in Bethlehem (vv. 1–7), the angels and the shepherds (vv. 8–20), the presentation in the temple with Simeon and Anna (vv. 21–40), and the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple (vv. 41–52). Together they establish three things about the child: he is born in the line of David and in fulfilment of Scripture; he is recognised by the Spirit-filled as the one Israel has been waiting for; and he understands himself, from the earliest age, as defined by a unique relationship with the Father that supersedes even the claims of family.

The presentation in the temple (vv. 21–40) is one of Luke's most theologically dense passages. In Simeon's song — the Nunc Dimittis — the scope of the child's significance is made explicit for the first time: he is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.” He is not merely the Messiah of Israel; he is the fulfilment of the universal promise of Isaiah (42:6; 49:6), the Servant who is to be the light of the nations. And the shadow of the cross falls even here: Simeon tells Mary that a sword will pierce her soul, that this child is set for the falling and rising of many, that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed. The manger casts the shadow of the cross from the very beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Birth of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of Jesus is introduced by one of the most politically freighted sentences in the New Testament: “In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus.” Augustus was the most powerful man in the world — the man who had ended a century of Roman civil war and inaugurated the Pax Romana.
