He called himself divi filius, son of the deified Julius. The Roman world hailed him as saviour, as lord, as the bringer of peace and of good news.

Luke places that decree at the head of the story of the one who is the true Son of God, the true Saviour, the true Lord, the true bringer of peace and good news. The contrast is not accidental. Luke's Gospel is, among other things, a counter-narrative to the propaganda of Rome — and it never once raises its voice to say so.

Augustus's census serves God's purposes without Augustus knowing it. He orders a registration for taxation; God uses it to bring a Galilean couple to Bethlehem, where Micah had said the ruler of Israel would be born (Mic. 5:2). The most powerful man on earth is, unwittingly, the instrument for keeping a seven-hundred-year-old promise.

This is the biblical theology of providential history. God works through the ordinary and sometimes brutal machinery of human politics to accomplish his purposes, and neither the emperor's ignorance nor his indifference can obstruct it. Nor does God remove the cost: the couple still walk ninety miles, and Mary still walks them at the end of a pregnancy.

The manger is the detail that has shaped two thousand years of Christian imagination, and rightly. Mary wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no place for them in the inn. The word rendered “inn” (katalyma) more often means the guest room of a private house — it is the word used of the upper room at the Last Supper (22:11) — and the likeliest picture is a crowded family home whose guest room was already full.

Either way the scene is the same: the one who is the bread of life is laid in the box the animals eat from; the one who made every star has nowhere to be put. The incarnation is the ultimate act of self-emptying, and Luke communicates it not with theological abstraction but with the concrete detail of the trough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The juxtaposition of Caesar Augustus and the infant Jesus is a statement about the nature of true power. Augustus commanded armies, controlled the Mediterranean, and issued decrees that moved millions across the empire. The child in the manger will command no army for thirty years, will spend his public life in a small region of a minor province, and will die as a criminal.

And yet it is the child, not the emperor, who is worshipped two thousand years later — whose kingdom, as Zechariah sang, has no end. Luke is asking his reader to see, from the first chapter onward, that the power which actually runs the universe does not look like the power that runs an empire.

The swaddling cloths are not merely a practical detail; they are a sign. When the shepherds are told they will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger, the cloths are part of the identifier. They say: he is truly human, wrapped as every newborn was wrapped, indistinguishable at a glance from any other child in Bethlehem.

The manger says the other half: that his humanity is received in the most vulnerable and dependent form imaginable. The eternal Son of God becomes a baby who cannot feed himself, cannot move himself, and cannot survive an hour without his mother.
verseByVerse.examples:
The census that brings Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem is a reminder that God uses inconvenient, uncomfortable, even oppressive circumstances to accomplish his purposes. Joseph and Mary did not choose to travel ninety miles at the end of a pregnancy. The Roman state imposed it. And in the imposition, the plan of God was fulfilled.

The Christian who finds himself in circumstances he did not choose — a redundancy that opens a door, a move that leads to an unexpected church, a disruption that turns out to have been an appointment — is living in the pattern of the incarnation. Being in the centre of God's will has never meant being outside other people's decisions.

The manger has been the comfort of every Christian who has ever felt overlooked, marginalised, or without a place. The Son of God did not insist on suitable accommodation. He took what was available, in the circumstances Providence had arranged, and made it holy.

No circumstance is too humble, and no situation too undignified, to be the place where God chooses to be present. The God who was born in a stable is found in the most improbable places — which is exactly where his people most often need to find him.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The emperor Augustus orders a census of the Roman world, the first while Quirinius was governing Syria.

Augustus. Hailed as saviour and bringer of peace. Luke quietly sets the real Saviour beside him (v. 11).

God uses Caesar. A decree in Rome brings Mary to Bethlehem, fulfilling Micah 5:2.

Where Christians differ: the census of Quirinius. Josephus dates a census under Quirinius to AD 6, after Herod’s death. Verdict: several solutions are possible: Quirinius may have held an earlier office in Syria; or the Greek may mean “before” the census under Quirinius. Luke is a careful historian (1:3), and the difficulty does not overturn him.

On a Tuesday. The powers that seem to run the world serve God’s purposes without knowing it.
verseByVerse.note: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14. The ESV notes that verse 2 can also be read “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria” — the dating of this census is debated.

parallels.desc: the revolt “in the days of the census”

verseByVerse.quote: And all went to be registered, each to his own town. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David’s town, to be registered with Mary, who is pregnant.

Bethlehem. David’s birthplace (1 Samuel 16), foretold for the ruler (Micah 5:2).

About ninety miles. A hard journey for a pregnant woman.

Betrothed. Legally bound, but not yet living together as husband and wife (Matthew 1:25).
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth to Bethlehem is a journey of roughly 80–90 miles.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were in Bethlehem, Mary gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the guest room.

Firstborn. The son with the rights of inheritance (Exodus 13:2). Where Christians differ. Roman Catholic and Orthodox tradition holds that Mary remained a virgin. Verdict: “firstborn” does not prove other children by itself, but the Gospels’ mention of Jesus’ brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3) most naturally means Mary had later children.

A manger. A feeding trough. The Lord of glory laid where animals eat.

The inn. Kataluma, usually a guest room (22:11). Probably a crowded family home, with the animals kept on the lower level. Not a heartless innkeeper.

For worship. Marvel that God came so low.
verseByVerse.note: Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn. A manger is a feeding trough. The word for “inn” can mean a guest room — the same word used for the upper room in 22:11.

parallels.desc: though he was rich, he became poor

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — The Shepherds and the Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The announcement of the birth is made not to the emperor, not to the high priest, not to the Sanhedrin, not to the scholars who could have quoted the prophecy from memory — but to shepherds keeping watch over their flocks in a field at night.

In first-century Jewish society shepherds occupied the lowest rungs of the ladder. Their work made ritual purity nearly impossible to maintain; later rabbinic rulings counted their testimony unreliable; and the settled respectable classes regarded them with suspicion. It is to these men, in this field, at this hour, that the glory of the Lord appears — the same glory that had filled the tabernacle and had not been seen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple.

The angel's announcement is one of the most compressed theological summaries in the New Testament: “For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.” Three titles in seven words. Saviour — the one who rescues; a title Caesar also claimed and could not fulfil. Christ (Christos) — the Anointed One, the fulfilment of Israel's whole prophetic tradition. Lord (kyrios) — the title Israel's Scriptures give to God himself. All three at once, all three together, all three true.

The sign given to confirm it is the inverse of every sign of power in human history: a baby, wrapped as every baby was wrapped, lying in a feeding trough. Kings are found in palaces and gods in temples. This one is identified by the humblest container in the village.

Then the sky fills. The heavenly host is a military picture — the armies of heaven drawn up over a hillside, praising God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.”

That last phrase is sometimes rendered “peace, good will toward men,” following a variant reading behind the older English versions. The better-attested text is the one the ESV follows: the peace comes to the people of God's good pleasure. That is not a colder reading but a warmer one — a goodwill announced to everyone in general is guaranteed to no one in particular, whereas this peace rests on the sovereign choice of God, which does not move.

The section ends where it must. The shepherds go with haste, find exactly what they were told they would find, tell everybody, and go back to work — glorifying and praising God, with the sheep still to be watched and nothing whatever in their circumstances altered.
verseByVerse.theology:
The choice of shepherds is Luke's first major instance of the great reversal that runs through his whole Gospel: the last are first, the humble are exalted, and those the world dismisses are the ones God chooses to honour. God shows here, in advance, the design he later carried out when he chose poor and uneducated fishermen for apostles.

The good news comes first to those who have nothing — no status, no ritual purity, no legal standing — because the good news is precisely that God's grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things.

The sign given to the shepherds requires a different kind of looking than a sign of glory would have required. A God who appears in unexpected humility can be walked past. The shepherds do not go looking for what they would have expected; they go looking for exactly what they were told to expect, and they find it.

And Luke is careful about the response of everyone else. The neighbours wondered — a word he uses often and never confuses with faith. Wonder is a doorway and not a destination. Mary, in the same room, does something different with the same information (v. 19), and the contrast is the point of the paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples:
The shepherds' response — “Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened” — is the model of responsive faith. They do not debate the vision. They do not wait for a second confirmation. They do not propose considering the matter carefully before acting. They go with haste, and they find exactly what they were told they would find.

The gap between hearing the word of God and acting on it is where faith most often quietly dies — not by a decision to disobey, but by a perfectly reasonable delay that becomes permanent. The shepherds closed the gap in about ten seconds.

They then became the first evangelists of the New Testament. Fishermen would follow; a tax collector would follow; a persecutor would follow. But the first to announce the birth of the Saviour were men whose word counted for little and who had nothing to commend them except that they had seen what they had seen.

That is the pattern of Christian witness in every generation: not credentials, not eloquence, not social standing, but the testimony of those who have met God and cannot keep quiet about it. And note what they proclaimed — not their experience of the light and the fear, but “the saying that had been told them.” The message, not the sensation.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shepherds keeping watch at night are terrified when an angel appears and the glory of the Lord shines around them.

Shepherds. Ordinary, often despised workers. God announces his Son to the lowly first (1:52).

David the shepherd. The Shepherd-King is born in the shepherd-king’s town.

The glory of the Lord. God’s visible presence, unseen since the exile (Ezekiel 10).

Where Christians differ: the date. Shepherds out at night have been used to argue against a winter birth. Verdict: the date is unknown. Christians are free to celebrate Christ’s birth on any day.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds were humble working men, often looked down on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel announces good news of great joy for all people: today in David’s town a Saviour is born, who is Christ the Lord.

Good news. Euangelizomai. The language Rome used of Augustus’s birthday.

Three titles. Saviour (rescuer), Christ (Messiah), Lord (God’s own title). No baby has ever been described like this.

For you. The shepherds, and all people.

On a Tuesday. This is good news for you, today.

For worship. Rejoice: a Saviour is born.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah; “Lord” was the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

parallels.desc: he will save his people from their sins
to us a child is born
the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign for the shepherds is a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger.

A strange sign. Not glory, but lowliness. A baby in a manger was unusual enough to identify.

Wrapped. Fully human, needing care.

parallels.desc: the LORD himself will give you a sign

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great army of angels praises God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!”

Heavenly host. An army, singing not fighting.

Peace. Peace with God, not mainly the absence of war (Romans 5:1).

Those with whom he is pleased. People on whom God’s favour rests: peace is God’s gift, not earned.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “goodwill toward men” (King James Version). One letter (eudokia or eudokias) makes the difference. The earliest manuscripts support the ESV, so the peace is for those God favours.

For worship. Glory to God in the highest.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV’s “among those with whom he is pleased” follows the better manuscripts; older translations read “good will toward men.”

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angels leave, the shepherds hurry to Bethlehem and find Mary, Joseph and the baby lying in the manger.

Let us go and see. Faith acts on God’s word.

With haste. Like Mary (1:39).

On a Tuesday. Go and see. Do not leave God’s word unacted on.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds tell what they were told about the child, and everyone who hears is amazed.

The first evangelists. Shepherds, whose testimony was not accepted in court.

Wondered. Amazement is not yet faith.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone what you have heard about Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary treasured all these things and pondered them in her heart.

Treasured. Stored up and kept.

Pondering. Putting things together, seeking meaning.

A source. Luke may hint that Mary was one of his eyewitnesses (1:2).

On a Tuesday. Take time to think over what God has done.

parallels.desc: his father kept the saying in mind

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds return, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen.

Back to work. The same field, changed hearts.

As it had been told. God’s word proved true.

For worship. Praise God for what he has shown you in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The presentation is the scene where the old covenant meets the new — where the long story of Israel's worship, sacrifice and waiting encounters the one the whole system had been pointing at.

Joseph and Mary come to Jerusalem for two duties, both required by the law: the purification of the mother forty days after the birth of a son (Lev. 12:1-8), and the presentation of the firstborn to the LORD (Exod. 13:2, 12-15; Num. 18:15-16). They bring the offering of the poor — two birds rather than a lamb and a pigeon — which tells us plainly what the family's circumstances were. The King of heaven and earth was raised in poverty.

Simeon is described in the language of the faithful remnant: righteous, devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him. That phrase, the consolation of Israel, comes from Isaiah 40 — “Comfort, comfort my people” — the promised end of exile and return of God to his people. Simeon has been waiting inside that chapter his whole life, and the Spirit has promised him he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ.

Now, as a young couple with the offering of the poor come into the courts, the Spirit moves him. He takes the child into his arms, and everything he has spent his life waiting for is a warm weight in his hands.

His song — the Nunc Dimittis — is among the most moving passages in Luke. The verbs are those of a sentry being stood down after a long watch. He can go now: his eyes have seen God's salvation, and the salvation he is holding is not for Israel only but “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” — the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs (42:6; 49:6) and the universal scope of the gospel announced before it has begun.

And then the shadow falls. The child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, a sign to be opposed; and a sword will pierce Mary's own soul. Joy and sorrow are not opposites in Luke's Gospel. They are twins, born of the same truth. The one who is the light of the world will be rejected, and the one whose birth the angels celebrated will die on a cross. Simeon holds the baby and sees all of it.

Anna is the second witness the law required (Deut. 19:15) — a daughter of Asher, one of the tribes long written off as lost, who has given decades of widowhood to fasting and prayer in that building and who arrives at exactly the right hour. And the section closes with the family's return to Nazareth and a single sentence covering the boy's whole childhood: he grew, became strong, was filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon's announcement that the child is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (v. 32) is the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs and the theological seed of the entire Gentile mission of Acts. From the moment of the presentation, Luke's Gospel contains within it the global church. The child in Simeon's arms is not merely the king of the Jews; he is the light of the world.

This is why Luke, writing for a Gentile reader, is the Gospel that most fully develops the universal reach of the good news. The trajectory is established here, in the temple courts, by an old man who has waited his whole life to say what he now says and who is ready to die.

Simeon's warning to Mary — that a sword will pierce her own soul — has been understood in the tradition as pointing to her presence at the crucifixion (John 19:25-27). The word is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, and Simeon does not soften it. The sword is the sword of grief, of the suffering that participation in the Son's mission inevitably involves.

But the clause “that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed” shows a wider purpose. The coming of Jesus forces a crisis of decision in every heart; he does not leave people neutral. He is “appointed for the fall and rising of many” — the stone of Isaiah 8:14 laid in the middle of the road. His presence divides, and in dividing it discloses what was already there.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simeon's “now you are letting your servant depart in peace” is the model of a death well prepared for — not the resignation of a man who has given up, but the discharge of a sentry who has received what he was waiting for. And notice what his peace does not rest on: not on achievement (we are told nothing of what he accomplished), not on longevity, but on what his eyes have seen.

The Christian who has seen that same salvation — not with physical eyes but with the eyes of faith, and has taken hold of it — has precisely what Simeon had, and may face death on precisely the same terms. Not because death is nothing, but because what lies beyond it is the same Christ known in life.

Anna is Luke's portrait of long faithfulness. She had been waiting most of her adult life — decades of widowhood — for the redemption of Jerusalem. She did not give up, did not grow cynical, and did not stop praying because the answer had not come. When it came, she was exactly where she had always been.

Her years were not the waiting room for her ministry; they were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family's arms when everyone around her saw a queue — and who knew, by name, everyone in Jerusalem who was waiting to be told. The reward of patient faithfulness is rarely glamorous. It is being in the right place when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day Jesus is circumcised and named Jesus, as the angel had said.

Circumcised. Jesus is born under the law (Galatians 4:4), obeying it fully for us.

Named. Mary and Joseph obey God’s word.

His first shedding of blood. A small foreshadowing of the cross.

parallels.desc: the name given by the angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the days of purification, Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, offering two birds as the law required.

Presentation. The firstborn belongs to God (Exodus 13:2, 12).

Purification. After forty days (Leviticus 12).

Two birds. The offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8). Jesus was born into poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “her purification”, which fits Leviticus. The ESV reads “their purification”, the earlier reading.

On a Tuesday. God’s Son was born to a poor family. Do not despise the poor.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days after the birth of a son the mother brought a purification offering. Firstborn sons belonged to the LORD and were redeemed. Two birds instead of a lamb was the offering of the poor.

parallels.desc: every firstborn is holy to the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon, a righteous and devout man waiting for Israel’s consolation, had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before seeing the Lord’s Christ.

The consolation of Israel. God’s comfort for his people (Isaiah 40:1).

The Holy Spirit upon him. Three mentions in three verses.

Waiting. The posture of faithful Israel.

On a Tuesday. Faithful waiting is not wasted.
verseByVerse.note: “The consolation of Israel” means the comfort God had promised his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Led by the Spirit into the temple, Simeon takes Jesus in his arms and blesses God.

In the Spirit. The timing is God’s.

In his arms. The old man holds God’s salvation as a baby.

For worship. Bless God for letting you see his salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon prays that God may now let him die in peace, for he has seen God’s salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel.

The Nunc Dimittis. From its first words in Latin, sung in evening worship for centuries.

Depart in peace. Ready to die.

Your salvation. Salvation is a person.

A light for the Gentiles. Isaiah 42:6; 49:6. From the start, Jesus is for the nations.

On a Tuesday. If you have seen Christ, you are ready to die.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon’s song is known as the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin.

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth
all the ends of the earth shall see

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ father and mother marvel at what Simeon said about him.

His father. Joseph is his legal father.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “Joseph and his mother”, perhaps to protect the virgin birth. The ESV reads “his father and his mother”, the earlier reading.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon blesses them and tells Mary that Jesus is appointed for the fall and rising of many, a sign opposed, so that hearts are revealed, and a sword will pierce her own soul.

Fall and rising. Jesus divides people (Isaiah 8:14; 28:16).

A sign opposed. Rejected, as the cross would show.

A sword. Mary’s grief at the cross (John 19:25).

Where Christians differ: Mary’s sorrows. Some Roman Catholic devotion sees Mary sharing in redemption as co-redemptrix. Verdict: Mary shares her son’s suffering as a grieving mother, not his saving work. Christ alone redeems (1 Timothy 2:5).

On a Tuesday. How you respond to Jesus reveals your heart.

parallels.desc: a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anna, an aged prophetess and widow who worshipped in the temple night and day, gives thanks to God and speaks of the child to all who wait for Jerusalem’s redemption.

Anna. “Grace”. Of the tribe of Asher: the northern tribes were not lost.

Prophetess. Luke often pairs men and women: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna.

Fasting and prayer. A life given to God after great loss.

She spoke of him. Testimony to all who were waiting.

On a Tuesday. Widowhood and old age can be years of fruitful devotion.
verseByVerse.note: Asher was one of the northern tribes. The ESV notes that verse 37 can also mean she had been a widow for eighty-four years.

parallels.desc: the widow who continues in prayers night and day

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having done everything the law required, they return to Nazareth, and the child grows strong, filled with wisdom, and God’s favour is on him.

The law kept. Luke stresses their obedience.

Grew. Jesus had a real childhood.

Matthew’s account. The wise men and the flight to Egypt (Matthew 2) come before this return.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels is this one: Jesus at twelve, in the temple, sitting among the teachers, leaving the learned astonished. Luke includes it not as a charming anecdote but as a theological statement. Before the public ministry begins, Jesus is already defined by a relationship with his Father that supersedes every other claim on him — including the entirely legitimate claim of his parents.

It is worth noticing what the story is not. The apocryphal gospels of later centuries are full of tales of the boy Jesus working wonders and settling scores. In the one childhood story Scripture preserves, he performs no miracle at all. He asks questions, and then goes home and does as he is told.

The setting is Passover — the feast of Israel's redemption, commemorating the night the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood. Jesus is twelve, the year before a Jewish boy took on personal responsibility for the commandments, and this is the last Passover of his childhood. The irony Luke intends is deep: the Passover Lamb has come up to keep the Passover.

When Mary and Joseph discover him missing from the caravan and search three days, her question is entirely natural and entirely human: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” Scripture lets her say it, and does not correct her tone.

Jesus's answer contains the first recorded words of his life, and they are a claim of identity: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” The word must (dei) is one of Luke's great theological words, marking the divine necessity that drives the whole redemptive plan. And the Father he names is not Joseph. He distinguishes — gently, but unmistakably — between the father who has been searching for him and the Father whose house he is in.

He had not run away, and he had broken no commandment; his surprise is genuine that after twelve years they had to be told where he would be. And then, having said it, he goes down with them to Nazareth and is subject to them for another eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word dei — “it is necessary,” “I must” — runs through Luke and Acts and marks the divine necessity driving the story forward: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22); he must rise on the third day (24:7); the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here, at twelve years old, Jesus uses it for the first time.

This is not a child defying his parents. It is the Son of God expressing the first law of his existence: he must be about his Father's business. The whole of Luke's two-volume work is the outworking of that single must, from the temple courts in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Jesus's submission after the episode — “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (v. 51) — is the answer to anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be exempt from ordinary human obligations. He is subject to his parents: not one act of compliance but a settled condition sustained for eighteen years.

And he genuinely grows (v. 52). The one who knows all things grows in knowledge; the one who is all-powerful grows in stature; the one in whom all wisdom is hidden grows in wisdom. This is the mystery of two natures in one person, and it means the incarnation was never a costume. It was real human life, lived fully from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary and Joseph “did not understand the saying that he spoke to them” (v. 50) — and Mary “treasured up all these things in her heart” (v. 51). For the second time in the chapter Luke shows her holding what she does not yet understand, refusing to let go of it, waiting for the understanding to arrive.

This is one of the most honest and most encouraging pictures of faith in the Gospel. The mother of the Son of God did not always understand what he was doing. But she did not discard what she could not explain. She kept it, turned it over, and waited — and she was still carrying this one twenty years later when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began to make sense.

The closing verse is the New Testament's summary of the hidden years: Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man. Eighteen years of silence before the public ministry begins — of growing, learning, working, and being formed in a village nobody wrote about.

The God who could have compressed everything into three years of public ministry chose instead to spend thirty in ordinariness. That is the pattern of divine formation: the long preparation, the hidden years, the slow work of wisdom and character before the public work begins. Anyone impatient to skip the hidden years has not yet understood how God shapes the people he uses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ parents go to Jerusalem every year for Passover, and when he is twelve they go as usual.

Every year. A devout family.

Twelve. On the edge of adult responsibility in the law.

On a Tuesday. Regular worship forms children.
verseByVerse.note: Every Jewish man was to go up to Jerusalem for the great feasts; families travelled together in large groups.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the feast ends, Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem without his parents knowing, and after a day’s journey they search for him.

A travelling group. Families from a village travelled together, so his absence was not noticed.

Searching. Every parent knows this fear.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days they find him in the temple among the teachers, listening, asking questions, and amazing everyone with his understanding.

After three days. Perhaps a hint of another three days (24:7).

Listening and asking. A learner, but with remarkable wisdom.

On a Tuesday. Ask questions of Scripture and of those who teach it.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law sat with their pupils in the temple courts, teaching by question and answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His astonished mother asks why he has done this, since they have searched anxiously; he replies, “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?”

Your father and I. Mary speaks of Joseph.

My Father. Jesus’ first recorded words point to God as his Father.

I must. Divine necessity (4:43; 9:22).

Textual note. The Greek is literally “in the things of my Father”. The King James Version reads “about my Father’s business”. The ESV’s “house” fits the setting.
verseByVerse.note: These are Jesus’ first recorded words.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not understand what he said.

Not understanding. Even Mary and Joseph grew in understanding gradually.

On a Tuesday. It is all right not to understand everything at once.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes home with them, submits to them, and grows in wisdom, stature and favour with God and people; and Mary treasures these things.

Submissive. The Son of God obeyed his parents (Exodus 20:12).

Grew in wisdom. Where Christians differ. How could the eternal Son grow? Some deny his full deity; others his true humanity. Verdict: Christ is one person with two natures. As God he knows all things; as man he truly learned and grew (Hebrews 5:8).

Favour with God and man. Like Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26).

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew ordinary family life. He understands yours.

For worship. Thank Christ for the hidden years of obedience he lived for you.

parallels.desc: the boy Samuel grew in favour with the LORD and with man

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the formal beginning of the story Luke has been preparing for since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and the ministry of preparation begins. Luke anchors the moment in history with a precision unmatched anywhere in the Gospels: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, the tetrarchies of Herod and Philip and Lysanias, the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. Seven named officials, layered like the rings of a tree, establishing exactly when the word of God broke in. Luke the historian is insisting: this happened. You can date it. You can place it. It is not legend.

John's ministry is introduced through Isaiah 40 — “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” — establishing that his role is not to be the destination but the signpost. He is the voice; another is the Word. His message is the message of the prophet: repent, be baptised, bear fruits worthy of repentance. The crowds who come to him receive not comfort but confrontation: “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” John is the great deflater of religious presumption — the man who tells Israel that Abrahamic descent is not a sufficient credential before the coming Judge. The axe is at the root of the trees. The one who comes after him will separate the wheat from the chaff with an unquenchable fire.

The chapter ends with two moments of quiet immensity: the baptism of Jesus, where the Trinity is revealed in a form no theologian could have anticipated — the Son in the water, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice from heaven — and the genealogy, which traces Jesus's lineage back through David, through Abraham, through Adam, to God himself. Luke's genealogy runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's and reaches further back: not just to Abraham (the Father of Israel) but to Adam (the father of the human race). Jesus is not merely the King of the Jews; he is the son of Adam come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry with a synchronism — a dating device borrowed from the great historians of the ancient world, who anchored their narratives in the reigns of known rulers. Seven officials are named: Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas.

This is the world into which the word of God intrudes: Roman imperial power, Jewish client kings, and a compromised religious leadership. And the word comes to none of them. It comes to John, in the wilderness, the son of a village priest. The contrast is pointed. All the power of the world is irrelevant to God's timing; the word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not trouble to look.

The names are also checkable, and they have been checked. Lysanias of Abilene was long cited as proof of Luke's carelessness until an inscription from the reign of Tiberius turned up near Damascus honouring exactly that man in exactly that office.

John's message has three parts. First, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins — a rite John did not invent, but radically reapplied. Jewish practice may already have had a baptism for Gentile converts entering the covenant people; John baptised Jews, which said out loud that being born inside the covenant was not enough and that Israel itself needed converting. It was scandalous, and it was meant to be.

Second, a demolition of presumption: “Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Ethnic heritage is no substitute for personal repentance, and the axe is already at the root.

Third, practical instruction to three specific groups who ask the same question — what shall we do? The crowds are told to share a spare tunic and their food. Tax collectors are told to collect no more than the authorised figure. Soldiers are told not to extort, not to lay false charges, and to be content with their pay. Notably, neither the tax collectors nor the soldiers are told to leave their work. Repentance in John's mouth has hands and feet, and all three answers land on money.

The climax is not John's own proclamation but his announcement of another: “He who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” The one who follows is not an improved John; he is of a different order altogether. And Luke calls the whole of this preaching — vipers, axe, unquenchable fire and all — good news (v. 18).

The section closes with Herod shutting John in prison for confronting him over his marriage to his brother's wife. The voice is silenced immediately before the Word begins to speak. The herald makes way for the King.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's declaration that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones is the most radical possible challenge to the theology of ethnic privilege. It disconnects the promise from the bloodline and reconnects it to faith and repentance.

This is not the abolition of the covenant with Abraham; it is the clarification of what that covenant always meant. Paul will develop the same argument in Galatians 3 and Romans 4: the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham's faith, not merely his biology. John stands at the hinge of the covenants and announces what the new covenant will make explicit — the community of God is defined by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire announces two aspects of the Coming One's work that belong together. The Spirit is the agent of new birth and renewal, the fulfilment of Ezekiel's new heart and Joel's outpouring. Fire is the agent of purification — the refiner's fire that burns away dross, and the thresher's fire that consumes chaff.

John does not separate these two; they are two sides of one coming. For those who receive him the fire purifies; for those who reject him it consumes. Everyone who meets Christ is touched by fire. The only question is which kind.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's instruction to the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers is one of the clearest demonstrations in the Gospels that repentance is not a feeling but a change of direction that shows. The crowd asks “what shall we do?” and the answer is not “attend synagogue more faithfully” or “pray more earnestly.” It is “share your tunic and your food.”

The tax collector's repentance looks like honest accounting; the soldier's looks like honest soldiering. Genuine repentance always takes the shape of the specific sin it is turning from — and in both those cases it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight, at real financial cost, alongside colleagues who would not.

John's willingness to confront Herod Antipas over his adulterous marriage (v. 19) — knowing what it would cost him — is the model of prophetic courage before political power. He did not reserve his hard message for crowds who could do him no harm; he took it to the palace, where it was entirely unnecessary and entirely dangerous.

The man who tells the crowd hard truths and comfortable things to the powerful has not yet learned from John. And John's own end is worth facing honestly: he did everything he was sent to do, and finished in a cell. Faithfulness is not always repaid in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke dates the start of John’s ministry by the rulers of the day, when God’s word came to John in the wilderness.

The fifteenth year of Tiberius. About AD 28–29.

Six rulers. Emperor, governor, tetrarchs and high priests: real history, and the powers that would oppose Jesus.

Annas and Caiaphas. Annas had been deposed by Rome, but kept great influence; Caiaphas, his son-in-law, held the office (John 18:13).

The word of God came. The formula for a prophet’s call (Jeremiah 1:2). Not to the palace or the temple, but to the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. God’s word comes into real history, and into your ordinary week.
verseByVerse.note: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian: Tiberius’s fifteenth year was about AD 28–29. Philip ruled lands north-east of the lake; Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. Annas had been deposed as high priest but still held great influence; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.

parallels.desc: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in the days of…

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John preaches a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, fulfilling Isaiah’s voice crying in the wilderness.

Repentance. A change of mind that turns the whole life to God.

Baptism. Gentile converts were washed; John tells Jews they too must come as outsiders.

For the forgiveness of sins. The baptism signified repentance, which looks for forgiveness. Where Christians differ. Some read baptism here as the means of forgiveness. Verdict: forgiveness comes through repentance and faith; baptism is the outward sign of them (Acts 2:38 with 3:19).

Isaiah 40:3. Preparing the way for the LORD himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s prophecy continues: every valley filled, every hill brought low, crooked made straight, so that all flesh will see God’s salvation.

Road-building. Preparing a highway for a king. The obstacles are in human hearts.

All flesh. Only Luke continues the quotation this far. Salvation is for all nations.

On a Tuesday. What in your life needs levelling to make way for Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke continues the quotation to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

parallels.desc: my eyes have seen your salvation

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls the crowds coming for baptism a brood of vipers and asks who warned them to flee the coming wrath.

Brood of vipers. Snakes fleeing a field fire. Some came for a ritual without repentance.

The wrath to come. John preached judgment as well as hope.

On a Tuesday. Religious ritual cannot hide an unrepentant heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John demands fruit that shows repentance, warns them not to trust in descent from Abraham, and says the axe is already at the root.

Fruit. Repentance is shown in changed living.

Abraham as father. Physical descent saves no one (John 8:39; Romans 9:6–8).

Children from stones. God can create a people from nothing. (In Hebrew, “children” and “stones” sound alike.)

The axe at the root. Judgment is near.

On a Tuesday. Do not trust your Christian family or background. Trust Christ, and bear fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds ask what to do, and John tells them to share their spare clothing and food.

What shall we do? The right response to preaching (Acts 2:37).

Two tunics. Practical generosity.

On a Tuesday. What do you have spare that someone else needs?
verseByVerse.note: The tunic was the inner garment; a second one was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tax collectors ask what to do, and John tells them to collect no more than they are authorised to.

Tax collectors. Hated as collaborators and cheats.

Not leave their jobs. John tells them to do them honestly.

On a Tuesday. Repentance shows in honesty at work.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors typically profited from whatever they could collect above the amount owed.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers ask what to do, and John tells them not to extort by threats or false accusation, and to be content with their wages.

Soldiers. Probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod.

Where Christians differ: may Christians serve as soldiers? Christian pacifists say no. Verdict: John does not tell soldiers to leave the army, nor does Jesus or Peter (7:1–10; Acts 10). The Reformed tradition holds that military service in a just cause is lawful, while abuses of power are forbidden.

Contentment. The root of honesty (1 Timothy 6:6–10).
verseByVerse.note: These were probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people wonder if John is the Christ, he says a mightier one is coming, whose sandals he is unworthy to untie, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire.

Unworthy to untie. A slave’s task. John’s humility.

Spirit and fire. Fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:3), with fire also meaning purifying judgment (v. 17).

Where Christians differ: baptism with the Spirit. Pentecostals teach a second experience after conversion, marked by tongues. Verdict: every believer is baptised with the Spirit at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13). Believers should seek to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18).

For worship. Praise Christ who gives the Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coming one holds a winnowing fork to clear his threshing floor, gathering wheat into his barn and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Winnowing. Throwing grain into the wind to separate it from chaff.

Unquenchable fire. Final judgment (Mark 9:43).

On a Tuesday. Jesus separates. Be found among his wheat.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back and the chaff blew away.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With many other exhortations John preached the good news to the people.

Good news. John’s warnings were good news, because they pointed to the Saviour.

For worship. Thank God for preachers who warn as well as comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod, rebuked by John for taking his brother’s wife Herodias and for his other evils, adds to them all by shutting John in prison.

Herodias. She had left her husband for Herod Antipas (Mark 6:17–18).

Speaking truth to power. John was imprisoned for confronting a ruler’s immorality.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness may cost you your freedom.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas. Herodias had been married to his half-brother. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, ahead of the story, to close his account of John.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The baptism of Jesus is narrated with remarkable brevity in Luke — briefer even than in Mark. Luke does not linger on the event; the baptism itself is a participle, almost an aside. What he focuses on is what happens while Jesus is praying afterwards.

This is characteristic. Luke consistently shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points of his ministry (3:21; 6:12; 9:18; 9:28; 11:1; 22:41). The baptism is not the centre of the scene; the prayer is. And what happens during it is the most explicit Trinitarian moment in the Synoptic Gospels: the Son in the water; the Spirit descending in bodily form like a dove; the Father's voice from heaven.

Why is Jesus baptised at all? John's baptism was for repentance and forgiveness, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. Matthew records John's protest and Jesus's answer: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

He is baptised not because he needs what the water signifies but because he is identifying himself with the people he came to save. He enters the water of repentance as the representative of those who need to repent; he will enter the waters of death as the representative of those who deserve to die. The Jordan is the first public act of the substitution that ends at Golgotha.

The Father's voice weaves two Old Testament texts together. “You are my Son” is Psalm 2:7, the royal psalm of the Davidic king. “With you I am well pleased” is Isaiah 42:1, the opening of the first Servant Song. Jesus is simultaneously the royal Son of David and the suffering Servant of Isaiah — the King who will reign and the Servant who will be crushed. Both identities are laid on him at the outset, and the whole ministry is the working out of what it costs to be both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
The descent of the Spirit “in bodily form, like a dove” is Luke's careful insistence that this was a visible, physical event — not a vision or an inward impression but something anyone standing on the bank could have seen.

The dove carries a layered background: the dove of Noah signalling that the judgment was over (Gen. 8:8-12); the dove of the poor person's offering (Lev. 5:7; and 2:24 in this Gospel); and, most significantly, the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Gen. 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. A new creation is beginning.

The Father's declaration comes before Jesus has performed a single public miracle, preached a single sermon, or won a single crowd. The pleasure of the Father in the Son is not contingent on performance; it is the expression of the love that existed between them before the foundation of the world (John 17:24).

That is the theological foundation of grace: the beloved Son is beloved before he does anything. And the Christian who is in Christ shares the status — not earned but given, not provisional but settled.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus praying at his baptism is the first instance of a pattern that runs through the whole Gospel. The implication is not that prayer is a mechanism that causes the Spirit to descend. It is that prayer is the posture of one who depends entirely on the Father rather than on his own resources.

The Son of God prays before every major act of his ministry — not because he lacks information or power, but because prayer is the expression of the relationship that defines him. The disciple who prays before decisions and transitions is not following a technique. He is following his Lord.

The Trinity is present at the Jordan in a way impossible to mistake and impossible to fully systematise. The three are distinct: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The three are simultaneously present, simultaneously active, simultaneously directed towards one redemptive event.

The doctrine of the Trinity is not a philosophical puzzle invented by later councils. It is the description of what happened at the Jordan. The church was simply trying to find words adequate to what the evangelists reported.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all the people had been baptised and Jesus was baptised and praying, heaven opened.

Why was Jesus baptised? He had no sin to repent of. He identified with sinners, fulfilling all righteousness (Matthew 3:15).

Praying. Luke often shows Jesus praying at key moments (5:16; 6:12; 9:18, 28).

Heaven opened. Isaiah 64:1: “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down.”

Where Christians differ: how was he baptised? Baptists point to immersion; others say the mode is not specified. Verdict: the word means to immerse or dip, and immersion best pictures burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:4), though Christians who differ on mode should not divide over it.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke notes that Jesus was praying.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit descends on Jesus in bodily form like a dove, and the Father’s voice says, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”

The Trinity. The Son baptised, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking.

Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1. The King and the Servant in one person.

Textual note. One Western manuscript reads “today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). Some have used it to say Jesus became Son at his baptism. The reading is weakly attested, and Luke has already shown Jesus to be God’s Son from conception (1:35).

For worship. In Christ, the Father is well pleased with you.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's genealogy is unlike Matthew's in three decisive ways: it runs backward, from Jesus to Adam rather than from Abraham to Jesus; it is placed after the baptism rather than before the birth narrative; and it extends past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God.

These are not inconsistencies but theological choices. Matthew writes for a Jewish readership and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's covenant story, beginning with Abraham. Luke writes with the world in view and presents Jesus as the answer to the human story, beginning at the Jordan — where his identity has just been declared by the Father — and tracing his lineage to the first man.

The genealogy also differs from Matthew's in many of the names between David and Joseph. Some hold that Luke traces the line through Mary; others that one evangelist follows legal succession and the other physical descent; others appeal to the complexities of levirate marriage. No solution is free of difficulty, and the church has lived with the two lists for two thousand years without resolving every detail.

What is clear is that the difference does work. Matthew's line runs through Solomon and the kings — the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and also the line under the curse pronounced on Jeconiah, that none of his offspring would prosper sitting on David's seat (Jer. 22:30). Luke's runs through Nathan, a son of David who never reigned and whose descendants never came under that word. On one common reading, the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child.

Most of the names between David and Joseph are otherwise unknown — dozens of men of whom Scripture records nothing except that the line ran through their houses. Further back the list passes through Ruth the Moabite, through Perez the son of Tamar, through Abraham who twice lied about his wife. God ran the promise straight through a family history containing foreignness, deception and disgrace, and did not clean it up first.

The placement after the baptism gives the list its frame. The Father has just said “You are my Son”; the genealogy answers the question whose son, exactly? He is the son of Joseph as registered; the son of David, which is his royal credential; the son of Abraham, which is his covenantal one; the son of Adam, which is his human solidarity. And at the end of the list — the son of God.

He is the Son of God who has become the son of Adam, so that the sons of Adam might become the sons of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The genealogy ending in “son of Adam, son of God” is Luke's most compact statement of the theology of the incarnation. Jesus traces his human lineage to the first human, establishing the full solidarity of his humanity with every person who has ever lived.

He did not merely appear in human form. He entered the long human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history — which is what Paul means by “born of woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Fully embedded in the situation he came to redeem.

The contrast between Adam and Jesus implicit here becomes explicit in Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49. Adam brought death; the second Adam brings life. Adam's disobedience constituted many sinners; the second Adam's obedience constitutes many righteous.

Luke's genealogy does not spell out that typology — that is Paul's work — but it establishes the premise on which the typology stands: Jesus is the son of Adam, which means Adam's story is part of his story, and his story is the answer to Adam's.
verseByVerse.examples:
The genealogy is one of the portions of Scripture readers habitually skip — a long list of unfamiliar names that looks like a necessary but uninspiring prelude. But it is the gospel in miniature. It announces that the salvation of the world came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding, sometimes scandalous history of real families making real choices.

Every name in the list is a person whose life contributed to the moment when the Son of God stood in the Jordan, and almost none of them had any idea of it. Providence is not abstract. It is as specific as a name — including the many names in this list about whom history has kept nothing else at all.

The final phrase, “the son of Adam, the son of God,” is the summary of everything the Gospel will demonstrate. Jesus is fully human and fully divine, and the two cannot be separated without destroying the gospel.

A Jesus who is only divine cannot save us, because he cannot represent us. A Jesus who is only human cannot save us, because he has no righteousness to give. The Jesus of Luke's genealogy — rooted in human history all the way back to Eden, and named by the Father as his Son — is the only Jesus who can do what needs doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus begins his ministry at about thirty, son, as was supposed, of Joseph, son of Heli.

About thirty. The age priests began service (Numbers 4:3), and David became king (2 Samuel 5:4).

As was supposed. Luke protects the virgin birth.

Where Christians differ: why does Luke’s genealogy differ from Matthew’s? Some say Luke gives Mary’s line, with Heli as her father. Others say both give Joseph’s, Matthew the royal succession and Luke the physical descent, linked by a levirate marriage. Verdict: either solution is possible. Both genealogies show that Jesus is the son of David with a legal claim to his throne.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Luke’s genealogy runs backward and differs from Matthew’s after David; many think Luke traces Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genealogy continues back through a list of mostly unknown names to Nathan, the son of David.

Through Nathan. Not Solomon, as in Matthew. Perhaps because of the curse on Jehoiachin’s line (Jeremiah 22:30).

Unknown names. God was working through ordinary, forgotten people.

On a Tuesday. Your faithful, unrecorded life may be part of God’s great story.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s line runs through Nathan, David’s son, not Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line goes back through David, Jesse, Boaz, Judah and Jacob to Abraham.

David and Abraham. The two great covenant names.

Textual note. Manuscripts vary over the names in v. 33 (Admin, Arni, Aram). Copyists struggled with unfamiliar names. Nothing important depends on it.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genealogy runs back past Abraham to Noah, Seth and Adam, the son of God.

To Adam. Matthew starts with Abraham; Luke goes back to Adam. Jesus is the Saviour of all humanity, the new Adam (Romans 5:12–21).

Son of God. Adam was God’s son by creation; Jesus is God’s Son by nature. The next scene tests him as Adam was tested (4:1–13).

Cainan. Luke includes a Cainan (v. 36) found in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11 but not the Hebrew.

A real Adam. Luke treats Adam as a historical person, like Paul (Romans 5).

For worship. Praise God for the Saviour who belongs to the whole human race.
verseByVerse.note: Luke traces the line back to Adam — Jesus belongs to all humanity. The Cainan of verse 36 appears in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11, not the Hebrew.

3.text: <sup>1</sup> In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, <sup>2</sup> during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. <sup>3</sup> And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>4</sup> As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. <sup>5</sup> Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, <sup>6</sup> and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’” <sup>7</sup> He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup> Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>9</sup> Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” <sup>10</sup> And the crowds asked him, “What then shall we do?” <sup>11</sup> And he answered them, “Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.” <sup>12</sup> Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” <sup>13</sup> And he said to them, “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.” <sup>14</sup> Soldiers also asked him, “And we, what shall we do?” And he said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.” <sup>15</sup> As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, <sup>16</sup> John answered them all, saying, “I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>17</sup> His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>18</sup> So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people. <sup>19</sup> But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, <sup>20</sup> added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. <sup>21</sup> Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened, <sup>22</sup> and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>23</sup> Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, <sup>24</sup> the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph, <sup>25</sup> the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, <sup>26</sup> the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, <sup>27</sup> the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, <sup>28</sup> the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, <sup>29</sup> the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, <sup>30</sup> the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, <sup>31</sup> the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David, <sup>32</sup> the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, <sup>33</sup> the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, <sup>34</sup> the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, <sup>35</sup> the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, <sup>36</sup> the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, <sup>37</sup> the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, <sup>38</sup> the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the chapter of beginnings and confrontations. It opens with the Spirit leading Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing — the place where Israel repeatedly failed, now entered by Israel's true representative who will not fail. It continues with the dramatic scene in the Nazareth synagogue where Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing — only to be driven out of the town by the same people who had initially marvelled at him. And it concludes with a succession of healings and exorcisms in Capernaum that demonstrate in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

The temptation narrative (vv. 1–13) is the interpretive key to the whole of Jesus's ministry. The devil offers Jesus three things — bread, power, and supernatural protection — and each offer is a shortcut around the path of obedience and suffering that leads to the cross. Jesus refuses each offer with the word of Scripture, demonstrating that the weapons of his warfare are not the weapons of power but the word of God and trust in the Father. The one who overcomes the devil in the wilderness will face him again, in various guises, throughout the ministry — and will face him definitively in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross. The wilderness is not the final battle; it is the first.

The Nazareth sermon (vv. 14–30) is Luke's programmatic statement of Jesus's mission — the equivalent of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. Luke places it at the beginning of the public ministry as the manifesto of the kingdom: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of the Lord's favour. The question the sermon raises — who is included in the “year of the Lord's favour”? — is answered by two Old Testament examples that the congregation finds intolerable: Elijah went not to an Israelite widow but to a Sidonian one; Elisha healed not an Israelite leper but a Syrian one. The good news of the kingdom is for the excluded, the foreigner, the unexpected. This is the gospel Luke has been writing toward since chapter 1 — and the congregation's response is homicidal rage.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temptation follows immediately on the baptism: the Spirit who descended at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The sequence is deliberate. The Father's declaration of sonship — “You are my beloved Son” — is at once followed by the devil's challenge to it: “If you are the Son of God…”

The wilderness is where the identity given at the baptism is tested, and where the question of what kind of Son Jesus will be is answered. Will he use divine power for his own relief? Will he take the world's kingdoms by the world's methods? Will he force the Father to prove his care? The answer each time is no — and the no is spoken not by supernatural force but with the word of Scripture.

The three assaults correspond to Israel's three great wilderness failures. Israel hungered and grumbled (Exod. 16); Jesus is tempted to turn stone into bread. Israel worshipped the golden calf (Exod. 32); Jesus is offered the kingdoms for an act of worship. Israel tested God at Massah (Exod. 17:1-7); Jesus is urged to throw himself from the temple. At every point where Israel failed, Jesus stands — and he does it by the means available to every Israelite: the word of God, believed and obeyed. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy, the book Moses gave Israel before they entered the land.

The final offer is the subtlest, because it comes with chapter and verse. The devil quotes Psalm 91 — accurately, so far as it goes. But he stops the quotation at “to guard you” and omits the psalm's own qualifier, “in all your ways.” The promise covers the paths of obedience; it does not cover a stunt.
