Chapter 6 is Luke's equivalent of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount — shorter, sharper, and structurally parallel, though not identical. Before the sermon comes the choosing of the twelve and two Sabbath controversies that frame the sermon's radical ethics with a theological question: by what authority does Jesus define what is lawful, and what kind of community does that authority create? The Sermon on the Plain (vv. 20–49) is the charter of the kingdom community — the description of what it looks like to live under the reign of God when that reign runs against every instinct of the natural self.

The beatitudes and woes (vv. 20–26) are the most direct statement in the chapter: the kingdom reverses the world's value system. The poor are blessed; the rich are warned. The hungry are filled; the full are emptied. Those who weep now will laugh; those who laugh now will mourn. This is not a promise that poverty is virtuous or that comfort is sinful; it is a statement about the direction of the kingdom. God's attention, God's blessing, God's purposes consistently run toward those whom the world has left behind — and consistently challenge those who have arranged their lives to need nothing from anyone, including God.

The ethical core of the sermon (vv. 27–45) — love your enemies, do not judge, produce good fruit — is the most demanding teaching in Luke's Gospel, and it rests entirely on the character of God. Love your enemies because your Father is kind to the ungrateful and evil. Do not judge because you will be judged by the measure you use. Bear good fruit because the tree is known by its fruit. The final image — the house on the rock — is the sermon's warning: hearing these words is not enough. The one who hears and does not do is building on sand. The storm will come, and only the house that is built on hearing and doing will stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two Sabbath controversies open the chapter, and together they establish the claim that makes everything in the sermon possible: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.

The first is about disciples plucking grain as they walk through fields. Plucking ears from a neighbour's standing grain was expressly permitted (Deut. 23:25), so the objection is not theft; it is that plucking counts as reaping and rubbing as threshing, both forbidden on the Sabbath by the scribal fence built around the commandment.

That fence did not begin in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people whose nation had gone into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment. And it had become unbearable — a gift turned into an audit, a day given to relieve working people now governed by case law only the leisured could master.

Jesus's response reaches back to 1 Samuel 21:1-6. David, on the run and hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which the law reserved for priests, and shared it with his men — and Scripture records it without a word of censure. The point is not that rules do not matter. It is that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. Jesus is not appealing over the head of Scripture; he is appealing to Scripture against a reading of it.

The choice of precedent is not accidental either. Of all the cases available, he reaches for the one about God's anointed king, rejected and on the run, with his own small band of followers, doing what the authorities called unlawful.

Then the conclusion: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” He does not argue that the Sabbath is unimportant. He claims that he is the one who determines its meaning — which, given that the Sabbath is rooted in creation, enshrined in the Ten Commandments, and named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel, is a claim about who he is.

The Pharisees are not wrong to take the Sabbath seriously. They are wrong to think their authority over it exceeds the authority of the one who instituted it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” is a divine claim in Jewish ears. The Sabbath is God's own institution — rooted in creation (Gen. 2:2-3), enshrined in the Ten Commandments (Exod. 20:8-11), and described as a sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exod. 31:12-17).

To be Lord of the Sabbath is to exercise authority over the covenant sign of God himself. Jesus is not relativising the day; he is claiming to be its author. This is among the most compact and most decisive of the implicit claims to deity scattered through the Synoptic Gospels.

And the title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7:13-14 — the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. It sounds modest in English and was not.

What is worth adding is what this lordship is for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest, but to give it back. The day always pointed at a person, and the person has arrived.
verseByVerse.examples:
The complaint about grain-plucking is a case study in confusing the purpose of a law with the law itself. The Sabbath was given as a gift — a day of rest for those who worked, and a sign of trust that God would provide without their constant labour.

The Pharisees' elaborate hedge of regulations (the Mishnah tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters) had turned that gift into a burden. When a law loses contact with the grace and wisdom that gave it, it becomes oppression. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he liberates it from the accretion that had buried what it was for.

The sequence is worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and does not require bad motives: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule — and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of the point.

The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending?

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a Sabbath Jesus’ disciples pick and rub heads of grain to eat, and some Pharisees accuse them of breaking the Sabbath.

Allowed by the law. Picking by hand from a neighbour’s field was permitted (Deuteronomy 23:25).

The charge. Rubbing grain was counted as threshing, one of thirty-nine forms of work the rabbis forbade.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “on the second-first Sabbath”, an obscure phrase probably from a scribal note. The earliest read simply “on a Sabbath”.
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking and rubbing counted as harvesting and threshing, work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus reminds them how David, when hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which only priests could eat, and gave it to his men.

1 Samuel 21:1–6. Human need outweighed the ceremonial rule.

Have you not read? They knew the Scriptures but missed their meaning.

David and his men. Jesus, the greater David, and his followers.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

Lord of the Sabbath. A staggering claim. God gave the Sabbath; Jesus claims authority over it.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Sabbatarians (the Westminster tradition) hold the fourth commandment binding, transferred to Sunday. Others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ’s rest. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), and the Lord’s Day is a privilege to keep gladly for worship and rest, not a set of rules binding the conscience. Hold the view charitably.

Textual note. One ancient manuscript (Codex Bezae) adds here a saying of Jesus to a man working on the Sabbath. It is not original to Luke.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second Sabbath controversy involves a man with a withered right hand — which, in a manual economy, meant an inability to earn a living. Luke the physician notes which hand.

The scribes and Pharisees are watching to see whether Jesus will heal, “so that they might find a reason to accuse him.” The watching is calculated and hostile, and it is worth registering how ugly it is: they are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. His hand interests them only as evidence.

Jesus knows exactly what they are doing, and he does not avoid the confrontation — he creates it. He tells the man to stand up in the middle, where everyone can see, and puts a question to the room: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?”

That question is the interpretive key to his whole Sabbath theology, and it is why they cannot answer. They came prepared to argue that healing is work and that a hand withered for years can wait until sundown — a reasonable position on their own terms. Jesus refuses the terms. He removes the neutral square marked “wait until tomorrow”: to be able to relieve suffering and to decline is not inaction but a choice, and it belongs in the other column.

The Sabbath is not a day of inaction. It is a day defined by the character of its author — and the God who rested on the seventh day is the God who sustains life on every day. Their silence answers the question for them.

Then he heals without touching. The man is simply told to stretch out the hand he cannot stretch out, and the strength arrives inside the obedience. There is nothing to accuse.

And the response is fury — the first time in Luke that the religious leaders plot against him. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The hardness that sets in at this point — “they were filled with fury” — begins the trajectory that ends at the cross. The fury is not primarily moral; it is theological. Jesus has publicly claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their interpretation, and refused to be intimidated by their watching.

Every confrontation confirms what they most fear: this man is either a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided he is a blasphemer, and from that decision every subsequent action follows with a terrible logic.

Their fury is a rage that has stopped thinking. It is what a framework does when it has been exposed in public and its owners are unwilling to revise it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were.

So these Sabbath controversies are not peripheral disputes about religious practice. They are the opening moves of the confrontation that will define history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man with the withered hand is told to stand up and come out into the middle — to be visible, exposed, in front of everyone. He obeys, knowing his disability will be on display, and Luke records that he rose and stood there.

There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. The person who keeps their need hidden, who manages a difficulty from the edge of the community, does not receive what the one standing in the middle receives. Jesus consistently calls his healings into the light.

And the command he gives is the one thing the man cannot do — stretching out that hand is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first so that obedience becomes possible. He is told to do the impossible thing, and discovers in the doing that it is possible.

That is very often the order in the Christian life. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience — which is why so much of following Christ feels like being told to move a hand that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On another Sabbath, a man with a withered right hand is in the synagogue, and the scribes and Pharisees watch to see if Jesus will heal, so they can accuse him; Jesus knows their thoughts and calls the man forward.

Right hand. Luke the physician notes it: his working hand.

Watching to accuse. Religion used to trap.

Come and stand here. Jesus heals in the open.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand. By the rabbis’ rule, healing a condition that was not life-threatening should wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save life or destroy it, and then heals the man’s hand.

Do good or harm. Refusing to do good is doing harm.

Looking around at them all. A silent challenge.

Stretch out your hand. Obedience and healing together.

On a Tuesday. Use the Lord’s Day for doing good.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are filled with fury and discuss what to do to Jesus.

Fury. Literally “senseless rage”. A healing makes them angry.

On a Tuesday. Religion that resents mercy has lost its way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before choosing the twelve, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer on the mountain. This is characteristic of Luke: the major decisions of the ministry are set in the context of prayer. And the placing is deliberate — Luke has just recorded the first plot against Jesus, and the next thing he records is a night on a hillside.

The choice of twelve from a larger body of disciples is not made lightly or impulsively. Luke gives the two stages precisely: he called the disciples, and from them he chose twelve.

The number is not convenient; it is theological. Israel had twelve tribes named for twelve sons, and no Jew could hear the number accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people — and at the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations bearing these men's names (Rev. 21:14).

They are called apostles here for the first time in Luke — apostoloi, sent ones. They remain disciples, learners; but a disciple who has been given an errand is something more.

The list itself is a study in unlikely combinations. Peter, who a chapter ago asked Jesus to leave because he was a sinful man. Matthew, the tax collector from the booth. And Simon the Zealot — a man whose title points to zeal for Israel and the law, and very possibly to sympathy with armed resistance to Rome. In ordinary life Matthew and Simon would not have shared a road. They shared a purse and a mission for three years.

Several of the twelve are almost unknown — James the son of Alphaeus above all, of whom the Gospels record no words and no deeds, nothing but a name in the lists.

And the list ends with Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor.” Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached, and the wording matters: not who was a traitor but who became one. He was chosen after the night of prayer, with the others, and heard and saw everything they did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are distinguished from disciples by a specific function: they are sent ones, commissioned witnesses rather than merely learners. Their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus will be the foundation of the church's proclamation.

Paul will later say the church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20). The night of prayer before the choice establishes that this foundation is not a human selection but a divinely guided one, even though the divine guidance works through a human process.

Luke's parenthesis on Judas — chosen deliberately, after a night of communion with the Father, and yet becoming a traitor — is a weight the reader is not permitted to set down. Election to office is not the same as salvation, and proximity to Christ is no protection.

He handled the money, was sent out with power like the rest, and heard every word of the sermon that follows. The verb Luke chooses describes a process, not a category — which should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time.
verseByVerse.examples:
The night of prayer before the choice models the principle that consequential decisions belong to God before they belong to us. Not every decision requires a night of prayer — but every decision that will shape the community of God's people belongs first to the Father.

The Jesus who spent a whole night praying before choosing twelve men puts a question to every leader, every elder board, every appointment committee: have we prayed as long and as seriously as this decision actually deserves?

And the composition of the twelve is a standing rebuke to congregations divided along political lines. Whatever holds a church together, it is not agreement about Rome, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be.

If a former agent of the Roman revenue and a man called the Zealot could eat from the same bag for three years, the divisions that currently make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus spends the whole night praying on the mountain, and in the morning he chooses twelve of his disciples and names them apostles.

All night. A major decision, made in prayer.

Twelve. A new Israel, with twelve founders, as Israel had twelve tribes.

Apostles. Sent ones, with authority.

Where Christians differ: are there apostles today? Some churches appoint modern apostles. Verdict: the Twelve and Paul were foundational and unrepeatable (Ephesians 2:20; Acts 1:21–22). Today the church has elders and deacons, not apostles in that sense.

On a Tuesday. Pray before major decisions.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Twelve are named: Simon Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

A mixed group. Fishermen, a tax collector who served Rome, and a Zealot who opposed Rome.

Judas son of James. Probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

Became a traitor. Chosen after a night of prayer, yet he betrayed Jesus. God’s plan included even this (John 6:70; Acts 1:16).

On a Tuesday. Jesus unites people who would otherwise be enemies.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s “Judas the son of James” is probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sermon on the Plain begins with a declaration that sounds like a mistake on first reading: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

Luke's beatitudes are addressed directly to the disciples — “blessed are you” — unlike Matthew's more generalised forms. And they are paired with woes Matthew does not include. The poor are blessed and the rich are warned; the hungry are promised satisfaction and the full are warned of hunger; those who weep now will laugh, and those who laugh now will mourn.

The poverty is not romanticised. Luke does not say “poor in spirit” but simply “poor” — the destitute, those with nothing of their own who depend entirely on what others give. This is not a spiritualisation of poverty; it is the announcement that the kingdom belongs to those whose condition leaves no room for self-sufficiency. Not because poverty is virtuous, but because the poor have no resources to trust except God.

Set beside Matthew's “poor in spirit,” the two hold opposite ends of one truth, and neither is safe alone. Luke without Matthew makes an empty purse a ticket. Matthew without Luke lets “poor in spirit” be quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing. Matthew names the poverty God blesses; Luke names the room such people are usually standing in.

The woes are the other edge of the same blade. “Woe” (ouai) is the prophets' word, carrying grief as much as warning (Isa. 5:8-23; Amos 6:1-7). It is not a wish for harm but a declaration that those who have “received their consolation” have been paid already and have nothing further outstanding.

The last woe is the most searching: “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.” Israel's true prophets were consistently unwelcome; the popular ones were the ones who told the king what he wanted to hear.

And the final beatitude (vv. 22-23) is the only one about something the disciples bring on themselves. Four escalating forms of social death — hated, excluded, reviled, name thrown out as evil — and the command attached is not endurance but leaping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes together express the eschatological reversal — the biblical pattern in which the last days invert the present order. Mary sang it in the Magnificat: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty.

This is not a programme of economic analysis; it is a prophetic announcement about the direction of God's kingdom. Those whose present condition drives them to dependence on God are in the right position to receive what the kingdom gives; those who can be self-sufficient are in the wrong one.

Read through the whole gospel, these blessings and woes are far more than social reversal — they are anchored in Christ himself, who entered the very conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Cor. 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept real tears, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us.

The great reversal is therefore no abstract law of history but a sure thing purchased in him. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the One who was made poor that we might be made rich, and who fills the empty out of his own fullness. And the woes are not cruelty but mercy raising its voice — a warning to the comfortable to loosen their grip on thin, passing riches before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples:
The beatitudes are often preached as comfort to those who suffer, and they are that. But they are also diagnosis and invitation. The question they put to every hearer is: in which column do you find yourself? The sermon does not allow a neutral answer; it creates a crisis of self-knowledge.

And the woes have to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading them is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. The question is not whether you enjoy good things but where your consolation actually comes from — what steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can?

“Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy” (v. 23) is the response Jesus commands to persecution — not stoic endurance, not grim determination, but leaping joy. The verb is the one used of the unborn John moving in Elizabeth's womb (1:41).

This is eschatological joy: the joy that knows how the story ends and can afford to leap because the future is secure. It is what Paul means in Romans 8:18 — the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. The leap is only possible if the landing is sure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes down to a level place where great crowds from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon gather to hear him and be healed, for power comes from him.

A level place. Hence “the Sermon on the Plain”.

Where Christians differ: the same sermon as Matthew’s? Some see two accounts of one sermon, others two different occasions. Verdict: Jesus surely preached similar sermons many times. Both accounts faithfully give his teaching, whether from one occasion or two.

Tyre and Sidon. Gentiles too.

Power came out. Divine power in Jesus’ person.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities to the north. Luke’s sermon is given on a “level place”; Matthew’s similar sermon on a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking at his disciples, Jesus says, “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

To his disciples. This blessing is for those who follow him.

The poor. Matthew says “poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3). Luke stresses actual poverty, among those who depend on God.

What it does not mean. Poverty does not save; it is not a virtue in itself. But the poor who trust God are blessed, and often more ready to receive the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. If you are poor and trust Christ, the kingdom is yours.

parallels.desc: has not God chosen those who are poor?

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are the hungry, for they will be satisfied, and those who weep now, for they will laugh.

Now. The present is not the end of the story.

The great reversal. As in Mary’s song (1:53).

For worship. Thank God for the laughter promised to those who weep.

parallels.desc: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you when people hate, exclude and insult you because of the Son of Man; rejoice and leap for joy, for your reward is great in heaven, as the prophets were treated the same.

On account of the Son of Man. Not for being difficult, but for Christ.

Leap for joy. Like the baby John (1:41, 44).

The prophets. You are in good company.

On a Tuesday. Rejection for Christ is a reason for joy, not shame.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the rich, who have received their comfort, and to the well-fed and laughing now, for they will hunger and mourn.

Four woes. Only in Luke, mirroring the four blessings.

Received your consolation. They have had their reward already (16:25).

What it does not mean. Wealth is not damnable in itself (Abraham, Job, Zacchaeus). The woe is on those whose comfort is in riches rather than in God (1 Timothy 6:17).

On a Tuesday. Where is your comfort really placed?
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings.

parallels.desc: woe to those at ease in Zion

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you when everyone speaks well of you, for that is how their ancestors treated the false prophets.

Popularity. Universal approval may mean you are not saying what God says.

False prophets. They told people what they wanted to hear (Jeremiah 6:14).

On a Tuesday. Are you seeking approval more than faithfulness?

parallels.desc: the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” This is probably the most demanding ethical command in the New Testament, and it is not an aspiration but an imperative, repeated in four parallel forms.

All four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling — which matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings; he commands treatment. And the four escalate in cost: do good can be done at a distance; bless requires words; pray for is hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long.

The natural instinct is reciprocity — love those who love you, do good to those who do good to you. Jesus points out that reciprocal love proves nothing: “even sinners love those who love them.” It requires no faith and no change of heart; self-interest produces it unaided. The question the passage forces is whether anything in a Christian's life could not have been produced by ordinary human decency.

The ground of the command is not the worthiness of the enemy. There is no suggestion that the enemy deserves love. The ground is the character of God, “for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.” The disciple who loves enemies is not performing an act of heroic willpower; he is showing a family resemblance.

The concrete instructions in vv. 29-30 — the cheek, the cloak, the beggar, the goods taken — have been read both as absolute commands and as radical illustrations of a disposition. What is certain is their subject: a backhanded blow was an insult to honour, and the cloak is taken by force. These are about personal affront and personal loss, and what is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of one's own dignity.

They are not, and have never been, a command to remain within reach of violence. Jesus walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29-30); Paul invoked his citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37).

“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (v. 36) is the summary — and mercy presupposes a real debt and then declines to collect it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is the most radical expression of grace in the New Testament — and it is exactly what God has done towards his own. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us… while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:8, 10).

The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies. The disciple who loves an enemy is not doing something beyond what God has done; he is doing what has already been done to him, and doing it because he received it. The ethics of the sermon flow from its gospel: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Luke's “be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” is a different formulation from Matthew's “be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), and the difference is instructive. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific attribute this whole section reflects. In a passage about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

And the order can never be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all — which is also why the sentence begins “your Father,” addressed to people who already hold the position they are being asked to display.
verseByVerse.examples:
The command to love enemies has been the most transformative teaching in Christian history — the basis of martyrdom (Stephen dying while forgiving, Acts 7:60), of peacemaking, of every real reconciliation in the church's story.

It has also been the teaching most frequently domesticated into something manageable: being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, or to former enemies who are now friends. The test is not whether we are kind to the kind. It is what we do with the person who is actively hostile, who has genuinely wronged us, and who continues to wish us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31) has parallels in nearly every ethical tradition — and almost all of them state it negatively: do not do to others what you would not want done to you. A man can keep that rule perfectly by doing nothing at all.

Jesus states it positively, which cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative, imagination, and going towards somebody at your own cost without being asked. And there is a mercy in how he frames it: he does not ask for an abstract theory of the good but for the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks — how you would want to be treated — applied in the other direction.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus commands those who hear to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who abuse them.

Love your enemies. The distinctively Christian ethic.

Four commands. Love in attitude, deed, word and prayer.

Christ’s example. He prayed for those crucifying him (23:34).

On a Tuesday. Name someone who has wronged you, and pray for their good today.

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If someone strikes your cheek, offer the other; if someone takes your cloak, let him have your tunic; give to all who ask, and do not demand back what is taken.

The cheek. A slap was an insult. Do not retaliate.

Where Christians differ: non-resistance. Pacifists read this as forbidding all use of force. Verdict: Jesus forbids personal revenge, not self-defence, the protection of others, or the state’s use of the sword (Romans 13:4). He himself challenged an unjust blow (John 18:23).

Give to all. Generosity, guided by wisdom (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

On a Tuesday. Let go of the right to get even.
verseByVerse.note: The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treat others as you would want them to treat you.

The Golden Rule. Others taught a negative version; Jesus puts it positively.

Active love. Not just avoiding harm, but doing good.

On a Tuesday. Before each conversation today, ask how you would want to be treated.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loving those who love you, doing good to those who do good to you, or lending to those who will repay earns no credit; even sinners do as much.

What credit? Literally “what grace?” Ordinary kindness is not grace.

Even sinners. Christian love must go beyond what everyone does.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love your enemies, do good, and lend expecting nothing back; your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, who is kind to the ungrateful and evil.

Sons of the Most High. Children resemble their Father.

Kind to the ungrateful. As God was to you.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “despairing of no one” rather than “expecting nothing”. The ESV follows the usual sense.

For worship. Thank God for his kindness when you were ungrateful.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.

The heart of the sermon. Matthew has “perfect” (Matthew 5:48); Luke “merciful”.

Like Father. God’s mercy to us is the pattern for ours.

On a Tuesday. Show mercy today where you would rather show judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The teaching on judging (vv. 37-42) and on fruit (vv. 43-45) form one unit held together by the theme of discernment: how we assess others and ourselves.

“Judge not” is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, taken to mean that no moral assessment of anyone is ever permitted. It cannot mean that. Four verses later Jesus tells his hearers to remove the log from their own eye so that they will see clearly to remove a brother's speck — an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified oneself to make it. Two verses after that he explains how to tell a good tree from a bad one.

What is forbidden is not discernment about conduct but condemnation — pronouncing a verdict on a person, assigning their final worth and destiny. That work belongs to a court, and there is only one. The difference is felt easily enough: “that was a lie” assesses an act; “he is a liar” delivers a summary of a life, and requires access to motives and history that no human being has.

The image of the measure in v. 38 is from a grain market: filled, pressed down to compact it, shaken so the grains settle, then heaped until it spills over into the fold of a man's garment. It is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous.

The blind guide and the log-and-speck follow, and the comedy is deliberate. A man with a plank in his eye leaning in to extract a splinter is an optical impossibility, and the audience can see it. Note that Jesus does not say “leave the speck alone.” The brother is still to be helped; what is corrected is the order. “First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly.”

The tree-and-fruit teaching is the positive counterpart: character produces conduct. This is not moralism — it does not say “try harder to produce good fruit.” It is a statement about the direction of causation. The fruit reveals the tree; what a person does consistently reveals what they are.

And the source is the treasury of the heart: “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” — out of the overflow. Speech is not what a person decides to say; it is what spills when the container is full and nobody is watching.
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of v. 38 recurs across both testaments (Matt. 7:2; Rom. 2:1; Jas. 2:13). It is not mechanical karma but a reflection of God's character — the God who shows himself merciful to the merciful and severe to the severe (Ps. 18:25-26).

The warning is not that God will be unkind to those who judge. It is that a person who approaches God without mercy will meet his justice applied with the rigour they themselves used. Someone who has received grace and then withholds mercy has fundamentally misunderstood what grace is.

The word “hypocrite” at v. 42 needs care. In ordinary English it means a conscious fraud. But the man Jesus describes genuinely does not see the log — it is stated twice. The hypocrisy is not deliberate pretence but a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere.

Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best — and the blind guide of v. 39 is in the same condition, sincerely certain he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log-and-speck has a sharp application for every relationship involving authority: parents with children, leaders with congregations, employers with employees, elders with members. The right to speak into another person's life is not conferred by position; it is earned or forfeited by the quality of one's own self-examination.

The mentor who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it can be trusted with somebody else's failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better about himself. There is a practical test before speaking: ask what this conversation will cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

“Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (v. 40) is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from. Formation works. The ceiling of what you become is set by the person you follow, whether or not you intend it.

And “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (v. 45) is the most usable diagnostic Jesus gave. Not what a person says when trying to impress, but what comes out when they are tired, unobserved, or talking about people who are not in the room. That is the overflow, and it is a straight readout of the treasury. Nor can it be fixed by monitoring speech — that produces a careful hypocrite. What must change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not judge or condemn, and you will not be judged or condemned; forgive and give, and it will be given back to you in full measure.

Judge not. Not a ban on discernment (v. 43–45; John 7:24), but on harsh, condemning judgment.

Good measure. A picture from the grain market: pressed down, shaken, overflowing into your lap.

What it does not mean. Not a prosperity formula: “give to get rich”. God is generous to the generous, in his way and time.

On a Tuesday. Give generously and forgive freely. God will not be in your debt.
verseByVerse.note: Grain was measured into a fold of the robe used like an apron; a generous seller pressed and shook it down so it held more.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks whether the blind can lead the blind, and says a disciple is not above his teacher, but when fully trained will be like him.

The blind leading the blind. Both fall in.

Like his teacher. Choose your teachers carefully: you will become like them.

On a Tuesday. Whom are you learning from? Whom are you leading?

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why look at the speck in your brother’s eye but ignore the log in your own? First remove the log, then you will see clearly to remove the speck.

A comic picture. A carpenter’s son speaks of planks.

Hypocrite. An actor.

What it does not mean. Not that we must never correct others, but that we must deal with ourselves first (Galatians 6:1).

On a Tuesday. Before you criticise anyone today, examine yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good tree bears good fruit and a bad tree bad fruit; each is known by its fruit, for out of the heart the mouth speaks.

The heart. Behaviour comes from what we are.

The mouth. Words reveal the heart.

Regeneration. Only God can make the tree good (Ezekiel 36:26).

On a Tuesday. Listen to your words today. What do they say about your heart?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends with two builders, two houses, and one storm — and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen.

It is preceded by the question that makes the parable necessary: “Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?” Jesus does not doubt that they call him Lord, or suggest they are insincere; the doubled address is the language of warmth. The problem is that the word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter — and to call a man Lord while deciding independently what to do with his instructions is a contradiction in terms.

The parable is not a contrast between a man who heard and a man who did not. Both come to Jesus. Both hear his words. Both build. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

The difference is entirely underground. The wise builder “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” — two verbs describing the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

Then the flood, and Luke is precise: the same stream breaks against both houses. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is weather, and it comes to everyone — which rules out the reading in which the obedient are protected from trouble. Both are hit equally. What differs is what happens next.

“Immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.” There is no gradual subsidence and no chance to shore it up. A life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

The storm is unspecified, and the vagueness is the point: bereavement, illness, betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Something always comes.

And the rock is not a set of principles. Jesus has spent thirty verses saying things no one can live out by admiration, and he ends by describing a man who hears my words and does them. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The eschatological note — the house that falls, and “the ruin of that house was great” — places the sermon's ethics in the context of final judgement. This is not moralism; it is eschatology.

The commands of the sermon are not useful guidelines for a better life. They are the description of the life that will stand on the day when every life is tested — which is why the sermon cannot be domesticated into a programme of self-improvement. It describes a life that is only possible through the transformed heart the kingdom produces, which is exactly what the tree-and-fruit teaching has just said.

And it is why the question at v. 46 is not an attack on assurance. It is a question about the relationship between what a person says about Christ and what they do about what Christ says. Every command in this chapter is checkable, and not one of them can be kept by admiring it.

The rock, finally, is not the sermon. It is the one who preached it. To hear these words and do them is to build on Jesus himself, and he is what the digging reaches.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the two builders has been used in Christian preaching from the earliest centuries as the description of the difference between nominal and genuine faith. Both builders heard Jesus; both began to build; both appeared to be doing the same thing. The difference was invisible until the storm came.

This is Jesus's own warning against the self-deception that hears the word, feels its power, admires its truth, and then returns to a life built on other foundations. The church in every generation has members who have heard much and built little.

The wise builder “dug deep” — the effort of foundation-laying is not passive. It requires excavation, the removal of everything covering the rock, the work of getting down to what will hold. That is spiritual formation: not merely hearing but digging, through prayer and Scripture, through accountability, through obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood and circumstance and social approval.

The digging is unglamorous and nobody sees it. The house is what people see. But the digging is what determines whether the house stands — and the way to start is not in general. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you call me “Lord, Lord” and not do what I say?

Lord, Lord. Fervent words without obedience.

A claim to authority. Jesus expects obedience as Lord.

On a Tuesday. What has Jesus told you to do that you have not done?

parallels.desc: if I am a master, where is my fear?

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever hears and does Jesus’ words is like a man who dug deep and built on rock, and his house stood in the flood; whoever hears and does not do is like one who built without a foundation, and it fell.

Dug deep. Only in Luke. Obedience takes effort.

The flood. Trouble and final judgment.

Hearing and doing. Both hear; only one obeys (James 1:22).

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “founded on the rock” rather than “well built”, from Matthew 7:25.

For worship. Thank Christ that he is the rock on which to build.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season.

said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?” <sup>3</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup> how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>6</sup> On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. <sup>7</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. <sup>8</sup> But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man For even sinners love those who love them. <sup>33</sup> And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. <sup>34</sup> And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. <sup>45</sup> The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. <sup>46</sup> “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? <sup>47</sup> Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: <sup>48</sup> he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. <sup>49</sup> But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

7.title: Faith, Doubt, and the Extravagance of Grace
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is one of the richest chapters in Luke's Gospel — four scenes that together compose a portrait of the grace of God operating at the edges of what respectable religion thought was possible. A Roman soldier sends word to Jesus about his dying servant; a widow's dead son is raised in a small village; the imprisoned John the Baptist sends messengers to ask if Jesus is really the one; and a woman known as a sinner anoints Jesus's feet with her tears and her perfume at a Pharisee's dinner table. In every scene, the expected is reversed: the Gentile soldier has greater faith than anyone in Israel; the dead man walks; the greatest prophet struggles with doubt; and the sinner, not the Pharisee, demonstrates the love that flows from forgiven debt.

The chapter's theological centre is the exchange between Jesus and John's disciples (vv. 18–35). John's question — “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” — is the most honest expression of faith-under-pressure in the Gospels. The forerunner who announced the Coming One from the womb, who saw the Spirit descend at the Jordan, who proclaimed the axe at the root of the trees — is now in prison, and the Coming One is not doing what John expected. Jesus's answer is not an argument but a recital: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them. He is, in other words, doing exactly what Isaiah promised the Servant would do. Blessed is the one who is not offended by him — even when he does not do what you expected.

The sinful woman at Simon's house (vv. 36–50) is the chapter's most searching scene. She comes uninvited, she weeps, she wipes Jesus's feet with her hair, she anoints them with perfume. Simon, the Pharisee host, draws the obvious conclusion: if Jesus were really a prophet, he would know who was touching him, and he would not allow it. Jesus's response is the parable of the two debtors — one forgiven a small debt, one a large one; which loves more? And the answer overturns Simon's entire moral framework. The woman's extravagant love is not the cause of her forgiveness; it is the evidence of it. She loves much because she has been forgiven much. Simon's cool hospitality reveals that he considers himself forgiven little — which means he considers himself to owe little, which means he loves little.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Jesus Heals a Centurion's Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The centurion whose servant is sick is the first Gentile whose faith is commended in Luke's Gospel — and it is commended in the strongest possible terms: “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

He is a Roman military officer, commander of a hundred men, the local face of the occupying power in a garrison town. He has also built the local synagogue — an extraordinary act of generosity towards a community he was not part of, and towards a God who was not his. And Luke's first fact about him is that a dying slave was “highly valued by him,” which in a world that classified slaves as speaking tools tells you a great deal before the man opens his mouth.

The Jewish elders who come on his behalf argue from merit: “He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” That is how human beings naturally think about who deserves help. The centurion contradicts every word of it.

“Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.” The elders said he was worthy; he says he is not. Nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation.

Then the reasoning, and it is the most penetrating theology anyone has produced in the Gospel so far: “For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me.” Note the first phrase. Not a man with authority but a man under it. He knows exactly why his orders are obeyed — when he speaks, Rome speaks — and that such authority operates through words, at any distance the words can travel.

He applies the framework to Jesus and concludes that illness is in the same position as a legionary: under orders. He is right, and he worked it out from his life in the army.

This is the faith the church has lived on since the ascension. Nobody now gets Jesus under their roof in the way the centurion declined. What is available is exactly what he asked for and received: the word, spoken at a distance, by one whose authority is not limited by where his feet are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The centurion's analogy is more profound than it first appears. He is not merely saying that Jesus is like a commanding officer. He is recognising that authority over illness has the same character as authority in a chain of command — it operates through words, at a distance, on the basis of what stands behind the speaker.

He knows that a soldier who refuses his order is refusing the emperor whose authority he carries. He perceives that the illness Jesus commands is in the same position, and he is right. The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Creator, and creation obeys its Creator.

Jesus's amazement — “he marvelled at him” — is one of only two places in the Gospels where Jesus is said to marvel; the other is at the unbelief of Nazareth (Mark 6:6). Faith where none was expected, and unbelief where all was.

How the eternal Son can be surprised is answered the way Luke answered it at 2:52: two whole natures in one person. According to his divine nature he knows all things and learns nothing; according to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man and was genuinely moved. The wonder was real. He was not acting.
verseByVerse.examples:
“I am not worthy to have you come under my roof” is the model of the humility that genuine faith produces. By every external measure this man is among the most impressive people in the narrative — authority, resources, a reputation for generosity — and he is the one who says he is not worthy. The elders say he is; he says he is not.

It is not false modesty. It is the accurate perception of a man who has understood who he is asking for help, and the awareness of that distance is precisely what Jesus names as great faith.

And there is a quieter thing worth taking from him. Everything remarkable he says about authority he learned at work, in the army, in the ordinary business of command — not from the prophets and not in a synagogue. The best theologian in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and what qualified him was his job.

The centurion never came in person and received everything he asked for. The word of Jesus is not constrained by geography, and the authority he trusted across the streets of Capernaum is the same one trusted across continents in every generation of the church's praying.

verseByVerse.quote: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Capernaum a centurion’s highly valued servant is sick and close to death.

A centurion. A Gentile officer commanding about a hundred soldiers, probably in Herod Antipas’s service.

Highly valued. The centurion cares about a slave, unusual in his world.

On a Tuesday. How do you treat those who work under you?
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion sends Jewish elders to ask Jesus to come, and they plead that he deserves it, for he loves the nation and built their synagogue.

He is worthy. The elders think in terms of merit.

A God-fearer. A Gentile drawn to Israel’s God, like Cornelius (Acts 10).

Where Christians differ: did he come or send? Matthew tells it as if the centurion came himself (Matthew 8:5). Verdict: Matthew condenses, treating those sent as the man’s own voice, as was normal. Luke gives the fuller detail.
verseByVerse.note: Luke tells us he sent elders; Matthew compresses the story as if he came himself. Some Gentiles admired Judaism and supported synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus nears the house, the centurion sends friends to say, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but say the word, and let my servant be healed.”

Not worthy. The elders said “worthy”; he says “not worthy.” Humility.

Under my roof. He knows a Jew would become unclean entering a Gentile house.

Say the word. Faith in the power of Jesus’ word alone.

On a Tuesday. Come to Jesus as one who deserves nothing.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion explains that he too is under authority and gives orders that are obeyed.

Authority understood. If his word moves soldiers, Jesus’ word can move disease.

Under authority. He recognises that Jesus’ authority comes from God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.' And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus marvels at him and tells the crowd he has not found such faith even in Israel; and the messengers return to find the servant well.

Jesus marvelled. Only twice in the Gospels: at this faith, and at Nazareth’s unbelief (Mark 6:6).

Not even in Israel. A Gentile’s faith surpasses that of God’s people.

Healing at a distance. Jesus’ word is enough.

For worship. Praise Christ whose word heals from afar.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The raising at Nain is one of the most tender scenes in Luke and one of the most deliberately crafted. Two crowds meet at the town gate: the crowd following Jesus, and a funeral coming out.

At the centre of the funeral is a widow carrying out her only son, and Luke underlines both facts because both are load-bearing. A woman's economic and legal standing ran through a man — father, then husband, then son. She has already buried the husband. She is now burying the son, and there is no fourth name on the list. This is not only the worst grief there is; it is destitution.

Nobody asks Jesus for anything. There is no centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart. She has not prayed and does not know who he is. He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief.

“And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her.” Two things in that sentence. This is the first time Luke himself calls Jesus the Lord in his own narration — not a title on somebody's lips but the evangelist's own description, and he uses it in front of a coffin. And the compassion is something involuntary and physical — Luke uses the same words of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20) and the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33).

He touches the bier, which under the law makes a man unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11) — and, as with the leper in chapter 5, the traffic runs the wrong way. Then one sentence to a corpse: “Young man, I say to you, arise.”

Luke, the physician, records the result in two clinical stages: he sat up, and he began to speak. And then the sentence that is the point of the whole scene — “and Jesus gave him to his mother” — which is almost word for word what is said of Elijah at Zarephath: he delivered him to his mother (1 Kgs. 17:23).

The crowd's response is fear, and then two acclamations: “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” Both are true, and both fall short. Elijah prayed three times and God raised the boy; this man gave an order.
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising of the widow's son is a sign of the kingdom with both an immediate and an ultimate reference. Immediately it is the reversal of the most final of all reversals, accomplished by the one who will himself die and rise. Ultimately it points forward to the general resurrection, when the dead will rise at the voice of the Son of God (John 5:25-29; 1 Thess. 4:16).

Jesus does not raise this young man permanently; he will die again. What the miracle demonstrates is not the abolition of biological death but authority over death as a power — the authority that reaches its final expression in Jesus's own resurrection.

The echo of Elijah is deliberate, and Luke has been preparing it since 4:26, when Jesus preached about the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth and the town tried to kill him. Both prophets meet a widow whose only son has died; both speak; both give the son back to his mother in almost the same words.

The echo establishes Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophetic tradition rather than its continuation. Where Elijah stretched himself over the boy and cried out to the LORD three times, Jesus simply speaks. The authority has been concentrated. The prophet gives way to the Lord of the prophets.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's compassion for the widow, unprompted and unsolicited, is the model of the grace that sees before it is asked. She did not pray. She did not seek him out. She was lost in her grief, and he saw her.

He was not the only person at that gate who could see her — the whole town was there. He was the one who looked at the woman rather than the coffin. The posture of compassion begins with seeing, and the Christian who prays to notice what God notices is asking to become like the man who walked into Nain and saw a widow in a crowd.

“Do not weep” — said to a woman at her only son's funeral — would be an outrage from anybody else. It is not a denial of her grief and not a rebuke; he wept himself at a friend's tomb. He says it because he is about to remove the reason.

That is the only circumstance in which the sentence is not cruelty, and it is the circumstance he was standing in. Nobody else may say it. He may — and one day, to everybody, he will (Rev. 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the gate of Nain, Jesus and a crowd meet a funeral: the only son of a widow is being carried out.

Two crowds. A crowd of life meets a crowd of death.

A widow’s only son. Her support and her future gone.

Elijah and Elisha. Both raised a widow’s son (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37). Shunem, where Elisha did it, is near Nain.
verseByVerse.note: Nain was a village south-east of Nazareth, near Shunem, where Elisha raised a widow’s son. A widow who lost her only son lost her means of support.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lord sees her, he has compassion and says, “Do not weep.”

The Lord. Luke’s first use of this title for Jesus in narrative.

Compassion. A gut-deep feeling. No one asked; he acts from pity.

Do not weep. Empty words from anyone else.

On a Tuesday. Jesus sees your grief before you ask.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus touches the bier, the bearers stop, and he says, “Young man, I say to you, arise,” and the dead man sits up and speaks, and Jesus gives him to his mother.

Touched the bier. Contact with death made unclean. Jesus makes death give way.

I say to you. No prayer for power, as with Elijah. His own word.

Gave him to his mother. The exact words of 1 Kings 17:23.

For worship. Praise the Lord whose word will one day raise all his people.
verseByVerse.note: The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day. Touching it made a person unclean.

parallels.desc: he gave him to his mother

verseByVerse.quote: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!' And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear seizes everyone, and they glorify God, saying that a great prophet has arisen and God has visited his people, and the report spreads everywhere.

A great prophet. True, but not the whole truth.

God has visited. Zechariah’s words (1:68). More true than they knew.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is in prison — Herod arrested him for confronting the tetrarch's marriage (3:19-20) — and the imprisonment has raised the question that was always implicit in his ministry. He sends two disciples with it: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”

Take in who is asking. The man who leapt in the womb at Christ's approach (1:41), who saw the heavens open and the Spirit descend, who said “Behold, the Lamb of God” — this man, in a cell, in the dark, wondering whether he had been wrong. If he could come to the edge of that question, the presence of doubt is not proof that a faith was never real. It is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

Jesus's answer is neither a rebuke nor a reassurance but a demonstration. First he works, in that very hour, in front of the messengers. Then: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them.”

The list is a mosaic of Isaiah — 26:19, 29:18, 35:5-6, 61:1 — the texts describing what it will look like when God finally comes to save. John knew every one by heart. Jesus is answering doubt not with an argument but with evidence, and the evidence is the Scriptures John built his life on, now enacted in front of his own men.

“And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” is a gentle warning that names John's actual difficulty without embarrassing him. He had announced an axe at the root and a winnowing fork (3:9, 17); what he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties. Everything promised is coming. Not everything is coming yet.

After the messengers leave — and only after — Jesus tells the crowd what he thinks of John: not a reed shaken by the wind, not a man in soft clothing, but a prophet, and more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1. “Among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

The section ends with the children in the marketplace. John came fasting and they said he had a demon; the Son of Man came eating and they called him a glutton. The objections were mutually exclusive, which proves the objections were never the reason.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's doubt from prison is the New Testament's most honest portrait of faith under pressure, and it is treated with complete respect. Jesus does not rebuke him, question his faith, or withdraw the commendation he is about to give. He answers the question with careful evidence.

That is the pastoral heart of the passage. Genuine doubt, honestly expressed, receives a genuine answer. A Christian tradition that treats doubt as a mark of spiritual failure has missed the model of Jesus himself. Honest wrestling with “is it really true?” is not the absence of faith; it is faith pushed to its limit by circumstance and still asking — and asking the right person.

The saying about the least in the kingdom is not a demotion of John but an elevation of the kingdom. It concerns position in redemptive history, not personal holiness or usefulness. John stood at the threshold: he announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out.

The least believer in the kingdom has what John did not yet have — an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, and the indwelling Spirit. Not because that believer is more faithful, but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's question is the question of every sincere believer facing a crisis of expectation: I believed this was true; this is not what I expected; am I wrong? And the answer Jesus gives is not “of course you are right, do not worry.” It is “look at the evidence.”

When faith is under pressure the antidote is not reassurance but the careful examination of what has actually happened — the Scriptures, the cross, the empty tomb, the testimony of those who met the risen Christ. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is a step towards evidence that has been examined.

Notice too what John did with his doubt. He did not sit in the dark nursing it, and he did not broadcast it. He sent it to Jesus. That is the one move available to a man in a cell, and it is the right one.

And the parable of the children diagnoses a condition that is not confined to Pharisees. There is a way of engaging with the things of God in which one is always, sincerely, weighing an objection — the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one a fanatic. Every objection may be individually reasonable. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated. The test is not whether you have a criticism, but whether anything has ever succeeded in getting you up.

verseByVerse.quote: The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John, in prison, sends two disciples to ask Jesus, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”

John’s doubt. John had announced a judge with an axe and fire (3:9, 17). Jesus is healing and eating with sinners, and John is still in prison.

He asks Jesus. The right thing to do with doubt.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “Jesus” for “the Lord” in v. 19.

On a Tuesday. Even great believers doubt. Take your doubts to Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: John was in prison, held by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very time Jesus heals many of diseases and evil spirits, and gives sight to many blind people.

In that hour. The answer is given in deeds before words.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them to report what they have seen: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news; and blessed is the one not offended by him.

Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1. The signs of the messianic age.

Not judgment yet. Jesus omits the vengeance part, as at Nazareth (4:19).

Offended. Stumbling because Jesus does not meet our expectations.

On a Tuesday. Do not let your expectations of Jesus become a stumbling block.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks the crowd what they went into the wilderness to see: not a reed in the wind, nor a man in fine clothes, but a prophet, and more than a prophet.

Not a reed. John was not fickle. His question did not mean he was weak.

Not soft clothes. John was no courtier.

More than a prophet. The forerunner himself foretold.
