verseByVerse.quote: This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is the messenger of Malachi who prepares the way, and no one born of women is greater; yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.

Malachi 3:1. The messenger before the Lord.

Greatest. In calling and privilege.

The least is greater. Not in character, but in privilege: even the least believer knows the finished work of Christ, which John only announced.

For worship. Thank God for the privilege of living after the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people and tax collectors who had been baptised by John declared God just, but the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves by refusing John’s baptism.

Declared God just. They agreed with God’s verdict on their sin.

Rejected the purpose of God. Where Christians differ. Arminians argue this shows God’s will can be defeated. Verdict: people can reject God’s revealed will and call (what he commands), but not his eternal decree (Ephesians 1:11; Isaiah 46:10). They are responsible for their refusal.

On a Tuesday. Agree with God about your sin.

verseByVerse.quote: 'To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus compares this generation to children in the market who complain that others will not dance to their pipes or mourn to their dirge.

Children’s games. Playing weddings and funerals.

Never satisfied. They want God on their terms.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John came fasting and they said he had a demon; the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they called him a glutton and drunkard, a friend of sinners; yet wisdom is justified by all her children.

No pleasing them. They reject both the ascetic and the feaster.

Friend of sinners. Meant as an insult; true as glory.

Wisdom’s children. Those who respond rightly prove God’s wisdom. Matthew has “by her deeds” (Matthew 11:19).

On a Tuesday. Do not make excuses for not responding to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to dinner. Jesus accepts — which is worth registering, since two verses earlier they were calling him a friend of tax collectors and sinners. He ate with the disreputable and with the respectable, and seems to have refused nobody.

The setting explains the story. Guests reclined on low couches, propped on the left elbow, feet extending away from the table; and such meals were semi-public, with uninvited townspeople free to come in and stand round the walls. That is how she gets in.

She is “a woman of the city, who was a sinner” — no name, no history, and in that context the description almost certainly means she was publicly known for sexual immorality. She comes uninvited, stands behind him at his feet, weeps enough to wet them, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with ointment from an alabaster flask.

Every one of those acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading. A respectable woman did not unbind her hair in public. The feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, and the anointing belonged on the head. She does not appear to notice any of it. She never speaks.

Simon's response happens entirely behind his face: “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is.” The logic is tidy, and what he cannot conceive is the third possibility — that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway. Jesus answers the unspoken thought, which settles Simon's question about prophetic knowledge before the conversation starts.

Then the parable of the two debtors, and Simon walks into it with a hedge that gives him away: “The one, I suppose.” Neither debtor could pay; the lender cancelled both; the one forgiven more loved more.

And then the mirror is turned on the table. No water for the feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for the head — three ordinary courtesies any Galilean host provided without thinking, and Simon omitted all three. Against each, what she did, and each of hers is enormously larger. He withheld the cheap minimum; she gave the costly maximum at the lowest place in the room.

“Your sins are forgiven… Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” Not her love — her faith. The love was the fruit. The faith was what got her through the door.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the two debtors is the theological key to the scene and to the chapter. Forgiveness is the cause; love is the effect. This is the reverse of the moralism that says “love more, and God will forgive you more.” The gospel runs the other way: the more you understand what you have been forgiven, the more you will love.

Her love is extravagant because her sense of her cancelled debt is accurate and large. Simon's love is cool because his sense of his own debt is small — or rather, because he does not yet believe he has one. A man who considers himself basically righteous will never produce the love that flows from a woman who knows she was lost and is not any more.

Verse 47 is regularly misread, and the passage itself supplies three corrections. The parable Simon has just endorsed runs cancellation first and love after. Her forgiveness is what brought her into the house. And three verses later Jesus names what saved her, and it is her faith.

The “for” is the for of evidence, not of cause — as in “it rained last night, for the ground is wet.” The second half of the verse proves it: “he who is forgiven little, loves little.” Forgiveness is the input; love is the output.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman is the chapter's portrait of what it looks like to be genuinely overwhelmed by grace. She is not performing for the guests; she seems unaware of them. She is not observing social convention; she has left it behind. She is not managing her reputation; she forfeited it years ago.

What she is doing is the only thing she can think of in the presence of the one who has forgiven her — giving everything she has left, her tears, her hair, her perfume and her dignity, because what she has received is worth more than all of it together. The question the scene puts to every reader is whether we feel forgiven like that.

Simon's failure is the failure of good morality without grace-shaped self-knowledge. He is not a bad man. He is careful, observant, theologically serious, and he has kept his reputation intact. What he has never seen is the size of his own debt.

A person who does not see the depth of their own sin cannot be overwhelmed by the grace that forgives it, cannot produce the love that flows from it, and cannot understand a woman weeping on the floor. The church that produces more Simons than sinful women has failed at the most basic level of gospel communication: it has not helped people grasp what they have been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus dines with a Pharisee, and a woman of the city, a sinner, brings an alabaster flask of ointment.

A Pharisee’s house. Jesus eats with Pharisees too.

A sinner. Probably known in the town as immoral.

Where Christians differ: who is she? Since Pope Gregory the Great (AD 591) she has often been identified with Mary Magdalene and Mary of Bethany. Verdict: Luke gives no name, and introduces Mary Magdalene separately (8:2). The anointing at Bethany (John 12) is a different event.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so a woman could stand at his feet. Doors were often open at such meals and onlookers could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she wets his feet with tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them.

At his feet. Guests reclined with feet behind them.

Loose hair. A shocking, intimate act in public.

Tears. Grief and gratitude together.

For worship. Bring Jesus your whole heart, without caring what others think.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon the Pharisee thinks that if Jesus were a prophet he would know what kind of woman she is, and Jesus says, “Simon, I have something to say to you.”

If he were a prophet. Jesus knows her, and Simon’s thoughts too.

What sort of woman. Simon sees her past; Jesus sees her present.
verseByVerse.note: Simon was a common name; this Pharisee is not Simon the leper of Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells of two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and one fifty, both forgiven; Simon rightly says the one forgiven more will love more.

A denarius. A day’s wage. Five hundred is over a year and a half.

Could not pay. Neither could. Simon is also a debtor.

Cancelled. Freely, as grace.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; five hundred denarii was more than a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus contrasts Simon’s lack of welcome—no water, no kiss, no oil—with the woman’s tears, kisses and ointment.

Do you see this woman? Simon had seen only a category.

Basic hospitality withheld. Simon had not honoured his guest.

On a Tuesday. Do you see people, or only their reputations?
verseByVerse.note: Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to a guest.

parallels.desc: let a little water be brought, and wash your feet
you anoint my head with oil

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much; but the one forgiven little loves little.

Where Christians differ: love as the cause? Some, especially in Roman Catholic tradition, have read this as forgiveness earned by love. Verdict: the parable shows love as the result of forgiveness: the debtor forgiven more loves more (v. 43). Her love was evidence she had been forgiven; her faith saved her (v. 50).

Forgiven little. Simon thinks he needs little forgiveness, so loves little.

On a Tuesday. If your love for Christ is cool, consider how much you have been forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price, as the parable shows.

parallels.desc: we love because he first loved us

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her, “Your sins are forgiven,” the guests ask who this is who forgives sins, and he says, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

Your sins are forgiven. Spoken publicly, restoring her.

Who is this? The question the Gospel wants every reader to ask.

Your faith has saved you. Faith, not love or tears, is the instrument of salvation.

Go in peace. Shalom: peace with God.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he forgives sinners publicly and completely.

parallels.desc: who can forgive sins but God alone?

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is organised around the question of hearing and responding to the word — the parable of the sower, the lamp under a jar, and Jesus's redefinition of family as those who hear the word and do it all converge on the same theme before the chapter moves into four great demonstrations of kingdom power. After the teaching section, the chapter becomes a series of astonishing encounters: Jesus calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, casts a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, heals a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, and raises Jairus's daughter from the dead. The four miracle stories are not loosely connected anecdotes; they form a theological argument. Jesus has authority over the forces of nature, over the powers of darkness, over the long suffering of a diseased body, and over death itself. Nothing is outside the reach of his word.

The opening note about the women who accompanied Jesus and provided for the ministry out of their means (vv. 1–3) is characteristic Luke — he notices and names women at a point in history when their testimony was not counted and their presence was not recorded. Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others: they are not background figures but named participants in the mission, financing the ministry that will change the world. Luke's Gospel is consistently attentive to those whom history overlooks.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the parable about parables — the key to how the whole teaching ministry of Jesus works. The word is the seed; the hearts of the hearers are the soil; the response to the word determines everything. But the parable also functions as a warning and a comfort simultaneously: a warning that most hearers will not bear fruit, for a variety of reasons; a comfort that some will — “an hundredfold.” The harvest is certain; it comes to those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke records that Jesus travelled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, accompanied not only by the twelve but by a group of women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities.

The list is striking in its specificity: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women “provided for them out of their means” — out of their own money.

So the Galilean ministry was funded by women. Thirteen men walking from village to village for the better part of three years, eating every day, with no visible income — and Luke tells us in half a verse where the money came from.

The significance of the passage is easily underestimated. In a culture where women were excluded from the travelling company of a rabbi, Jesus's entourage included them as named, active participants — and it exposed him to precisely the accusation his enemies had already made (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

Each woman is identified by what was done for her rather than by what she brought. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising; it is a collection of the rescued.

Mary Magdalene needs rescuing from a long misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the lake, and the name says only where she came from. What Scripture tells us of her past is that seven demons came out of her — which is affliction, not scandal. She is not the unnamed woman of the previous chapter; the accident of neighbouring paragraphs invited that merger, and a sixth-century sermon fixed it in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it in the text.

Joanna is a court wife whose husband managed the estate of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell. Whatever her presence here cost her at home, she is named again at the empty tomb (24:10) — as is Mary Magdalene, who will still be there at the cross when the men have gone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The inclusion of women in the travelling band is a quiet revolution in the social world of first-century Judaism. Rabbis did not travel with female disciples; the association would have been scandalous, and Jesus's opponents were already looking for material.

His practice reflects the consistent pattern of including those the religious establishment excluded, and it anticipates the full participation of women in the life of the new covenant community (Acts 2:17-18; Gal. 3:28). The kingdom of God does not replicate the social hierarchies of the world it enters.

It matters, too, that the women are introduced immediately before the parable of the soils. Luke has just shown a company of people in whom the word took root and bore fruit — and their fruit was that they gave everything they had to keep the sowing going.

These same women are at the cross when the twelve have scattered (23:49), and at the tomb on the third morning (24:1-11). They are not peripheral figures. On the two occasions when the testimony mattered most, they are the witnesses Luke has.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women who supported the ministry “out of their means” are the New Testament's first and clearest model of financial stewardship in service of the gospel. They did not merely believe; they paid for it, and they kept paying.

The theology of giving that runs through Paul's letters (2 Cor. 8-9; Phil. 4:14-19) has its roots here: those who share in the blessings of the gospel share their resources with those who carry it forward. It is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel and pretend they were not there. They were. Somebody bought the bread.

And notice what these women could not do. They could not preach in a synagogue, and there is no sign they tried. What they had was money and mobility, and they put both under the mission for years, and were named once and then never mentioned in that connection again.

There is a whole doctrine of unglamorous service in that. The four Gospels exist partly because a group of women paid the bills of an itinerant preacher and did not require anybody to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus travels through towns and villages preaching the kingdom, with the Twelve and some women he had healed, including Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.

The kingdom of God. God’s saving rule arriving in Jesus.

Women disciples. Unusual for a rabbi. Luke gives them names.

Mary Magdalene. From Magdala. Delivered from seven demons, not, as later legend said, a prostitute.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ followers are people he has rescued.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake. Nothing in Scripture says she was the sinful woman of chapter 7.

parallels.desc: from whom he had cast out seven demons

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joanna, wife of Herod’s steward Chuza, Susanna, and many others support Jesus and the disciples from their own means.

Joanna. From Herod’s court. She will be at the empty tomb (24:10).

From their means. Women funded the mission.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “provided for him” rather than “for them”.

What it does not mean. Luke honours women’s discipleship and service. It does not follow that Jesus appointed women among the Twelve. He did not.

On a Tuesday. Support gospel work with what you have.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas; Joanna came from his court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why his disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells it publicly (vv. 4-8), then explains it privately (vv. 9-15), with a hard word about the purpose of parables in between.

Note when he tells it. Not to a disappointing turnout, but to a great crowd — and what he says is a story in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is telling the truth about crowds.

The picture was entirely ordinary. In that agriculture, sowing came before ploughing: a man walked the field broadcasting seed by the handful, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed genuinely did fall everywhere. The sower is not careless; that is simply how the job was done, and it matters — the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

The disciples ask what it means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in the Gospels on parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” The quotation is Isaiah 6:9-10, the commission given after the vision of the throne — the hardening that follows persistent rejection of revelation.

This should not be softened, and three things hold it together. It is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given; Luke has shown a Nazareth that tried to kill him and a delegation plotting his death. A parable is also a door held ajar, hiding the thing from the casual and rewarding the man who comes back and asks — which is exactly what has just happened in verse 9. And it is mercy as well as judgement: to be told plainly and reject it plainly is a far more terrible position.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God, which settles a great deal. The variable in this parable is never the seed; it is the ground. The path is hardened by ordinary traffic. The rock is shallow soil over limestone, where the fastest growth in the field is the first to die. The thorns are already rooted and simply grow at the same time, for the same water and light. And the good soil holds the word fast in an honest heart and bears fruit with patience.

It is not a rigid psychological classification. It is a mirror, and every hearer is invited to hold it up.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark records Jesus saying, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” (Mark 4:13). It establishes the principle governing all his teaching: the response to the word determines everything.

The seed does not change. It is the same word in all four soils, and the same generous hand scattering it. What varies is the condition of the heart it lands in — which is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of what has been given.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” — describes a heart that is not simply admirable. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one but the honest one: the heart that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, and does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering.

And the last word is patience, patient endurance. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable is a diagnostic tool. The question it puts to every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?”

Has it been taken away before it could go in — by distraction, by noise, by a life with no quiet in it? A footpath is not naturally hard ground; it is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get into it, and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent.

The rock soil frightens sincere believers, and it should be handled carefully. It describes someone who fell away — who is no longer there — not someone who is struggling and worried about it. Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes (Phil. 1:6; John 10:28), and John's own comment on those who left is that “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The remedy is never introspection; a plant cannot inspect its own roots. It is to go deeper, in the unspectacular disciplines nobody sees, before the drought arrives — because the sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

The thorns are the most dangerous soil, because nothing appears to be wrong. And not one of the three Jesus names is a sin: cares, riches, and the ordinary pleasures of life. The choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things — which is exactly why it is so hard to see, and why the outcome is stated so precisely: their fruit does not mature. Not nothing at all. Perpetually promising, and never actually there.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To a great crowd Jesus tells the parable of a sower whose seed falls on the path, where it is trampled and eaten by birds.

The sower. Seed was scattered by hand, then ploughed in.

The path. Hard, trodden ground.

A parable. A story from ordinary life with a spiritual point.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some seed falls on rock and withers, some among thorns that choke it, and some on good soil yielding a hundredfold; and Jesus calls, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Four soils. Same seed, different results.

A hundredfold. An extraordinary harvest.

Ears to hear. The point is how we listen.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples ask its meaning, Jesus says the secrets of the kingdom are given to them, but others hear in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing not understand.

Given to you. Understanding is a gift.

Isaiah 6:9–10. Judicial hardening: those who refuse light are given darkness.

What it does not mean. Jesus does not hide the truth from seekers; parables reveal to the willing and conceal from the unwilling.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed is God’s word; those on the path hear, but the devil takes the word from their hearts so they will not believe and be saved.

The seed is the word. Everything depends on God’s word.

The devil. An enemy who opposes faith.

On a Tuesday. After hearing God’s word, think it over before the day steals it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those on the rock receive the word with joy but have no root; they believe for a while and fall away in testing.

With joy. Emotional response is not the same as root.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall away? Arminians read this as true believers losing salvation. Verdict: they had no root. Their faith was temporary and shallow, not saving (1 John 2:19). True faith perseveres.

On a Tuesday. Put down roots through prayer, Scripture and fellowship before testing comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those among thorns hear, but are choked by worries, riches and pleasures, and their fruit never ripens.

Three thorns. Anxiety, wealth, pleasure. Two are not obviously sinful.

As they go. Slowly, over time.

On a Tuesday. What is crowding out God’s word in your life?

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those in good soil hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.

Hold it fast. Keeping, not just receiving.

Honest and good heart. A heart God has prepared (Acts 16:14).

Patience. Endurance. Fruit takes time.

For worship. Ask God to make your heart good soil.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable, and both apply it.

The lamp saying comes first, and its placing is deliberate. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after saying that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not others. A disciple could easily draw the wrong conclusion: we have been let into something, and it is ours.

“No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” Both absurdities are exact: a jar smothers the flame for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed burns the house down. Neither preserves light; both destroy it while pretending to keep it.

And note the purpose clause — so that those who enter may see. Not so the lamp may be admired, and not for the household's benefit. The secrets of the kingdom were given to be put where strangers can see by them.

“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest” cuts both ways. Forward, it is a promise: the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house, and Luke is writing the second volume that proves it. But everything concealed also comes out eventually — which is terrifying for anyone hiding something, and one of the great comforts of Scripture for anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off.

“Take care then how you hear” is the imperative that gathers up the whole chapter. And the principle attached to it — to the one who has, more will be given — is not a cruelty but a description of how understanding actually behaves. Capacity grows by use, and atrophies without it. Luke alone adds the sharpest phrase: “even what he thinks that he has.” The man's holdings were never what he supposed.

Then Jesus's mother and brothers arrive, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” It is not a rejection of Mary. It is the good soil of verse 15, six verses on, given a family name — and it is the same hearing-and-doing that ended the sermon at 6:47-49.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying and the redefinition of family are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they received is the lamp; the world they are being sent into is the stand.

The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils. The lamp saying describes what those in whom it took root are to do with it.

And the family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already established about Mary. She is not being demoted; she is the founding member of the category. The woman who said “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38) heard the word of God and did it, and Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the one she walked through.

Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing — which is why the brothers standing outside at this point in the story, who did not yet believe in him (John 7:5), are outside in more senses than one.
verseByVerse.examples:
The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it.

This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community the ancient world had no category for. It remains the miracle of every congregation that takes hearing-and-doing as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

“Take care then how you hear” is worth turning into a practical question, because the parable has just made hearing the decisive variable. Not what was preached, but what was done with it between the car park and Tuesday.

And “even what he thinks that he has” is aimed precisely at the person who is quite sure they are fine. Both the rock soil and the thorn soil had something, and both would have described themselves as having it, and neither had what they supposed — and each found out at the worst possible moment. There is a mercy in being told now, in a season of quiet, rather than in a season of testing.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one lights a lamp and hides it; nothing hidden will stay hidden.

A lamp. The word received must shine out.

Nothing hidden. The truth of the kingdom will be revealed, and everything will come to light (12:2).

On a Tuesday. Let what you have heard be seen in your life.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care how you hear: to the one who has, more will be given; from the one who has not, even what he seems to have will be taken.

How you hear. Listening is a moral act.

More given. Using what you hear brings more understanding.

What he thinks he has. Hearing without obeying leaves a person with an illusion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ mother and brothers come but cannot reach him, and he says, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.”

A new family. Those who obey God’s word.

Not a rejection. Jesus honours Mary as the model hearer (1:38, 45).

His brothers. Where Christians differ. Roman Catholics say cousins; Orthodox say Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. Verdict: most naturally Mary and Joseph’s later children (Mark 6:3; Matthew 1:25).

On a Tuesday. In Christ’s family, obedience counts more than blood.

parallels.desc: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake at his own initiative — “Let us go across to the other side.” They are in that boat, in that weather, because he told them to get in. The storm is not a consequence of any failure; obedience put them there.

He falls asleep. It is the only place in the Gospels where he is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity: he had been preaching all day, and the moment the boat was under way he was unconscious in the stern.

Then a windstorm comes down on the lake. The geography explains it — the lake sits some two hundred metres below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling cold air off the heights into the warm basin without warning. A small, shallow lake goes from flat to lethal in minutes. It still does.

And these are professional fishermen who have worked this water all their lives. When they wake him with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” it is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown — which is worth saying to anyone taught that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is an accurate reading of the instruments.

He “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same verb Luke used of the demon in the synagogue (4:35) and of a fever (4:39). There is no prayer. He speaks to the weather in the imperative.

“And they ceased, and there was a calm.” Luke's word is calm, a dead flat calm — and anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When wind drops, the swell runs on. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant.

“Where is your faith?” is gentler than it looks. He does not ask why they have none; he asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some and mislaid it. What was missing was not courage but the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen.

And they were more frightened afterwards than during. The wind had threatened their lives; what came next threatened their categories. “Who then is this?”
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator over the natural world.

In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea. “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Ps. 107:29). “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Ps. 89:9). “Who shut in the sea with doors… and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther?” (Job 38:8-11).

The disciples' question — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — has only one available answer, and every man in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood. Luke leaves the question hanging; it will not be answered aloud until Peter's confession (9:20).

The sleeping is theologically as significant as the stilling. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned but because he is at peace — the one who will say “do not be anxious” (12:22) practising it in a sinking boat. And it is the fullest possible statement of the incarnation: the Lord of the storm, too tired to stay awake, four feet from men who thought they were dying.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon, seen the healings, received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes they are afraid and amazed.

That is the honest portrait of early discipleship, and of most later discipleship too. Knowing who Jesus is in the abstract is not the same as trusting him in the specific, wet, embodied crisis. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis; it is mislaid — and “where is your faith?” is a search rather than an accusation.

The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure. It is about the one who was in the boat with them. He did not abandon them in the storm and he did not scold them for waking him. He stilled it, and then invited them to examine where their faith had been — not to condemn but to grow.

And the sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these. It heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus and his disciples set out across the lake, he falls asleep, and a windstorm swamps the boat.

He fell asleep. His true humanity: tired.

A windstorm. Galilee lies low among hills; sudden storms are common.

His idea. “Let us go across.” Obedience can lead into storms.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They wake him crying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!”, and he rebukes the wind and waves, and there is calm.

Rebuked. As he rebuked demons and fever.

Psalm 107:29. God stills the storm. Jesus does what only God does.

For worship. Praise Christ who rules wind and water.

parallels.desc: he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks, “Where is your faith?” and they, afraid and amazed, ask, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?”

Where is your faith? They had it, but forgot it.

A greater fear. Fear of the storm gives way to awe of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. In your storm, where is your faith? Look at who is in the boat.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the far shore — Gentile territory, east of the lake, with pigs on the hillsides — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet.

The description is harrowing and deliberate. He wore no clothes; he did not live in a house but among the tombs; he had repeatedly broken the chains put on him and been driven into the desert. Stripped of clothing, of community and of self-determination, he is not described as a man with a problem but as a site.

Two puzzles meet a careful reader here. Gerasa lay thirty miles inland, and Gadara six miles off; neither is on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, modern Kursi, was the spot — a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water — while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast. And Matthew names two men where Mark and Luke name one: Matthew adds a second, he does not subtract one, and the other two follow the man who spoke and who was left with a story to tell.

The demons recognise Jesus at once and their theology is impeccable: “Son of the Most High God” — a title Jews and Gentiles alike used of Israel's God, fitting on this side of the lake. But look at the verb. They beg. Three times in this scene the powers of darkness plead, which is Luke's way of showing how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore.

“Legion” was nominally six thousand men, and a legion is not a crowd but an occupying force. The word would have had an edge in the Decapolis, where people had watched real ones march. And the answer comes from the occupation rather than the man: asked his own name, there is no I left to reply.

They beg not to be sent to the abyss — the sealed prison of rebel spirits (Rev. 20:1-3) — but into the pigs. Jesus permits it, and it is the demons who stampede the herd, doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had done to one man for years. The lake full of drowned swine is the plainest possible evidence of what he had been living under.

The townspeople find him clothed, in his right mind, and sitting at the feet of Jesus — the posture of a disciple. And they ask Jesus to leave. The man himself begs to come along; that is the one request in the chapter that is refused. “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.”
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels, and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile herdsmen. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel.

The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the demonised man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33) — both liberated by the same word, with the same authority, and neither able to put up the slightest resistance.

The restored man is “in his right mind” — sober, self-possessed — and he is sitting at Jesus's feet, where a disciple sits (cf. 10:39; Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has not merely been evicted; the ground has been given to somebody else.

That distinction matters, because a deliverance that only removes does not hold. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24-26). The sitting at the feet is not incidental colour. It is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave are the cautionary portrait of a community that values what it can calculate over what it cannot control. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The arithmetic should be straightforward.

But the fear is real, and Luke names it: something has happened here that they do not control. A lunatic in the tombs can at least be chained. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or manage it into something more comfortable — and Jesus does not argue with them. He gets into the boat and goes. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

The man's desire to follow, and Jesus's refusal, is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. That is a harder road than the boat. Everyone who has been converted where their old life is public knowledge understands it.

And he is sent to declare not a doctrine but a testimony — the one subject on which he is the world's leading authority. Then Luke does something quietly enormous and leaves it without comment: Jesus said “declare how much God has done for you,” and the man went and proclaimed “how much Jesus had done for him.” The two sentences sit side by side, and Luke sees nothing to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sail to the country of the Gerasenes, and a demon-possessed man from the town meets Jesus; for a long time he had worn no clothes and lived among the tombs.

Gentile territory. Across the lake, in the Decapolis.

Among the tombs. Unclean and isolated. Satan dehumanises.

Textual note. Manuscripts read Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes. Gerasa and Gadara were towns of the region; Gergesa may have been a village on the shore.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gadarenes, some Gergesenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing Jesus, he falls down and shouts, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me,” for Jesus had commanded the spirit to come out.

Son of the Most High God. A title used by Gentiles for Israel’s God.

Torment. The demons fear judgment.

Chains could not hold him. No human power could help.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked his name, he says “Legion,” for many demons had entered him, and they beg Jesus not to send them into the abyss.

Legion. A Roman unit of about six thousand.

The abyss. The prison of demons (Revelation 20:3).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers. The abyss is the place where evil spirits are confined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demons beg to enter a herd of pigs, Jesus permits it, and the herd rushes into the lake and drowns.

Pigs. Unclean animals in a Gentile land.

Visible proof. The man can see that the demons have gone.

The destruction. Some have objected to the loss of the herd. A man’s soul is worth more than many pigs.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The townspeople come and find the man clothed, in his right mind, sitting at Jesus’ feet, and they are afraid and ask Jesus to leave.

At the feet of Jesus. The posture of a disciple.

Clothed and in his right mind. Restored humanity.

Asked him to leave. They preferred their pigs to the presence of such power.

On a Tuesday. What would you rather keep than have Jesus near?
verseByVerse.note: Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple.

parallels.desc: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healed man begs to go with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell what God has done, and he proclaims throughout the town what Jesus has done.

Go home. Not every disciple is called away; many are sent home.

God and Jesus. Jesus says “God”; the man says “Jesus.” He has understood.

A missionary to the Gentiles. Before Paul, a healed madman took the news of Jesus to the Decapolis.

On a Tuesday. Tell your family and neighbours what God has done for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — a healing folded inside a raising, with each story interpreting the other.

Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue: a lay official who organised the services and carried the community's respect, and a member of the class that had been watching Jesus with hostility since chapter 5. He falls at Jesus's feet in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. His only daughter, about twelve, is dying, and every consideration of position has gone.

Jesus goes with him. The crowd presses. And a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years — exactly as long as the girl has been alive — reaches through the crowd and touches the tassel on the corner of his garment.

Her twelve years had cost far more than health. Leviticus 15:25-27 put a woman in her condition under continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her: anything she sat on, anyone who touched her. Twelve years without the synagogue, without normal contact, very likely without a husband — and none of it her fault. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching: she had spent everything and was no better.

Her approach is furtive because it had to be; by the law she understood, her touch would defile him. And once again the traffic runs the wrong way. The bleeding stops.

Jesus stops the whole procession to ask who touched him — a question he already knows the answer to. Peter's exasperation is reasonable and Luke lets it stand. But he will not take a transaction where a person is available: she had tried to take the gift and stay invisible, and that would have left her physically healed and socially exactly as she was. He makes her say it out loud, in public — which puts her restoration on the record where her whole town can hear it — and then calls her “Daughter,” the only time in the Gospels he uses that word to a woman.

And while he is still speaking, the message comes: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” From where Jairus stands, the delay killed her. Somebody else's twelve-year problem was attended to first, and his child ran out of time.

“Do not fear; only believe.” Then the mourners are put out, the girl is taken by the hand — “Child, arise” — and her spirit returns. And the first thing Jesus says afterwards is that somebody should get her something to eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman healed on the way to Jairus's house teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for her has more than enough for a dead girl.

Jairus is being taught, at his own cost and in real time, to resist the word that says “it is too late.” The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life, and Jairus had just watched, at close range, what this man does for somebody who ran out of options twelve years ago.

“She is not dead but sleeping” is not a correction of the diagnosis, and Luke — a physician — gives three signals that she was genuinely dead: the professional mourners had arrived, the crowd knew, and “her spirit returned.” Jesus is changing a category, not disputing a fact. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and that is now what death is for those who belong to him (1 Thess. 4:13-15; John 11:11).

The woman's touch of the “fringe” may point to the tassels of Numbers 15:38-40, worn as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 had promised that the sun of righteousness would rise “with healing in its wings,” and the Hebrew for wings is the word for the corners of a garment. She may have been reaching, knowingly or not, for exactly that.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years, her exhausted resources, her uncleanness and her invisibility are the conditions in which she finally comes. She did not come while she still had options; she came when she had nothing left.

And Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, calling her “daughter,” declaring her faith in front of everyone — is the public vindication of a person who arrived at the bottom of her resources. Her faith was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it aloud.

Jairus's journey is faith pushed to its absolute limit. He did everything right: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked in time. Then the delay, and then the word that it was over. This has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many lives feel like and pious hurry past it is worthless.

“Only believe” is not a technique, and it is not an instruction to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead — that reading crushes bereaved people. It is a word to a man who has just been told it is finished, asking him to keep hold of the person beside him for another ten minutes.

And the last instruction in the house is the one that could not have been invented. A girl has been raised from the dead, the room is beyond speech, and the Son of God says: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back across the lake, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, falls at Jesus’ feet and begs him to come, for his only daughter, about twelve, is dying.

A ruler. A man of standing, humbled by need.

Only daughter. Like the widow’s only son (7:12).

Twelve. She has lived as long as the woman has suffered (v. 43).
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman who had bled for twelve years, and could not be healed by anyone, comes behind Jesus and touches the fringe of his garment, and the bleeding stops at once.

Twelve years unclean. Cut off from worship and touch (Leviticus 15:25).

The fringe. The tassels commanded in Numbers 15:38.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “though she had spent all her living on physicians”. Luke the physician may have softened Mark’s comment that doctors made her worse (Mark 5:26).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the words about the physicians. Her condition made her ritually unclean. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks who touched him; when all deny it and Peter points to the crowd, Jesus insists someone touched him, for he felt power go out.

Who touched me? Not ignorance, but to draw her out.

Power went out. Not magic in his clothes, but his personal power responding to faith.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “and those with him”, and Peter’s words “and you say, Who touched me?”

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing she cannot hide, the woman comes trembling, falls down and tells everyone why she touched him and how she was healed, and Jesus says, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”

In the presence of all. Her healing is made public, so she can be restored to the community.

Daughter. The only time Jesus addresses anyone so.

Your faith. Faith, weak and secret, is honoured.

Made you well. The same word as “saved”.

For worship. Thank Jesus who calls the outcast “daughter”.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A messenger arrives: the girl has died, so do not trouble the Teacher; but Jesus says, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.”

Too late. The delay seemed costly.

Only believe. Faith when all seems lost.

On a Tuesday. When you hear “it’s too late,” hear Jesus: “Do not fear.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes Peter, James, John and the parents inside, tells the mourners she is not dead but asleep, and they laugh at him, knowing she is dead.

Three disciples. The same three at the transfiguration (9:28).

Sleeping. For Jesus, death is like sleep, because he will wake her (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

What it does not mean. Not that she was in a coma. Luke says she was dead (v. 53, 55).

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes her hand and says, “Child, arise,” her spirit returns, she gets up at once, and he tells them to give her something to eat and to tell no one.

Her spirit returned. Death is the spirit leaving the body (James 2:26).

Something to eat. Tender, practical care.

Tell no one. Jesus avoids fame as a wonder-worker.

For worship. Praise Christ who will one day take your hand and say, “Arise.”

parallels.desc: the child’s life came into him again

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross.
