The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together, gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Two words, and not synonyms: power (dynamis) is the capacity, authority (exousia) is the right. Both are given, and neither is earned.

The instructions are deliberately spartan — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. Between them those five items cover security, supply and comfort, and he takes all five away. The messengers are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house first receives them and not moving on to a better one.

A reader comparing Gospels will find a difficulty: Mark records that they were to take nothing except a staff (Mark 6:8). Several explanations have been offered, and none is certain; what is plain is that both accounts fit the point of the list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet — the gesture a Jew used at the border when returning from Gentile territory, here applied to Jewish villages that refuse the kingdom's messengers. The old boundary has moved. It now runs not around the nation but around the message.

Luke reports the whole mission in one verse: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere. What is absent is as striking as what is there — no account of the first house, the first refusal, the first demon. The instructions were not an ideal held up for admiration; they were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Herod's perplexity closes the section. He has killed the greatest of the prophets and is now hearing that something greater is happening. The three theories on offer — John raised, Elijah appeared, one of the old prophets risen — are all respectful and all too small. His question, “who is this about whom I hear such things?”, is exactly the right question. And “he sought to see him” is the tragedy: he gets his wish at the trial (23:8), and Jesus does not answer him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sending of the twelve is the first instance of the apostolic mission. The word apostle means simply one who is sent; it says nothing about the man's qualities and everything about his commission.

The authority they receive is delegated — the same authority Jesus has been exercising since chapter 4, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will run through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world.

Note who receives it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), propose incinerating a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready.

And the errand has two halves held together: to proclaim and to heal. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The instructions to take nothing are not a travel policy but a structural embodiment of dependence. The messengers carry no resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to, which creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver, and the receiver depends on the message.

The rule about staying in the first house is more pointed than it looks. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on. A messenger who upgrades has begun to be paid — and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale.

The shaking of the dust takes a refusal seriously enough to mark it, without bitterness and without a backward argument. Two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing until the gospel becomes an irritation attached to a person, or to shrug it off and privately conclude they were never going to anyway. The dust does neither.

And Herod is the standing warning that the right question is not enough. A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask exactly the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives the Twelve power and authority over demons and diseases, and sends them to preach the kingdom and heal.

Power and authority. Delegated by Jesus. The apostles act as his representatives.

Preach and heal. Word and deed together, with preaching first.

Where Christians differ: healing today. Some expect all believers to heal as the apostles did. Verdict: these powers marked the apostles in a unique, foundational mission (2 Corinthians 12:12). God still heals in answer to prayer (James 5:14–15), but the church’s commission is to preach the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells them to take nothing for the journey, no staff, bag, bread, money or spare tunic, and to stay in whatever house welcomes them.

Travel light. Total dependence on God and on hospitality.

A special mission. Later Jesus changes the instructions (22:35–36). These were for a short mission in Israel.

On a Tuesday. What are you carrying that keeps you from depending on God?
verseByVerse.note: The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies; a second tunic was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where people do not welcome them, they are to shake the dust off their feet as a testimony against them.

Shaking off dust. What pious Jews did leaving Gentile land: this town is treated as outside God’s people.

A testimony. A solemn warning, not personal spite.

On a Tuesday. You are responsible for faithful witness, not for the response.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

The mission multiplies. Jesus’ work now spreads through others.

For worship. Thank God for those who first brought the gospel to your town.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod hears of it and is perplexed, because some say John has been raised, others that Elijah or a prophet has appeared; he says, “John I beheaded, but who is this?” and seeks to see Jesus.

Who is this? The great question of the chapter (vv. 18–20).

A guilty conscience. Herod beheaded John and is troubled.

He sought to see him. He will, at the trial (23:8).
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Luke records that he later saw Jesus at his trial.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The twelve return from their mission and Jesus withdraws with them to Bethsaida for rest. Mark gives his reason in his own words: “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” The crowds find out where the boat is going and get there first.

So the rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out the destination — and Luke records that “he welcomed them.” The verb means received gladly. He met the people who had wrecked his only plan for the week as though they had been invited, and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and cured those who had need of healing, until the day was nearly over.

The disciples' suggestion is sensible and they are right about almost everything: it is late, the place is desolate, thousands need food and lodging, and the villages are the only source of either. Sending away is not wickedness; it is arithmetic, done honestly, by tired men. What the arithmetic never includes is the person standing next to them.

“You give them something to eat” is emphatic in the Greek — you give them — and there is no reading on which the twelve can obey it. Their answer is what an honest man says when handed an impossible order: here is the inventory. Five barley loaves and two fish, which John tells us belonged to a boy. They have even costed the alternative: Mark records two hundred denarii, two-thirds of a year's wage, and even that would not be enough.

They are right. Five loaves and two fish do not feed five thousand men — and Luke's andres means adult males specifically, so with women and children (Matt. 14:21) the real number is far higher. No amount of faith changes that arithmetic and Jesus never suggests otherwise. What he does is ask for the loaves. Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over.

The four verbs over the bread — took, blessed, broke, gave — are the ordinary actions of a Jewish householder, and Luke fixes them in the reader's memory because they return twice: at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus, where “their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (24:30-31).

All ate and were satisfied — the satisfaction the Psalms say God gives (Ps. 107:9; 132:15). And twelve baskets of fragments were gathered: one for each man who had done the arithmetic.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle besides the resurrection recorded in all four Gospels, which signals its weight. The typology is dense: a multitude fed in a desolate place, as Israel was fed in the wilderness; the crowd seated in ordered companies of fifty, as Moses set the people in fifties (Exod. 18:25); the one greater than Moses giving bread not prayed down from heaven but broken from his own hands.

It is the New Testament's great sign of the messianic banquet — the feast Isaiah promised (Isa. 25:6-9) and Revelation describes as the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9). Every time the church gathers at the Lord's table it is taking a foretaste of that feast.

And the eucharistic action defines the church's life: receiving grace, returning it in blessing, breaking it in service, giving it away. He could have distributed the bread himself. Instead it goes from his hands into the disciples' and from theirs to the people — so that the men who said “send them away” spent the next hour giving away food they did not have.

The twelve baskets left over say what the whole scene says: the kingdom of God does not issue minimum rations. There was more at the end than at the beginning, and it was not close.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Send the crowd away” is the reasonable option in far more situations than this one — the pastoral problem genuinely beyond a church's capacity, the person whose needs are more than anyone in the congregation can carry, the ministry that cannot be staffed.

And notice what had just happened to these men. They had come back that same week from a mission in which they healed the sick with nothing in their pockets, and were still telling him about it two verses earlier. Experience of God's provision has a remarkably short half-life, and it is almost never available in the moment it would be most use.

“Bring what you have” can be preached as though the trick were to be optimistic about the loaves. It is not. The loaves are genuinely insufficient and everyone in the story knows it. The command is to put them in his hands anyway, in full knowledge that they will not do, and see what he does with them.

The rhythm of withdrawal and interruption is worth having by anyone who works with people and has learned, rightly, to guard their time. The guarding is not unspiritual — Jesus withdrew constantly. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when what was properly and prayerfully arranged is taken by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles report back, and Jesus takes them away privately to Bethsaida, but the crowds follow, and he welcomes them, speaks of the kingdom and heals those in need.

Withdrew. Rest after ministry.

He welcomed them. Interrupted rest, yet no irritation.

On a Tuesday. How do you respond to interruptions?
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Late in the day the Twelve ask Jesus to send the crowd away to find food and lodging, since they are in a desolate place.

Desolate. Like Israel in the wilderness, where God gave manna.

A sensible suggestion. But Jesus has a different plan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says, “You give them something to eat,” and they protest that they have only five loaves and two fish.

You give them. Jesus puts the responsibility on them.

Only five loaves. Our resources measured against the need.

On a Tuesday. Bring Jesus what little you have.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are about five thousand men, and Jesus has them sit in groups of about fifty.

Five thousand men. With women and children, far more.

Groups. Order, like Israel’s camp in the wilderness (Exodus 18:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes the loaves and fish, looks to heaven, blesses and breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to serve.

Took, blessed, broke, gave. The same words as at the Last Supper (22:19) and Emmaus (24:30).

Through the disciples. Jesus provides; they distribute.

For worship. Give thanks before meals, as Jesus did.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All eat and are satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers are collected.

Satisfied. Not just a taste. Jesus is the true bread (John 6:35).

Twelve baskets. One for each apostle: more than enough.

For worship. Praise Christ who satisfies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying — Luke alone tells us so, as he does at every hinge of this Gospel — and out of that prayer comes the question the whole book exists to answer.

“Who do the crowds say that I am?” The answers are the same three that reached Herod's court: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Every one is respectful; every one is wrong in the same way, placing him within the prophetic tradition rather than beyond it.

“But who do you say that I am?” It is a question no survey can answer. Peter says: “The Christ of God.”

And immediately, without celebration, Jesus charges them to tell no one — and begins to teach what the title actually means. “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”

The silence is not modesty. In Galilee in that decade Messiah meant a son of David who would raise an army and break Rome; John records a crowd trying to make him king by force (John 6:15). The word is embargoed until it can carry the meaning he is about to give it. And the rejection is specified by office — the Sanhedrin, which is to say the entire official religious leadership of the people of God. Not Rome. The men who had the Scriptures.

The call to discipleship follows on the same terms, and Luke marks the audience: “he said to all.” This is not advanced material for the twelve. “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”

To deny the self is not to deny oneself things. The verb is the one Luke will use of Peter's denials in the courtyard (22:34, 61). And “take up his cross” was not a metaphor to anyone hearing it: crucifixion was a live Roman practice, and the phrase described a condemned man carrying the beam of his own execution to the place where he would be nailed to it.

Then “daily,” which is Luke's addition — Matthew and Mark do not have it. It takes the most final image available and makes it a routine, which means it is not chiefly about martyrdom and not reserved for the exceptional.

The section closes with a promise that has troubled readers ever since: “there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” Luke answers it in the very next sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's confession is correct, and Luke records no commendation of it — Matthew's account has the blessing on Peter; Luke, writing for a Gentile church, moves straight to the reframing. The Christ of God is the suffering, dying, rising Son of Man.

“Son of Man” is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying “a human being.” It comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is a claim of enormous weight wrapped in a phrase that sounds humble — which is exactly why he could use it in public.

The word must (dei) is the divine-necessity word Luke uses at every turning point. The cross is not an accident, a miscalculation, or the defeat of the mission. It is the appointment. And he never once announces the death without the rising in the same breath.

On “will not taste death,” three answers are given and they are not equally strong. The weakest strains the words. The second, and much better, takes the kingdom in Luke's usual sense — God's reign breaking in — and points to the resurrection, Pentecost, and the spread Luke describes in his second volume, all within the lifetime of the hearers. But the strongest is the one Luke himself supplies: eight days later, three of them went up a mountain and saw the Son of Man in glory.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Daily” is the word that brings the cross within reach of an ordinary believer. It is not the dramatic act of martyrdom reserved for the exceptional disciple; it is the ordinary Tuesday in which the self is again told it does not rule here.

And self-denial needs guarding, because it can be twisted into something poisonous. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to.

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?” is put at the extreme deliberately: if the trade fails at the maximum price it fails at every price below it. Nobody reading this will gain the whole world. The prices most people actually pay are small — a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

And shame is the right word, chosen over “deny” or “reject.” Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ; a great many are embarrassed by him, and by his words particularly. What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After praying alone, Jesus asks the disciples who the crowds say he is, then who they say he is, and Peter answers, “The Christ of God.”

Praying. Again at a turning point.

Who do you say? Not opinion polls, but personal confession.

The Christ of God. The Messiah God sent.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. Matthew’s account includes the “rock” saying used to support the papacy (Matthew 16:18). Verdict: Luke records only the confession. The rock is Christ as confessed by Peter, and Peter’s foundational role as apostle was shared with the others (Ephesians 2:20). It does not establish a line of popes.
verseByVerse.note: Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi) but notes that Jesus was praying. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus strictly charges them to tell no one, saying the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the leaders, be killed, and on the third day be raised.

Tell no one. “Messiah” meant a political liberator to most people.

Must. Divine necessity.

Suffer, rejected, killed, raised. The first passion prediction.

For worship. Thank Christ who went to the cross of his own will.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow; for whoever would save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it for Jesus will save it.

Deny himself. Say no to self as master.

The cross. An instrument of execution.

Daily. Only in Luke. An ongoing, everyday dying to self.

Lose to save. The paradox of discipleship.

On a Tuesday. What cross is yours to take up today?
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Only Luke adds “daily.”

verseByVerse.quote: For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What good is it to gain the whole world and lose yourself? Whoever is ashamed of Jesus and his words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of when he comes in glory.

The whole world. No gain is worth the soul.

Ashamed. Of Jesus and of his words, his teaching.

Coming in glory. His return as judge.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide that you belong to Jesus?

verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says some standing there will not die before they see the kingdom of God.

Where Christians differ: what did they see? The transfiguration, the resurrection, Pentecost, the fall of Jerusalem, or the second coming. Verdict: the transfiguration that follows immediately is a preview of the kingdom’s glory, and the resurrection and Pentecost brought the kingdom in power. Jesus was not mistaken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
About eight days after the confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray — and Luke alone tells us that is why he went. It happened while he was praying.

Luke is careful with his words. Mark and Matthew say he was transfigured; Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, describes what was seen: his face became different, his clothing turned a white that flashed. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus becoming something more than he was; it is the covering coming off something always there.

Moses and Elijah appear in glory — the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on the same mountain, Sinai and Horeb; both had asked in their way to see him and been given a back and a whisper. Now they stand in the light, talking with him.

And Luke alone tells us the subject. They “spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word is exodos. The man who led the first one — out of Egypt, through the blood of a lamb, through the sea — is standing there while the word is applied to a death in Jerusalem. It is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens: not a defeat but a deliverance, accomplished by a lamb, on a fixed date, by a leader who goes ahead of his people. And the verb is accomplish, not suffer.

The three were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it — and Luke will find the disciples asleep again in Gethsemane (22:45). Peter's proposal to build three tents comes as Moses and Elijah are leaving: a man trying to stop something ending, and Luke's aside is candid and gentle, “not knowing what he said.” The proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, three equals.

The cloud interrupts him mid-sentence. It is the shekinah — the cloud of Sinai, of the tabernacle, of Solomon's temple, unseen in Israel for centuries — and the verb “overshadowed” is the one Gabriel used to Mary (1:35).

“This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” Then the cloud lifts, and Moses is gone, and Elijah is gone, and there are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration is at once christological and eschatological — revealing who Jesus is, and what the coming kingdom will look like. What the disciples see is not a separate divine form he can put on and take off; it is the radiance belonging to who he always is, momentarily unrestrained. The humanity that veiled the glory at Bethlehem is for a few minutes transparent to it. This is what John means by “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).

Moses and Elijah's conversation is the most extraordinary discussion never recorded — two of the greatest figures of the Old Testament speaking with the Son of God about the cross that will accomplish the ultimate Exodus. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it.

Some Bibles read “my Beloved” at v.35 rather than “my Chosen One,” and the manuscripts do differ. “Chosen One” is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading — a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the baptism and the parallel in Matthew. And the phrase is deliberate: “my chosen” is Isaiah's word for the Servant (Isa. 42:1). On a mountain where they have just discussed his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant's title.

“Listen to him” is the only imperative in the scene, and it is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's desire to build three tents is the perennial temptation to institutionalise a moment of glory — to capture the experience, preserve it, replicate it. Every significant encounter with the living God carries it. The glory was never given to be housed; it was given for the road down.

And the road down is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Jesus comes off that mountain the next morning into a crowd, a boy in convulsions, and a ministry that has failed. Moses came down Sinai carrying the tablets of God and found a golden calf.

“Listen to him” is the transfiguration's practical legacy. The disciples have been given an extraordinary visual confirmation, and are told the appropriate response is not to build but to listen. The Christian life is not primarily about spectacular experiences of divine glory, though God gives those in his mercy. It is about listening to the voice of the Son, in Scripture, in prayer, in the community of faith.

And the placing of it is a mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them he will be rejected and killed, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About eight days later, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray, and as he prays his face changes and his clothes become dazzling white.

As he was praying. Only Luke mentions it.

Transformed. His hidden glory shines out.

Like Moses. Whose face shone on the mountain (Exodus 34:29). But Jesus’ glory is his own.
verseByVerse.note: “About eight days” counts inclusively; Matthew and Mark say “after six days.” Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak with him of his departure, which he was about to fulfil in Jerusalem.

Moses and Elijah. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to him (24:27).

Departure. Literally exodos. His death, resurrection and ascension are the new exodus.

Fulfil. He goes to Jerusalem to accomplish it.

Life after death. Moses and Elijah were alive.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “departure” is exodus — his death, resurrection and ascension as a new rescue of God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, waking, sees his glory and suggests making three tents, not knowing what he is saying.

Heavy with sleep. As at Gethsemane (22:45).

Three tents. Perhaps to prolong the moment, or to treat all three as equals.

Not knowing. Glory without the cross is not yet.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cloud overshadows them, and a voice says, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” and then Jesus is found alone.

The cloud. God’s presence (Exodus 40:34).

My Chosen One. Isaiah 42:1.

Listen to him. Deuteronomy 18:15. The prophet like Moses.

Jesus alone. Moses and Elijah fade; Jesus remains.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “my beloved Son”, from Mark 9:7. “My Chosen One” is earlier.

For worship. Listen to him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “my Beloved” for “my Chosen One.”

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen
my chosen, in whom my soul delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets a father whose only child is seized by a spirit that convulses him — and the disciples who were not on the mountain had tried and failed.

The father's description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, then flattened exhaustion. So was the boy ill or possessed? Luke is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and he consistently keeps the categories apart: those sick with various diseases, and demons also came out of many (4:40-41); a crowd healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits (6:17-18). Jesus speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do real harm and Luke's care rules out both — that every seizure or darkness of mind is the enemy's work, and that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose. But Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

“O faithless and twisted generation” is addressed to the whole scene, not the father — the word “twisted” is Moses' word for Israel in the wilderness (Deut. 32:5). And it is followed immediately by “Bring your son here.” He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy anyway.

Luke ends the miracle as he ended the one at Nain: “he gave him back to his father” (cf. 7:15). Not “the boy was healed.” A son handed back to the man who brought him.

Then, at the height of the crowd's enthusiasm, the second passion prediction — “let these words sink into your ears.” They did not understand, it was concealed from them, and they were afraid to ask. Afraid of the answer, almost certainly; Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32).

And what fills the silence is an argument about which of them is greatest. Jesus takes a child — a person with no legal standing and nothing to offer — and stands the child beside himself. Then John reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, and gives his reason: “he does not follow with us.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' failure at v.40, after their success in vv.1-6, raises the question of what changed. Matthew records Jesus naming it as “little faith” (Matt. 17:20). The lesson is what the whole chapter teaches: the authority delegated to them is not their own. It flows from the one who gives it and is sustained by the relationship of trust with him.

“Delivered into the hands of men” — handed over. There is a bitter wordplay the English keeps: the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of men.

Luke's “it was concealed from them” is a passive without an agent, and probably deliberately so. Two things are true at once: there is a hiddenness God appoints (cf. 19:42; 24:16), and there is a hiddenness they are manufacturing, since the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead.

On “the one who is not against you is for you” — a reader will notice the apparent opposite at 11:23, “whoever is not with me is against me.” The difference is in the pronouns. There the subject is a man's own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground. Here it is one servant's judgement of another. About my own standing, assume nothing; about another doing good in his name, assume the best.
verseByVerse.examples:
The child placed beside Jesus is a searching challenge to every form of Christian leadership measured by influence, platform, numbers or reputation. A first-century child had no legal rights, no property, no voice, and no capacity to confer honour on anybody — which is exactly why he was chosen for an argument about greatness.

So the test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats those who cannot advance him, repay him, report him, or do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching.

“I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not” is an honest report of ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. It belongs in the Gospel and it is a comfort of a hard kind: the record of the church's work has always included the things that did not work.

And John's “he does not follow with us” — not “he does not follow you” — names the instinct precisely. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history, and they are not to be stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day a man in the crowd begs Jesus to look at his only son.

From glory to need. Down from the mountain into a suffering world.

Only son. Again Luke notes an only child (7:12; 8:42).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A spirit seizes the boy and convulses him, and the disciples could not cast it out.

Convulsions. Symptoms like epilepsy, but caused here by a spirit.

What it does not mean. Not that epilepsy is demonic. Scripture distinguishes illness from possession (4:40–41).

The disciples failed. Even with authority given (v. 1).

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus laments a faithless, twisted generation, rebukes the spirit, heals the boy and gives him back to his father, and all are astonished at God’s majesty.

Faithless generation. Deuteronomy 32:5.

Gave him back. As at Nain (7:15).

The majesty of God. Seen in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When others fail you, bring your need to Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While all marvel, Jesus tells the disciples that the Son of Man is about to be handed over to men, but they do not understand and are afraid to ask.

Let these words sink in. Amid applause, he speaks of the cross.

Concealed from them. Understanding would come after the resurrection (24:45).

On a Tuesday. Do not be afraid to ask Jesus about what you do not understand.

parallels.desc: they understood none of these things

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
An argument starts about which of them is greatest, and Jesus, knowing their thoughts, puts a child by his side.

Right after the cross was mentioned. They argue about status.

A child. Without status in that world.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever receives this child in Jesus’ name receives him and the one who sent him; the least among you is the greatest.

Receives me. Jesus identifies with the lowly.

The least is great. Greatness by service (22:26).

On a Tuesday. Serve someone who can give you nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John reports that they stopped someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name because he did not follow with them, and Jesus says, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.”

Not with us. Group loyalty.

Not against you. Compare 11:23. Here the issue is those who truly act in Jesus’ name.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone using Jesus’ name is genuine (Acts 19:13–16), or that truth does not matter.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice in gospel work done by Christians outside your church or tradition.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” With that sentence Luke's narrative pivots. The Galilean ministry is over, and the journey that runs from here to 19:44 begins. Everything that follows — the parables, the healings, the controversies — happens on the road that leads to the cross.

“Taken up” reaches past the cross to the ascension. Luke has the whole arc in one word: the death, the rising, the going home.

“Set his face” is the language of the Suffering Servant: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 50:7) — from a passage whose preceding verse reads, “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard.” He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies. He turns and starts walking.

The route runs through Samaria, which some Jewish pilgrims avoided by going round through the Jordan valley. He goes straight through. And the village refuses him precisely because his face is set toward Jerusalem — the ancient dispute over Gerizim and Jerusalem. On the first day of the journey to the cross, what he is rejected for is going to the cross.

James and John ask to call down fire, reasoning from Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:10-12), and reasoning badly: Elijah faced armed men sent to seize a prophet, and these two are facing a village that declined to provide beds. Jesus rebukes the disciples, not the Samaritans, and they go on to another village. Samaritan villages like it would be evangelised within a few years (Acts 8:5-8, 25), and no one there was burned.

Three encounters close the chapter. A man volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head — a saying that fits the refusal he has just met. A second is called and asks to bury his father first; in that world burial happened the same day, so the request may well mean “let me stay until my father dies,” an indefinite postponement. A third asks only to say goodbye — which is what Elisha was granted (1 Kgs. 19:20) — and is answered with a ploughing image, the difference being that Elisha destroyed his plough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The travel narrative beginning at 9:51 is Luke's unique structural contribution. Matthew and Mark move quickly from Galilee to Jerusalem; Luke devotes ten chapters to the journey. The structure is theological before it is geographical: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, which is to say on the road to the cross. The whole of it is lived in the shadow of the set face of 9:51.

“Leave the dead to bury their own dead” is among the most shocking sayings in the Gospels — an apparent violation of the fifth commandment and of an obligation so weighty that the Old Testament names its absence as a mark of judgement (Jer. 22:18-19). It is not an abolition of family duty. It is a refusal of one word, and the word is first. And the saying is wordplay, not cruelty: let those who are spiritually dead attend to the socially necessary; you have been called by the one who gives life.

“Fit for the kingdom of God” is the language of usefulness. It is not a statement about whether such a man is saved. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while facing the wrong way.

And the instinct James and John show — to destroy those who reject Jesus — is answered by the direction he is walking. The one who has set his face toward a cross does not call down fire on those who refuse him; he presses on toward the sacrifice that will make it possible for even Samaritans to receive him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled through stony ground; it had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A man who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment, and a crooked first furrow makes every furrow after it crooked, because they are all set by the first. The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

The three would-be disciples represent three ways of not following. The first underestimates the cost — “wherever you go” sounds easy until it means homelessness. The second and third both say first. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective at postponing everything.

Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided. He never does. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing.

And a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite — that coming to Christ secures a settled life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the days near for him to be taken up, Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem, and a Samaritan village refuses to receive him.

Taken up. His ascension, through the cross.

Set his face. Determination (Isaiah 50:7).

The journey begins. Luke 9:51–19:27 is the long journey to Jerusalem.

Samaritans. Hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

For worship. Thank Christ who set his face towards the cross for you.
verseByVerse.note: Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins. “Taken up” points to the ascension. Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea and were often hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: I have set my face like a flint
Jews have no dealings with Samaritans

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John offer to call down fire on the village, but Jesus rebukes them, and they go to another village.

Sons of thunder. Elijah called down fire (2 Kings 1:10).

He rebuked them. Not the way of the Son of Man.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “as Elijah did”, and Jesus’ words, “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.” They are not in the earliest manuscripts, though they express Jesus’ mind.

On a Tuesday. When rejected, do not call down fire. Go on to the next village.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “as Elijah did,” and a further saying: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Someone promises to follow Jesus anywhere, and Jesus answers that foxes have holes and birds nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

Count the cost. Following Jesus may mean losing security.

Nowhere to lay his head. Rejected just now in Samaria.

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To another Jesus says, “Follow me,” and when he asks first to bury his father, Jesus says, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; go and proclaim the kingdom.”

Bury my father. Perhaps his father was alive and he wanted to wait until he died.

The dead bury the dead. Let the spiritually dead handle it.

What it does not mean. Not contempt for parents (Exodus 20:12; Mark 7:10–13). Jesus demands first loyalty.

On a Tuesday. What “first let me” is delaying your obedience?
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another wants first to say goodbye at home, and Jesus says no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom.

Elisha. He asked to say goodbye, and was allowed (1 Kings 19:19–21). Jesus demands more.

Looking back. A ploughman who looks back ploughs crooked furrows.

On a Tuesday. Keep your eyes forward on Christ.

For worship. Thank Christ, who never looked back from the cross.
verseByVerse.note: A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow.

parallels.desc: Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 gives us three of Luke's most theologically rich scenes — each one, in its own way, a complete world. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) expands the mission beyond the twelve, shows what kingdom authority looks like in practice, and culminates in the most intimate expression of Jesus's joy in the entire Gospel. The parable of the Good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) is the world's most famous story about neighbourly love — and simultaneously one of its most searching challenges to religious self-justification. And the scene at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) is the New Testament's most precise statement about the one thing that is necessary in a life pulled in every direction by legitimate demands.

The chapter is the opening movement of the great travel narrative (9:51–19:44) — the long road to Jerusalem during which Jesus pours himself into his disciples and into the crowds that gather around him. The sending of the seventy-two models the missional multiplication that will characterise the church after Pentecost. The Samaritan parable models the ethics of the kingdom in the most concrete possible terms. The Mary-and-Martha scene models the devotional centre that makes the mission and the ethics sustainable. Together, the three scenes answer three questions: What does the kingdom produce in the world? What does the kingdom demand of its citizens? And what does the kingdom require of those who would receive it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others — beyond the twelve — and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town and place he is about to go.

If your Bible says seventy, nothing is wrong: the manuscripts divide almost evenly here and at v. 17, and both figures carry the same symbolism. Moses appointed seventy elders to help carry a burden he could not carry alone (Num. 11:16), and two more prophesied in the camp (Num. 11:26); and the nations listed in Genesis 10 come to about seventy. Either way, the expansion from twelve signals that the mission is wider than the twelve tribes.

They go two by two — the two witnesses the law required (Deut. 19:15) — and they go ahead of him. They are not independent agents but an advance party, and everywhere they arrive he is coming behind them.

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” inverts the instinctive picture. The field is not the problem; the field is ready. And faced with a labour shortage, Jesus does not say “go” but “pray” — and he says it to the seventy-two he is about to send out that hour. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the shortage is not finally ours to solve: it is “the Lord of the harvest” and “his harvest,” twice in one sentence.

“Lambs in the midst of wolves” is candid. A lamb among wolves is food; there is no version of that scene where the lamb wins. Jesus does not promise safety, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending.

The instructions echo those to the twelve, with additions. “Greet no one on the road” is not rudeness but urgency — an Eastern roadside greeting could consume a large part of a day, and Elisha said the same to Gehazi on an errand that would not wait (2 Kgs. 4:29). The “son of peace” is a Semitic idiom for a person already prepared to receive what is being brought; and where there is none, the peace “returns” — nothing is wasted.

“Eat what is set before you” is far more than manners. It sends Jewish men into households whose kitchens were the daily boundary of the covenant, and it plants the seed of Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10:14-15).

And the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are among the most severe words in Luke's Gospel — aimed not at pagan cities but at the three villages where most of the ministry had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chain of representation in v.16 — “the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” — governs all Christian mission. It rests on the ancient principle that an authorised envoy carries the standing of the one who sent him: insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king.

The comfort in that is enormous. A believer stammering through an explanation to a colleague is not offering a private opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger's inadequacy does not degrade what is carried.

The weight is equally real. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken. But note the limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant: the chain runs through the message, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to shield leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. What could not be refused without consequence was a specific announcement: the kingdom of God has come near.

The woes introduce graduated accountability — judgement proportional to light received. Paul develops it (Rom. 2:12-16), and Hebrews applies it to those who have known the covenant (Heb. 10:26-31). The privileged place in the kingdom is also the most exposed position under judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Chorazin appears in the whole New Testament exactly twice — here and in the Matthew parallel — and not one miracle done there is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of “the mighty works done in you” as though his hearers knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books (cf. John 21:25): a town condemned for a history of miracles no evangelist thought to write down.

“It will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town” is not a claim that inhospitality outranks Sodom's sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in her streets announcing that the kingdom of God had come near.

And the last word a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer, repeated. “Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near” is almost word for word what the receiving towns were told (v. 9). The kingdom came as near to Chorazin as to anywhere — and nearness is not reception.

The principle bites hardest where most has been given (12:48), which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others and sends them in pairs ahead of him, telling them to pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers, for the harvest is great.

Seventy-two. Perhaps recalling the seventy nations of Genesis 10: a hint of mission to the world.

Two by two. Companionship and a valid witness (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Pray first. The first command is prayer for more workers.

Textual note. Manuscripts are divided between seventy and seventy-two. Genesis 10 has seventy nations in Hebrew and seventy-two in Greek, which may explain both.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for more gospel workers.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy. The number may recall the nations listed in Genesis 10, or the seventy elders who helped Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sends them out like lambs among wolves, carrying no money or bag or sandals, and greeting no one on the road.

Lambs among wolves. Vulnerable, yet sent by the Shepherd.

Greet no one. Urgency: no long social courtesies on the road.
verseByVerse.note: Travellers’ greetings could be long and elaborate; there was no time for them.

parallels.desc: if you meet anyone, do not greet him

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In each house they are to say, “Peace be to this house,” and stay there, eating what they are given, for the labourer deserves his wages.

A son of peace. Someone open to the message.

Do not move around. Not looking for better lodging.

The labourer deserves his wages. Quoted by Paul (1 Timothy 5:18). Gospel workers should be supported.

On a Tuesday. Support those who minister to you.
verseByVerse.note: A “son of peace” means a person open to God’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where a town welcomes them, they are to eat what is set before them, heal the sick, and say, “The kingdom of God has come near to you.”

Eat what is set before you. Do not fuss about food laws (Acts 10; 1 Corinthians 10:27).

The kingdom has come near. In Jesus and his messengers.

parallels.desc: eat whatever is set before you

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where a town rejects them, they are to wipe its dust off their feet, yet still say the kingdom has come near; it will be more bearable for Sodom on that day.

Still the kingdom. Rejection does not change the fact.

Sodom. Greater light brings greater responsibility.

Degrees of punishment. Judgment is according to light received (12:47–48).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces woe on Chorazin and Bethsaida, which saw his mighty works and did not repent, and on Capernaum, which will be brought down to Hades.

Tyre and Sidon. Pagan cities that would have repented.

God’s knowledge. God knows what would have happened.

Capernaum. Jesus’ base, now under the heaviest warning.

On a Tuesday. Great privilege brings great accountability. What have you done with what you have heard?
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever hears them hears Jesus, and whoever rejects them rejects Jesus and the Father who sent him.

Christ’s representatives. The message carries his authority.

What it does not mean. Not that every preacher speaks for Christ in everything. Faithful messengers do so as they speak his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two return elated: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” The word even gives them away — they expected the preaching to work and did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name.

“I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels. It may look back to the primordial fall, or forward to the cross and the final defeat (cf. Rev. 12:9); but the tense and the context favour a comment on what has just happened. They came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins “I saw.” He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing.

Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. The Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work — only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it.

Then the authority over serpents and scorpions, and the promise that nothing shall hurt them — both of which have been badly misused and both of which the passage itself guards.

And then the redirection: “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The joy was not wrong; it was aimed at the wrong thing. Authority is about what they can do, and anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance.

Jesus then rejoices in the Holy Spirit — one of the very few places where Luke tells us what he was feeling, and it is exultation. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father, and the occasion is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

The prayer thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and then makes one of the highest claims in the Synoptic Gospels: all things handed over, and a mutual knowing of Father and Son that admits no third party except by the Son's choosing.

Finally the private beatitude: “blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Not blessed for perceptiveness — blessed for what happens to be in front of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The joy of Jesus “in the Holy Spirit” is a Trinitarian moment: the Son's joy is given in the Spirit and directed to the Father in prayer. The mutual delight of Father, Son and Spirit overflows into the mission and into the lives of those who share in it.

Verses 21-22 have long been called the Johannine thunderbolt, because they drop into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel. “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” is not authority in a defined area but everything. And the mutual knowing is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others; it is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door only he can open. That he opens it is why the prayer is joy rather than terror.

“The wise and understanding” are not scholars in general — the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is the most educated writer in the New Testament. They are the professionally religious who have watched everything and concluded he is a problem. And the “little children” are the seventy-two. The dividing line is not intelligence but whether a man will come with empty hands; learning is no obstacle to that, it simply supplies one more thing to hold onto.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” reorients the worker's identity from achievement to grace. The image is a citizen register — the book of life in which names are written (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 21:27).

Every feature of it reverses what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else — and it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

This belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness. The minister whose standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children's faith as a report card on himself. The Christian who has been ill for two years, can no longer do any of the things he used to do, and quietly suspects he has become surplus.

And the beatitude of vv.23-24 is a rebuke to the boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time. Abraham died with one son of the promise and a burial plot. Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown a back. Isaiah described the Servant's wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Every one of them longed for this. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two return with joy that even demons submit in Jesus’ name, and he says, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.”

In your name. The authority was Christ’s.

Satan fall. Where Christians differ. Some see his original fall before creation; others his defeat through Jesus’ ministry. Verdict: the context points to Satan’s defeat in Jesus’ mission, which the cross completes (John 12:31; Revelation 12:9–11).

For worship. Praise Christ who has broken Satan’s power.

parallels.desc: how you are fallen from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has given them authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the enemy’s power, and nothing will hurt them.

Serpents and scorpions. Pictures of evil powers (Psalm 91:13).

What it does not mean. Not a command to handle snakes in worship, as some groups have done with fatal results. Do not put God to the test (4:12).

Nothing shall hurt you. Spiritually secure, though believers may suffer (21:16–18).

parallels.desc: you will tread on the lion and the adder

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rejoice that spirits obey you, but that your names are written in heaven.

The greater joy. Not power or success, but belonging to God.

Written in heaven. The book of life (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12).

On a Tuesday. When ministry goes well or badly, rejoice most that you are God’s.

parallels.desc: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
