Jesus rejoices in the Spirit and thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children, for so it pleased him; and no one knows the Son except the Father, or the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

The Trinity. The Son rejoices in the Spirit, praising the Father.

Hidden and revealed. God reveals truth to the humble, not the proud.

Your gracious will. Election is cause for Jesus’ joy.

To whom the Son chooses. Knowing God is a gift of Christ’s sovereign grace (John 6:44; Matthew 11:27).

For worship. Thank God that he revealed himself to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the disciples privately that their eyes are blessed, for many prophets and kings longed to see and hear what they see and hear.

Prophets and kings. They looked forward (1 Peter 1:10–12).

Blessed eyes. To see the fulfilment.

On a Tuesday. Do not take for granted what you know of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer — an expert in the law of Moses — stands up to test Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” The wording gives him away twice over. What shall I do assumes the answer is an action; and an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for, since it comes by belonging to a family. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence without noticing.

Jesus answers with two questions. “What is written in the Law?” asks for the text. “How do you read it?” asks for the man — and a reading is never neutral. The examination has quietly moved.

The lawyer's answer is superb: Deuteronomy 6:5 welded to Leviticus 19:18, the spine of the law in a sentence. And Jesus commends it: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.”

Which is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. The catch is not in the offer but in the doer. Jesus is using the law as it was meant to be used — not a ladder to climb but a mirror to look into (Rom. 3:20; Gal. 3:24).

And it works. The lawyer does not go home content; he starts negotiating, “desiring to justify himself.” His question — “who is my neighbour?” — sounds like scholarly precision and is a search for a boundary. If neighbour has edges, there are people outside them, and a man can be entirely obedient and still walk past the rest. It was a live question with real answers on offer: neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite, and the Qumran sect required its members to hate the sons of darkness.

The story refuses him a category from its first line: not a Jew, not a Gentile, just “a man.” Stripped and beaten unconscious, he has lost the two things — clothing and speech — by which anyone could have identified him.

A priest passes. A Levite passes. Every listener now expects the third man to be an ordinary Israelite; that is the shape of the joke. What arrives is a Samaritan — and the hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. It is only a chapter since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to burn it.

Then the reversal: not “who is my neighbour?” but “which of these three proved to be a neighbour?” The lawyer cannot say the word. He says “the one who showed him mercy.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The usual defence of the priest is ritual purity: contact with a corpse made him unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11-13), and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead. But note the direction of travel — he was going down, away from Jerusalem, towards Jericho, where many priests lived between rotations. His duty is behind him, not ahead.

And the law he was protecting had a clause about exactly this. The same Torah commands a man to help even his enemy's fallen animal (Ex. 23:4-5), and forbids standing by the blood of your neighbour (Lev. 19:16) — two verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

Luke offers the priest and Levite no mitigation whatever. He simply says they passed by on the other side, and adds of the second that he “came to the place” — he got closer, looked from nearer, and crossed anyway. The Samaritan, by contrast, “when he saw him, had compassion.” The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

The parable has been read allegorically since Origen: the traveller is humanity, the robbers the devil, the priest and Levite the law and prophets that cannot save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the two denarii the sacraments. The reading is not without insight — Jesus is indeed the one who binds wounds, pays the debt and promises to return. But the surface command is non-negotiable: “Go and do likewise.”
verseByVerse.examples:
“Had compassion” — compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses the word at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and of the Samaritan.

The care is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it. Bandages torn from his own clothing; his own oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, now gone; his own animal, which means he walked; a night spent nursing a stranger; two denarii, two days' wages, enough for a fortnight's board; and then an open-ended undertaking — “whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.” A blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despised him.

“Go and do likewise” is not “go and feel compassion,” which is sentiment, or “go and have good intentions,” which are cheap. It is the specific, costly, schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening action of the Samaritan.

Which is unbearable if read honestly — and that is the moment it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road, to where we were lying, when we were in no condition to ask; he paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy, but mercy received and then passed on (1 John 4:19). The command remains binding — and it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lawyer tests Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus asks what is written in the law.

A lawyer. An expert in the law of Moses.

What shall I do? He assumes eternal life is earned.

What is written? Jesus points him to Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lawyer answers with love for God with all one’s being and love for neighbour as oneself, and Jesus says, “Do this, and you will live.”

Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. The two great commandments.

Do this and live. Leviticus 18:5. Where Christians differ. Does Jesus teach salvation by works? Verdict: the law truly promises life to those who keep it perfectly, but no sinner does (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–12). Jesus’ answer is meant to show the lawyer his need, as his next question proves.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer asks, “And who is my neighbour?”

To justify himself. To limit his duty, and so manage to keep it.

Who is my neighbour? A question meant to draw a boundary.

On a Tuesday. Watch for ways you narrow your obligations to love.

parallels.desc: those who justify yourselves before men

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells of a man robbed and left half dead on the Jericho road, and how a priest and a Levite saw him and passed by on the other side.

The Jericho road. Steep and notorious for robbers.

Priest and Levite. Religious professionals. Perhaps afraid of defilement from a corpse, or of danger.

The other side. Deliberate avoidance.
verseByVerse.note: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through barren, rocky country, and was notorious for robbers. Touching a dead body made a priest unclean.

parallels.desc: no priest shall make himself unclean for the dead

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Samaritan sees him, has compassion, bandages his wounds with oil and wine, takes him to an inn on his own animal, and pays for his care.

A Samaritan. Hated by Jews as half-breeds and heretics.

Compassion. The same word as Jesus’ compassion (7:13).

Costly love. Time, money, risk and his own reputation.

Where Christians differ: an allegory of Christ? Augustine read the Samaritan as Christ, the inn as the church, and so on. Verdict: the main point is to show what neighbour-love looks like (v. 37). Christ is its supreme example, who came to us when we were his enemies, but the details are not a code.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage — two could cover some days at an inn.

parallels.desc: the captives clothed, anointed and carried on donkeys to Jericho

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks who proved to be a neighbour; the lawyer answers, “The one who showed him mercy,” and Jesus says, “Go and do likewise.”

The question reversed. Not “who is my neighbour?” but “am I a neighbour?”

He cannot say “Samaritan”. He says “the one who showed mercy.”

Go and do likewise. The lawyer, if honest, will see he has not, and needs mercy himself.

On a Tuesday. Who on your road needs your mercy today?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes in a house in a village — Bethany, though Luke does not name it — and the placing is deliberate. The Samaritan has just poured out his time and money on a road, with “go and do likewise” still in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something.

Martha “welcomed him into her house” — her house, Luke says, which is unusual enough to notice, and she received him as an honoured guest. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching,” and both halves of that would have struck a first-century reader. Sitting at a teacher's feet is the technical posture of a disciple — Paul describes his own training as being brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3). And that place was not open to a woman. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and in three verses he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it in a subordinate clause, as though it were ordinary — which, from now on, it is.

Martha is “distracted with much serving” — pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not being busy but being torn. And the thing tearing her is service: she is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for.

Her complaint takes three steps and each goes further. She interrupts his teaching; she accuses her sister in front of the guests; and then she accuses him. “Do you not care?” is not a request but a charge, levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed in — and then “tell her,” which does not even ask him to intervene but tells him what to say.

Every word of it is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance — and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score.

“Martha, Martha” is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person: the same register as “Simon, Simon” (22:31), “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” (13:34), “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). And the diagnosis is not of her workload but of her interior — “anxious,” the worry he will forbid his disciples (12:22-26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mary sitting at the Lord's feet is the posture of discipleship, and Luke has used the phrase once already of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). In the first century women did not ordinarily receive rabbinic instruction, and the posture of female discipleship was itself a quiet revolution. Jesus does not redirect Mary to help; he defends her right to receive what he is giving.

“The good portion” plays on a word for a share at a meal — and Martha, of all people, would have felt it, since she is in the kitchen dividing portions while Mary has taken the one that matters.

“Which will not be taken away from her” carries the force of a promise. What Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week's end; the word Mary is taking in is permanent, the living and abiding word of God (1 Pet. 1:23).

Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one” at v.42; the shorter reading is very likely original and the sense is unaffected either way. What lasts defines what is necessary, and what is necessary defines what must not be sacrificed to the urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene speaks to the perennial tension between doing and being. It does not abolish the tension; it orders it. Martha's service is not wrong — her anxiety is. And this is not a rebuke of practical work: Luke has just spent a chapter praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills.

It is a statement about order. Martha's work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

“Do you not care?” is worth naming for anyone who has prayed like it, because a good many have. It is the same accusation the disciples threw at him in the boat (Mark 4:38) — what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where she is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping — including, in the end, with the Lord it was all being done for. The cure is not less service. It is the recovery of the one thing that makes service a gift rather than a grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, and her sister Mary sits at the Lord’s feet listening to his teaching.

Martha. The host.

At his feet. The posture of a disciple (Acts 22:3). Unusual for a woman then.

His word. Mary chooses to hear.
verseByVerse.note: John places Martha and Mary in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha, distracted by much serving, asks Jesus whether he cares that Mary has left her to serve alone, and tells him to make Mary help.

Distracted. Pulled in many directions.

Do you not care? Like the disciples in the storm (Mark 4:38).

Tell her. Martha commands the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary; Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

Martha, Martha. Tender, not harsh.

One thing. Hearing Jesus.

Where Christians differ: action or contemplation? Medieval writers made Mary and Martha types of the contemplative and active life, ranking monks above workers. Verdict: service is good; Martha’s fault was anxiety and distraction, not work. Sitting at Jesus’ feet is the source of right service.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one”.

On a Tuesday. Before the busyness of today, sit at Jesus’ feet.

For worship. Choose the good portion.

parallels.desc: one thing have I asked of the LORD
the LORD is my chosen portion

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Chapter 11 divides into three movements of escalating intensity. It opens with the disciples' request — “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples” — and Jesus's response: the Lord's Prayer and two parables about persistent asking. It continues with the controversy over Beelzebul, where Jesus is accused of casting out demons by the power of the prince of demons, and responds with the parable of the strong man, the sign of Jonah, and a warning about the darkness that replaces expelled light. And it closes with the most sustained series of woes in Luke's Gospel — six pronouncements against the Pharisees and lawyers that are simultaneously the most confrontational and the most sorrowful words Jesus speaks in public.

The chapter's movement from prayer (vv. 1–13) to spiritual warfare (vv. 14–36) to religious condemnation (vv. 37–54) is not a random sequence. The prayer section establishes the relationship with the Father that makes spiritual life possible. The Beelzebul controversy shows what happens when the kingdom's power is at work in the world — it provokes opposition, demands decision, and warns against the neutrality that is actually a form of hostility. And the woes reveal what becomes of religious life when it loses the relationship with the Father — when the form of religion remains but the substance has been evacuated, replaced by the performance of piety for the wrong audience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying, and when he finishes one of the disciples asks: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” Of everything on offer in three years beside the Son of God — the healings, the stilled storm, the knowledge of men's thoughts — the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father.

Luke's version is shorter than Matthew's (Matt. 6:9-13), and that difference has unsettled readers who learned the prayer by heart as children. Where is “who art in heaven”? Where is “thy will be done”? An older Bible will have them at this very verse and a modern one will not.

There is nothing sinister in it. Luke's prayer was always the shorter of the two, but the version the church actually prayed aloud, week after week for centuries, was Matthew's — and scribes copying Luke knew that fuller wording by heart. Line by line, over generations, they filled Luke out to match what their lips already said. It is one of the most understandable corrections in the history of copying and one of the easiest to detect: the earliest manuscripts of Luke are short, and the additions match Matthew word for word. Nothing was lost. Every phrase you were taught is genuinely the Lord's; it is simply Matthew who recorded it.

And Luke's shorter form is worth having in its own right, because two versions tell us something one could not. Jesus plainly gave this prayer more than once, and not in identical words. Matthew says “pray then like this”; Luke says “when you pray, say.” Set them side by side and the conclusion is unavoidable: this was never handed down as a formula to be recited syllable-perfect on pain of not counting. It is a shape for praying — a floor to build on, not a ceiling.

The prayer opens with one word that was a revolution. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation; what is almost entirely absent is an individual addressing him that way in prayer. The word Jesus himself uses in Gethsemane is the Aramaic Abba (Mark 14:36) — family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of that period addressed God with it in prayer.

Then five petitions: his name, his kingdom, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God first, then us — and the order is not decoration. A prayer that begins with God's honour can bring every human need afterwards without becoming a list submitted to a dispenser.
verseByVerse.theology:
The address “Father” is the theological revolution of this prayer. Paul will name what has happened: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” (Rom. 8:15). The address is not a warmer name for the same relationship; it is a different relationship — the Son's own, opened to people with no natural claim to it.

“Hallowed be your name” asks that God be treated as holy, since his name cannot be made more holy than it is. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known, so the petition asks that he be known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is — first by the one praying, and then by everybody else. It is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to.

“Your kingdom come” is the central petition and the shortest, and it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God's rule to come is to ask for one's own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he was hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

“Daily” bread — the ESV margin gives “our bread for tomorrow,” enough for the coming day. It is a small request, deliberately: enough for today, asked today, and again tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples:
The “for” in “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive” has troubled readers, and it must not become a bargain. God's forgiveness is not purchased by ours; the prayer has just called him Father, which nobody earns.

What the clause does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed — a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour; and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all. Matthew makes the connection explicit (Matt. 6:14-15).

Note the tense, too: “we ourselves forgive,” present and continuing. Not “we forgave, once, years ago.” It is a standing policy.

And “lead us not into temptation” is not a fear that God might try to make us sin, which James forbids (Jas. 1:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it — which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for strength to survive the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Jesus finishes praying, a disciple asks him to teach them to pray, as John taught his disciples.

Watching Jesus pray. His example made them want to learn.

Teach us. Prayer must be learned.

On a Tuesday. Ask Jesus to teach you to pray, and learn from his prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus teaches them to pray: “Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.”

Father. Abba: intimate trust, given to those adopted in Christ (Romans 8:15).

Hallowed. May God’s name be treated as holy. God’s glory first.

Your kingdom come. Longing for God’s rule to be complete.

Textual note. Later manuscripts expand Luke’s shorter prayer to match Matthew’s: “Our Father in heaven”, “your will be done”, “deliver us from evil”. A few read instead, “May your Holy Spirit come upon us and cleanse us.” The shorter form is original to Luke.

For worship. Pray this prayer today, slowly.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer is shorter than Matthew’s; the ESV notes that some manuscripts add phrases from Matthew’s form. “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.”

Daily bread. Dependence for today’s needs.

Forgive us. Sin is a debt we cannot pay.

As we forgive. Where Christians differ. Is God’s forgiveness conditional on ours? Verdict: we do not earn forgiveness by forgiving; but those who are forgiven become forgiving. An unforgiving spirit shows we have not grasped grace (Matthew 18:21–35).

Lead us not into temptation. Keep us from testing that would overcome us.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you need to forgive before you can pray this honestly?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two illustrations follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater.

The first is the friend at midnight. To feel it you have to see the house: one room, the family asleep together on a raised platform, a single door barred at night with a beam that cannot be lifted quietly. Getting up wakes everybody. And there is no bread in the house, because bread was baked daily and eaten daily.

The man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. Hospitality in that culture was an obligation with the weight of law, and a traveller arriving at night was the whole village's guest; to fail him was a public disgrace. He asks a friend, at the worst possible hour, for three loaves — enough for one meal — and he asks to borrow them.

The sleeper's excuses are all true. The door is barred, the children are asleep, getting up will wake them. And he gets up anyway, “because of his impudence” — anaideia, shamelessness.

Whose shamelessness has been argued over. The traditional reading takes it as the asker's brazen persistence. A second reading, with a good deal to be said for it, takes it as the sleeper's — he rises to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. Both land in the same place: if even this man gives, how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced.

What the parable licenses is boldness. Most prayer dies of good manners, and this story was told to kill that.

Then “ask, seek, knock” — after that parable, keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking — and a promise unconditional in form: “everyone who asks receives.” Which raises the honest problem, because a great many people have read that verse and then buried someone they prayed for.

Jesus answers it with a picture of a father and a child. A fish and a snake are roughly the same shape; an egg and a coiled scorpion are roughly the same shape. What is described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he asked for and will hurt him — and no father does that.
verseByVerse.theology:
The three imperatives are in the present tense, implying continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. And there is a progression. Asking is words; seeking involves the feet; knocking is standing at a closed door that has not yet opened, and staying there.

On the difficulty in v.10, three things have to be said. Scripture itself never treats the promise as a blank cheque and says so in the same breath: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14), and “you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4:3). Jesus himself prayed a prayer not granted in the form he asked it — “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). And the next three verses are his own commentary, which is where the weight lies.

A request denied is not a father who is deaf. It is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless, and it is not meant to. What it removes is the one conclusion that would be unbearable — that the silence means indifference.

And Luke's ending is his own. Matthew has “how much more will your Father give good things” (Matt. 7:11); Luke has “the Holy Spirit.” Luke's version tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance; it is himself, present, in a person.
verseByVerse.examples:
“You, who are evil” is dropped in without emphasis, as agreed common ground. He is talking to ordinary decent parents and takes it as obvious that they are bad — and that even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

The parable of the friend at midnight is also worth noticing for what the man needs. He is not asking for himself. He wants bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them — which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty.

And “give us each day our daily bread” has a hard edge for anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight (Ex. 16:19-20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment.

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, this is where the passage lands. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself — and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells of a man who goes to a friend at midnight to borrow three loaves for an unexpected guest.

Hospitality. A sacred duty. The whole village’s honour was at stake.

Midnight. The worst possible time.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty; villagers baked daily, and a household might have nothing left at night.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friend refuses at first, but because of the man’s shameless persistence he gets up and gives him what he needs.

Impudence. Anaideia: shamelessness, boldness.

The contrast. If a grumpy neighbour gives, how much more will God, who is no grumpy neighbour.

What it does not mean. Not that we must pester God into answering, as if he is unwilling. The point is bold confidence before a generous Father.
verseByVerse.note: A peasant family slept together in one room; opening the barred door would wake everyone. The ESV notes that “impudence” can also be rendered “persistence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So ask, and it will be given; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened.

Keep asking. The verbs are present tense: continual prayer.

Everyone who asks. A promise to all who come to God in Christ.

What it does not mean. Not a blank cheque for anything we want, but a promise that God answers his children’s prayers for their good (James 4:3; 1 John 5:14).

On a Tuesday. Ask, seek, knock today about the thing you have stopped praying for.

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No father gives his son a snake for a fish or a scorpion for an egg; if evil fathers give good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

You who are evil. Total depravity in a subordinate clause.

How much more. The argument from lesser to greater.

The Holy Spirit. Matthew has “good things” (Matthew 7:11). The Spirit is God’s best gift.

What it does not mean. Not that believers lack the Spirit until they ask for a second blessing. Believers have the Spirit (Romans 8:9), and pray for his fuller work.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “a good spirit” or “good gifts”.

For worship. Ask your Father for more of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew.

parallels.desc: the gift of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus casts out a demon that has made a man mute, and the crowd marvels. Two responses come from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

The first is the Beelzebul charge — that he works by the prince of demons. Notice what it concedes: nobody disputes that the man is speaking, and nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter to the fact that it happened.

The second is a demand for “a sign from heaven” — a real one, not this business with a local demoniac. Made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, that is not scepticism; it is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable.

Jesus dismantles the charge twice over. A divided kingdom cannot stand, so Satan casting out Satan is destroying his own operation. And “by whom do your sons cast them out?” exposes a standard applied to him and not to their own exorcists — which means the objection is not the real reason.

Then his own account: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” The phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament — Pharaoh's magicians conceding they are out of their depth (Ex. 8:19), and the tablets written by God's own finger (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10). Deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, in three words. And the verb is “has come upon you” — not near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but arrived.

The parable of the strong man is the interpretation of everything he has done. The strong man is fully armed, on his own ground, and while that holds his goods are safe. Then one stronger attacks, overcomes, strips the armour he trusted in, and divides the spoil. And the goods, in this context, are people.

The section closes with two warnings. Neutrality is abolished — “whoever does not gather with me scatters.” And the swept house: a life cleaned up and left empty is not a neutral state on the way to better. It is a vacancy, advertised.
verseByVerse.theology:
The warning about the returning spirit is the parabolic form of the New Testament's consistent warning against reformation without regeneration. Everything in the description is good news — swept, put in order, the mess dealt with, the habits sorted. One word is missing, and it is the whole point: nobody is living there.

Jesus's assessment of that condition is not “an improvement, as far as it goes.” It is “worse than the first,” because an empty swept house has been made attractive. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation — and Luke has just named who is available, and how he is described: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either; he was found sitting at the feet of Jesus (8:35).

“Whoever is not with me is against me” must be read alongside 9:50, “the one who is not against you is for you,” and the two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There the subject is you — the disciples' judgement of a stranger. Here it is me — a person's own standing before Christ. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

And note what Jesus assumes in passing while making his argument: that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom — organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against. He says it as something too obvious to argue.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's beatitude on Jesus's mother is well meant and entirely ordinary in that culture: praise the son by praising the woman who produced him. Elizabeth said something very like it in this Gospel's first chapter (1:42).

The word “rather” is doing careful work in the reply. It is not a contradiction but a redirection, and it refuses the assumption underneath the compliment — that blessedness is a matter of proximity. If that were true the whole thing would be closed to everybody else, since there is exactly one womb that bore him.

What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd: “hear the word of God and keep it” — two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. And Mary is the outstanding instance of exactly that: “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). The correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

And the swept-house warning is worth turning into a question by anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing. Not “what have you got rid of?” but “who lives there now?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus casts out a mute demon and the man speaks; some say he does it by Beelzebul, prince of demons, and others demand a sign from heaven.

Beelzebul. “Lord of the house”, a name for Satan.

Two responses. Slander and demand.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that a kingdom divided against itself falls; if Satan is divided, his kingdom cannot stand.

Knowing their thoughts. Again.

Logic. Satan would not undermine his own rule.

Your sons. Other Jewish exorcists. Would they say the same of them?
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” means the critics’ own followers.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Jesus casts out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon them.

The finger of God. Exodus 8:19: Pharaoh’s magicians admitted it.

Has come. The kingdom is present in Jesus’ ministry.

For worship. Praise God that his kingdom has come in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong man guarding his palace keeps his goods safe, until a stronger one overpowers him, takes his armour and divides his spoil.

The strong man. Satan.

The stronger one. Jesus (Isaiah 49:24–25; 53:12).

Divides his spoil. Rescued captives.

On a Tuesday. Christ is stronger than whatever binds you.

parallels.desc: he shall divide the spoil with the strong

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with Jesus is against him, and whoever does not gather with him scatters.

No neutrality. With Jesus or against him.

Compare 9:50. There, those working in his name. Here, those standing aloof from him.

On a Tuesday. Where have you been trying to stay neutral about Jesus?

parallels.desc: the one who is not against you is for you

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it returns to find the house swept and in order, and brings seven worse spirits, so the last state is worse than the first.

Swept but empty. Reform without Christ.

Worse. Moral improvement without new life leaves a person exposed.

On a Tuesday. Do not simply remove sin; fill your life with Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Waterless places were thought to be the haunt of demons.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman calls out a blessing on the womb that bore him, and Jesus replies, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!”

Blessed rather. Not denying Mary’s blessing, but placing it rightly.

Where Christians differ. This verse is often cited against Marian devotion. Verdict: Mary is blessed, but chiefly as one who heard and kept God’s word (1:38, 45; 8:21). That blessing is open to all.

On a Tuesday. Hear God’s word and keep it.

parallels.desc: all generations will call me blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowds are increasing — and Luke notes it, because that is when Jesus says “this generation is an evil generation.” Popularity has never once altered what he told people.

They want a sign from heaven, and he refuses; but the refusal is not of evidence. It is of evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain — which is exactly what happened fifteen verses earlier when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

The sign of Jonah works two ways, and they are not rivals. Jonah himself was a sign to Nineveh: a foreigner walking into the greatest city of the ancient world with a single sentence of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented (Jon. 3:4-9). And behind that stands what happened before he arrived, which Matthew makes explicit — three days in the belly of the fish, and three days in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40). Luke leaves it unstated and lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic.

Two witnesses are then called, and both are chosen to sting. The Queen of Sheba travelled over a thousand miles by camel, on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody's God. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria — the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, a byword for a people beyond hope — and it repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there and was furious when it worked.

Neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. And twice the refrain: “something greater than Solomon is here… something greater than Jonah is here.” Not someone greater but something — broader and stranger. No prophet in Israel's history ever spoke about himself like that.

The lamp sayings close the section. The lamp is not hidden; it has been on a stand in Galilee for three years. So the problem cannot be the lighting — it is the window. “Your eye is the lamp of your body,” and its two conditions are not merely medical: Scripture speaks of “a bountiful eye” for a generous man (Prov. 22:9) and, as the ESV margin renders it, “a man whose eye is evil” for a stingy one (Prov. 28:22; cf. Deut. 15:9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation, because both responded to far lesser messengers. It is the graduated-accountability principle of the woes on Chorazin and Bethsaida, sharpened: it will not be the ignorant who are condemned by Nineveh, but the well-informed.

“Something greater than Solomon” is worth weighing. Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived, and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. Jesus does not argue for it; he says “behold,” and leaves it there.

The eye sayings are not about eyesight or intellect. Ancient thinking often understood the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person — so the picture is a house with a window: clear, and the house is bright; blocked, and the house is dark however strong the sun outside.

Which explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person's capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true — and nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Be careful lest the light in you be darkness” is the warning that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say “be careful in case you are in the dark” — a man in the dark generally knows it and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness.

That is a different order of danger. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries. Be careful — look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument.

The context names who it is for. The next paragraph is a dinner party with a Pharisee that ends in six woes. The people at greatest risk are not the irreligious but those with the most exposure — long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two feel identical.

And then, after the warning, the promise, which is unexpectedly warm. “Having no part dark” is the condition — not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut. And the result is not an impressive person but a useful one: “as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in.

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As crowds grow, Jesus calls this generation evil for seeking a sign, and says no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah.

Seeking a sign. Demanding proof on their terms.

The sign of Jonah. Jonah came back from death, as it were, and preached to Nineveh. Jesus’ resurrection and preaching are the sign.

A sign to Nineveh. Jonah himself was the sign.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will condemn this generation at the judgment, for they responded to Solomon and Jonah, and something greater is here.

The queen of Sheba. She travelled far to hear Solomon (1 Kings 10).

Nineveh. Pagans who repented at Jonah’s preaching.

Something greater. Jesus is greater than Solomon and Jonah.

On a Tuesday. You have heard more than they did. What is your response?
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, probably in south-west Arabia. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one lights a lamp and hides it; your eye is the lamp of your body: when it is healthy you are full of light, when bad, full of darkness.

A healthy eye. Literally “single”: focused and sincere.

A bad eye. Evil or envious.

On a Tuesday. What are you looking at? It shapes your whole inner life.
verseByVerse.note: A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess or an evil desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be careful that the light in you is not darkness; if your whole body is full of light, it will be as bright as a lamp shining on you.

Light that is darkness. The danger of thinking you see while you are blind (John 9:41).

Wholly bright. A life open to Christ, with no dark corners.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine, and he goes. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel and every one ends badly — and Jesus accepts every invitation. Whatever is said in this room is said by a guest who came when he was asked.

He does not perform the ritual handwashing, and the omission may well be deliberate. That washing was not hygiene and it was not in the law of Moses; nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating. The Pharisees had taken the priestly standard and applied it to everybody, all the time — a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

His answer takes their own debating point about the cleansing of vessels and turns it on them. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup; it is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And the first word for what is inside is greed — the grasping that takes. Something is being taken.

“Give as alms those things that are within” is his prescription, and it is remarkable: they asked how to be clean and the answer is not a better ritual but to give the contents away. The remedy for greed is not scouring the cup; it is giving away what was grasped.

Then six woes — three against the Pharisees and three against the lawyers. The word itself needs setting straight: ouai is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict, the sound a man makes watching somebody walk towards a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later in this Gospel (19:41).

They tithe mint and rue and neglect justice and the love of God — and “these you ought to have done” refuses to abolish the small duty. They love the best seat and the public greetings. They are unmarked graves. The lawyers load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and have taken away the key of knowledge.

And it hardens them. The chapter ends with respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions to get a sentence they can use.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe turns on a trade nobody consciously makes. The law required a tithe of grain, wine and oil (Deut. 14:22-23); it said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. These were not lazy men — they were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt. And “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” is regularly ignored: he does not condemn the herb-tithing.

The mechanism is universal. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off — and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not.

The unmarked-grave woe depends on a detail of the law. Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Num. 19:16), so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, conspicuously, so pilgrims could see them and go round. The marking was a public service; it kept people clean. An unmarked grave is the exact opposite — one a man walks straight over and finds out afterwards, if he finds out at all.

And “the key of knowledge” is the heaviest charge. The knowledge in question is not information about God but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce. These men were the keyholders legitimately — and they did not enter themselves, and they blocked the door for people who were already moving towards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lawyer's interruption — “in saying these things you insult us also” — is wonderfully revealing. He does not say “that is untrue.” He concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, which is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite.

The burdens woe puts a simple test to anyone who teaches. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself. Set it against “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

The tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet; he has stopped saying the things that got him killed. Meanwhile a living one is at the table, and they are about to arrange his death. Every generation of the church admires the awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. A dead prophet requires a subscription; a live one requires repentance.

And the key-of-knowledge woe puts a question to anyone who teaches anything to anybody. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine; he transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine. Not whether what you say is correct, which is the easier test — whether someone who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder.

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus dines with a Pharisee, who is astonished that he did not wash first before dinner.

Washing. Not hygiene, but ritual purity (Mark 7:3–4).

A host who watches. Hospitality turned to judgment.
verseByVerse.note: The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the Pharisees they clean the outside of the cup but inside are full of greed and wickedness; the one who made the outside made the inside, so give as alms what is within, and everything will be clean.

Outside and inside. Appearance versus the heart.

Fools. God sees both.

Give alms. Where Christians differ. Some have read this as almsgiving earning purity. Verdict: Jesus calls for a changed heart, shown in generosity. A heart given to God makes ritual worries unimportant. Purity comes from God, not from our gifts.

parallels.desc: to the pure, all things are pure

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the Pharisees who tithe even garden herbs but neglect justice and the love of God; these they should have done, without neglecting the others.

Mint and rue. Tiny amounts, scrupulously tithed.

Justice and love. The weightier matters.

Without neglecting. Jesus does not dismiss the small things.

Where Christians differ: tithing today. Some hold the tithe binding on Christians. Verdict: the New Testament calls for generous, proportionate, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 8–9), for which the tithe is a helpful guide, not a legal requirement.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to garden herbs such as mint and rue.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the Pharisees who love the best seats in synagogues and greetings in the market.

Status. Religion used for honour.

On a Tuesday. Do you serve to be seen?

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to them, for they are like unmarked graves that people walk over without knowing.

Unmarked graves. Touching a grave made you unclean (Numbers 19:16). They defile others without anyone realising.

Hidden corruption. Their influence spreads it.
verseByVerse.note: Touching a grave made a person unclean; an unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lawyer protests that Jesus insults them too, and Jesus pronounces woe on lawyers who load people with burdens they will not lift a finger to help carry.

Lawyers. Scribes, experts in interpreting the law.

Burdens. Rules added to God’s law.

Not a finger. No help, no compassion.

On a Tuesday. Do not burden others with rules God has not given.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to them who build tombs for the prophets their fathers killed; they approve their fathers’ deeds.

Honouring dead prophets. While rejecting living ones.

Witnesses. They complete their fathers’ work by plotting against Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s Wisdom sent prophets and apostles who would be persecuted, so that this generation will answer for the blood of all the prophets from Abel to Zechariah.

The Wisdom of God. God speaking in his wisdom, perhaps Jesus himself.

Abel to Zechariah. The first and last murders in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis to Chronicles (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), which was the last book in the Hebrew order.

The canon. Jesus’ phrase covers the whole Hebrew Old Testament, without the Apocrypha. This is one support for the Protestant Old Testament canon.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the lawyers who have taken away the key of knowledge, not entering themselves and hindering those who were entering.

The key. Understanding of Scripture.

Hindering others. Bad teaching shuts people out.

On a Tuesday. Pray for teachers who open Scripture rather than close it.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus leaves, the scribes and Pharisees press him hard, trying to catch him in something he says.

Lying in wait. Hunters’ language.

The cost of truth. Jesus’ honesty increased their hostility.

For worship. Thank Christ who spoke the truth whatever it cost.

parallels.desc: to trap him in his talk

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is one of the most urgent chapters in Luke's Gospel — a sustained call to a particular quality of life in the light of the coming judgment. Jesus addresses a massive crowd (v. 1 — “so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another”) and then moves between the crowd and the disciples in a series of teachings that together form a comprehensive call to undivided allegiance. Do not fear those who can kill the body; fear the one who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Do not covet or stockpile; the rich fool who planned bigger barns died the night he planned them. Do not be anxious about food and clothing; seek the kingdom first. Be dressed for action, with lamps burning, waiting for the master to return.

The chapter's emotional register is high throughout. Jesus speaks of fire he has come to cast on the earth and a baptism he has to undergo before it — and he is distressed until it is accomplished. He warns that he has not come to bring peace but division — a division that runs through the family. He rebukes the crowd for its ability to read the weather and its inability to read the present moment. And he calls everyone to settle accounts with their adversary before they arrive at the judge — because once you are before the judge, the outcome is fixed. The urgency is eschatological: the crisis of the kingdom's arrival is not a background hum; it is the defining emergency of every human life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowd is so large that people are being trampled — and in the middle of it Jesus turns his back on the thousands and addresses the handful. This is a word for those inside about a temptation specific to religious people.

“The leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Leaven was a lump of soured dough kept back from the last batch: small, invisible once mixed in, working by itself, changing everything it touches. And Luke alone gives us Jesus's own definition. Hypocrisy is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part.

The argument against it is not moral but practical: “nothing is covered up that will not be revealed.” The performance has a fixed run and a closing date. Whether that sentence is the most frightening in the chapter or the most liberating depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The teaching on fear is the application. Do not fear those who kill the body — after that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out. What is commanded instead is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror; and the effect is the opposite of paralysis, since a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else. Every tyranny in history has run on the fear of what can be done to a body, and this sentence cuts the supply line.
