The chapter closes with three sayings of escalating urgency, and the first is the most emotionally exposed moment in Luke outside Gethsemane.

“I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled!” The fire is most likely the one John announced at the start of this Gospel — “he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (3:16) — and Luke's second volume opens with tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). It is also the fire of judgement and purifying, and the two are not separable: the same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on.

“I have a baptism to be baptized with.” To be baptized is to go under — and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. In the Psalms the waters are often death: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Ps. 42:7). He is talking about the cross, and calling it a drowning.

And “how great is my distress” is the cry of a man hemmed in, pressed on every side. Read the two verses together and the shape is precise: the fire cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. Pentecost waits on Golgotha, and he is pressed between them.

Then the division saying, which shocks — not least because angels announced “on earth peace” over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14). Both are true. What he brings is peace with God, which every human being needs and cannot manufacture. What he never promised is the peace of everybody getting along, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked. The household list is quoted from Micah 7:6, where it describes a society coming apart — and every pair is named in both directions.

Finally the weather. West of Israel is the Mediterranean, so cloud coming inland meant rain; a south wind off the desert meant the scorching sirocco. Two confident readings, and Jesus grants they are right. These people are competent. And they will not apply the skill where it matters.
verseByVerse.theology:
“How great is my distress until it is accomplished” is not a man dreading the cross and hanging back — Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what was underneath it. He wants what is on the far side badly enough that the waiting is a torment. He went to that cross wishing it were already over, not because the pain was unendurable but because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

The charge of hypocrisy at v.56 is precise. It is not that the crowd is stupid; it is that they are perfectly capable of reading evidence and drawing conclusions, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite but illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what stands in front of him has made a choice and is pretending it was a limitation.

And the evidence he expects them to have read is not a secret sign. The “present time” is the whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor given good news, thousands following, and the authorities plotting a death.

“Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” assumes the resources for the judgement are already in their possession. It needs a guard — Scripture is emphatic that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Prov. 14:12; Jer. 17:9) — so the question is not “why not decide what suits you?” It is narrower: given what you can already read, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something.
verseByVerse.examples:
The division saying has real pastoral weight, because someone reading it is living inside it. He does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens — and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted has very often concluded that he handled it badly, or that a wiser person would have avoided it. This verse says the fracture was in the nature of the case.

Every generation is expert at reading something — markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career — and the skill is genuine. The same person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or in his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

And “you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny” has carried theological weight it was never built to bear — one of the two verses historically cited for purgatory. But this is practical advice about a lawsuit used to illustrate urgency, and doctrine cannot be quarried from an illustration's scenery. A man in a debtors' prison could not earn, which was the point of the prison; “until you have paid the last penny” is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out. And a doctrine supplying a further opportunity to settle after death removes the urgency of the only sentence that mattered. Settle now, on the road — and know that the settlement is not a schedule of payments but an amnesty, purchased at the judge's own expense (7:41-42; Col. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: 'I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled!

For two verses the mask of the teacher comes off, and Luke lets us hear what it was like inside him.

What fire? The most likely answer is the one John the Baptist announced at the start of this Gospel: he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire (3:16) — and Luke's second volume opens with tongues of fire resting on each of the waiting disciples (Acts 2:3). It is also the fire of judgement and of purifying, and the two are not separable: the same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on.

Would that it were already kindled. The Greek is an unfinished exclamation, and translators have struggled with it because it is not a tidy sentence. It is a man wishing out loud.

I have a baptism to be baptized with.

The word means to be plunged, immersed, submerged — and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. To be baptized in the Old Testament's imagery is to go under the waters, and the waters in the Psalms are often death: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Ps. 42:7); save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck (Ps. 69:1).

He is talking about the cross, and he is calling it a drowning.

And how great is my distress until it is accomplished!

The verb is synechomai — to be gripped, hemmed in, pressed on every side. Luke uses it elsewhere of being seized by a fever (4:38) and of a besieging army closing on a city (19:43). It is the word for something with no room left in it.

Read the two verses together and the shape is unbearable and precise. The fire he longs for cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. Pentecost waits on Golgotha. He cannot have the one without going through the other, and he is pressed between them.

So this is not a man dreading the cross and hanging back — Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what was underneath it. He wants what is on the far side badly enough that the waiting is a torment.

He went to that cross wishing it were already over, not because the pain was unendurable but because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.
verseByVerse.note: Fire can picture judgment or purifying; “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed by suffering.

parallels.desc: the baptism with which I am baptized

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division.

The sentence is a shock, and it is meant to be — not least because the angels announced on earth peace over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14), and Zechariah sang that he would guide our feet into the way of peace (1:79).

Both are true, and the resolution is not a compromise between them.

What he brings is real peace — peace with God, which is the thing every human being most needs and cannot manufacture (Rom. 5:1). What he does not bring, and never promised, is the peace of everybody getting along, because that peace was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked.

For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three.

Five is a household — parents, a married son, his wife, an unmarried daughter. And the arithmetic is deliberately awkward. Three against two, then two against three: the same fracture described from both sides, because in a divided house both halves feel like the ones being left.

They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.

The list is quoted, and the source matters. It is Micah 7:6, where the prophet describes a society coming apart — the son treats the father with contempt… a man's enemies are the men of his own house. In Micah it is a picture of national breakdown. Jesus applies it to what his own arrival does.

And note that every pair is named in both directions. The father rejects the son and the son the father. There is no suggestion that the believing half will find it easy or behave well.

Now the pastoral weight, because someone reading this is living inside it.

He does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens — and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted has very often concluded that he handled it badly, or that a wiser person would have avoided it. This verse says the fracture was in the nature of the case.

It does not license tactlessness; a great deal of family division is caused by Christians being insufferable rather than by Christ. But when everything has been done gently and the division comes anyway, it is not evidence of failure. It is the thing he warned about, happening.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the crowds, 'When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, A shower is coming. And so it happens.

He turns from the disciples to the crowds, and begins with the weather — which in that country was entirely predictable if you knew the geography.

West of Israel is the Mediterranean. Cloud building over the sea and coming inland meant rain, and the peasant standing in his field did not need to think about it. South is the Negev and the Arabian desert; a south wind meant the sirocco, the scorching wind that could strip a crop in a day.

Two signs, two confident readings, and Jesus grants that they are right: and so it happens. These people are competent. Their instincts about the sky are reliable and hard-won.

You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?

The charge is precise. It is not that they are stupid. It is that they are perfectly capable of reading evidence and drawing conclusions, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters.

And notice what he expects them to have read. Not a secret sign. The present time — the whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor being told good news, thousands following, and the religious authorities plotting a death. Any of it could have been interpreted by a man who reads clouds for a living.

What makes it hypocrisy rather than error is that the failure is selective. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite; he is illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what is standing in front of him has made a choice, and is pretending it was a limitation.

Which is worth turning on ourselves before it is enjoyed at their expense. Every generation is expert at reading something — markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career. The skill is genuine. And the same person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once sat down and asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or in his own house, or in the last five years of his own circumstances.

The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.
verseByVerse.note: Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain; the south wind blew hot off the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?

One short question, and it deserves an entry of its own because of what it assumes.

He has just told them they can read the sky and will not read the times. Now he asks why they do not work it out themselves.

Which means the failure is not for want of a teacher. They are not being told to go and consult somebody. They are being told that the resources for the judgement are already in their possession, and that they are declining to use them.

The verb is the one for reaching a verdict. And for yourselves puts the responsibility exactly where the crowd would least like it. They had spent the chapter asking him to settle things: adjudicate my inheritance (v. 13), give us a sign (11:16), tell us whether this parable is for us (v. 41).

He hands it back.

Now this needs a guard, because it is not an invitation to make it up. Scripture is emphatic that the human heart is unreliable and that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Prov. 14:12; Jer. 17:9). The question is not why not decide what suits you?

It is narrower and harder. Given what is in front of you — the evidence you can already read, the conscience you already have, the Scriptures you already possess — why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion?

And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something. The crowd's problem is not a shortage of light but an unwillingness to act on what the light shows. Which is precisely why the next two verses are about a man on his way to court, running out of road.

There is a particular kind of religious passivity that this question is aimed at, and it survives well in churches. It is the habit of waiting to be told — of treating every question as one for the experts, so that nothing is ever settled and nothing therefore has to be done about it. Jesus calls it what it is by asking why.

verseByVerse.quote: As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way.

The picture is a lawsuit already in motion. The two parties are walking to court together, which is how it worked — the plaintiff brought the defendant himself — and the road is the last stretch of time in which anything can be done.

Make an effort is a strong verb: work at it, put yourself into it. This is not a suggestion to be reasonable if convenient.

Lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison.

Three handovers in a row, and the man is passed down the chain like a parcel. Once the process starts, he has no further say in it — which is exactly the point. On the road he is a man who can negotiate. In the courtroom he is a case.

I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.

That last clause has carried a great deal of theological weight it was never built to bear. With its parallel in Matthew 5:26, it is one of the two verses historically cited for purgatory: a state after death in which the sins of the faithful are paid off before entry into heaven. The word until seems to promise a way out at the end of the paying, and a prison that is temporary is not hell.

Three things make that reading impossible.

First, look at what this is. It is practical advice about a lawsuit, used as an illustration of urgency. Doctrine cannot be quarried from the scenery of an illustration. Push the method and Luke's own parable of the persistent widow would make God a magistrate who grants justice only to stop being pestered (18:1-8) — which nobody believes and Jesus never meant. The magistrate, the officer, the prison and the penny are the furniture of the story, not a floor plan of eternity.

Second, the idiom runs the other way. A man in a debtors' prison could not earn — that was the entire point of the prison. To say he will not get out until he has paid the last penny is not to hold out a release date; it is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out at all.

Third, and most decisively, it reverses what this passage exists to say. Every line here presses one point: act now, because afterwards is too late. A doctrine that supplies a further opportunity to settle the account after death takes the urgency out of the only sentence that mattered. If there were a way to pay later, the advice to settle on the road would be optional.

And what of the debt itself? Luke answered that five chapters back, in a house where a woman wept over Jesus's feet. Two debtors owed sums they could not repay, and when neither of them could pay, he cancelled the debt of both (7:41-42). The record that stood against us was not put on an instalment plan. It was set aside, nailed to the cross (Col. 2:14).

So take the urgency with full seriousness — settle now, on the road, while it is still called today. But know what the settlement is. It is not a schedule of payments. It is an amnesty, and it was purchased at the judge's own expense.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” was the smallest coin in circulation.

12.text: <sup>1</sup> In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. <sup>2</sup> Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>3</sup> Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops. <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>6</sup> Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. <sup>7</sup> Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>8</sup> “And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, <sup>9</sup> but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. <sup>10</sup> And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>11</sup> And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, <sup>12</sup> for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” <sup>13</sup> Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” <sup>14</sup> But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” <sup>16</sup> And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully, <sup>17</sup> and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ <sup>18</sup> And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. <sup>19</sup> And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ <sup>20</sup> But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ <sup>21</sup> So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. <sup>23</sup> For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. <sup>24</sup> Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! <sup>25</sup> And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>26</sup> If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? <sup>27</sup> Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>28</sup> But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! <sup>29</sup> And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. <sup>30</sup> For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them. <sup>31</sup> Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. <sup>32</sup> “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <sup>33</sup> Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. <sup>34</sup> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <sup>35</sup> “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, <sup>36</sup> and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. <sup>37</sup> Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. <sup>38</sup> If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! <sup>39</sup> But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. <sup>40</sup> You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” <sup>41</sup> Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” <sup>42</sup> And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? <sup>43</sup> Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>44</sup> Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>45</sup> But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, <sup>46</sup> the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. <sup>47</sup> And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. <sup>48</sup> But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more. <sup>49</sup> “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! <sup>50</sup> I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! <sup>51</sup> Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. <sup>52</sup> For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. <sup>53</sup> They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” <sup>54</sup> He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. <sup>55</sup> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. <sup>56</sup> You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time? <sup>57</sup> “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? <sup>58</sup> As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. <sup>59</sup> I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

13.title: Repent or Perish; the Narrow Door; Jerusalem's Lament
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is structured around the call to repentance and its refusal — three overlapping statements that together describe what happens when the opportunity for repentance closes. It opens with Jesus's response to news of a Galilean massacre and the fall of the tower of Siloam — two disasters that the crowd assumes were punishments for exceptional sinfulness. Jesus refuses the assumption and turns both events into a summons to universal repentance: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Then he tells the parable of the fruitless fig tree — one more year of patient cultivation before the axe comes. Then on a Sabbath he heals a woman bent double for eighteen years, and the synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus names the synagogue ruler's hypocrisy before the entire crowd.

The middle section (vv. 18–30) moves through the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven — the kingdom's hidden but irresistible growth — to the question about the number of the saved, and Jesus's answer: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” The door will close. The day will come when the master of the house rises and shuts the door, and those who knock and say “we ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” will hear “I do not know where you come from.” Familiarity with Jesus is not relationship with Jesus; proximity to the gospel is not reception of it.

The chapter ends with one of the most heartrending passages in the Gospel: the lament over Jerusalem. Some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him; Jesus refuses to be deflected (“I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem”). And then he speaks to the city itself: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” The willingness is on his side; the unwillingness is on theirs. And the house will be left desolate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Repent or Perish; the Barren Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The massacre Pilate carried out on Galilean pilgrims is recorded nowhere else in ancient literature — which is itself telling, since this is exactly the kind of local atrocity that filled a province and left no trace in the histories. It fits everything known about the man.

The crowd assumes the victims' fate was a verdict on their exceptional sinfulness, and Jesus brings the assumption into the open before they can state it: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners…? No, I tell you.” Flat, immediate, unqualified.

That was not a fringe view he was demolishing. It was the working theology of the ancient world — Job's friends spent most of a book on it, and the disciples will ask it about a blind man (John 9:2). It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

He then supplies a second case himself, and the choice is deliberate because it is a different kind of disaster. The first was murder; the second is an accident — masonry giving way near the pool of Siloam. Between them the two cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. And the answer is identical, word for word, twice, so that neither case is left open.

The parable of the fig tree extends the urgency and adds the intercession. The tree is planted in a vineyard — prime cultivated ground, occupying space that would otherwise carry vines. Three years is not impatience: a fig takes about three years to bear at all, and the law required the first three years' fruit to be left untouched (Lev. 19:23), so the owner has waited the full statutory period and then come three times on top of it.

And the charge is precise. Not that the tree has done harm, but that it is “using up the ground.” Barrenness here is not a neutral condition; a tree that produces nothing is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else.

The vinedresser disputes none of it. He accepts the whole case and asks for time — and offers to do the work himself: digging round compacted roots, and dunging. Heavy, unpleasant labour on a tree that has given him nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's answer refuses both the question and the assumption behind it. He does not say “God never punishes” — the Old Testament would contradict that. He says this is not the special punishment of especially sinful people. All are sinners; all face mortality; all need to repent.

So the disasters are not explanations of why those particular people died. They are reminders to the living that they are not exempt from the mortality those people have just experienced. The right response to someone else's death is not theological analysis of their sins but examination of one's own soul while there is time.

The fig tree and the vineyard together would have been unmistakable. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5 — “he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes” — and Israel is the fig tree in which God came looking and found nothing (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; Mic. 7:1). The one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year and offering to do the digging himself, is standing in that room saying it.

But the intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period and concedes the outcome. Which puts this parable in its proper relation to the two disasters: those verses said the axe is real, and this one says the axe is being held — and by whom. Separating the two halves ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Take this into the real world, because it will be needed there. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered and this passage forbids them both.

The first is the one Jesus is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, and about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either — he does not remove these deaths from his Father's world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts.

Between those two errors is where a Christian must stand, and it is a narrow place: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it. The honest answer to why them? is that we are not told; the answer we are given instead is that our own footing is no firmer than theirs was.

And there is a sting in the wording. “You will all likewise perish” was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple courts and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. It came true in the very forms they had just been discussing.

The vinedresser's response to three barren years is the model of patient labour with an apparently hopeless case — a church that has not grown, a child who will not turn. He neither writes the tree off nor pretends there is fruit. He asks for another year and goes and gets the spade.

verseByVerse.quote: There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And he answered them, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.

The incident is recorded nowhere else in ancient literature, which is itself worth noting: this is exactly the kind of local atrocity that filled a province and left no trace in the histories. Galileans killed on Pilate’s orders while they were offering sacrifice, so that their blood was mingled with their offerings; Luke gives no further detail.

It fits everything known about Pilate, whom Josephus records provoking riots and putting them down brutally more than once.

Now, why do they raise it? Luke does not say, and the silence is suggestive. They may be testing him — Herod's threat is coming at the end of this chapter, and a Galilean teacher's opinion on a massacre of Galileans would be useful to somebody. But the answer Jesus gives tells us what they were actually thinking.

Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way?

There it is, and he brings it out into the open before they can say it. The assumption behind the report is that the manner of a man's death is a comment on his life.

That was not a fringe view. It was the working theology of the ancient world and of a good deal of the Old Testament's readership. Job's friends spent most of a book on it. The disciples will ask it about a blind man — who sinned, this man or his parents? (John 9:2). It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

No, I tell you.

Flat, immediate, unqualified. He does not say probably not, and he does not explore the possibility. The equation is broken.

But unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

And then the turn nobody was ready for. He does not merely deny that the dead were worse. He tells the living they are in the same position — and the only difference between them and the men on that pavement is a matter of timing.

The question they brought was about somebody else's guilt. He has handed it back with their own name on it.
verseByVerse.note: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Many assumed disaster was punishment for a particular sin.

parallels.desc: who that was innocent ever perished? see: John 9:1–3 = who sinned, this man or his parents?

verseByVerse.quote: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them.

He supplies a second case himself, and the choice is deliberate, because it is a different kind of disaster altogether.

The first was murder — a cruel man with soldiers, doing something wicked on purpose. The second is an accident: masonry giving way near the pool of Siloam at the south end of Jerusalem, probably during building work, and eighteen people underneath it.

Between them the two cases cover the whole field. Evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. Whatever category a bereaved person's loss falls into, one of these two covers it.

And the answer is identical. No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Word for word, twice — which is Jesus making certain that neither case is left open.

Take this into the real world, because it will be needed there. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered, and this passage forbids them both.

The first is the one he is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, and about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved.

The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either. He does not remove these deaths from his Father's world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts. Between those two errors is where a Christian must actually stand, and it is a narrow place: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it.

So what may be said? Very little about the dead, and a great deal to the living. The honest answer to why them? is that we are not told. The answer we are given instead is that our own footing is no firmer than theirs was — which is not a change of subject but the only useful thing that can be said to people standing near a fresh grave and quietly assuming they are safe.

And there is a sting in the wording. You will all likewise perish was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple courts and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. It came true in the very forms they had just been discussing.
verseByVerse.note: Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem; the tower’s collapse is otherwise unknown.

parallels.desc: not wishing that any should perish

verseByVerse.quote: And he told this parable: 'A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.

Notice the setting before anything else. A fig tree in a vineyard — not in an orchard, and not wild on a hillside. It has been deliberately planted in prime cultivated ground, in the best soil the estate has, and it is occupying space that would otherwise carry vines.

Which is the first half of the case against it. This tree has had every advantage.

And the two images together would have been unmistakable to anyone who knew the prophets. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5 — he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes — and Israel is the fig tree of Hosea and Jeremiah, in which God came looking and found nothing (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; Mic. 7:1).

Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none.

Three years is not impatience. A fig takes about three years from planting to bear at all, and the law required that the first three years' fruit be left untouched in any case (Lev. 19:23). So the owner has waited the full statutory period and then come three times on top of it. This is a man who has given the tree every year it was owed and several it was not.

Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?

And here is the charge, stated exactly. Not it has done harm. Not it is diseased. It is using up the ground — drawing water and nutrients out of good soil, taking the light, occupying a space where something fruitful could stand.

Barrenness in this parable is not a neutral condition. A tree that produces nothing is not simply failing to help; it is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else.

Which is a hard word, and it is worth letting it land before the vinedresser speaks. The question the owner asks is not whether the tree has done wrong. It is what the tree is for.
verseByVerse.note: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: the vineyard that yielded wild grapes

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure.

The vinedresser does not dispute the verdict. He does not argue that the tree is fruitful, or that the owner has been hasty, or that three years is too short. He accepts the whole case and asks for time.

And notice what he offers along with the request. Not merely a delay — let it alone is only half his sentence. He undertakes to work: to dig round the roots, breaking up compacted ground so water can reach them, and to dung it. That is heavy, unpleasant, unglamorous labour on a tree that has given him nothing for three years, and he volunteers for it.

The identification is not difficult. The vineyard is Israel, and the one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year and offering to do the work himself, is standing in that room saying it.

Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.

And here the parable does something most of its readers would rather it did not. The intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period, and he concedes the outcome if nothing changes.

Which puts this parable in its proper relation to the two disasters that preceded it. Those verses said the axe is real. This one says the axe is being held — and by whom.

Both halves are needed, and separating them ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years' time. Jesus puts them in the same paragraph.

And there is one thing here for anyone praying over an apparently hopeless case — a church that has not grown, a child who will not turn, a life that has produced nothing for as long as anyone can remember. The vinedresser's response to three barren years is not to write the tree off and not to pretend there is fruit. It is to ask for another year and go and get the spade.

parallels.desc: God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A Woman with a Disabling Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke notes almost in passing that Jesus is teaching in a synagogue — the last time in this Gospel he is recorded doing so. The doors are closing.

The woman had been bent double for eighteen years and could not straighten herself. Luke the physician gives the clinical picture in a line. Consider what it means: she has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body, and has not looked another adult in the face in nearly two decades. She sees feet, floors, and the lower half of the world.

And she is in the synagogue. Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming — eighteen years of asking and receiving nothing, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict — and she is in her place. She asks for nothing when he arrives, which is what makes everything that follows one-sided.

Three things happen and all three are his: he saw her, in a crowded room, teaching, with a woman folded double probably out of everyone's sightline; he called her over, which made her healing public when it could have been quiet; and he touched her, which nobody had needed to do for a long time. “You are freed from your disability” — released, and the release stands; four verses later he calls it being “loosed from this bond.”

She stands up straight for the first time since the middle of another decade, and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look for eighteen years.

The synagogue ruler is indignant, and he does not address Jesus. He addresses the people — public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. And his argument is not stupid: the fourth commandment says what he quotes. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which produces the sentence that gives the whole thing away: “come on those days and be healed.” He is proposing a schedule for a miracle, to a woman who has not been healed on any working day of any week for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
“A disabling spirit” should not be flattened either way. Luke does not call her possessed or record a demon being cast out; Jesus says Satan had bound her — and chapter 11 showed a stronger one overpowering the strong man (11:21-22). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

“Daughter of Abraham” occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Luke will pair it later with Zacchaeus — “he also is a son of Abraham” (19:9).

The argument from lesser to greater is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice. An animal tied in a stall cannot reach water, and leaving it thirsty for a whole day was not an option any farmer would entertain; the rulings of the period permitted untying and leading, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem: “on the Sabbath day.” Not in spite of it. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler's manoeuvre is worth naming because it is recognisable. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the target — the sermon everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And underneath it is the real failure, which is not legalism exactly: he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem. There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure, and it does not feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.

The woman glorifies God before anyone can tell her what she should feel — not the carefully considered religious expression calibrated for an audience, but the overflow of a life that has just been changed.

Two responses close the section, set side by side in a single verse: the adversaries put to shame, the people rejoicing. Nothing in the evidence separated them. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up, and what divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end. Being put to shame is not the end of a man; shame is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.

Luke notes it almost in passing, and it is the last time in this Gospel that Jesus is recorded teaching in a synagogue. The doors are closing.

And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years.

The behold is Luke pointing. She is not mentioned by anyone else in the room.

The phrase a disabling spirit should not be flattened either way. Luke does not here call her possessed or say a demon was cast out of her; Jesus will say Satan had bound her (v. 16). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it — the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.

Luke the physician gives the clinical picture in a line, and it is the detail of a man who has examined such people. She is folded forward and cannot lift herself upright.

Consider what that means for eighteen years of ordinary life. She has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body. She has not looked another adult in the face; every conversation of nearly two decades has been conducted with the top of her head. She sees feet, floors, and the lower half of the world.

And she is in the synagogue. That is the thing to sit with. Eighteen years bent double, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict, and she is still coming to worship on the Sabbath.

Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming. She has been asking God for eighteen years and receiving nothing, and she is in her place.

Luke does not tell us she prayed for healing, and she asks for nothing when he arrives. It is likely she had stopped expecting anything — which is what makes what happens next entirely one-sided.

Eighteen years is also worth measuring rather than reading past. It is longer than a childhood. That is eighteen years of looking at the ground.

Is sickness caused by Satan? Here Luke says this woman’s condition came from a spirit, and Jesus calls her one whom Satan bound (v. 16). But Scripture never teaches that every illness is demonic: the man born blind was not (John 9:3), and Paul’s thorn was a messenger of Satan that God used for his good (2 Cor 12:7–9). A believer cannot be owned by Satan, though God may permit him to be afflicted. The ordinary response to illness is prayer and medicine, not exorcism.

And nobody in that synagogue had done anything about it. She had presumably been coming for most of those years, past the same faces, and it had become the settled furniture of the place: the bent woman at the back, whom everybody knew and nobody expected to change.

parallels.desc: another synagogue healing on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her, he called her over.

Three things happen in that half-verse, and all three are his.

He saw her. In a crowded synagogue, teaching, with a woman folded double at the back and probably out of the sightline of everyone facing the front, he noticed her. Luke uses the same verb of him seeing the widow at Nain (7:13) and it always precedes an action.

He called her over. Which means she had to cross the room, slowly, bent, with every eye following her — and it means he made her healing a public event when he could have done it quietly. Whatever else is coming, nobody in that building will be able to say afterwards that they did not see it.

And she has still asked for nothing.

Woman, you are freed from your disability.

The verb is a perfect passive — you have been released, and the release stands. It is the vocabulary of untying, and it is the same root Jesus will use four verses later of the ox untied from its manger.

He does not say be healed. He says the knot has been undone.

And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight.

He touched her, which nobody had needed to do for a long time.

Eighteen years, and it takes one sentence and a pair of hands.

And she glorified God.

The first thing she does with her new body. Not thank him, though presumably she did; Luke records that the first use she made of standing upright was worship.

Which is worth seeing exactly. For eighteen years she had not been able to lift her face towards heaven in a building built for lifting faces towards heaven. She stands up straight for the first time since the middle of another decade — and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look for eighteen years.

parallels.desc: the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.

A woman has just stood upright for the first time in eighteen years and is praising God at the front of his synagogue, and this man is angry.

Notice first who he speaks to. Not to Jesus, who did it. To the people — and effectively to her, since she is the one being told when to come for healing. He has a grievance against a man he does not dare address and takes it out on a congregation that cannot answer back.

That is a recognisable manoeuvre and it is worth naming. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target — the sermon that everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And look at his argument, because it is not stupid. He is right that the Sabbath forbids work, and the fourth commandment says so in the words he is quoting: six days you shall labor and do all your work (Ex. 20:9). He is not inventing a rule.

What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which leads to the sentence that gives the whole thing away: come on those days and be healed. Say it slowly and it collapses. He is instructing a woman who has been bent double for eighteen years — who has not been healed on any of the six working days of any week for nearly two decades — to come back on Monday.

He is proposing a schedule for a miracle. As though the healing were a service Jesus provided on request, and the only issue were the opening hours.

Underneath that is the real failure, and it is not legalism exactly. It is that he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem.

There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure. It is not rare, and it does not usually feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hypocrites!

The plural is deliberate. One man spoke; Jesus answers a whole way of thinking, and everyone in the room who agreed with him is included.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it?

The argument is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice, and everybody present did it.

An animal tied in a stall cannot get to water. Leaving it thirsty from Friday evening to Saturday evening was not an option any farmer would have entertained, and the rabbinic rulings of the period made allowance for exactly this — untying and leading were permitted, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work.

So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering. Jesus is not asking them to adopt a new rule. He is asking them to apply the one they use every week of their lives.

And now the comparison, which is the sharpest thing in the chapter.

And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?

Every term is chosen.

This woman — over against his ox or his donkey. The animal has an owner who will take trouble for it. The woman has been in that congregation for years.

A daughter of Abraham. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is being handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries.

Whom Satan bound. He names the one who tied the knot — the strong man of chapter 11, whom a stronger one overpowers (11:21-22). This is not a medical misfortune. It is an occupation, and someone is being dispossessed.

Eighteen years — against the ox's overnight thirst.

Be loosed from this bond. The loosing of the woman matches the untying of the animal, and that is the hinge of the whole argument: they untie; he unties.

Does the Sabbath still bind Christians? Jesus shows here what the Sabbath was for: rest and release, which he himself brings. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day binds the conscience (Col 2:16–17; Rom 14:5). Christians gather on the Lord’s Day as a glad and ancient practice, and works of mercy are always fitting.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem. On the Sabbath day. Not in spite of the Sabbath. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.
verseByVerse.note: Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath.

parallels.desc: he also is a son of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.

One verse, two reactions, and Luke sets them side by side without comment.

All his adversaries were put to shame. Humiliated by exposure — not shouted down, but shown up. Nobody argued them into silence; the argument and the standing woman did it between them.

Note also the word adversaries — those set against him, opponents in a case. The synagogue ruler is no longer merely indignant. He belongs to a party.

And all the people rejoiced.

The ordinary crowd, who had nothing invested in the ruling about Sabbath work, are simply delighted. And the word Luke chooses for what they were delighted about is glorious — splendid things.

It is an unusual word for a healing. They have not merely observed something useful. Something of the weight of God has been visible in their synagogue, and they know it.

Two responses, then, to exactly the same event — and this is the point of putting them in one sentence. Nothing in the evidence separated these people. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up. What divided them was what they brought into the building.

Which is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel, and for the rest of the story. The same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end of the verse that is easy to miss. Being put to shame is not the end of a man. Shame is what a person feels when he has been shown to be wrong, and it is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the synagogue ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties the parables to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, been attacked for it, and sent a happy crowd home — and it is a fair question whether that is what the kingdom of God amounts to.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled. And it is sowed in his garden — deliberately put in the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort. Black mustard grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet; calling it a tree is a stretch, and probably meant to be.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's and Daniel's, and it always means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins; this starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

The leaven parable ought to bring a reader up short, since one chapter ago leaven was the picture of everything that ruins (12:1). That is its usual role in Scripture — scoured out before Passover (Ex. 12:15), and Paul's image for malice and evil (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

But the sentence refuses the warning reading. Jesus does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says it is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading, and everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy makes it a good image for the kingdom.

Then someone asks whether the saved will be few, and gets no number. “Strive to enter through the narrow door” — strain, exert everything, as an athlete does in a contest. And the door is narrow: not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question “will those who are saved be few?” was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and notice how it is framed — a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking has placed himself outside the calculation.

That is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. There is a particular safety in the general: as long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing. And Jesus's reply is to them, plural, though one man asked.

If striving is required, is salvation earned? No — and notice what the striving is for. Not to become worthy, and not until enough has been done. Strive to enter. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal with nothing to offer is told “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Nobody buys this door open — but plenty intend to go through it later, and later is a door that shuts.

“I do not know where you come from” is not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational (Amos 3:2), and “where you come from” is a householder's question about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The closing vision fulfils Isaiah's feast on the mountain for all peoples (Isa. 25:6-8) and the gathering from far off (Isa. 49:12). The seats do not stand empty; the table is full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.
verseByVerse.examples:
The plea of those outside is entirely true and entirely beside the point. They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording — and he had taught in their streets and they were there. These are not people making things up.

But every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached. Nobody says we trusted you — and a modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion. All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

Which raises the question that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside? The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing the entering all along in ordinary people. The centurion who says “say the word” (7:7). The woman told “your faith has saved you; go in peace” (7:50). The leper who came back (17:19). The blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39). Not one was admitted for being impressive; each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside.

And “some are last who will be first” should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is not disadvantage but grace — and grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore, What is the kingdom of God like?

The therefore ties this to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, and been attacked for it, and the crowd went home happy. Now he explains what that was.

It is a fair question to have been asking. If this is the kingdom of God arriving, it does not look like much. One woman. One synagogue. One argument won against a minor official, and the establishment more hostile than it was that morning.

It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled — rabbinic sayings used it as the standard unit of the negligible, and Jesus uses it that way himself when he talks about faith (17:6).

And note that it is sowed in his garden. Not scattered in a field, and not dropped by accident. Somebody deliberately put a thing that small into the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort.

And it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.

Black mustard in that country grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet — large enough for birds to perch and shelter in, which is what the text says, though calling it a tree is a stretch and is probably meant to be. There is a touch of exaggeration in the picture and it is doing work.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's, and Daniel's, and it always means the same thing: a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Ezekiel's version is a promise — God will plant a sprig on a high mountain and it will become a noble cedar, and in the shade of its branches birds of every sort will nest.

So Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb.

Which is the joke, and it is also the whole doctrine of how God works. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins. This starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he said, 'To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.

The second parable ought to bring a reader up short, and if it does not, it is worth stopping to notice why it should.

One chapter ago, in this same Gospel and from this same speaker, leaven was the picture of everything that ruins: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy (12:1). That is leaven's usual role in Scripture. Israel scoured it out of the house before Passover (Ex. 12:15); the feast at the start of the passion is the feast of Unleavened Bread (22:1); and Paul takes the image for granted — a little leaven leavens the whole lump — and means malice and evil by it (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

So when Jesus says the kingdom of God is like leaven, some have concluded he must be issuing a warning: corruption spreading quietly through the church.

That reading cannot stand, and the sentence itself refuses it. He does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says the kingdom of God is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, in the same breath, as the matching half of a pair. Both parables answer one question: how does something this small end up being everything? Turn the second into a warning and you have broken the pair in half.

The resolution is simpler than the difficulty suggests. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading. Everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy — that it is small, hidden, works from the inside, and does not stop until the whole batch is changed — is exactly what makes it a good image for the kingdom. The same yeast that ruins the loaf when it is the wrong yeast transforms it when it is the right one. Luke's own two uses prove the point rather than embarrassing it: at 12:1 something false permeates a community; here something true permeates the world.

And do not miss the quantity, because Jesus chose it. Three measures of flour is a great quantity — not a household baking but bread for a hundred people and more, an absurd amount for one woman to be kneading in a kitchen. The comedy is deliberate. A pinch of yeast, invisible the moment it goes in, and a mountain of dough; and the pinch wins.

That is the answer to anyone who has looked at the size of the world and the size of the church and quietly concluded that the arithmetic is hopeless.
verseByVerse.note: Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

verseByVerse.quote: He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him, 'Lord, will those who are saved be few?' And he said to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem.

Luke reminds us where the road is going. He has been noting the direction of travel since 9:51, and it is not filler. Everything in these chapters is being said by a man walking towards his own execution.

And someone said to him, Lord, will those who are saved be few?

The question was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and it was discussed with some relish. How many of Israel would have a share in the age to come? Some held that all Israel would be saved except a named list of exceptions; others were considerably tighter.

And notice how the question is framed. It is a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking it has placed himself outside the calculation and is enquiring about the statistics.

That is worth naming, because it is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. Questions like what about those who have never heard? and are most people lost? and what happens to those who die as infants? are genuine questions, and some of them have good answers. They are also, very often, a way of discussing eternity in the third person.

There is a particular safety in the general. As long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing.

And he said to them.

Two small things before the answer itself.

He does not tell him the number. Anywhere in the Gospels where curiosity presses for information God has not given — the times and seasons, who is greatest, what will happen to that man — the answer is a redirection, and it is never rude and never satisfies.

And the reply is to them, plural, though one man asked. Whatever was said next was aimed at everybody in earshot, and the questioner was not going to be allowed to receive it as a matter of general interest.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive to enter through the narrow door.

He does not answer the question asked. He answers the question that should have been asked, and it is not how many? but are you going in?

The verb is agōnizesthe — the root of agony, and in ordinary Greek the word for what an athlete does in a contest. It means to strain, to exert everything, to compete as though something depended on it.

And the door is narrow — not locked, not hidden, and not high. Narrow. Which says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.

Two questions come straight off this verse, and a reader deserves both answered.

The first: if I must strive, am I not earning my way in after all?

No — and notice what the striving is for. He does not say strive to become worthy, or strive until you have done enough. He says strive to enter. The effort is not payment offered at the door; it is the urgency of a man who will not be talked out of going through it. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal who has nothing whatever to offer is told today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43).

Nobody buys this door open. But plenty of people intend to go through it later, and he is telling them that later is a door that shuts.

For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.

Which raises the second question, and it is the one that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside?

The passage is about to be unsparing on false assurance, so it is worth saying plainly what genuine entering looks like. The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing us the entering all along in ordinary people. It is the centurion who says say the word (7:7). It is the woman told your faith has saved you; go in peace (7:50). It is the leper who came back (17:19), and the blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39).

Not one of them was admitted for being impressive. Each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside. If that is what you are doing, you are not outside knocking.

verseByVerse.quote: When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door.

The scene changes from a doorway to a house at night, and the decisive action has already happened before the verse begins. The master has got up and shut the door, and everything after that is on the wrong side of it.

Note that he is not described as refusing to open it. He shut it, once, at a time of his choosing, and the shutting is presented as ordinary — what any householder does at the end of the day.

And you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, open to us.

They know the address. They know what to call him. They are at the right house, and they are asking the right person.

Then he will answer you, I do not know where you come from.

It is a strange formula, and it is not a failure of memory. To know in the Hebrew idiom is relational — God knew Israel among all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). And where you come from is the question of a householder about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The answer is that there is none.

Then you will begin to say, We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.

And here is the plea, and every word of it is true.

They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording all through this Gospel. He had taught in their streets, and they had been there to hear it. These are not people making things up. Their credentials are entirely genuine.

They are also entirely beside the point, and it is worth being exact about why. Every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached.

Nobody says we trusted you.

Depart from me, all you workers of evil.

Which lands hardest on the most religiously exposed people in any generation. A modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years. I sat under good preaching. I took communion.

All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out.
