Weeping is grief and gnashing of teeth is commonly taken as anguish or even anger — so what is described may be not merely sorrow but sorrow with fury still in it.

And the specific torment named is a sight. They will see the patriarchs inside. Whatever else exclusion means, this text says it involves knowing exactly what has been lost and who is at the table.

Note who the people outside are. Not pagans. Men who could recite their descent from Abraham, and whose whole assurance rested on it — we have Abraham as our father, which John the Baptist had already demolished at the start of this Gospel (3:8).

And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God.

Four directions, which is the ancient way of saying everywhere, and it is a deliberate echo of the prophets. Isaiah had promised a feast on the mountain for all peoples, with the covering removed and death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8), and the gathering from far off, from the north and from the west (Isa. 49:12).

So the seats do not stand empty. The table is full, and it is full of people nobody in that synagogue would have expected to see there.

And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.

This is Luke's signature and it has been running since the Magnificat — the mighty brought down and the humble exalted (1:52). But it should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog.

What determines the order is not disadvantage. It is grace, and the fact that grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

Weeping and gnashing of teeth describes conscious grief and anguish at being shut out (cf. Matt 8:12; 25:30). Some evangelicals hold that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist; but this picture is of people who are present and aware of what they have lost, and Jesus elsewhere speaks of eternal punishment (Matt 25:46). The more likely reading is that the punishment is conscious and lasting.

Which is why the warning falls where it does. It is not aimed at people far from God. It is aimed at people who were sure they were near him — and the seats were taken by strangers who knew they had no claim at all.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him — the only occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of a danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain. Not every Pharisee was an enemy; Luke records three who invite him to dinner. But Herod ruled Galilee, and a man frightened out of that territory would be driven towards Judea, where his real opponents were waiting.

“That fox” is contemptuous in a specific way. In Jewish usage the fox was not primarily crafty but the small predator set against the lion — a rabbinic saying speaks of being the tail of lions rather than the head of foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power, which is what he was: Rome never let him be king, and he ended his days exiled to Gaul.

The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else. Herod does not set the date. “I finish my course” is the language of completion — the same English as the word from the cross, “it is finished” (John 19:30). And the last clause is grim irony: he is not saying Jerusalem is dangerous but that it is the appointed place, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

Then the lament. “How often” is not the language of a man who has been in Jerusalem three or four times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time — and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. The one speaking is the one who sent them.

The image has a long history in Israel's Scriptures: the eagle stirring her nest (Deut. 32:11), the wings under which Ruth took refuge (Ruth 2:12), the shadow of the wings in the Psalms (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 91:4). But a hen is not an eagle, and the difference matters. A hen has no talons and cannot fight; what she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way she saves her chicks in a fire is to spread them and stay where she is. Farmers have found them afterwards, burnt through, with the chicks alive underneath.

That is the image he chose for himself, on the road on which he had set his face towards a city that was going to kill him.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Your house is forsaken” — and the first two words are the devastating ones. It had never been their house — Solomon built it and God filled it, and it is called “my house” in every prophet, as Jesus himself will say in that very building (19:46). To hand it back with the possessive changed is to say the owner has moved out.

Israel had seen it before. Ezekiel watched the glory rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23) — and the temple stood a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple; it is masonry.

The closing quotation is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts, and the crowd will shout it over him within six chapters (19:38). Some read the promise as fulfilled there, and the words very nearly match; but the entry is one day, not an era, and what follows it does not look like a welcome. Others read it as pointing further on — to a day when the city that would not be gathered finally says it and means it, which is the hope Paul holds out (Rom. 11:26). The second fits the words better, since “Blessed is he who comes” is a welcome, not a cry of terror.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lament is the model of prophetic grief — the sorrow a faithful preacher feels for those who hear the word and do not receive it. It is not anger; it is love that has been refused, and the grief of knowing what the refusal costs.

Every pastor who has watched someone hear the gospel clearly and walk away, every parent who has prayed for a child who will not turn, every evangelist who has seen the door closing on someone who came so close, has tasted something of it.

“And you were not willing” is five words and the whole tragedy. Every verb before them is his — would I have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other. He does not say they were unable; he says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

And what matters most about the last verse is its shape. It ends with until. He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line — and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, 'Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.' And he said to them, 'Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.

It is the only recorded occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of a danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain.

They may mean it. Not every Pharisee was an enemy — Luke records three who invite him to dinner, and Nicodemus was of that party. Or the warning may be a manoeuvre: Herod ruled Galilee and Perea, and a man frightened out of that territory would be driven towards Judea, which is where his real opponents were waiting. Luke does not tell us, and it is better not to decide.

Either way, the threat is credible. This is the Herod who had beheaded John (9:9), and who has been wanting to see Jesus ever since.

Go and tell that fox.

The message is sent back to Herod personally, and the word is contemptuous in a specific way. In Jewish usage a fox was not primarily crafty; it was the small predator, set against the lion — a rabbinic saying speaks of being the tail of lions rather than the head of foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power.

Which is what he was. Rome never let him be king; he was a tetrarch, and he would end his days exiled to Gaul.

Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.

The reply is not defiance for its own sake. It is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else.

Herod does not set the date. Jesus will go on doing exactly what he is doing until the work is finished — and the verb for finishing is teleioumai, the language of completion and of a thing brought to its proper end. It is the same root as the word from the cross: it is finished (John 19:30).

Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.

There is the must again — dei, the divine necessity that has driven this Gospel since a boy in the temple (2:49).

Did Jesus insult a ruler? He spoke as a prophet with authority over Herod, giving God’s verdict on a cunning and destructive man. It is not a pattern for Christians to speak of rulers with contempt; Paul apologized for speaking against the high priest (Acts 23:5), and Peter says Honor the emperor (1 Pet 2:17). And today and tomorrow, and the third day is an idiom for a short, fixed time: Jesus’ work will go on until God’s appointed end, which no ruler can hasten or prevent. The third day may echo the resurrection, but the point is that his course is in his Father’s hands.

And the last clause is grim irony. He is not saying Jerusalem is dangerous. He is saying it is the appointed place — that the city which exists to bring men to God has a settled record of killing the men God sends, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John. A fox was a picture of cunning and destructiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem.

The doubled name again — the same register as Martha, Martha and Simon, Simon. It is what he says when he sees the whole of someone and grieves.

The city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it.

This is what the city does, habitually, as a settled practice. And the charge is historical, not rhetorical. Zechariah was stoned in the temple court on the king's orders (2 Chr. 24:21). Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern to die. Tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh.

How often would I have gathered your children together.

How often is the phrase to stop at, because it is not the language of a man who has been in Jerusalem three or four times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time — and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. The one speaking is the one who sent them.

As a hen gathers her brood under her wings.

The image is maternal, and it is the tenderest thing Jesus ever says about himself.

It has a history in Israel's Scriptures, and he is drawing on it deliberately: the eagle stirring up her nest and bearing her young on her wings (Deut. 32:11); under whose wings you have come to take refuge, said to Ruth (Ruth 2:12); hide me in the shadow of your wings (Ps. 17:8; cf. 36:7; 57:1; 91:4).

But a hen is not an eagle, and the difference matters. A hen has no talons and cannot fight. What she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way a hen saves her chicks in a fire is by spreading them and staying where she is — and farmers have found them afterwards, burnt through, with the chicks alive underneath.

That is the image he chose for himself, on the road on which he had set his face towards a city that was going to kill him.

And you were not willing.

Five words, and they are the whole tragedy. Every verb before them is his — would I have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other.

Does this show that God’s saving will can be thwarted by human will? Arminian Christians read it so: Christ wanted to save Jerusalem, and its people refused. The Reformed answer distinguishes God’s revealed will, his sincere call and desire that sinners turn, from his decree, what he has purposed to do. Jesus here speaks as the incarnate Son, weeping over a city that would not come, and the refusal was truly theirs. Both are true: God does all that he purposes (Eph 1:11), and those who refuse him do so by their own will and are justly judged. Christ’s tears are real.

He does not say they were unable. He says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, your house is forsaken.

Your house. Two words, and they are devastating.

It had never been their house. Solomon built it and God filled it, and it was called my house in every prophet — my house shall be a house of prayer, which Jesus will say in that very building (19:46). To hand it back to them with the possessive changed is to say that the owner has moved out.

And Israel had seen this before. Ezekiel watched the glory of God rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23) — and the temple stood for a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple. It is masonry.

And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

The quotation is Psalm 118:26, the psalm sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts, and the crowd will shout it over him within six chapters as he comes down the Mount of Olives (19:38).

So does that settle it? Some read the promise as fulfilled at the triumphal entry, and the words very nearly match. But the entry is one day, not an era, and what happens after it does not look like a welcome. Others read it as pointing further on — to a day when the city that would not be gathered finally says it and means it, which is the hope Paul holds out when he writes that all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11:26).

The second fits the words better, since Blessed is he who comes is a welcome, not a cry of terror. What is certain is the shape of the sentence, and the shape is what matters.

It ends with until.

He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line — and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

The hen is still on the road, still walking towards Jerusalem, still saying how often would I have gathered you. And the sentence that ends her lament is not never. It is not until you are ready to say: blessed is he who comes.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
this house shall become a desolation

13.text: <sup>1</sup> There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. <sup>2</sup> And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? <sup>3</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. <sup>4</sup> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? <sup>5</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” <sup>6</sup> And he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. <sup>7</sup> And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’ <sup>8</sup> And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. <sup>9</sup> Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’” <sup>10</sup> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. <sup>11</sup> And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. <sup>12</sup> When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your disability.” <sup>13</sup> And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. <sup>14</sup> But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” <sup>15</sup> Then the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? <sup>16</sup> And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” <sup>17</sup> As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. <sup>18</sup> He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? <sup>19</sup> It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” <sup>20</sup> And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? <sup>21</sup> It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” <sup>22</sup> He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. <sup>23</sup> And someone said to him, “Lord, will those who are saved be few?” And he said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. <sup>25</sup> When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ <sup>26</sup> Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ <sup>27</sup> But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’ <sup>28</sup> In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. <sup>29</sup> And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. <sup>30</sup> And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” <sup>31</sup> At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” <sup>32</sup> And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ <sup>33</sup> Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. <sup>34</sup> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>35</sup> Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

14.title: The Banquet, the Invitation, and the Cost
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is built around a dinner table — and it is one of the most dramatically productive dinner tables in the Gospels. Jesus is at a meal in the house of a prominent Pharisee, being watched carefully. A man with dropsy appears; Jesus heals him on the Sabbath and challenges the watching lawyers and Pharisees. He observes the guests scrambling for the best seats and tells a parable about table manners that is really about the kingdom's reversal of honour. He turns to the host and tells him who to invite to dinner — not the friends and family who will reciprocate, but the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, who cannot repay. And when a guest at the table says “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God,” Jesus responds with the parable of the great banquet — the most complete statement of grace and rejection in the Gospel.

The chapter's second movement (vv. 25–35) shifts from the dinner table to the crowd following Jesus on the road, and the tone shifts from parable to direct confrontation. “Whoever does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple.” Two parables of counting the cost — the tower-builder and the king going to war — press the same point. “Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” This is not the Christianity of added benefits; it is the Christianity of total claim. The banquet of grace and the cross of discipleship belong to the same Gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the Sabbath Jesus goes to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees — the third such invitation Luke records, and every one of them ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway.

“They were watching him carefully.” The verb is one used of keeping something under observation for a purpose; Luke uses it in Acts of men watching the gates day and night to kill Paul (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity but surveillance. There is food on the table, a host at the head of it, and a set of guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

A man with dropsy is “before him.” Dropsy is what would now be called oedema: fluid retention, the limbs and abdomen swelling, usually a symptom of failing organs. And the ancient world understood something about it we might miss — a man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty, which made it the standing image in Greek moralists for insatiable greed: a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him. Worth holding, in a chapter about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Note the staging, too. Luke does not say how he came to be there; he may well have been put there to see what Jesus would do.

Jesus does not wait for the trap; he springs it himself, asking the question out loud before touching anybody — and framing it exactly as they would have framed it. Their silence is not puzzlement. They cannot say yes without undercutting their own position, and cannot say no with a swollen man standing in the room.

Then he heals him and sends him away, which is a mercy on its own: the man does not have to stand there for the argument that follows.

And the second question silences them completely — “a son or an ox” put in one sentence, as items in the same category, because that is where their practice puts them. They could not reply.
verseByVerse.theology:
The silence of the lawyers and Pharisees — both times — is the silence of people who know they have no answer and will not give the answer they do have. It is worth naming, because it is the commonest form cowardice takes among religious people: not denial, not opposition, but a careful and dignified silence held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked.

The argument is the same shape as the one in the previous chapter but sharpened in two ways. There, the animal was thirsty and being led to water; here something has fallen into a well and is drowning, and the word is immediately. This is an emergency, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling.

The manuscripts vary slightly at v.5 and some read “a donkey or an ox,” which is the more expected pair and very likely why some copyists produced it. “Son or ox” is the harder reading and almost certainly what Luke wrote — and it is the one that does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both?

They are beaten by their own practice, which is the only argument that cannot be got round. He has not quoted an obscure text or appealed to his own authority; he has described what every man in that room does on a Sabbath afternoon when something valuable falls down a hole.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus heals the man before making the argument. That is not bad pedagogy but the right order: the principle of Sabbath mercy is not established by syllogism and then applied — it is demonstrated in flesh and blood and then defended. The compassion leads the argument.

And there is a hard general truth in the second silence. Most people's real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking, and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself.

The two-tier system is the thing being dismantled: their own emergencies justify Sabbath flexibility, and somebody else's does not. That instinct did not die out in the first century. It is at work wherever a rule is applied rigorously to people at a distance and generously to oneself and one's own — and it is almost never noticed by the person doing it, because the exceptions feel like common sense.

Note also that Jesus sends the healed man away before the debate begins. He will not have a person used as an exhibit, even in an argument he is winning.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees.

He accepted the invitation. That is the first thing, and it is the third time Luke has recorded it (7:36; 11:37) — and every one of these dinners ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway.

A ruler of the Pharisees is a man of standing, perhaps a member of the Sanhedrin. This is a formal Sabbath meal, the best meal of the week, and Jesus is the guest of honour in the sense that he is the one everybody has come to see.

They were watching him carefully.

The verb is one used of watching for a purpose — the word for keeping something under observation, and in Luke's second volume it is used of a plot to kill Paul, watching the gates day and night (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity. It is surveillance.

So the room is not what it appears. There is food on the table, a host at the head of it, and a set of guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.

Luke's behold is his usual signal to look, and the medical term is his own — hydrōpikos, a word that appears nowhere else in the Greek Bible and belongs to the physicians' vocabulary. Dropsy is what would now be called oedema: fluid retention, the limbs and abdomen swelling, usually a symptom of failing heart, liver or kidneys.

And the ancient world understood one thing about it that we might miss. A man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty — the more fluid he retains, the more he craves. It was the standing image in Greek moralists for insatiable greed: a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him.

Which is a detail worth holding, because the rest of this chapter is about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Note also the staging: before him, in a private house, at a formal dinner, on the Sabbath. Luke does not say how he came to be there; he may well have been put there to see what Jesus would do.
verseByVerse.note: Dropsy is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?' But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?

Luke says he responded, though nobody has said anything. He is answering what is in the room.

And notice who moves first. They have set the trap and are waiting for him to walk into it; he asks the question himself, out loud, before touching anybody. There is nothing to catch him at, because he has put the whole matter on the table in advance.

The question is also framed exactly as they would have framed it. Is it lawful? — the technical language of their own debates, addressed to the experts, inviting a ruling.

But they remained silent.

And here is the answer, and it is the loudest thing in the chapter.

They cannot say yes, because their whole position depends on saying no. And they cannot say no, because there is a swollen man standing in the room and everybody can see him.

So they say nothing — which is not neutrality. Silence is a decision, and this one has been taken in front of a suffering man. The most learned religious men in that district have been asked a straight question about mercy, and every one of them has calculated that answering would cost him something.

It is worth naming, because it is the commonest form that cowardice takes among religious people. Not denial. Not opposition. A careful, dignified silence, held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked.

Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.

Three verbs, and each is worth a moment.

And the Sabbath today? Jesus defends works of mercy on the Sabbath under the old covenant. For Christians the Sabbath is fulfilled in him (Col 2:16–17), and no day binds the conscience; but the lesson stands for every day: need is never an interruption to be ignored.

He took him — took hold of him, which is contact with a diseased body at a Sabbath dinner in front of men obsessed with purity. He healed him. And he sent him away, which is a mercy on its own: the man does not have to stand in that room for the argument that is coming. Whatever he was brought there for, he is not going to be used for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?' And they could not reply to these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?

The argument is the same shape as the one in the previous chapter — from what they already do to what they will not allow — but it has been sharpened in two ways.

There, the animal was thirsty and being led to water. Here, something has fallen into a well and is drowning, and the word is immediately. This is not routine care. It is an emergency, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling.

And the pairing is deliberately shocking: a son or an ox. He puts them in one sentence, as items in the same category — because that is where their practice puts them. A man will haul either one out without pausing to think about the day.

The manuscripts vary slightly here and some read a donkey or an ox, which is the more expected pair and is very likely why some copyists produced it. Son or ox is the harder reading and almost certainly what Luke wrote, and it is the one that does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both?

And they could not reply to these things.

The second silence, and Luke reports it as an inability rather than a choice. The first time they remained silent; this time they could not reply.

They have been beaten by their own practice, which is the only argument that cannot be got round. He has not quoted an obscure text at them or appealed to his own authority. He has described what every man in that room does on a Sabbath afternoon when something valuable falls down a hole.

And there is a hard general truth in it. Most people's real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking — and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Places of Honour; Inviting the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus has been watching the guests arrive. Seating at such a meal was not casual — guests reclined on couches around a U-shaped arrangement graded by proximity to the host, a visible ranking of the room that everybody could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself. These men have just come from a Sabbath service, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

The parable begins as pure social advice, and the scenario would have made everyone wince. Honour in that culture was public and finite, gained and lost in front of witnesses. Follow the mechanics of the humiliation: the man is not merely demoted but has to get up and walk the whole length of the room, because the only seat left is the last one. And “begin with shame” is exact — the shame is not a moment; it starts, and goes on all evening.

Then the reversal, which would be shrewd manoeuvring if it stopped there. What closes the trap is the last verse: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” Neither verb says who does the humbling and the exalting, and neither needs to: God will do it. This is not about how the evening goes; it is about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Which is what makes false modesty useless rather than merely distasteful. A man who takes the low seat in order to be moved up has exalted himself, and the verse has already seen it.

Jesus then turns to the host — at the host's own table, having eaten his food. The four categories he names are the entire ordinary guest list, and the objection is stated plainly: “lest they also invite you in return.” Hospitality in that world ran on reciprocal obligation; an invitation created a debt discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date.

The alternative list is the exact opposite: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none. And the reason given is not that they are more deserving — it is that they “cannot repay you.” The inability is the qualification.
verseByVerse.theology:
“He who humbles himself will be exalted” appears repeatedly in Luke (14:11; 18:14; and in substance in the Magnificat). It is the law of the kingdom inverting the law of the world, and it is grounded eschatologically: “you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” The accounts are not settled in this life, but they are settled.

The parable cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing — and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat; he is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation rather than merit.

Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening at the bottom of the table costs him nothing.

And the promise on the other side is not a better seat at a dinner party. The one saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is, and Paul describes the outcome in the same two movements: “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Phil. 2:8-9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Read flatly, the instruction to the host bans Christmas dinner, and someone will read it flatly. Is a believer forbidden to have his own family round a table?

No — and the same chapter shows why. A dozen verses on, Jesus says a disciple must “hate” his father and mother (v.26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends but do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends — at Levi's feast, in Martha's house, and at this very Pharisee's dinner while he says it.

So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does. Put the two lists side by side and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves: the guests who will have you back, or the guests who cannot. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so — and this is a command with a doorbell, not a principle to admire.

The host who invites only those who will invite him back has not given; he has traded. The host who invites those who cannot repay has given, and in doing so has imitated the God who invites sinners to his table knowing they have nothing to offer him. And note that the account is not cancelled but moved: what is on offer is a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, 'When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor.

He has been watching them arrive.

The seating at such a meal was not casual. Guests reclined on couches around a U-shaped arrangement, and the positions were graded by proximity to the host — a visible ranking of the room that everybody present could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself.

So this is a room of men who have just come from a Sabbath service, at the house of a Pharisee, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

And Luke says Jesus noticed. He watched the whole performance from wherever he had been put.

Then he tells a parable, and it opens as pure social advice — the sort of thing a wise uncle might say.

When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him.

The scenario is entirely realistic and would have made everyone wince. Honour in that culture was public and finite; it was gained and lost in front of witnesses, and a man's standing was whatever the room said it was.

And he who invited you both will come and say to you, Give your place to this person, and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.

Follow the mechanics of the humiliation, because Jesus has thought it through. The man is not merely demoted. He has to get up, in front of everybody, and walk the whole length of the room — because the only seat left is the last one. Every guest between the top and the bottom watches him go past.

And the phrase begin with shame is exact. The shame is not a moment; it starts, and it goes on for the rest of the evening while he sits where everyone can see he ended up.

That is what the grasping actually costs, and the parable has not yet said a word about God.
verseByVerse.note: Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host.

parallels.desc: better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, Friend, move up higher.

The advice is exactly reversed, and if it stopped here it would be a piece of shrewd manoeuvring — take the bottom seat as a tactic, and enjoy being moved up in front of everybody.

Anyone who has read it that way has been outmanoeuvred by the parable, and the last verse is what closes the trap.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

Neither verb says who does the humbling and the exalting, and neither needs to: God will do it. This is not about how the evening goes. It is a statement about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Which is what makes false modesty useless here rather than merely distasteful. A man who takes the low seat in order to be moved up has exalted himself; the manoeuvre is the exaltation, and the verse has already seen it.

So the parable cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing — and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is.

And here is where the parable turns from advice into gospel. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat. He is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation and not by merit.

Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening spent at the bottom of the table costs him nothing at all.

And the promise on the other side is not a better seat at a dinner party. The one saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is — and Paul will describe the outcome in the same two movements, humbling and exalting: he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him (Phil. 2:8-9).

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said also to the man who had invited him.

Having dealt with the guests, he turns to the host — at the host's own table, having eaten his food. It is one of the least comfortable moments in the Gospels.

When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid.

The four categories are the entire ordinary guest list, and the objection is stated plainly: lest they also invite you in return.

That was not a hypothetical in that world. Hospitality ran on an understood system of reciprocal obligation; an invitation created a debt, and the debt was discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date.

But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you.

The four categories here are the exact opposite: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none. And the reason given is not that they are more deserving. It is precisely that they cannot repay you — the inability is the qualification.

Read flatly, though, this verse bans Christmas dinner, and someone will read it flatly. Is a believer actually forbidden to have his own family round a table?

No, and the same chapter tells you why. A dozen verses on, Jesus will say that a disciple must hate his father and mother (v. 26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends; it is do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends — at Levi's feast, in Martha's house, and at this very Pharisee's dinner while he says it.

So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does. Put the two lists side by side and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so.

For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.

Not you will not be repaid. The account is not cancelled; it is moved. And it is worth seeing what the host is being offered: a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection — which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return.

parallels.desc: the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow shall eat

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A guest breaks the silence with something entirely correct: “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” The picture he invokes was the settled hope of Israel — the feast on the mountain, rich food for all peoples, death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8).

So why does Jesus answer with a parable about people who refuse an invitation? Listen to the sentence again. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense, and nobody in the room is implicated by it. Jesus has just told them to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them — both remarks about this table, tonight — and what comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The parable changes the tense. And it turns on a custom: a formal banquet involved two invitations, the first well in advance so the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals, the second on the day to say it was ready. So these guests are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They accepted weeks ago, and the host has slaughtered on the strength of it.

“Come, for everything is now ready” is the gospel in six words. Not would you consider coming? The work is done, the cost has been met, and the only thing missing is the guests. And notice who carries it — not the host but a servant, sent on foot to men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own.

Then the excuses, and not one is disreputable. A field already bought; five yoke of oxen already bought; a new marriage. Property, work, family — every one a good thing, and not one a sin. Nobody says “I do not want to come.” They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.

Which is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say “I refuse Christ.” A great many say “not now — there is something I have to deal with first,” and go on saying it politely for forty years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The master's anger is the only emotion attributed to him, and it is easily made into something it is not. It is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He has been given his guests' word and spent accordingly — and in that economy a great banquet meant slaughtered animals that could not be kept, so the cost was already unrecoverable. What has been refused is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved.

But the anger does not cancel the banquet; it redirects it. And the four categories the servant is sent to fetch are the same four Jesus gave the host eight verses earlier (v.13) — which is the parable's quiet accusation to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. God does exactly what he told them to do.

The parable's geography follows the movement of Acts: the original guests, then the streets and lanes of the city, then the highways and hedges outside it — Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. The original guests are the religious establishment that has had the invitation through the whole Old Testament and is declining it with polite excuses; the poor and lame of the city are the tax collectors and sinners responding to his ministry; the people beyond the walls are the Gentiles.

And the exclusion is stated without qualification: “none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.” The feast does not wait indefinitely, and the door does not stay open after the house is full.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room” is the most hopeful sentence in the parable. The servant has swept every street and every alley and brought in everyone he found, and the hall is not full. Whatever else this house is, it was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

One phrase has done real damage and should be handled plainly: “compel people to come in.” Augustine, pressed by the Donatist controversy, used it to justify the state coercing schismatics back to the church, and it was quoted for centuries afterwards in defence of forced baptisms and penal laws.

Which is exactly the opposite of force. Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will. If the verse presses anything on the church, it is urgency in persuading the people who assume the gospel cannot possibly be for them.

And “that my house may be filled” is the heart of it. Not that the food may not be wasted. He wants the room full.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!

Somebody breaks the silence, and what he says is entirely correct.

The picture he is invoking was the settled hope of Israel: the great feast on the mountain, when the LORD of hosts would spread a banquet of rich food for all peoples and swallow up death for ever (Isa. 25:6-8). Every devout Jew at that table believed it and looked forward to it.

So why does Jesus answer him with a parable about people who refuse an invitation?

Listen to the sentence again and the reason surfaces. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense — blessed is everyone who will eat. Nobody in the room is implicated by it. It is the kind of thing a man says at a dinner table when the conversation has become uncomfortable and he wants to return it to safe and elevating ground.

And the timing gives it away. Jesus has just told this room to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them. Both remarks were about this table, tonight. What comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come.

It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

Which is a manoeuvre worth recognising, because it is very hard to object to. Nothing false has been said. The speaker has agreed enthusiastically with the general direction of everything, and in doing so has moved the entire discussion somewhere it can cost him nothing.

Jesus's reply changes the tense. The parable that follows is not about who will be blessed at a future feast. It is about a banquet that is ready now, and a servant already at the door, and a set of men who all had something else on.

The man wanted to talk about the guest list of the kingdom. He is about to be told that the invitations have gone out and the replies are coming in.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man once gave a great banquet and invited many.

Note the two stages, because the custom matters and the parable turns on it.

In that world a formal banquet involved two invitations. The first went out well in advance, and it was accepted or declined then — the host needed to know the numbers before he killed the animals, since an ox fed a hundred and could not be stored. The second was sent on the day, when everything was ready, to tell the guests who had already accepted that it was time to come.

So the people in this story are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They said yes weeks ago. The host has bought and slaughtered on the strength of it, and the food is on the table.

And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, Come, for everything is now ready.

That is the second summons, and it is worth hearing what it actually says.

Not would you consider coming? Not are you free? Everything is now ready — the work is done, the cost has been met, the table is laid, and the only thing missing is the guests.

Which is the gospel in six words, and it is why the parable is not really about hospitality at all. The invitation Jesus brings is never an invitation to do something. It is the announcement that something has been done and is finished, and that the only remaining question is whether a man will come and sit down.

And notice who carries it. Not the host. A servant, sent out on foot to the houses of men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own.

That is the shape of every gospel errand since. The servant does not prepare the feast, cannot add to it, and has nothing to offer but the message that it is ready — and the message is the whole of his commission.

The parable has not yet mentioned refusal. At this point in the story there is a full table, a completed preparation, and a host who has gone to considerable expense on the strength of a promise.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all alike began to make excuses.

All alike — with one accord, as though it had been arranged. And these are men who had already accepted.

Three are given as samples, and the striking thing about them is that not one is disreputable.

I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it.

Property — and the transaction is already complete. He has bought it, which in that world meant he had seen it; nobody purchased land unexamined. Going out to look at it now is pleasure, not necessity, and it will still be there tomorrow.

I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them.

Business, and the same shape. Five yoke is a substantial holding — a man farming on that scale is prosperous. He has bought them and now wants to try them out, which again could be done any morning that week.

I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.

Family, and this one is different in tone. The first two say please have me excused, which is at least polite. This one does not ask. He states it as a fact: I cannot come.

And there was a legal provision he may be leaning on — a newly married man was exempt from military service and public duty for a year (Deut. 24:5). But a banquet is not a war, and the law he is standing on was given to protect a marriage, not to excuse a man from an evening out.

Property, work, family. Every one of them a good thing; not one of them a sin.

Which is the point, and it is why the parable is more searching than a story about wicked men would have been. Nobody here says I do not want to come. Nobody attacks the host. They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.

That is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say I refuse Christ. A great many say not now — there is something I have to deal with first, and go on saying it, politely, for forty years.

And Jesus classifies that answer without hesitation. It is not a postponement. It is the refusal.
verseByVerse.note: The law excused a newly married man from war for a year — but not from a feast.

parallels.desc: a newly married man free at home one year

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry.

The anger is worth stopping at rather than hurrying past, because it is the only emotion attributed to the host in the whole parable and it is easily made into something it is not.

It is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. Consider what has actually happened. He has been given his guests' word. He has spent accordingly — and in that economy a great banquet meant slaughtered animals that could not be kept, so the cost was already unrecoverable. Then, on the day, with the food on the table, every one of them sent back a message about a field.

What has been refused is not an evening's entertainment. It is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual.

So the anger is the proper response of generosity treated as an inconvenience, and it belongs in the parable because Jesus is describing something true about God. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved.

Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.

And then the astonishing turn: the anger does not cancel the banquet. It redirects it.

Quickly — the food is ready and the evening is going ahead. The streets and lanes of the city — the public thoroughfares and the narrow back alleys, which is where a man goes to find people who have nowhere else to be.

And the four categories are the same four Jesus gave the host eight verses earlier: invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind (v. 13).

Which is the parable's quiet accusation, delivered to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. God does exactly what he has told them to do. The people who cannot repay him are the ones who end up at the table — not as a second-best arrangement forced on him by circumstances, but because that was always the kind of guest list he wanted, and the men reclining in that Pharisee's dining room had already declined to draw one up.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.

The most hopeful sentence in the parable, and it is spoken by the servant.

He has swept the city — every street and every alley — and brought in everyone he found, and the hall is not full. Whatever else this house is, it was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled.

Now he is sent outside the city altogether. The highways are the roads between towns; the hedges are the field boundaries where a man with no roof sleeps. These are not the poor of the city. These are people with no address at all — and, to the men listening, they are foreigners.

One phrase here has done real damage and should be handled plainly: compel people to come in. Augustine, pressed by the Donatist controversy, used this line to justify the state coercing schismatics back to the church, and it was quoted for centuries afterwards in defence of forced baptisms and penal laws.

It will not carry that weight. The compulsion is urging — pressing, insisting — and the setting is the ordinary courtesy of that world, where a man summoned from a hedgerow to a nobleman's banquet would assume a mistake had been made and would need pressing hard before he believed the invitation was meant for him. The compulsion in view is a servant taking a beggar by the arm and saying: no, truly, he means you.

Which is exactly the opposite of force. Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will — the whole grief of the story is a master who will not do that.

That my house may be filled. There is the whole heart of it. Not that the food may not be wasted. He wants the room full.

For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.

And the last line is spoken past the servant, in the plural, to somebody else — which is Jesus stepping out of the parable and addressing the dinner party he is sitting at.
verseByVerse.note: “Compel” means press them to come — the invitation is so generous it must be urged.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Great crowds are travelling with him, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel — which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a following.

“Hate” is Semitic idiom for loving less by comparison, and the usage is well attested: Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah,” and in the next verse Leah is described as “hated” (Gen. 29:30-31). Matthew records the same saying in the plainer form — “whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

The idiom explains the word, but the softer reading is not a rescue operation; it is the only one the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity — when the scribes devised Corban to avoid supporting aged parents, he called it making void the word of God (Mark 7:9-13), which is precisely the manoeuvre a literal reading of this verse would license. He kept the commandment himself in his last hours, giving his mother to John (John 19:26-27). And Paul states it flatly: a man who does not provide for his household “has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

And note the last name on the list, which governs the rest: “and even his own life.” Family is not being singled out for sacrifice; the self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation.

The cross image was not a metaphor to that crowd. A cross-bearer was a specific sight: a condemned man, already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets, with the jeering going on around him. It carries finality, shame, and submission — and the man saying it was going to do it himself within the year.

Then two parables, both beginning “sit down first.” The tower is probably a farm watchtower, not a monument, and the failure is public and permanent: an abandoned foundation sits in the field for as long as anybody remembers, and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say. The king's case adds a third option the builder does not have — sue for peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cost teaching is addressed to those already following, already enthusiastic, already in the crowd. They are not being warned before they commit; they are being warned that what they think they have committed to may not be what discipleship requires. The danger is not the uncommitted outsider but the enthusiastic follower who has not counted the cost.

He is not recruiting. He has just watched thousands attach themselves to his procession and his response is to tell them to stop and calculate — the exact opposite of every technique for gathering a following that has ever been used. A crowd that has not counted the cost is not an asset; it is a field full of abandoned foundations waiting to happen.

The king's parable changes the register. The builder's alternatives are to finish or be mocked; the king can send a delegation and ask for terms. And who is the greater king in that picture? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. What is left is the delegation — going out, while there is still distance, and asking for terms. That is not defeat in this parable; it is the only wise move on the board, and it is what the counting of the cost is actually for.

“Renounce” is not primarily get rid of but let go of: a man at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind.
verseByVerse.examples:
What the hate-saying means is a matter of collision, not everyday temperature. Most of the time there is no conflict at all — loving Christ makes a man a better son, husband and father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured: when following Jesus will cost you your family's approval, or your inheritance, or your place at their table.

If you are living inside that collision, take two things from it. The cost is real and Jesus never pretends otherwise — he has already said he came to divide households (12:51-53), and he says this to a crowd, not to specialists; the grief you feel is not a sign you have done something wrong. And the command does not license coldness. Nothing here permits writing your family off, arguing at every meal, or making your faith a weapon. You go on loving them, and usually better than before; you simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ.

“Renounce all that he has” is comprehensive in a way that goes past property — reputation, plans, the rights a man believes his circumstances have granted him, the future he has drawn up. Here is a test that is not about percentages: think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the hardest to lose — the thing quietly filed as not up for discussion. Whatever came to mind has not been renounced.

And the salt saying is the chapter's last word on what a half-committed disciple is for. The salt of Palestine was gathered from Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum; if the sodium leached out with damp it left a white powder that looked exactly like salt and did nothing. Still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt — and it has stopped working.

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them.

The setting is the point. He has an enormous following, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel — which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a crowd.

If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.

Hate is Semitic idiom for loving less by comparison, and the usage is well attested in the Old Testament: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and in the next verse the text says Leah was hated (Gen. 29:30-31). Matthew records the same saying in the plainer form: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37).

The idiom explains the word, but a reader may still suspect the explanation of being convenient — a hard saying softened because we do not like it. So it is worth showing that the softer reading is not a rescue operation but the only one the rest of Scripture will allow.

The same Lord who says this upheld the fifth commandment and enforced it with unusual severity. When the scribes had devised Corban — a way of declaring money dedicated to God so that it need not be spent supporting aged parents — Jesus called it making void the word of God by their tradition (Mark 7:9-13). That is precisely the manoeuvre a literal reading of this verse would license, and he condemned it in the strongest terms he ever used about religious practice.

He also kept the commandment himself at the last possible moment: dying, in his last hours, he arranged for his mother's care and gave her to John (John 19:26-27). And Paul states the principle flatly: anyone who does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Tim. 5:8).

A man who neglects his family in order to serve Jesus more freely has not obeyed this verse. He has broken a commandment that Jesus defended.

What the saying does mean is a matter of collision, not of everyday temperature. Most of the time there is no conflict at all — loving Christ makes a man a better son, a better husband, a better father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured: when following Jesus will cost you your family's approval, or your inheritance, or your place at their table.

And note the last name on the list, which governs the rest: and even his own life. Family is not being singled out for sacrifice. The self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation of the two.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Matthew’s parallel says “loves father or mother more than me.”

parallels.desc: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — “Leah was hated”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

He has said this before, after Peter's confession (9:23), and there it was daily. Here it is put differently: not take up but bear, and not his cross but his own cross.

Both changes are worth having.

Bear is the ordinary word for carrying a load — not a single act of lifting but the sustained business of walking under a weight. And his own makes it particular. There is no generic cross issued to disciples in one size. Each man carries the one that has his name on it, and it will not look like anybody else's.

The image itself was not a metaphor to that crowd, and it has been worn smooth by two thousand years of use. A cross-bearer in the Roman world was a specific sight: a condemned man, already sentenced, carrying the crossbeam of his own execution through the streets to the place where he would be nailed to it, with the jeering going on all around him. Everyone in that crowd had seen it, probably more than once.

So the picture is not hardship. It is a man walking to his death in public, and it carries three things.

It carries finality. Nobody carrying a crossbeam is coming back down that road. The sentence has been passed.

It carries shame. Crucifixion was designed to be degrading; the Romans reserved it for slaves and rebels, and Roman citizens were exempt. The walk was part of the punishment.

And it carries submission. A man carrying his cross has stopped fighting. Whatever else is true of him, he is going where he is being taken.

Which is why this saying and the last one belong together. To hate your own life is not an inward feeling; this is what it looks like on the road, and there is nothing romantic in it.

And there is one thing more, which the crowd could not yet have known. The man saying it was going to do it himself within the year — through those same streets, condemned, shamed, submitting.

He never asks anyone to walk a road he has not walked first.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?

Having said what discipleship costs, he insists that people work out whether they can pay.

The tower is probably a farm building — the watchtower in a vineyard, for guarding the crop at harvest. Not a great civic monument; an ordinary piece of work that an ordinary landowner might undertake.

And the verb is sit down. Not consider in passing. Stop, sit, and do the arithmetic before the first stone is laid.

Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, This man began to build and was not able to finish.

The failure described is public and permanent. An abandoned foundation does not go away. It sits in the field, visible from the road, for as long as anybody in the district remembers — and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say, which is the detail that makes it sting.

Now, this is a startling thing to say to a crowd that is following him, and it needs to be taken at face value before it is softened.

He is not recruiting. He has just watched thousands of people attach themselves to his procession, and his response is to tell them to stop and calculate whether they can afford it — which is the exact opposite of every technique for gathering a following that has ever been used.

And the reason is that he is not after numbers. A crowd that has not counted the cost is not an asset; it is a field full of abandoned foundations waiting to happen, and every one of them will be quoted against him by people who watched.

Which has something uncomfortable to say about how conversions are sometimes sought. There is a kind of appeal that works by keeping the cost out of sight until the decision is made — get them in, and explain later. Jesus does the reverse, in public, to the largest crowd he ever had.

The counting is not meant to deter anybody. It is meant to make the commitment real, so that what begins actually gets finished — and so that the tower, when it is up, is a witness rather than a joke.
verseByVerse.note: A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm.

verseByVerse.quote: Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?

The second parable is the same lesson from the opposite direction, and the change of scale is deliberate: from a farmer with a half-built shed to a king with an army, from money to survival.

Sit down first again. The same phrase as the builder's, and the same instruction: do the sum before you move.

And the odds are exact — ten thousand against twenty thousand. Not hopeless, but outnumbered two to one, which is the kind of arithmetic that requires an honest man to face a difficult conclusion.

And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

Here the two parables part company, and the difference is the whole point.

The builder's alternatives are to finish or to be mocked. The king has a third option, and it is the one Jesus names: he can sue for peace. He sends envoys before the armies are in sight of each other, and asks what the terms are.

Which changes the register of the passage entirely. The first parable asks have you got what it takes? This one asks a different question, and the honest answer is no.

Because who is the greater king in this picture? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size, in a chapter about what it costs to follow Jesus, is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. He cannot. Nobody can.

What is left is the delegation — going out, while there is still distance between you, and asking for terms.

And that is not defeat in this parable. It is the only wise move on the board, and it is the one the king is commended for making. The disaster is not surrender; the disaster is a man who marches out with ten thousand against twenty thousand because he never sat down and did the sum.

Which is what the counting of the cost is actually for. It is not to establish that you can afford discipleship. It is to bring you to the point of sending the delegation.

verseByVerse.quote: So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.

The so therefore ties this to both parables. This is the conclusion the builder and the king were drawn for, and it is the third time in eight verses that the phrase cannot be my disciple has fallen.

The verb is apotassetai, and it is worth having exactly. In ordinary Greek it meant to take leave of somebody — to say goodbye, to detach oneself from. Luke uses it that way five chapters back, of the man who wanted to say farewell to those at home (9:61).

So it is not primarily get rid of. It is let go of. The picture is of a man saying goodbye at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind.

Which is the difference between this and a rule about liquidation. Jesus is not requiring every disciple to sell up; Luke himself will not allow that reading.
