Zacchaeus gives half and is told salvation has come to his house (19:8-9). The women of 8:3 funded the ministry out of means they must still have had. Peter's rebuke to Ananias turns on the fact that the property was his to keep (Acts 5:4).

What is required is that a man stop holding.

And all that he has is comprehensive in a way that goes past property. It reaches the reputation, the plans, the rights a man believes he has been granted by his circumstances, the future he has drawn up. Everything the sentence this is mine can be said about.

Here is a test that can be run without much difficulty, and it is not about percentages. Think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the thing you would find hardest to lose — the thing you have quietly filed as not up for discussion.

Whatever came to mind has not been renounced. It is still being held, and this verse says so.

And there is a mercy in the severity, which the chapter has already supplied. A man who has let go of everything cannot be robbed, cannot be blackmailed, and cannot be moved from the low seat because he has nothing to defend. The renunciation is not a fee charged at the door. It is what makes a man free enough to walk through it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored?

The saying closes the chapter, and it is not a change of subject. The crowd has just been told what discipleship costs; this is what happens to a disciple who does not pay it.

Salt in that world was genuinely valuable: it preserved meat, seasoned food, and was scattered on the dunghill and dug into fields as a fertiliser. It was one of the few things a poor household could not do without.

Can salt actually lose its taste? Pure sodium chloride cannot. But the salt of Palestine was not pure — it was gathered from the Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum and other minerals, and if the sodium leached out with damp it left a white powder that looked exactly like salt and did nothing at all.

Which is the whole force of the image. This is not salt that has disappeared. It is salt that is still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt — and it has stopped working.

It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile.

Luke's detail is the sharpest of the three Gospels. Even the dunghill will not take it. Whatever else can be thrown on a manure heap and do some good, this cannot.

It is thrown away.

And that is a fair description of what a half-committed disciple is for. Not wicked. Not an enemy of anybody. Simply useless for the one thing that was the point of him — because a follower of Christ who has kept his own life, his own family loyalties and his own possessions out of the arrangement has retained the appearance and lost the function.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

Luke says he called out the same words after the parable of the soils (8:8), and it is the same demand. Anybody can take in a saying about salt. What is being asked for is the hearing that goes past the surface and lets the thing in.

And it is a good sentence to end on, because it hands the whole chapter back to the reader. There is nothing more to explain. A man has counted a cost or he has not; a table serves people who can repay or people who cannot; a seat has been grasped or given up.

Can a true Christian lose his saltiness and be thrown away? Arminian Christians read the verse that way. The more likely reading is that Jesus is warning those who follow at a distance without counting the cost: a disciple in name who will not carry his cross shows that he never truly had the salt (cf. 1 John 2:19; John 15:6). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which Christ keeps his true disciples faithful.

The teaching has been given. What is left is the hearing.
verseByVerse.note: Impure salt could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

14.text: <sup>1</sup> One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. <sup>3</sup> And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?” <sup>4</sup> But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?” <sup>6</sup> And they could not reply to these things. <sup>7</sup> Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, <sup>8</sup> “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, <sup>9</sup> and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. <sup>10</sup> But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. <sup>11</sup> For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>12</sup> He said also to the man who had invited him, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. <sup>13</sup> But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, <sup>14</sup> and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” <sup>15</sup> When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” <sup>16</sup> But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. <sup>17</sup> And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ <sup>18</sup> But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ <sup>19</sup> And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ <sup>20</sup> And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ <sup>21</sup> So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’ <sup>22</sup> And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ <sup>23</sup> And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. <sup>24</sup> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’” <sup>25</sup> Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, <sup>26</sup> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <sup>27</sup> Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <sup>28</sup> For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? <sup>29</sup> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, <sup>30</sup> saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ <sup>31</sup> Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? <sup>32</sup> And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. <sup>33</sup> So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. <sup>34</sup> “Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? <sup>35</sup> It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological heart of Luke's Gospel — the chapter that more than any other earns Luke the title “the Gospel of grace.” It contains three parables told in response to a single complaint: the Pharisees and scribes grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” The three parables are Jesus's answer to the grumbling — not an argument but a story, or rather three stories that together form a single, overwhelming answer to the question: why does the Son of God eat with sinners? Because this is what God is like. He is the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep. He is the woman who lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house until she finds the one lost coin. He is the father who runs to meet his returning son while he is still a long way off.

The three parables form a crescendo: from a sheep (something lost through its own wandering nature), to a coin (something lost through its owner's carelessness, possibly), to a son (someone lost through deliberate, calculated rebellion). The lostness becomes more personal, more chosen, more culpable at each step — and the joy at the finding becomes more extravagant, more communal, more absolutely centred on grace rather than on the condition of the lost. The sheep does nothing to return; it is carried home. The coin does nothing; it is found. The son turns around and prepares a speech about his unworthiness — and the father interrupts the speech with the best robe and the ring and the sandals and the fatted calf. The grace always exceeds the repentance.

The chapter's most searching moment is the elder son (vv. 25–32) — the one who has never left, who has served faithfully, who is furious at the welcome given to the prodigal. He is the Pharisees in the parable — the ones whose complaint prompted all three parables. And the father's final words to him are the most tender and most open-ended in the chapter: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” The chapter ends without the elder son's response. Luke does not tell us whether the Pharisees came in to the feast. The question is left open — which is where Jesus leaves the invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything in this chapter depends on the first two verses. Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to hear him — a settled pattern rather than one occasion — and the Pharisees and scribes grumble.

Grumbling is what Israel did over and over in the wilderness (Ex. 16:2, 7-8). It is not argument; it is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

“This man receives sinners and eats with them” is meant as an accusation and is completely accurate. The charge is not that Jesus preaches to sinners — nobody objected to that. It is the table. A shared meal in that world was the single clearest social statement a person could make about who his people were, and he was making it, often enough for everyone to have noticed.

What follows is his answer: three parables, all about something lost, all ending in a party — and the charge is never denied. Luke calls them one parable (v.3), singular, which is worth noticing. They are one argument in three movements.

He begins by putting his critics inside the story. “What man of you” compels agreement: any shepherd here would do this. He is not defending an eccentric practice but describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to.

The detail is realistic. A hundred sheep is a substantial flock, likely with hired help, so leaving the ninety-nine “in the open country” is not the recklessness it sounds. And a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct, and a separated animal will lie down and refuse to move.

“Until he finds it” governs the whole search — there is no clause allowing the shepherd to come home empty. And he does not drive the animal back; an exhausted sheep cannot be herded, so he hoists seventy or eighty pounds across his shoulders and carries it home over the same country he searched, rejoicing.

Then he throws a party, over one sheep out of a hundred, quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.
verseByVerse.theology:
The shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine is the most dramatic possible image of divine initiative. The sheep does not seek the shepherd; the shepherd seeks the sheep. This is the consistent pattern of grace: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19); “no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The lost sheep contributes nothing to its rescue — it is found, lifted, carried.

Note also where the word repents falls. It appears in the application, not in the story. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried. The repentance and the being-found are the same event seen from two sides.

The phrase “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” can be taken two ways and both are held by serious readers. It may be straightforward: there really are people already safe in the fold, and no slight is intended.

But remember who Jesus is answering. On the lips of the men grumbling at verse 2, “righteous persons who need no repentance” is exactly how they would have described themselves — and by the end of this chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father's house. Read against that ending, the phrase carries a dry edge: there is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine, not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ninety-nine left “in the open country” looks irresponsible, and it reveals something about the community that belongs to the shepherd: they are safe in his care even while he is searching for the one. The gathered community is not threatened by the shepherd's pursuit of the wanderer; it is the context from which he goes and to which he brings the found sheep.

The church that begrudges the energy spent on the lost has misunderstood its own situation. It was once the one, and is now among the ninety-nine.

And the arithmetic of the parable is the thing to sit with, because it is deliberately disproportionate. Heaven does the sum the shepherd did. One sheep out of a hundred, and the whole neighbourhood is called in.

If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, it is worth asking which number you have quietly assigned yourself. The men it was told to were quite certain they were among the ninety-nine, and the parable was constructed so that they would agree with every word of it right up to the moment it closed on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in this chapter depends on these two verses, and a reader who skips them will misread all three parables.

Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him.

They were drawing near, and kept doing it. This is not one occasion. It is a settled pattern, and by this point in the ministry it has become the most conspicuous fact about him.

Tax collectors were Jews who had contracted with Rome to collect its revenue, and were regarded as traitors as well as extortioners; a tax collector was barred from serving as a witness in court. Sinners is broader and vaguer — the word covered the openly immoral, but it was also used by the scrupulous of anybody who did not keep the purity code, which meant most ordinary working people.

And note why they came: to hear him. Not for bread, not for healing. They came to listen to a preacher, which is the last thing anyone would have predicted of that crowd.

And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled.

The verb Luke chooses is the one the Greek Old Testament uses over and over of Israel in the wilderness — the people grumbled against Moses about the water and the bread (Ex. 16:2, 7-8). It is not argument. It is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

This man receives sinners and eats with them.

It is meant as an accusation, and it is completely accurate.

Receives means welcomes, takes to oneself. And eats with them was the part that mattered most, because a shared table in that world was not a casual thing. To eat with a man was to accept him — his standing, his company, his reputation attached to yours for the evening. It was the single clearest social statement a person could make about who his people were.

So the charge is not that Jesus preaches to sinners; nobody objected to that. It is that he sits down and eats with them, and does it often enough for everyone to have noticed.

What follows is his answer. Three parables, all about something lost, all ending in a party — and the charge is never denied.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together signalled acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he told them this parable.

Singular. Luke calls the whole of what follows one parable, which is worth noticing, because three stories are coming. They are one argument in three movements.

What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost?

He begins by putting his critics inside the story. What man of you — and the question is framed to compel agreement. Any shepherd here would do this; the answer is obvious.

Which is the move that traps them. He is not defending an eccentric practice. He is describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to.

The detail is realistic. A hundred sheep is a substantial flock, likely with hired help, which is why leaving the ninety-nine in the open country is not the recklessness it sounds — they are in pasture, and there is somebody with them. And a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct, and a separated animal will lie down and refuse to move.

Until he finds it.

Four words that govern the whole search. Not until dark. Not until it seems hopeless. There is no clause in this sentence that allows the shepherd to come home empty.

And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.

He does not drive it. A sheep that has been lost for a day or two on rough ground is exhausted, and a frightened animal cannot be herded — so the shepherd hoists it across his neck, front legs held in one hand and back legs in the other, and carries seventy or eighty pounds home over the same country he searched.

And the word Luke attaches to that is rejoicing. Not exhausted, not relieved, though he must have been both. The whole weight of the animal that caused the trouble is on his shoulders, and he is glad about it all the way home.

parallels.desc: I myself will search for my sheep
he will carry them in his bosom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.

He throws a party. Over one sheep, out of a hundred, and quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth.

That is the third thing the shepherd does that nobody would predict, and it is the one that answers the grumbling at verse 2. The Pharisees have objected to a man who eats with sinners. Jesus has just described a man who, having recovered what was lost, cannot keep it to himself and calls in the neighbours for a meal.

The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.

Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.

And there is the application, and it is deliberately disproportionate. Heaven does the arithmetic the shepherd did.

Note also that the word repents appears here for the first time in the parable — and it appears in the application, not the story. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried. The repentance and the being-found are the same event seen from two sides.

The phrase ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance should be handled with care, because it can be taken two ways and both are held by serious readers. It may be straightforward: there really are people already safe in the fold, and no slight is intended.

But remember who Jesus is answering. On the lips of the men grumbling at verse 2, righteous persons who need no repentance is exactly how they would have described themselves — and by the end of this chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father's house, refusing to come in.

Read against that ending, the phrase carries a dry edge. There is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine — not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.

If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, it is worth asking which number you have quietly assigned yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman — deliberate, and not likely to be accidental in the Gospel that records more about women than any other. God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a housewife on her hands and knees.

The coins are drachmas, each roughly a day's wage. Ten is not a fortune, but for a peasant household it is ten days' living. It may be more serious still: in some parts of that world a woman's ten coins were her dowry, strung together and worn on her headdress — both her security and the visible sign of her marriage, so that the lost coin is a gap in something she wears.

Every detail of the search is exact for the house she lived in. A peasant home had few windows and a beaten earth floor, so even at midday the corners were dark — hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying; it is dragging a broom across the floor to hear the coin move, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

“Until she finds it” is the shepherd's clause again, and the same refusal to stop. And the ending is the same: friends and neighbours called in, and a party quite possibly costing more than a drachma.

One difference from the first parable deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin can do nothing at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position. Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found — and it made almost none — the coin makes less.

The application changes in two small ways. The tense moves from future to present: not “there will be joy” but “there is joy,” now, and every time. And the location becomes “before the angels of God” — which puts the angels in the position of onlookers, watching somebody else be glad.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whose joy are the angels watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already answered it. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted.

So the picture is this: somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round — and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

That is a very long way from the God the grumblers at verse 2 were defending, and a long way from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable, and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

The angels are elsewhere described as “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). They are not detached observers of the gospel; they are invested in its outcomes. The finding of one lost sinner is a cosmic event, celebrated at every level of the created order that understands what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's method is the model of the kind of prayer and pastoral work that refuses to give up. She does not glance round and conclude it is not there. She lights the lamp — creating the conditions for seeing clearly. She sweeps — removing what might be covering it. And she seeks diligently until the finding.

Intercession for the lost follows the same method: create the conditions for light, remove what obscures the gospel, and keep at it. And the sweeping is worth holding on to, because it is the least glamorous part and the part that actually finds the coin. It is repetitive, unremarkable work done on hands and knees in a dark room, and it is how the thing was recovered.

And the completeness of the coin's helplessness is a comfort rather than an insult. Anyone who has watched a person they love become entirely unable to help themselves — through addiction, or illness of the mind, or a hardness they cannot seem to break — is looking at the coin. It cannot call out. It cannot move towards the light.

What the parable says is that this changes nothing about the search.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it?

The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman — which is deliberate, and which Luke, who records more about women than any other evangelist, is not likely to have included by accident. God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a housewife on her hands and knees.

The coins are drachmas, each roughly a day's wage. Ten of them is not a fortune, but for a peasant household it is ten days' living, and the loss of one is serious.

It may be more serious still. In some parts of that world a woman's ten coins were her dowry, strung together and worn on her headdress — both her security and the visible sign of her marriage. On that reading the lost coin is not merely money. It is a gap in something she wears.

Does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently.

Every detail is exact for the house she lived in. A peasant home had few windows and a beaten earth floor, so even at midday the corners were dark — hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying; it is dragging a broom across the floor to hear the coin move, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

Until she finds it. The same clause as the shepherd's, and the same refusal to stop.

And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.

And the same ending: a party, and quite possibly one costing more than a drachma.

One difference from the first parable is worth registering, because it deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin cannot do anything at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position.

Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found — and it made almost none — the coin makes less. It is simply lost, and then it is simply found, and everything in between was done by somebody with a lamp.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius — about a day’s wage. Houses were dark, with small windows and earthen floors.

verseByVerse.quote: Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.

The same application as the sheep, with two changes, and both repay attention.

The first is the tense. Over the sheep it was there will be more joy in heaven — future. Here it is there is joy — present. Not a celebration held later when the accounts are settled. It is happening now, and it happens every time.

The second is the location: before the angels of God.

That is an odd way to put it, and it is odd on purpose. He does not say the angels rejoice, though Scripture elsewhere shows them singing at creation and worshipping at the throne. He says there is joy in front of them — which puts the angels in the position of onlookers watching somebody else be glad.

Whose joy are they watching?

The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already told us. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. And in the parable still to come, a father will run down a road and kill the best animal on the farm. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted.

So the picture is this. Somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round — and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

That is a very long way from the God the grumblers at verse 2 were defending, and it is a long way from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable, and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself.

There is a search, and then there is a party.

And the arithmetic never changes. One sheep out of a hundred; one coin out of ten; one sinner, of no particular importance to anybody, whose repentance stops heaven in its tracks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“There was a man who had two sons.” The story is announced as being about two — worth remembering, since it is usually preached as though it were about one.

The younger son's request is difficult to convey in its full shock. An estate passed at the father's death; a son had no standing to ask early, and the request carried an unmistakable meaning: I want what I will get when you are dead, and I do not want to wait for you to die. And he calls it “the share that is coming to me” — not a gift but something owed.

The father grants it without a recorded word. Note the plural: “he divided his property between them.” Two-thirds went to the elder son on the spot, and he never asked — which will matter enormously when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything.

Liquidating that land was a public act. Land in Israel was the family's portion in the inheritance of God's people, with laws to keep it in the family (Lev. 25:23-28), so the whole district watched the transactions and drew the obvious conclusion. And the far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved.

The descent is calibrated: the money goes, then a famine removes any possibility of recovery, then he attaches himself to a Gentile who sends him out of sight to feed pigs — the floor, for a son of Israel — and then he is hungry enough to envy the carob pods and cannot get them. “No one gave him anything.” The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

“He came to himself” is exact. He does not become someone else; he comes round, the way a man does after a blow to the head — which says that everything from verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and repentance is sanity returning.

His prepared speech gets two things right and one wrong. He names it as sin, against God first and his father second. Then he proposes to work his way back as a hired labourer — he has understood his guilt and entirely misunderstood his father.

And the father, seeing him a long way off, runs.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father running is the most shocking thing in the parable. An elderly man of standing in a Middle Eastern village did not run; it required gathering up the robe and exposing the legs, which was humiliating, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. He deliberately and publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village.

And he may have had a further reason. The boy had sold family land to Gentiles and lost it, and could expect a hostile reception. The father reaches him first, on the road, before anyone else can get to him. The same logic runs through the fattened calf: everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father's verdict on his son, and it is very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Every gift is a specific restoration. The best robe is the finest in the house and probably the father's own — so anyone entering afterwards sees a son of the house and nothing else. The signet ring is authority, the instrument for sealing contracts in the father's name, handed to the one member of the family who has proved beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money. Slaves went barefoot; the shoes settle the question the boy had rehearsed all the way home.

An objection has to be met here, because it is raised by critics and by thoughtful believers alike: there is no atonement in this parable. No sacrifice, no blood, no mediator — the father simply forgives. Some have built on that silence the claim that the doctrine of atonement was a later invention laid over a simpler gospel.

But the parable is not costless; we have been reading it from the son's side. The younger son's portion was real property, squandered and not coming back — the father is permanently poorer for having let him go. And the robe, the ring, the sandals and the calf all come out of what remains. The father does not forgive at no cost. He absorbs the entire cost himself, in silence, and never once mentions it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The boy did not come home because he missed his father. He came home because he was hungry, and the text is entirely candid about it — so a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold. I turned to God when my marriage collapsed. I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real?

Watch what the father does with it. He does not interrogate the motive or wait at the gate to establish whether the boy has come for love or for supper. He sees him a long way off and runs. Luke has been showing this all through: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes came out of sheer misery and went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal on the cross came with a few hours left and nothing else on earth to try (23:42-43).

Nobody's repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace — the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards.

Then the elder brother, and the parable's real target. He describes his life in his father's house as service — “these many years I have served you” — and thinks he is stating a credential. He wanted a goat to celebrate with his friends; even his imagined party does not have his father in it. And the complaint is false: two-thirds of that estate had been legally his since verse 12, and he could have killed a goat any week he liked.

He cannot say “my brother.” The servant managed it without effort; the elder son says “this son of yours.” And he supplies the prostitutes, which Luke never mentioned and which he was several days' journey away from witnessing — resentment filling in the blanks in the worst available way and calling it honesty.

The parable then stops. A man standing in the dark outside a lit house, being begged by his father, with the music still playing. Jesus told this to the men who grumbled at verse 2, and left them on the doorstep. The ending was theirs to write.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man who had two sons.

Eight words, and everything in the chapter has been leading to them. Note that the story is announced as being about a man and two sons — which is worth remembering when the parable is preached, as it usually is, as though it were about one.

And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.

It is difficult to convey how shocking that sentence was, and the shock is the doorway into the whole parable.

An estate passed at the father's death. A father could distribute property early, but the son had no standing to ask, and the request carried an unmistakable meaning: I want what I will get when you are dead, and I do not want to wait for you to die. One rabbinic writer of a later period discusses a man who divided his estate in his lifetime and treats it as folly. Nobody treats the son's request as normal.

And the word he uses is careful. He asks for the share of property that is coming to me — which he calls his by right. He has not asked for a gift. He has asked for what he considers already owed.

What he is really asking for is the father's death without the inconvenience of a funeral.

And he divided his property between them.

And the father does it, without a recorded word.

That silence is one of the most extraordinary things in the parable. There is no argument, no attempt to talk him out of it, no condition attached. The father hears the request, understands exactly what it means, and grants it.

Note also the plural: between them. The elder son is given his share at the same time, and he never asked. Two thirds of the estate goes to him on the spot — which will matter enormously at the end of the story, when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything.

Everything both sons will need is already in their hands by the end of verse 12. What remains to be seen is what kind of man each of them is when he has it.
verseByVerse.note: A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive a third — the elder son had a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country.

Not many days — he did not even wait. The property had to be liquidated first, which takes some doing, and he clearly set about it at once.

And it is worth registering what that liquidation would have meant in that village. Land in Israel was not merely an asset; it was the family's portion in the inheritance of God's people, held in trust across generations, and there were laws to keep it in the family (Lev. 25:23-28). To sell up was a public act, and the neighbours would have watched every transaction and drawn the obvious conclusion about what the boy thought of his father.

By the time he left, the whole district knew.

Gathered all he had — everything convertible, converted. Nothing left behind that could bring him back.

Took a journey into a far country.

Distance was the point. Not the next town, where he would be known; a far country, where nobody had heard of his father and nobody would report on him.

Which is the honest anatomy of the thing, and it is why the parable has never dated. The far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved — and every generation has its own version, and the current one has more of them than any before it.

And there he squandered his property in reckless living.

Squandered is dieskorpisen — scattered, dispersed to the winds. It is the same verb Mary sang of God scattering the proud in the thoughts of their hearts (1:51).

And reckless is asōtōs, an adverb built on a negative: literally unsavingly — without keeping anything back, without a thought for what comes next. The older versions render it riotous living, and it is a fair translation, but the root is less about vice than about the absence of any brake.

Luke does not itemise. His brother will, at the end of the chapter, and Luke does not confirm it.
verseByVerse.note: A far country is Gentile land.

parallels.desc: a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country.

Watch the sequence, because it is the ordinary sequence and it is merciless.

First the money runs out — which was always going to happen, and would have happened without a famine. Then the famine arrives on top of it, and the two together remove any possibility of recovery. A man with capital can survive a famine; a man in a famine cannot rebuild capital.

And notice how much of this he did not choose. He chose the far country and the spending. He did not choose the famine. Sin puts a man in a place where circumstance can destroy him, and then circumstance does not require his permission.

So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country.

The ESV margin gives the Greek as joined himself to, which is stronger than hired himself out. This is not applying for a post. It is a starving man fastening himself to a stranger who does not want him.

And the employer's response reads as a way of getting rid of him. He is sent to the fields, out of sight, to do the one job no Jewish boy could take.

Who sent him into his fields to feed pigs.

Pigs were unclean (Lev. 11:7), and a later rabbinic saying pronounces a curse on the man who raises them. For a son of Israel this is the floor. There is no lower employment available anywhere in that country.

And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.

The pods are carob — the long dark seed pods of the carob tree, used as animal fodder and eaten by the very poor in hard times. Coarse, barely nourishing, and he cannot get them.

Because that is what the last clause means. He is not eating them; he is longing to. Even the pig food is not his to take, and there is nobody in that whole country who will hand him anything at all.

He left home with a third of an estate, and he now ranks below the livestock.

And it is the last clause that finishes him: no one gave him anything. There were plenty of people around him while the money lasted. The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean under the law; a Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had sunk as low as possible. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he came to himself.

One of the most exact phrases in the Gospels, and it says something about sin that a great deal of preaching misses.

He does not become someone else. He comes to himself, which is what we say of a man recovering from a faint, or coming round after a blow to the head. The implication is that everything from the request in verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and that this is the boy waking up.

Sin, on this account, is not a man being true to himself. It is a man out of his mind, and repentance is sanity returning.

How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!

His first clear thought is about bread, and about his father's household — and the detail he remembers is that even the lowest grade of worker on the estate has more than enough. He is remembering his father's generosity, which is the one thing he had never valued.

I will arise and go to my father.

The decision, in eight words, and there is no agonising. He has been in the pigsty long enough.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.

The prepared speech has three parts, and the first two are exactly right. He names it as sin, not misfortune. He names it against God first and his father second, which is the correct order (cf. Ps. 51:4). And he concedes he has forfeited the standing of a son, which he has.

The third part is where he goes wrong. Treat me as one of your hired servants — the hired servant was a day labourer, the lowest rank on an estate, hired in the morning and paid at night, not part of the household at all.

He is proposing to work his way back. He has understood his guilt and has entirely misunderstood his father.

And this raises a question that troubles more honest Christians than almost any other, so let it be answered plainly. The boy did not come home because he missed his father. He came home because he was hungry — the text is entirely candid about it. So a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold: I turned to God when my marriage collapsed. I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real, or was I just desperate?

The truth is that nobody's repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace — the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards.
verseByVerse.note: Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family.

parallels.desc: against you, you only, have I sinned

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he arose and came to his father.

Luke gives the journey half a sentence. Whatever it cost him to walk back into that village with the smell of pigs on him, past the neighbours who had watched him sell the land, it is not described.

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him.

Which tells you what the father had been doing.

You do not identify a figure at that distance unless you are looking, and you do not look unless you have been looking for a long time. Nothing in the parable says the father knew he was coming — there was no message from the far country, and the son had left with the whole of his inheritance and no intention of returning. The old man had been watching a road for a boy who had every reason never to appear on it.

And felt compassion.

The compassion that turns over inside a person. Luke uses the word at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the Samaritan seeing the beaten man (10:33), and here.

And ran.

Two words, and it is the most shocking thing in the parable.

An elderly man of standing in a Middle Eastern village did not run. Running required a man to gather up his long robe and expose his legs, which was undignified to the point of humiliation, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. Aristotle had said the great-souled man moves slowly and speaks in a deep voice.

So the father, seeing his son on the road, deliberately and publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village.

And there is a reason he might have run beyond simple joy. The boy had sold family land to Gentiles and lost it. In such a village he could expect a hostile reception — some scholars point to a later Jewish ceremony in which a community formally cut off a son who had done exactly that. If anything of that kind was waiting, the father reaches him first, on the road, before anyone else can get to him.

And embraced him and kissed him.

Literally fell on his neck. And the verb for kissing is intensive — kissed him repeatedly.

He is filthy, he stinks of a pig field, and he is ceremonially unclean. The father has him by the neck before a word has been said.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run.

parallels.desc: Esau ran to meet him and embraced him
you who once were far off

verseByVerse.quote: And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the son said to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

He gets two-thirds of the way through the speech he had rehearsed in the pigsty — and then it stops.

Compare it with what he planned in verses 18-19 and one line is missing: Treat me as one of your hired servants. The confession is delivered in full. The proposal is not.

Why not? Two readings, and both are worth having.

He may have been interrupted. He is speaking into his father's shoulder, being kissed, and the next verse begins but the father said to his servants — which reads like a man not waiting for the end of a sentence.

Or he may have stopped himself. Something happened on that road between the seeing and the embrace, and a boy who arrived planning to negotiate terms of employment may have found, with his father's arms round him, that the offer had become absurd.

Either way, the plan to work his way back never gets said out loud, and the parable is careful about that. Everything the son had worked out in the far country about how to be received is left unspoken, because it was answered before he opened his mouth.

And notice what he does keep. He does not skip the confession. He is not embraced into a situation where nothing needs to be said; he says all of it — I have sinned, and I am no longer worthy — and both statements are entirely true.

Which is the shape of real repentance and it is worth being clear about, because grace is regularly preached in a way that makes the confession unnecessary. It is not. The son says the words. What he does not get to do is set the terms on which he will be taken back.

There is only one thing a returning sinner has to bring, and he brought it: an honest account of himself. Everything else in this scene is supplied by somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the father said to his servants, Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.

He does not answer the son at all. He turns and gives orders about clothing — and every item is a restoration of something specific.

Quickly comes first, and it governs the rest. There is no interval. Nothing is put on probation; nobody is sent to wash first.

The best robe — the finest in the house, which in a household of that kind would be the father's own. The boy is dressed in his father's clothes, and the rags of the far country disappear underneath them. Anyone entering the room afterwards would see a son of the house, and would see nothing else.

A ring on his hand. Almost certainly a signet ring, carrying the family seal — the instrument by which contracts were sealed and business transacted in the father's name. It is not jewellery. It is authority, handed to the one member of the family who has demonstrated beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money.

Shoes on his feet. Slaves went barefoot; sons wore sandals. It is a small detail and it settles the question the boy had been rehearsing all the way home. He had come to ask for a place among the hired men. Before he can propose it, his father has put shoes on him.

Three things, then, and between them they restore his standing, his authority and his freedom — in that order, immediately, and without a single condition attached.

Not one of them is deserved, and everybody watching knows it. That is what makes the scene so uncomfortable and so exactly like the gospel. The father does not restore him gradually as he proves himself. He restores him completely at the gate, before the boy has done one honest day's work, and then lets him live the rest of his life as what he has been declared to be.

Does the parable teach forgiveness without atonement? No. A parable is not a full doctrine; this one shows the Father’s welcome, not how it was made possible. The father bears the cost himself, the shame of running and the loss of the inheritance. The cost of our welcome was met at the cross (Rom 3:25–26), as Jesus says at the end of this Gospel: that the Christ should suffer, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name (24:46–47).

And is the prodigal a believer who fell away? The parable is aimed at the Pharisees’ complaint about tax collectors and sinners (vv. 1–2), and the younger son stands for sinners coming home to God. He is a son throughout; the father calls him my son (v. 24). It may also comfort a believer who has wandered for a season, but it does not teach that sonship can be lost and regained.

Which is the doctrine Paul spent his letters explaining, told as a story about a coat.
verseByVerse.note: The robe honoured him, the ring gave him authority, and sandals marked a son, not a barefoot slave.

parallels.desc: Pharaoh gives Joseph his ring and garments

verseByVerse.quote: And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate.

A peasant household did not eat meat often, and a fattened calf was not ordinary meat. It was one animal, deliberately grain-fed and kept back for a single great occasion — a wedding, or a visit from someone important. Killing it fed a crowd.

So this is not a family supper. The father is calling in the village — the same village that had watched the boy sell his father's land and leave.

Which is a further piece of protection, and it is easy to miss. Everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father's verdict on his son. It becomes very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.

Twice over, and the second half of each pair is what makes the parable.

My son — the first word, and the boy had just finished saying he was no longer worthy to be called it. The father does not argue the point. He simply uses the word.

Was dead, and is alive again. Not a figure of speech reached for casually. In that culture a son who had done what this one did was reckoned dead to the family, and the father is using the household's own language and reversing it.

He was lost, and is found. And here the three parables of the chapter close into one. A sheep was lost and found; a coin was lost and found; a boy was lost and found — and every one of them ended in the same thing, which is a party.

And they began to celebrate.

Luke's phrasing is worth noticing: they began. The celebration is under way and is not finished when the chapter ends. It is still going on in the last verse, with music audible from the field, and one son standing outside it.

Somebody paid for that calf, and it was not the boy, who came up the road with nothing but the smell of pigs on him. Every single thing he receives in this scene is drawn from his father's own resources — and the father never once mentions the cost.
verseByVerse.note: A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now his older son was in the field.

The camera turns, and the second half of the parable begins. Everything from here is about the son who never left — and the chapter was announced at verse 11 as being about a man with two sons.

He is in the field, which is where he has been all day and every day. Whatever else is true of him, he is not a bad son by any ordinary measure. He is out working while his brother is being kissed at the gate.

And as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing.

He hears it before he understands it. Music from his own house, and he has no idea why.

That detail is doing work. It means nobody sent for him. A party is under way at his father's expense, involving the whole village, and the elder son of the household learns about it by getting close enough to hear the band.

And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant.

He does not go in and ask his father. He stops outside, gets hold of a servant and interrogates him.

Which is the first sign of the distance, and it is a considerable one. He is standing in his own yard, treating his own home as somewhere he needs to be briefed about before entering.

Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.

The servant's answer is entirely artless and entirely accurate, and it contains every fact the elder brother will later distort.

Your brother — the servant says it without hesitation. The elder son will refuse the word in three verses' time.

Because he has received him back safe and sound. That is the reason given, and it is worth weighing. Not because your brother repented, not because he has been forgiven. The stated cause of the celebration is simply that he is home and he is well.

A servant boy who has been in that house all his life has understood the father exactly. The son standing in the yard is about to demonstrate that he never has.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he was angry and refused to go in.

Both verbs matter and neither is a passing mood.

He was angry — a settled state rather than a flash. And he refused to go in, which is an act, and a public one. Every guest at that party knows the elder son is outside and will not come.

Consider what that does to his father in front of the village, on the one evening he had asked them all to come. The younger son had shamed him by leaving; the elder is now shaming him by standing in the yard.

And it is worth registering the symmetry the parable has been building. Two sons, both outside the father's house, both by their own decision. One went to a far country; one is standing just outside the door. The distance is not measured in miles.

His father came out and entreated him.

And for the second time in one evening, the old man leaves his house and goes out to a son who has humiliated him.

It is the same movement as the running in verse 20 — he does not summon the boy, or send a servant with a message, or wait for him to see sense. He walks out of his own celebration, in front of everybody, and goes to find him.

And entreated is a gentle word: he begged, he pleaded, he urged him. There is no command in it. The father, who has every right to order his son indoors, stands in the dark asking.

Which is the answer to anyone who reads this parable as being about the kindness of God to the disreputable and the severity of God to the religious. It is not. The father goes out twice, and the second time is harder, because the second son does not want to be found.

Whatever else the elder brother is about to say, he says it to a father who came out and asked.

And there is a warning in the staging for anyone who has ever been the one outside. Standing in the yard feels like taking a position. It usually is not; it is usually just standing in a yard, in the dark, near a house where people are happy, waiting to be persuaded to enjoy something you have already decided not to enjoy.

The father will not force him in. That is the last mercy and the hardest one — the door is open, the music is audible, the invitation has been delivered in person, and after that the yard is a choice.

verseByVerse.quote: but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command.

The word he chooses for what he has been doing is douleuō — I have slaved for you. Not lived with, not worked alongside. He describes his life in his father's house in the vocabulary of a servant, and he thinks he is stating a credential.

It is the whole tragedy in one verb. He has been a son for the entire story and has experienced it as employment.

Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.

Note the scale. He is not asking for a fattened calf; a young goat is a modest animal, and this is a small grievance carefully preserved. And note who he wanted to celebrate with: my friends. Not you. Even his imagined party does not have his father in it.

And the complaint is, as a matter of fact, false. Two-thirds of that estate had been legally his since verse 12. He could have killed a goat any week he liked. He had been living on his own property, asking permission he did not need, and resenting a father who had already given him everything.

But when this son of yours came.

He cannot say my brother. The servant managed it without effort three verses ago; the elder son says this son of yours, which puts the boy in relation to his father and cuts him out of his own family.

Who has devoured your property with prostitutes.

Luke never said that. Verse 13 says reckless living and nothing more, and the brother was several days' journey away when it happened.

He may be right. He does not know, and the detail he reaches for is the one that will do the most damage — which is what resentment does when it finally gets to speak. It fills in the blanks in the worst available way and calls it honesty.

You killed the fattened calf for him!

And there it is. Not a complaint about justice. A complaint about somebody else's welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.

The word for son here is not the ordinary one. It is teknon — child, the tender word, the one a parent uses. After everything that has just been said in the yard, the father's first word is an endearment.

You are always with me. Which was the elder son's privilege and he had experienced it as a sentence. He has had, every day for years, the one thing his brother threw away — proximity to his father — and he has been counting goats.

And all that is mine is yours. A flat statement of fact, and it demolishes the complaint. Everything remaining on that estate was already his, legally, since verse 12. There was no goat he needed permission for.

Which is the sharpest thing in the parable, and it is not aimed at the disreputable. A man can live in his Father's house for forty years, keep every rule, resent the whole arrangement, and never once take anything out of a storehouse he has always owned.

It was fitting to celebrate and be glad.

Not it was generous of me, and not I hope you will understand. Fitting — edei, the word of necessity that Luke has used all through this Gospel of what God's purpose requires. Given what has happened, a party was the only proper response, and any other response would have been wrong.

For this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.

This your brother. The elder son said this son of yours; the father hands the word back, corrected. There is only one relationship in dispute here, and it is not the one between the father and the younger boy.

And then the parable stops.

We are not told whether he went in. Luke ends the chapter with a man standing in the dark outside a lit house, being begged by his father, with the music still playing.

That is not an oversight. Jesus is telling this story to the men who grumbled at verse 2 that he receives sinners and eats with them, and he has just put them on the doorstep of the party and left them there.

The ending was theirs to write. It still is.

parallels.desc: to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants

15.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. <sup>2</sup> And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” <sup>3</sup> So he told them this parable: <sup>4</sup> “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? <sup>5</sup> And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. <sup>6</sup> And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ <sup>7</sup> Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. <sup>8</sup> “Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? <sup>9</sup> And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ <sup>10</sup> Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” <sup>11</sup> And he said, “There was a man who had two sons. <sup>12</sup> And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them. <sup>13</sup> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <sup>14</sup> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <sup>16</sup> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <sup>17</sup> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <sup>18</sup> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. <sup>19</sup> I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”’ <sup>20</sup> And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. <sup>21</sup> And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ <sup>22</sup> But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. <sup>23</sup> And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. <sup>24</sup> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate. <sup>25</sup> “Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. <sup>26</sup> And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. <sup>27</sup> And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ <sup>28</sup> But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, <sup>29</sup> but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup> But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’ <sup>31</sup> And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup> It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’”

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Luke 16 is one of the most challenging chapters in all the Gospels. It contains two sustained teachings — the Parable of the Dishonest Manager and the story of the Rich Man and Lazarus — that bracket a cluster of sayings about the law, divorce, and divine valuation. What holds it together is money as a spiritual diagnostic: how a person handles wealth reveals the true condition of their heart before God.

The Parable of the Dishonest Manager shocks its hearers because Jesus appears to commend a fraudster. The commendation, however, is carefully qualified: the manager is praised not for his dishonesty but for his shrewdness — his ability to think clearly about the future and use present resources to secure it. Jesus turns the parable into an indictment of disciples who exercise less practical wisdom in spiritual things than worldly people do in material ones.

The story of the Rich Man and Lazarus is the only parable in which a character has a proper name, and it closes the chapter with one of Scripture's most sobering statements: if people will not be persuaded by Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. This is both a claim about the sufficiency of Scripture and a prophecy about the response to Jesus's own resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells this to his disciples while the Pharisees are also listening (v.14), which is why the chapter ends where it does.

The manager is an oikonomos — the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts and ran the property in his master's name. And what he had been doing is what the prodigal did in the far country (15:13). The parable opens with a second man squandering another man's property.

Note the order of the dismissal: he is sacked first and the audit demanded second, which means he is finished and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap — no longer trusted, not yet stripped of authority, the debtors not yet told, the seal still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application.

His options are closed: he cannot dig, and he will not beg — and the difference in the two clauses is a fair sample of the man. He is not able to dig; he is ashamed to beg. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

What he then buys is not money. He does not embezzle; what he wants is houses — an open door somewhere when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth can be converted into them while he still controls it.

The reductions are uneven — fifty per cent on oil, twenty on wheat — which is the clue. If he were simply defrauding his master the discounts would be arbitrary; that they differ by commodity suggests he is removing something that varied by commodity, and the obvious candidate is his own commission. On that reading he waives his fee and takes a large personal loss, which would explain the otherwise baffling commendation.

It cannot be settled with certainty and the parable does not require it. What is commended is neither the honesty nor the dishonesty but the structure of the act: he took a resource about to stop being his and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would outlast the deadline.
verseByVerse.theology:
The commendation is careful about what it does and does not say. He is still called the dishonest manager. What is praised is his shrewdness: practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act. A commander can admire an enemy's manoeuvre without approving the war.

“Sons of light” was a term the devout used of themselves — the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at reading a situation and acting in time.

The observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. A man will plan a pension he may never draw, take advice about a mortgage, insure a house he expects to keep. Set beside that the way the same qualities are deployed in the things of God by people who genuinely believe they will stand before him: the forward thinking stops, and a man who would never let a financial decision drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it.

The three descriptions of money in vv.10-12 are each deflating. It is unrighteous — the currency of a fallen order, and nobody's money is clean all the way back. It is a very little, said to people for whom it was the difference between eating and not eating. And it is another's. But the promise on the other side is easily missed: the true riches, and that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 9 is the hardest sentence in the chapter and needs facing. Read flatly it appears to say a man can purchase his welcome into heaven — and it has been read that way in defence of almsgiving as accumulated merit.

Who are “they”? Three readings are held by careful Christians: the friends themselves, the angels, or — most likely — God himself, whose name the wording leaves unspoken.

And on whether salvation is for sale, the verse answers itself in three words that are easy to read past: when it fails. The money is explicitly the thing that runs out. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity — and in this very chapter a rich man's fortune procures him not one drop of water.

What the verse teaches is that generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with “you cannot serve God and money,” which is where the saying is travelling.

And that closing sentence is a statement about what is possible, not advice about priorities. A man may hold two jobs; nobody has ever had two owners. Note too that both outcomes are the same outcome — whichever way it falls, one master gets the loyalty and the other the contempt. Most people serving money would sincerely say they love God, and the conflict only becomes visible when the two masters give conflicting orders.

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the disciples.

The audience has changed. Chapter 15 was aimed at the grumbling Pharisees; this is for the men who follow him — though verse 14 will tell us the Pharisees were still listening, which is why the chapter ends where it does.

There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions.

The manager is an oikonomos — the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or a freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts, collected rents and ran the property in his master's name. He was not a servant among servants. He had the seal and the keys, and the owner might be an absentee who saw the place twice a year.

And the word for what he had been doing is the one Luke used of the prodigal in the far country — diaskorpizōn, scattering (15:13). The parable opens with a second man squandering another man's property, which is not a coincidence in a Gospel arranged as carefully as this one.

Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.

Two things, and the order matters. The dismissal is announced first and the audit demanded second — which means he is finished, and the paperwork is a formality.

What that gives him is a gap. He is no longer trusted and not yet stripped of authority; the debtors have not been told; the seal is still in his hand. He has a short, precisely bounded interval in which he can still act in his master's name.

The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application. Every person in this chapter is holding something on somebody else's behalf, has been told the arrangement is ending, and has an unspecified amount of time left in which the seal still works.

Notice also what the man does not do. He does not dispute the charges. Luke never says whether they were true — but the manager's silence, and his immediate move to plan for unemployment, answer the question well enough.
verseByVerse.note: A manager (steward) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers to make deals in his name.
