verseByVerse.quote: And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the manager said to himself, What shall I do?

The parable now goes inside his head, which is where Luke has taken us twice already — the rich fool talking to his own soul (12:17), and the prodigal coming to himself in the pigsty (15:17). It is the same construction each time, and it is always a man at the end of his options.

I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg.

Two doors, and both shut.

He cannot dig. A steward's life was clerical, not physical, and he is honest about what a lifetime of it has done to him — a middle-aged administrator suddenly facing labouring work and knowing his back will not last a week.

And he will not beg. Note the difference in the two clauses: he is not able to dig, and he is ashamed to beg. The first is a limitation and the second is a decision — and it is a fair sample of the man. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.

And there is the plan, and the thing to notice is what he is actually buying.

Not money. He does not embezzle; there is no suggestion he takes anything for himself, and a man with a bag of stolen silver would be in a far worse position than a man with friends. What he wants is houses — an open door somewhere, hospitality, a place at a table when he has nothing.

He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships — and that the wealth, while he still controls it, can be converted into them.

That is the entire insight of the parable, and Jesus is about to say so.

What is striking is how late it comes. He has run that estate for years with the whole apparatus of value in his hands, and it took a dismissal notice to make him ask what any of it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, summoning his master's debtors one by one.

One by one, and quickly — before the news gets out. These are not petty debtors; the quantities are enormous.

A hundred batous of oil is somewhere near nine hundred gallons, the yield of a substantial olive grove. A hundred korous of wheat is perhaps a thousand bushels, the crop of a large field. These are tenant farmers or merchants with serious contracts, and each debt represents something in the region of several years' wages.

Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.

The debtor writes it himself, in his own hand, on his own bond — which is important. What the manager produces is a document that looks entirely legitimate and carries no trace of him.

And the reductions are curiously uneven: fifty per cent on the oil, twenty per cent on the wheat.

That unevenness is the clue that has led many readers to the likeliest explanation. If the manager were simply defrauding his master, the discounts would be arbitrary; the fact that they differ by commodity suggests he is removing something that varied by commodity — and the obvious candidate is his own commission, the surcharge a steward customarily added to a contract as his cut.

On that reading he is not stealing at all. He is waiving his own fee, taking a very large personal loss to buy goodwill — which explains the otherwise baffling fact that his master, on discovering what he has done, commends him.

It cannot be settled with certainty, and the parable does not require it to be. Either he sacrificed his own margin or he defrauded his employer, and Jesus commends neither the honesty nor the dishonesty. What is commended is the structure of the act.

He took a resource that was about to stop being his, and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would still exist after the deadline.

And notice the tempo, because it is part of what is being praised. Sit down quickly. He summons them one by one and gets it done before the news travels, because the window is measured in hours and he knows it.

Nobody in this parable is described as clever. He is described as fast.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the size of these debts: a hundred measures of oil was about 800–900 gallons, a hundred measures of wheat about 1,000–1,200 bushels. Cutting them won the debtors’ gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness.

Which is startling, and the sentence is careful about what it does and does not say.

He is still called the dishonest manager — literally the steward of unrighteousness, a man characterised by it. The commendation does not rehabilitate him. What is praised is phronimōs: prudence, practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act on it.

A commander can admire an enemy's manoeuvre without approving of the war, and that is roughly what is happening here.

For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.

And here is the sting, and it is one of the most uncomfortable sentences Jesus ever spoke about his own people.

Sons of light was a term the devout used of themselves; the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at this.

Better at what, exactly? At dealing with their own generation — at reading a situation, seeing where it is going, and acting in time.

And the observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. Consider the ordinary competence of the world. A man will spend real effort on a pension he may never draw, take advice about a mortgage, insure a house he expects to keep, plan a career over decades. He thinks forward, calculates, and acts while he still can.

Now set beside that the way the same qualities are usually deployed in the things of God, by people who genuinely believe they are going to stand before him. The forward thinking stops. The strategy disappears. A man who would never leave a financial decision to drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it.

Who is the master who commends the manager? Most likely the rich man in the story, since Jesus speaks in his own voice in the next sentence. Some take it as the Lord himself. Either way, what is praised is the manager’s foresight, not his dishonesty.

Jesus is not asking his disciples to become worldly. He is asking them to become as intelligent about eternity as they already are about money — and observing, without much apparent hope, that mostly they are not.
verseByVerse.note: The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

The hardest sentence in the chapter, and it needs facing rather than hurrying past. Read flatly, it appears to say a man can purchase his welcome into heaven by spending money on the right people — and it has been read that way, in defence of almsgiving as a work that accumulates merit.

Two questions have to be answered: who are they, and is this salvation for sale?

On the first, three readings are held by careful Christians. Some take they as the friends themselves — those helped in this life standing at the door of the next, glad to see their benefactor arrive. Some take it of angels, who will carry Lazarus a few verses later.

But the likeliest is simpler: this is the Semitic way of saying you will be received without naming God directly, a reverent third-person plural. Luke has used the identical idiom already — this night your soul is required of you (12:20), where the Greek literally reads they require your soul, and nobody supposes a committee. It is God who receives; the wording keeps his name off the sentence.

On the second question the verse answers itself, and it does so in three words that are easy to read past: when it fails.

The money is explicitly described as the thing that runs out. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity.

And Luke will not let the merit reading stand a moment longer. The tax collector who could offer nothing but his breast went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal a few hours from death bought nothing whatever and was told today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43); and in this very chapter a rich man's fortune procures him not one drop of water. If money could buy an eternal dwelling, the man in torment was the best-funded soul in the story.

What the verse teaches is that generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with you cannot serve God and money — which is where this saying is travelling. How a man treats his wealth shows which master owns him.
verseByVerse.note: “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: rich in good works, storing up treasure

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much.

The parable is finished and the application widens, and this is the principle underneath it. Character does not change with scale. The way a man handles a small thing is not a warm-up for how he would handle a large one; it is a sample of it.

Which cuts against a very common self-assessment. Most people privately believe they would be generous if they had more, honest if the stakes were higher, disciplined if the work were more important. Jesus says the evidence is already in, and it is in the small things, and it has been all along.

If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?

Three descriptions of money follow, and each is deflating.

It is unrighteous wealth — not evil in itself, but the currency of a fallen order, inevitably entangled with things God hates. Nobody's money is clean all the way back.

It is a very little. That is an extraordinary thing to say to people for whom money was the difference between eating and not eating, and Jesus says it anyway. Whatever the sums involved, they are small.

And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?

And it is another's. Not yours. You are the steward of the parable, running an estate you did not buy, and the audit is coming.

Then the promise on the other side, which is easily missed under the warnings: the true riches, and that which is your own.

There is something coming that will actually belong to you. Everything held now is on loan and will be handed back; what is being trained for is an inheritance that cannot be taken away — and the training ground is a bank account.

Which is why God appears to care so much about a subject that seems beneath him. He is not interested in the money. He is watching what a man does with a small sum of somebody else's cash, because that is the most reliable evidence available of what he would do with anything.

verseByVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No servant can serve two masters.

Think of a slave, not an employee, and the sentence settles the argument before it starts, because a man may hold two jobs but nobody has ever had two owners. A slave's time, body and will belonged wholly to one person.

So the sentence is not advice about priorities. It is a statement about what is possible.

For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other.

Note that both outcomes are the same outcome. Whichever way round it falls, one master ends up with the loyalty and the other with the contempt. There is no third arrangement in which both are served.

And the strength of the language is deliberate. Not prefer and neglect, but love and hate, devoted and despise. The divided man does not end up mildly disappointing one of his masters; he ends up with something like contempt for him.

Which is worth sitting with, because most people who are serving money would say they love God. They would say it sincerely. What Jesus is describing is not what they would say but what is actually happening — and it becomes visible only when the two masters give conflicting orders, which is why so much of life passes without the conflict ever surfacing.

You cannot serve God and money.

The word for money is mamōnas — Mammon, an Aramaic term for wealth or property, and Jesus treats it here as a name. Not a thing you own but somebody who owns you. He has personified it, and the personification is the point: money is not a neutral tool in this sentence. It is a rival lord, and it makes demands, and it has slaves.

Then the flat impossibility: you cannot. Not should not, and not will find it difficult.

Which means the division that most people are actually attempting — God at the centre, money in a firm second place, both properly managed — is not a compromise between two positions. It is one of them, held by a man who has not noticed which.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees are described as lovers of money, which is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. But it was not a secret vice among them and did not feel like a vice at all, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. A wealthy Pharisee could regard his estate as a testimonial.

Their response is not argument. They ridiculed him, and that is the tell. There is no counter-exegesis, no appeal to Scripture. Ridicule is the cheapest defence available and the most effective: it requires no reasoning and lets a whole room off the hook at once by making the speaker faintly absurd.

Jesus goes past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. “You justify yourselves before men” describes the exhausting business of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience. And “abomination” is a heavy word, not chosen loosely — in the Old Testament it is a standard word for idols. He is not saying human and divine values sometimes differ. He is putting visible success, honour and social standing in the same category as an idol.

Then two verses that must be held together. “The Law and the Prophets were until John” dates an era, and John stands on the seam — the last of the old order and the herald of the new (cf. 7:28). But “not one dot of the Law” will become void: the dot is the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another, and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does.

The word holding them together is fulfilment. The Law's era as the way God's people related to him has closed; the Law itself has been kept — by the man saying this — and its moral claim stands exactly where it stood. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it.

Which is why the divorce saying follows, and the placing is not a change of subject. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things, by the party of permissive divorce rulings. He takes the point where their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law and shows who is actually relaxing it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Everyone forces his way into it” is a strange phrase and the translations divide: everyone is pressing in, or, as the ESV margin gives it, everyone is forcefully urged into it. Either way the point stands and it is not gentle: since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door (cf. Matt. 11:12).

There is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are shoving their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

The two verses guard against two opposite errors that are always with the church. One man reads “the Law and the Prophets were until John” and concludes the commandments no longer trouble him — that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity. Verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes nothing has changed at all — that he is still under a covenant of works and must produce a righteousness of his own. Verse 16 exists to stop him: the good news is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

And the permanence of the Law is why the sexual ethic is not negotiable. The Pharisees were known for liberal divorce interpretations — Hillel's school allowed it for almost any reason — and Jesus reaffirms the original design of Genesis 2:24 as the Law's continuing moral claim, not as something the kingdom relaxes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke gives the divorce saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke will conclude that every divorce and remarriage is adultery. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in: Matthew records the same teaching twice with an exception for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor. 7:15). On that basis the Reformed churches have historically recognised two grounds, and that is the position confessed in the Westminster standards.

Luke leaves the exception out because he is giving the rule, not the case law — which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says “never take this on an empty stomach” is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. The exceptions are narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

But there is a further question, and it is the one that keeps people out of church: what about the man or woman already divorced and already remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18) — he calls them husbands, names the truth exactly, and does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage; it is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that exists and carries real obligations.

Where there was sin it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross rather than dragged out every morning. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: “and such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Cor. 6:9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him.

Luke tells us two things and the second follows from the first.

Lovers of money is philargyroi — literally silver-lovers, and it is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. But it was not a secret vice among them, and it did not feel like a vice at all, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. A wealthy Pharisee could regard his estate as a testimonial.

They ridiculed him. The verb is vivid — literally they turned up their noses at him.

And that is the tell. They do not argue. There is no counter-exegesis, no appeal to Scripture, no attempt to show that the teaching is wrong. They sneer — which is what people do when something has landed and cannot be answered.

Ridicule is the cheapest defence available and the most effective. It requires no reasoning, it costs nothing, and it lets a whole room off the hook at once by making the speaker faintly absurd.

You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts.

He goes straight past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. Justify yourselves before men — the effort of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience, which is exhausting, and which is the only thing sustaining the position they have just defended with a sneer.

For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.

Abomination is a heavy word and it is not chosen loosely. In the Greek Old Testament it is the standard term for idols and for the practices of the nations — the things that provoked God to jealousy.

So the sentence is stronger than it first appears. He is not saying that human values and divine values sometimes differ. He is saying that the thing this society most admires — visible success, honour, the standing these men had spent their lives accumulating — is in the same category as an idol.

parallels.desc: the LORD looks on the heart

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.

A hinge verse, and it divides history in two.

The Law and the Prophets is the standard way of naming the whole Old Testament, and Jesus dates its era: until John. Not abolished at John, and the next verse will make that emphatic. But the age in which the Scriptures pointed forward to something not yet arrived has closed, because the thing they pointed to has come.

John stands on the seam. He is the last of the old order and the herald of the new — which is what Jesus meant when he said no one born of women is greater than John, and yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he (7:28).

Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached. Not argued, not required. Announced, as news is announced.

And everyone forces his way into it.

A strange phrase, and worth a pause, because the Greek verb can be read two ways and the translations divide. It may be middle voice — everyone is pressing into it, straining to get in. Or passive — everyone is being urged in, pressed to enter, which the ESV notes in its margin.

Either way the point stands, and it is not gentle. Since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is not drifted into. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door — with decision, urgency, and everything he has (cf. Matt. 11:12).

And there is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to the men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are shoving their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

Which is worth turning on any settled congregation. The kingdom in this verse is not a place people are gently ushered into over a lifetime of respectable attendance. It is somewhere people are visibly fighting to get.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.

Immediately after saying that an era has ended, he says the Law is untouchable — and the but is there to stop exactly the conclusion a hearer would otherwise draw.

The dot is the keraia, literally a little horn: the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. In Hebrew script the difference between certain letters is a mark smaller than the head of a pin — and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does.

So the two verses have to be held together, and they are held together by one word: fulfilment.

The Law's era as the way God's people related to him has closed. The Law itself has not been cancelled; it has been kept — by the man saying this — and its moral claim stands exactly where it stood. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it.

Which is why the very next thing he says is about divorce, and why the placing has puzzled readers. It is not a change of subject. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things; the Pharisees who sneered at his teaching on money were also the party of permissive divorce rulings. So he takes the point at which their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law, and shows who is actually relaxing it.

And there is a word here for two opposite errors that are always with the church.

One is the man who reads the Law and the Prophets were until John and concludes that the commandments no longer trouble him — that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity. Verse 17 exists to stop him.

Must Christians, then, keep the Old Testament law? Reformed Christians distinguish its ceremonial laws, sacrifices, food laws and festivals, which are fulfilled in Christ (Heb 9–10); its civil laws, given to Israel as a nation; and its moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still guides believers. Not a dot of the law fails because Christ fulfils all of it, some by completing it and some by writing it on our hearts.

The other is the man who reads verse 17 and concludes that nothing has changed at all — that he is still under the covenant of works and must produce a righteousness of his own. Verse 16 exists to stop him. The good news of the kingdom is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.
verseByVerse.note: The “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

Luke gives the saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke will conclude that every divorce and every remarriage without qualification is adultery.

Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in. Matthew records the same teaching twice and both times includes an exception for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9). Paul adds a second case: if an unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). On that basis the Reformed churches have historically recognised two grounds on which a marriage may be dissolved without sin — adultery and desertion — and that is the position confessed in the Westminster standards.

Why then does Luke leave the exception out? Because he is giving the rule, not the case law, which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says never take this on an empty stomach is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. Luke's flat form is the shape of the thing: marriage is for life, and the exceptions are exceptions — narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

But there is a further question, and it is the one that keeps people out of church. What about the man or woman already divorced and already remarried, on no ground the New Testament allows? Is every day of the new marriage a fresh sin? Is the only repentance available to break the second home apart?

No. Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18) — he calls them husbands, he names the truth exactly, and he does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage; it is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that now exists and carries real obligations to a real spouse and real children.

Where there was sin, it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin — and then left at the cross, not dragged out and re-committed every morning. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: and such were some of you. But you were washed (1 Cor. 6:9-11).

None of which is a loophole, and it must not be heard as one. The fence stands exactly where Jesus put it, and he put it there to protect something — chiefly the wife who in that world could be dismissed at her husband's convenience and left with nothing. But a fence is not a cage, and the gospel does not leave a man locked outside his own forgiveness.

Some Christians hold that there is no ground for remarriage while a former spouse lives, reading this verse without exceptions; others allow remarriage on wider grounds. The verdict given elsewhere in this commentary is that Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matt 19:9) and Paul for desertion by an unbeliever (1 Cor 7:15), and that in those cases the innocent party is free to remarry. Luke gives the principle; Matthew and Paul give its exceptions.

If that is your history, the word to you is not go back. It is be washed, and be faithful now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The most extended treatment of life after death in the Synoptics, told as the direct sequel to the teaching on money.

Every detail of the opening is a price tag. Purple came from the murex shellfish and took thousands of them to colour a garment; the fine linen was a costly luxury cloth, and he feasted every day, not on feast days when ordinary people ate meat.

Lazarus was laid at the gate — passive, because he could not get there himself — and the gate is the great portal of a walled estate, which means the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him. He wanted what fell: not a place at the table but the scraps on the floor. And he did not get them. The dogs are not a comfort but the final degradation — scavenging pariah animals reaching him when no human being would.

Then the reversal, and it is total. Lazarus is carried — the same passivity as at the gate, and he does nothing in either case. “Abraham's side” is, as the ESV margin gives it, his bosom: at a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbows, so the guest of honour lay with his head near the host's chest, which is the phrase John uses of the beloved disciple (John 13:23). The beggar who longed for what fell from a table is in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

The rich man is buried — a few words, and the last good thing that happens to him. And the first thing he sees from Hades is Lazarus: the one face he had trained himself not to register, and he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Everything he then says shows that nothing has been learned. He pleads descent — “Father Abraham,” exactly what John the Baptist warned against (3:8) — and twice says “send Lazarus,” still treating him as somebody who ought to be running errands.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story teaches several interlocking truths. There is conscious existence after death, prior to the resurrection: the rich man sees, recognises, feels pain and argues. This is consistent with 23:43 and with Paul (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:23). The final state of the wicked involves real torment. And it is irreversible — the chasm “has been fixed,” established and standing established, and it is described as working in both directions. That second clause rules out something a sentimental reading would like: it is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him.

One caution on reading the scene rightly. Jesus is not drawing a surveyor's map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God's justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets. The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography.

But the warning must not be softened by that caution — and the gulf of verse 26 is not a new thing. There was a gulf in verses 19 to 21 as well. It was a gate, and it could be crossed by anybody who chose to. One man had the power to cross it every day of his life and never did.

Abraham's “Child, remember” is tender and it is not an accusation. Nothing new is introduced; no list of sins is produced. He simply asks the man to recall a life in which he received his good things — got exactly what he had chosen, all of it, for as long as he lasted.
verseByVerse.examples:
One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story's shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything, and the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns.

That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was wealthy. Note also the one name in the story: the rich man, who had every name worth having in this life, is anonymous, and the beggar is called Lazarus — named, and known. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily; what saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

“They have Moses and the Prophets” is one of the most important sentences in Luke. They had not been left without warning: the Law commands provision for the poor at your gate (Lev. 19:9-10; Deut. 15:7-11), and the Prophets say almost nothing more often — Amos on those who lie on beds of ivory and are not grieved, Isaiah on fasting that does not share bread with the hungry (Amos 6:4-6; Isa. 58:6-7). The rich man heard it read every Sabbath of his life, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner.

And the final line is devastating for two reasons. The problem is never a shortage of evidence but an unwillingness to hear — miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it. And somebody did rise from the dead. When another Lazarus was raised at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him too (John 12:10). The test was run, and it went exactly as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day.

Every detail is a price tag. Purple dye came from the murex shellfish, and it took thousands of them to colour a single garment; it was so costly that some societies restricted it by law to royalty. The fine linen was a costly luxury cloth, worn by the very rich.

And he feasted sumptuously every day — not on feast days, which is when ordinary people ate meat. Every day.

And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus.

The verb is passive: he was laid there, by somebody, because he could not get there himself.

And the gate is not a garden gate. It is the great portal of a walled estate — which tells you the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him.

Covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.

He wants what falls. Not a place at the table; the scraps that go on the floor. And he does not get them.

The dogs are not a comfort. They are the scavenging pariah dogs of a Near Eastern town, unclean animals, and they can reach him when no human being will — which is the final degradation and Luke means it as one.

One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story's shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything; the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns, and a poor man is safe on the strength of his sores.

That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was a wealthy man.

Note also the one name in the story. The rich man, who had every name worth having in this life, is anonymous. The beggar is called Lazarus — Eleazar, meaning God has helped — which is the single hint the parable gives about where his hope actually lay.

What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily. What saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.
verseByVerse.note: Purple dye was costly and fine linen a luxury — the clothing of the very rich. Lazarus, the Greek form of Eleazar, means “God has helped”; he is the only character in Jesus’ parables, apart from Abraham, who is given a name.

parallels.desc: whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side.

Luke does not say he was buried. A man in his condition, with nobody to claim him, would have gone into a common pit outside the walls — and the parable simply passes over it, because something else was happening that nobody at the graveside could see.

He was carried. The same passivity as verse 20, and the same helplessness — he was laid at a gate by men, and he is carried through death by angels, and he does nothing in either case.

To Abraham's side — literally into Abraham's bosom, which is the language of a banquet. At a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbows, so the person in the place of honour lay with his head near the chest of the host. It is the phrase John uses of the beloved disciple at the Last Supper (John 13:23).

So the beggar who longed for what fell from a table is now in the place of honour at the greatest table there is, next to the father of the nation.

The rich man also died and was buried.

A few words, and they are the last good thing that happens to him. He got what Lazarus did not — a funeral, and given his wealth, presumably an impressive one.

The burial is the final entry in the ledger of a life that had everything the world can supply, and the sentence moves straight past it.

And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

Hades is the Greek term for the realm of the dead, used in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew Sheol. And what the parable describes is conscious existence: he sees, he recognises, he is in pain, he will shortly argue.

Then the detail that finishes him. The first thing he sees is Lazarus.

The man he had walked past at his own gate, every day, for years — the one face he had trained himself not to register — is the first thing visible from where he now is. And he knows his name.

Is this story a parable or a real event? It begins like other parables, There was a rich man, but names Lazarus, which no other parable does. Most likely it is a parable, told to make a point about wealth, repentance and the sufficiency of Scripture; so its details should not be pressed. But Jesus does not use false pictures. What it teaches plainly is that after death there is conscious existence, that the righteous are comforted and the wicked in torment, and that the separation is fixed (v. 26).

Hades here is the place of the dead before the final judgment, not yet the lake of fire (Rev 20:13–15), and Abraham’s side is the blessedness of believers with God (cf. 23:43). Some evangelicals hold that the lost will finally be destroyed rather than suffer for ever, and they rightly note that this is not yet the final state. But Jesus speaks elsewhere of eternal punishment (Matt 25:46), and the more likely reading is that the judgment is conscious and without end.

Does this mean the dead can see us or speak with us, or that the saints can pray for us? No. The story gives no warrant for contact between the living and the dead, and Scripture forbids seeking it (Deut 18:10–12; Isa 8:19). The rich man’s request is refused, and the point is that the living have Moses and the Prophets.

He had always known his name.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom” — the place of honour beside the host at a banquet. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue.

Two things in that request tell you the man has not changed at all.

The first is Father Abraham — he is pleading descent, which is exactly what John the Baptist had warned against at the start of this Gospel: do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father (3:8). His claim is ancestry, and it is the only one he makes.

The second is worse. Send Lazarus. He knows the name, he can see the man in the place of honour beside Abraham — and his instinct is to have him fetched, like a servant, to bring water.

Nothing has been learned. In torment, with everything gone, he still cannot conceive of Lazarus as anything but somebody who ought to be running errands for him.

And note how small the request is. Not release, not reversal. The end of a finger, dipped. Even that is refused.

Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.

Abraham's answer opens with Child. There is no cruelty in this scene, and no gloating. The word is tender.

And what he says is not an accusation. It is an accounting, and it turns on one word: remember.

Nothing new is being introduced. Abraham does not produce a list of sins; he asks the man to recall his own life, in which he received his good things — and the possessive is exact. Your good things. He got what he had chosen, and he had all of it, and it lasted exactly as long as he did.

Which is the whole indictment, and it does not require a single charge to be laid. The rich man had received everything he wanted. The tragedy is not that he was punished for enjoying it. It is that he wanted so little.

parallels.desc: men whose portion is in this life

verseByVerse.quote: And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.

A second reason, on top of the first, and this one is not about what the man deserves. It is about what is possible.

Has been fixed — it was established, and it stands established. Somebody fixed it, and there is no doubt who.

And the barrier is described as working in both directions: nobody crosses from there, and nobody crosses from here. That second clause is worth registering, because it rules out something a sentimental reading would like. It is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him. It is that the door is shut, and it is shut from the side that had every reason to want it open.

Which is the parable's answer to the hope that there might be a second chance after death — and it is the plainest statement of it in the Gospels. Whatever was decided in the life is now settled.

One caution on reading the whole scene rightly. Jesus is not drawing a surveyor's map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew — Abraham's side, a fixed gulf, a cry across the divide — to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God's justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets. The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography.

But the warning itself must not be softened by that caution, and it is the reason this parable exists in a chapter about money. The gulf in verse 26 is not a new thing. There was a gulf in verses 19 to 21 as well, and it was a gate, and it could be crossed by anybody who chose to.

One man had the power to cross it every day of his life and never did. He is now on the far side of a chasm he cannot cross, and it is the same chasm.

parallels.desc: to die once, and after that comes judgment

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house — for I have five brothers — so that he may warn them.

The second request, and it is usually read as the one decent thing the man does. He has given up on himself and is thinking of his family.

There is something in that, and it should not be dismissed. He does not want them where he is, and the sentiment is real.

But notice that it is still send him. Twice now, and both times the same instinct: Lazarus is a resource, to be dispatched on an errand. And notice which house he wants him sent to — my father's house, where five brothers are presumably still feasting sumptuously and stepping over somebody at the gate.

There is also something in the request that reads, very faintly, like a complaint. If somebody had warned him, he might not be here. That is not stated, and it is worth not pressing too far — but Abraham's answer meets it exactly.

They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.

That is the answer, and it is one of the most important sentences in Luke's Gospel.

They have not been left without warning. They have the Scriptures — which are full of this. The Law commands that the poor at your gate be provided for and that the corners of your field be left standing (Lev. 19:9-10; Deut. 15:7-11). The Prophets say almost nothing more often: Amos on those who lie on beds of ivory and are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph; Isaiah on fasting that does not share bread with the hungry (Amos 6:4-6; Isa. 58:6-7).

The rich man had all of it. He heard it read in synagogue every Sabbath of his life, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner.

So the request for a messenger is not really a request for information. Nobody in that house lacks information. What is being asked for is something more compelling than the word of God — and Abraham's reply is that they already have the word of God, and it is enough, and the problem was never the evidence.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures.

parallels.desc: if you believed Moses, you would believe me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.

He contradicts Abraham flatly — no — which is a remarkable thing to do from where he is standing, and entirely in character. He has been managing people all his life and is still doing it.

And his theory is one that a great many people hold. The Scriptures are not enough; what would really work is something dramatic. A miracle. A visitation. Some undeniable event that would settle the question.

It is worth admitting how reasonable that sounds. Most Christians have thought it about somebody they love: if he could only see something, he would believe.

If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.

And that is the answer, and it is devastating for two reasons.

The first is what it says about the human heart. The problem is not a shortage of evidence; it is an unwillingness to hear. A man who will not be moved by the word of God will not be moved by anything, because the resistance is not located in his mind. Miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it — they only raise the stakes.

The second reason is the one Luke's first readers would have heard immediately, and it is why this sentence ends the chapter.

Somebody did rise from the dead.

Not long after this was spoken, a man came out of a tomb outside Jerusalem, and the men who had heard this parable were among those who arranged for the guard on it and paid for the story that explained it away. John's Gospel records that when another Lazarus was raised at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him too (John 12:10).

The test was run. It went exactly as he said.

Which puts the whole chapter in its place, and puts a Bible in the reader's hands with a particular weight. There is no further evidence coming. What we have is Moses and the Prophets, and now the record of the one who rose — and if that is not heard, nothing else will be.

There is no dramatic sign that will do what a page of Scripture, honestly attended to, is able to do.

parallels.desc: after Lazarus of Bethany is raised, they plot to kill Jesus

16.text: <sup>1</sup> He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. <sup>2</sup> And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’ <sup>3</sup> And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. <sup>4</sup> I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’ <sup>5</sup> So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ <sup>6</sup> He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ <sup>7</sup> Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’ <sup>8</sup> The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. <sup>10</sup> “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. <sup>11</sup> If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? <sup>12</sup> And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own? <sup>13</sup> No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.” <sup>14</sup> The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. <sup>16</sup> “The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. <sup>17</sup> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. <sup>18</sup> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. <sup>19</sup> “There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. <sup>20</sup> And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, <sup>21</sup> who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <sup>22</sup> The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, <sup>23</sup> and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. <sup>24</sup> And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ <sup>25</sup> But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. <sup>26</sup> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’ <sup>27</sup> And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— <sup>28</sup> for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ <sup>29</sup> But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ <sup>30</sup> And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ <sup>31</sup> He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Luke 17 gathers teachings that might appear loosely connected but share a common thread: the shape of life in the kingdom as it moves toward its final consummation. Disciples are warned about causing others to stumble, commanded to forgive repeatedly, confronted about the nature of faith, and then — after the extraordinary healing of ten lepers — taught about gratitude. The chapter then pivots to sustained teaching about the coming of the Son of Man: apocalyptic instruction that would be at home in the Olivet Discourse.

The healing of the ten lepers is one of the most poignant episodes in Luke, precisely because of what does not happen: nine healed men simply walk away. The one who returns is a Samaritan — an outsider — and his return becomes the occasion for Jesus to say something remarkable: “your faith has made you well” — or, as the ESV margin gives it, “has saved you.” The nine received physical healing; the one received something more.

The eschatological teaching (vv. 20–37) is deliberately disorienting. The kingdom does not come with observable signs (v. 20); it is already in your midst (v. 21). Yet the day of the Son of Man will come with lightning-like sudden visibility (v. 24). The tension is not a contradiction: the kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus, but its final manifestation remains future — and when it comes, it will be unmistakable, inescapable, and final.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Four short teachings, each pressing the disciples on a different part of their calling.

The ESV margin gives “temptations to sin” as “stumbling blocks” — not primarily an enticement but an obstacle set in somebody's path. Drowning carried a particular horror for a Jew who expected burial in his own ground, and it is offered as the preferable outcome.

The weight of the saying falls on the influential, because nobody trips a person who is not following them. The “little ones” include children and reach wider: the young in faith, the recently converted, anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

The forgiveness command opens with “pay attention to yourselves,” and the order governs everything after it — a man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not. Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, and it is meant to kill the arithmetic: anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgement, not sincere, and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself. The test is not whether the repentance convinces but whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

The apostles respond “Increase our faith!” — and note when. Not before a storm or a demon. They have been told to forgive, and they say they have not got enough of whatever it takes. The answer is not what they asked for: he tells them the quantity was never the issue.

Then the servant parable, which checks the pride that obedience produces. And note the condition: “when you have done all that you were commanded” — this is the sentence for the best possible day, with nothing outstanding. Even then there is no credit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching anticipates the Lord's Prayer — “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes the effect of justification on a heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47).

The mulberry saying needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and made into a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once about the tumour and the child. It cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where it sits: the apostles asked for help to forgive, and this is his answer about that. Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel — if this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed, and men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer offered in perfect faith: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). Nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small.

Achreioi — “unworthy” — means unprofitable, contributing no surplus. It does not mean worthless in God's sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. And it must be guarded from the opposite error, because the same Lord says he will gird himself and serve his watching servants (12:37) and set the faithful man over ten cities (19:17). There is no wage; there is a Master who pays anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents and leaves the other case open. What if he never says “I repent”? That silence is where most real wounds live.

The answer begins with a distinction: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and Jesus attaches it to “if he repents.” You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally; you cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

That protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

And the servant parable has a reader for whom the whole scene will sting: anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement, doing the work that is simply expected and eating after everybody else. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said that when the master comes he will gird himself and have them recline at table and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come!

The word is skandala — and it is not primarily about enticement. A skandalon was the baited trigger-stick of an animal trap: the innocent-looking thing that brings the whole apparatus down. What is being described is not a tempting offer but a snare somebody has set.

And the first half is a flat acknowledgement of the world as it is. They are sure to come. Jesus does not promise a church in which nobody is ever tripped up, and a man who expects one will be disillusioned within a year.

But the inevitability changes nothing about the responsibility. Woe to the one through whom they come — and Luke's woe is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict.

It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea.

The image is deliberately extreme: a millstone, a wheel of rock a man could not lift.

And drowning carried a particular horror for a Jew, who expected burial in his own ground. This is being described as the preferable outcome.

Than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.

Who are the little ones? The phrase can cover children, and it certainly includes them. But in this context it reaches wider: the young in faith, the recently converted, the weak — anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

Which is where the weight of the saying falls, and it falls on the influential. Nobody trips a person who is not following them.

So this is a word for parents, and for anyone who teaches, leads, or is simply admired by a younger believer — and the terms of it are severe beyond anything else Jesus says about the consequences of a bad example. To ruin your own soul is a catastrophe. To be the stumbling block under somebody else's is worse, and he measures it with a millstone.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to yourselves!

The imperative comes first and it governs everything after it. Before a word is said about rebuking anybody, the man doing the rebuking is told to look at himself.

If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him.

Three obligations, and the middle one is the least popular. The rebuke is not optional and it is not unkind; it is what love does when it sees somebody going wrong and would rather they did not arrive.

What makes it bearable is the order. A man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not.

And if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, I repent, you must forgive him.

Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, and it is meant to kill the arithmetic. Anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgement, not sincere — and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself.

The test is not whether the repentance convinces. It is whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

But Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents, and leaves the other case open. What if he never says I repent? The silence is worth pressing, because that is where most real wounds live.

The answer begins with a distinction Luke's own wording invites: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury, declining to make yourself the creditor. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and that takes two; Jesus attaches it to if he repents.

You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally. You cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

And that protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from the cruelty of having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for.

This private rebuke is the first step Jesus describes more fully in Matthew 18:15–17, where unrepentant sin is taken to one or two others and then to the church. And the seven times a day is the same limitless forgiveness Jesus gives Peter: seventy-seven times (Matt 18:22).

Hold the two together and the opening command does its work. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles said to the Lord, Increase our faith!

Note when they say it. Not before a storm, not facing a demon, not in front of a crowd of five thousand. They have just been told to forgive a brother seven times in a day, and their response is that they have not got enough of whatever it takes.

It is an honest request and a good one, and it is worth registering that they were right to be daunted.

If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, Be uprooted and planted in the sea, and it would obey you.

The answer is not what they asked for. They wanted more; he tells them the quantity was never the issue.

The mustard seed is the standard image of the negligible, and the mulberry — the black mulberry of Palestine — was proverbially deep-rooted and long-lived, said to stand for six hundred years. Uprooting one and planting it in the sea is doubly absurd: a tree that cannot be moved, put where nothing grows.

But the verse needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and turned into something else: a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once, that the tumour did not shrink and the child did not recover for the same reason. That has been preached to a great many people at the worst hour of their lives, and it cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where the saying sits. The apostles have not asked for power to work wonders. They have asked for help to forgive, and the mulberry tree is his answer about that. To pull it out and make it a lever for moving circumstances is to use a sentence about pardoning your brother as a technique for rearranging your life.

Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel. If this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed — and in the whole of that book, men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer in history offered in perfect faith: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). The cup was not removed, and nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small.

What is promised is not that faith is a force whose output rises with its volume, but that its power lies in what it is attached to. What you already have, actually used, is enough for the seventh apology today.
verseByVerse.note: The mulberry (sycamine) tree has a deep, spreading root system.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, Come at once and recline at table?

The question expects the answer no, and every man listening would have given it without hesitation.

Picture the household. This is a small farm, not a great estate — a man with one servant, who does the ploughing and the shepherding, and who has been out all day. There is no second slave in the kitchen. When he comes in, the supper has not been made, because he is the one who makes it.

And recline at table is the posture of a guest at a formal meal. The suggestion is not that the master might let him sit down; it is that he might treat him as an honoured visitor in his own master's house.

Will he not rather say to him, Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink?

The arrangement is not cruel by the standards of that world and Jesus is not commending it as a model for employment. It is simply how a household ran, and everybody knew it.

Dress properly is, in the ESV margin, gird yourself — tuck up the robe for work, as the servants waiting for their master did in chapter 12.

And note the last clause, because it is easy to miss under the severity: and afterward you will eat and drink. The servant is not going hungry. He eats; he simply eats second.

Which is worth holding, because this parable is about to say something very hard about deserving, and it says it inside a picture where the servant is fed.

There is also a reader for whom the whole scene will sting, and it is worth saying now rather than at the end. Anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement will recognise this household exactly — the work that is simply expected, the meal made after everybody else has eaten.

Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said, in this same Gospel, that when the master comes he will gird himself and have them recline at table and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded?

Again the answer is obvious and again it is no — not because thanks would be wrong, but because thanks are for something over and above. Nobody is owed gratitude for meeting the terms.

So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.

Note the condition attached: when you have done all that you were commanded. This is not addressed to a man who has failed. It is the sentence he is to say on the day he has done everything — the best possible day, with nothing outstanding.

And even then there is no credit. Not a small credit; none. Duty done is duty done.

Unworthy here means unprofitable, contributing no surplus. It does not mean worthless in God's sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. It means that at the end of the accounting there is nothing on the credit side that God did not first supply.

Which is why this parable exists where it does. Chapter 17 has just demanded three enormous things — do not trip the weak, forgive seven times a day, exercise the faith you have. A disciple who manages any of that will feel something rise in him, and what rises is the thought that God now owes him a little.

That thought is the target.

And it needs guarding from the opposite error, because this saying has been used to flatten people who were already flat. It does not mean God is indifferent to what his servants do, and Luke will not allow that reading. The same Lord says he will gird himself and serve his watching servants (12:37), and that the faithful man will be set over ten cities (19:17). He is generous past anything owed.

The two sit together without strain once the direction is right. There is no wage. There is a Master who pays anyway — and the whole point of the parable is that the second sentence is a gift and not an invoice.

parallels.desc: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is in the border country where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory — a detail that will matter in five verses.

The ten stand at a distance because the law required it: a man with the disease lived outside the camp, in torn clothes, calling “unclean” as anyone approached (Lev. 13:45-46). “Leprosy” covered a range of skin conditions, but the social consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis — total exclusion from worship, family, work, and touch.

And ten of them are together, which tells its own story. Whatever each had been before, the disease had stripped it off and left them with the one thing they now had in common. Which is what makes verse 16 so striking: one of these ten is a Samaritan. Nine Jews and a Samaritan are living together outside a village, because the disease has done to their divisions what nothing else could.

“Master” is, everywhere else in this Gospel, on the lips of disciples. And they ask not for cleansing but for mercy, leaving the content of it to him.

He does not touch them and does not pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand that only makes sense afterwards — the inspection of Leviticus 14 is what you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence.

“And as they went they were cleansed.” Not before they went. There would have been a stretch of that road during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed.

One turns back — and it is worth being clear that the other nine were obeying. Until a priest certified them they could not go home or touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards the thing they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them stops.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story illustrates the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing; only one responded to the Giver. And the nine were not ingrates by worldly standards — their failure was not defiance but distraction. They moved from the gift to the system without pausing to return.

The Samaritan's outsider status is theologically loaded in Luke, who shows Samaritans in a positive light three times: the good Samaritan (10:33), this leper, and Samaria as the first step beyond Jerusalem in Acts (1:8; 8:5).

And the point is sharper than it first appears. The nine were going to the priests in Jerusalem — to the temple, the sacrifices, the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. He could not have gone with them. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place open to him, and it turned out to be the right one.

“Foreigner” at v.18 is allogenēs, a word found only here in the New Testament — and it is the word carved on the stone barrier in the temple court warning Gentiles not to pass beyond on pain of death. That inscription has been dug up. Jesus names this man by the very status the sign held against him, and the only man in the story fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Your faith has made you well” — or, as the ESV margin gives it, “has saved you.” Luke has used those words to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48).

Which answers the obvious difficulty: all ten were cleansed, so what is left for this man to receive? Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved. A man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

And notice what his faith actually consisted of, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men, obeyed an instruction that made no sense, and when he saw what had happened, turned round and went back to the one who did it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in his story.

The three questions at v.17 are among the few places where Jesus expresses something like disappointment at how he has been treated. He does not do it elsewhere for himself — not when a village will not house him, not when a Pharisee omits the courtesies at dinner.

And the nine are not villains but ordinary. Nobody in that group decided to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago. A family prays for a sick child and the child recovers; within weeks the thankfulness has given way to relief and resumed normal life. The story calls ordinary people to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee.

Luke reminds us of the destination again, and gives us the geography — the border country, the strip where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory.
