He is not a warning about scandalous living but about a life that passes every test a person can be set. A man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

“One thing you still lack” sounds like a small outstanding balance, which is how he would have heard it. It is not. The one thing is the whole thing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Is Jesus prescribing poverty as a universal requirement? No — the command was specific to this man, whose particular idol was wealth. He does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8-9); he does not say it to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3). What has happened is that the first table of the law, quietly left out of the list two verses earlier, has been applied: you shall have no other gods before me, tested in the one area where it would cost him. It is a diagnostic instrument, precisely calibrated to one patient.

The camel and the needle should not be softened, and two softenings should be set aside. There is no evidence that “the eye of the needle” was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall — that story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages. And the suggestion that a copyist confused the word for camel with the word for rope is speculation about a text nobody has; a rope will not go through a needle either. Jesus picked the largest animal in the country and the smallest opening in common life, and the sentence means what it appears to mean.

The crowd's reaction — “then who can be saved?” — surprises modern readers, and the surprise is important. They shared the assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16, that prosperity evidenced God's approval. On that theology the rich were at the front of the queue.

“What is impossible with man is possible with God” is the pivot of the whole chapter. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did. The infants could not come; they were carried.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's “we have left our homes” is easy to hear as boasting, and it is fairer to hear it as a question with the question mark missing. He has just watched a man grieve because he could not give up his possessions, and heard that entry is impossible for such a man — and Peter has done the thing the ruler would not. And “our homes” is understated: Luke has recorded boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

Note the qualifying phrase in the answer: “for the sake of the kingdom of God.” This is not a promise attached to loss in general, and certainly not a licence for abandoning a family — Luke has already ruled that out (cf. 1 Tim. 5:8).

And what is returned is not usually the same currency. Mark's version specifies houses and brothers and mothers and children (Mark 10:30), which is not a promise of replacement relatives but a description of what the church turned out to be. A man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses. Anyone who has watched a convert lose his relations and gain a congregation has seen this verse work.

But Mark adds two words Luke omits — with persecutions. The return is real and it is not comfortable, and Luke's silence should not be read as a promise of an easier settlement than his brother evangelist offers.

A wealthy member of a congregation serves faithfully — on the board, in generous giving, in every visible way — and there is one area he has never submitted to Christ's scrutiny. The rich ruler was, by most measures, exemplary. The issue was not what he had done but what he would not surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: And a ruler asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a ruler asked him, Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?

Luke calls him a ruler — a man of official standing, probably a synagogue ruler or a member of a local council. Matthew tells us he was young; all three Gospels tell us he was rich.

And he asks the best question in the Gospel, sincerely. Mark says he ran up and knelt (Mark 10:17), which is not the behaviour of a man laying a trap. Whatever is wrong here, insincerity is not it.

But listen to the shape of the sentence, because the whole problem is in it. What must I do to inherit? — the same collision Luke recorded from the lawyer at 10:25, a doing-word and a receiving-word in one breath. An inheritance is the one thing nobody works for.

And it comes one verse after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to infants.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

This has been used to argue that Jesus denied his own deity, and it will not do the work. He does not say I am not good. He asks a question about a word.

Good Teacher was not a standard form of address; the rabbinic sources have nothing quite like it, and it reads as a compliment paid to a man whose approval the ruler wants. So the question is a challenge to think about what has just been said.

Only God is good in the absolute sense. So either the title is loose — flattery, a pleasant thing to say to a teacher one admires — or it is exact, and the ruler has said far more than he intended.

Jesus does not resolve it. He leaves the man holding both halves.

Is Jesus denying that he is good, or that he is God? Neither. The title is true: Jesus is good because he is God, without sin (Heb 4:15). His question presses the man to think about what he is saying: if only God is good, and you call me good, what do you think I am?

And there is a reason he starts here rather than answering the question. A man who hands out the word good that easily has a scale on which the word can be applied to people, and he is standing somewhere on it. Everything that follows is going to be about where.
verseByVerse.note: Luke calls him a ruler; Matthew adds that he was young.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’' And he said, 'All these I have kept from my youth.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments.

Note the assumption, and it is not a compliment. He does not teach him anything. This man knows.

And then a list, and the selection is the thing to watch: Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.

Five commandments, all from the second table of the Decalogue — the ones governing how a man treats his neighbour. And they are the observable ones, the commandments a community can check.

What is not quoted is the first table. Nothing about having no other gods, nothing about idols, nothing about the name or the Sabbath. And nothing about the tenth commandment, you shall not covet — the only one in the list that is entirely interior and cannot be verified by anybody.

That is not an accident, and the omission is going to be filled in at verse 22.

And he said, All these I have kept from my youth.

It is worth taking his claim seriously, because Jesus does. There is no suggestion anywhere in the passage that the man is lying, and Mark records that Jesus looked at him and loved him (Mark 10:21).

By any measure a first-century community could apply, this is an exemplary man. He has not committed adultery, killed anybody, stolen, perjured himself or dishonoured his parents — and he has managed it since boyhood.

From my youth. A lifetime of it, and no exceptions claimed.

Which is precisely the position of a great many decent people, and it is why this passage is so uncomfortable. The ruler is not a warning about scandalous living. He is a warning about a life that genuinely passes every test a person can be set — and a man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

Was the ruler really blameless? Only by outward measure. No one keeps the law as God requires (Rom 3:20; Gal 3:10–11), and Jesus had taught that anger and lust break the commandments (Matt 5:21–28). Jesus is not offering a ladder of law-keeping to eternal life; he is using the law to show the man his need. His next words expose that his wealth was his god (v. 22), and the answer comes at vv. 26–27: what is impossible with man is possible with God.

He has measured himself by what he can see and has not yet found his limit. It is about to be located for him with a single sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard this, he said to him, 'One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One thing you still lack.

After a lifetime of commandment-keeping, one item outstanding — and the arithmetic of that is worth pausing on. It sounds like a small remaining balance on an otherwise settled account, which is exactly how the man would have heard it.

It is not. The one thing is the whole thing.

Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.

Four imperatives, and the last is the point of the other three. This is not primarily a command about money; it is a call to discipleship with an obstacle removed first, and the obstacle is named because Jesus can see it.

And it is worth being clear that this is not a universal rule. He does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8-9); he does not say it to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3), or to Martha, whose house he was glad of. Luke has been careful about this all through.

What has happened is that the first table of the law, quietly left out of the list two verses ago, has just been applied. You shall have no other gods before me — and the man is being asked to demonstrate that he has not, in the one area where it would cost him.

It is a diagnostic instrument, precisely calibrated to one patient.

But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.

Luke's word is strong — deeply grieved, not merely disappointed. He is not indignant and he does not argue. He is heartbroken, which means he understood exactly what was offered and exactly what it cost.

And Luke's last clause is the diagnosis in five words: for he was extremely rich.

The Gospel does not tell us he went away, though Matthew and Mark do. Luke simply leaves him standing there, sad, in front of Jesus — and it is one of the few conversations in the Gospels that ends with the man losing.

He came with the right question, and was offered treasure in heaven and the company of the Son of God, and he could not do it. Nothing in the passage suggests Jesus was wrong to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, 'How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!

He says it while looking at him. This is not a general observation delivered afterwards; it is spoken over a grieving man who is still in front of him.

For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

The image is deliberately absurd and it should not be softened.

Two softenings have been attempted over the centuries and both should be set aside. One is that the eye of the needle was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall through which a camel could pass on its knees with its load removed; there is no evidence any such gate existed, and the story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages. The other is that the Greek word for camel is a near-miss for the word for rope, and a copyist confused them; that is speculation about a text nobody has, and a rope will not go through a needle either.

The camel was the largest animal in that country and the needle's eye the smallest opening in common life. Jesus has picked the two extremes on purpose, and the sentence means what it appears to mean: this cannot be done.

Which raises the obvious question about why. And it is not that wealth is wicked, or that God objects to comfort.

It is that entering this kingdom requires arriving with empty hands, and wealth is the most effective device ever invented for keeping them full. A rich man's difficulty is not that he loves money more than a poor man does — that is often untrue. It is that his life is arranged so that he never has to depend on anybody, and the kingdom is entered only by people who have run out of alternatives.

The needle's eye is not too small for a camel because God is stingy about the entrance. It is exactly the right size for a person carrying nothing.

And by any global standard, almost everybody reading this is the camel.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who heard it said, 'Then who can be saved?' But he said, 'What is impossible with man is possible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who heard it said, Then who can be saved?

The reaction is not what a modern reader expects, and the surprise is the important thing about it.

We hear hard for a rich man and think: yes, wealth is a spiritual danger, that is a familiar idea. They heard it and concluded that nobody could be saved at all.

Why? Because they shared an assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16 — that prosperity was evidence of God's approval. On that theology the rich were the front of the queue. They had the means to give alms, to keep the law without economic pressure, to be visibly blessed. If they cannot get in, the rest of the field is hopeless.

So the question is despairing and it is entirely logical. It is also, at last, the right question — and it is the first thing anybody in this chapter has said that does not begin with I.

The ruler asked what must I do? The crowd asks who can be saved? — passive, and with no candidate in mind.

But he said, What is impossible with man is possible with God.

One sentence, and it is the gospel.

Note that he does not soften the diagnosis. He does not say it is difficult but manageable, or produce a technique for wealthy disciples. He grants the whole of the objection: it is impossible. The camel does not get smaller and the needle does not get wider.

What he adds is a different actor.

Which is the pivot of the entire chapter, and everything before it has been preparing for it. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did it. The infants could not come; they were carried. And a rich man cannot enter the kingdom — and God can put him there.

Salvation, on this account, is not a difficult thing made possible by effort. It is an impossible thing done by somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, 'See, we have left our homes and followed you.' And he said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter said, See, we have left our homes and followed you.

It is easy to hear this as boasting, and it is worth being fairer to Peter than that.

He has just watched a man grieve in front of Jesus because he could not give up his possessions, and heard that entering the kingdom is impossible for such a man. And Peter has done the thing the ruler would not. His sentence is not a claim to merit so much as a question with the question mark missing: we did it — is it all right?

And our homes is understated. Luke has recorded what they left: boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.

The answer is generous and it is exact.

Note the qualifying phrase: for the sake of the kingdom of God. This is not a promise attached to loss in general, and it is certainly not a licence for abandoning a family. What is in view is what discipleship costs when it costs something — and Scripture elsewhere rules out the reading that would make this an excuse for neglect (1 Tim. 5:8).

Many times more in this time. Not only in the age to come. Something is returned now.

And what is returned is not usually the same currency. Mark's version specifies houses and brothers and mothers and children (Mark 10:30), which is not a promise of replacement relatives but a description of what the church turned out to be. A man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses; the community became what he had given up, multiplied.

Anyone who has watched a convert lose his relations and gain a congregation has seen this verse work.

But it is worth being honest that Mark adds two words Luke omits — with persecutions. The return is real and it is not comfortable, and Luke's silence should not be read as a promise of an easier settlement than his brother evangelist offers.

And in the age to come eternal life. Which is what the ruler asked for at verse 18, and was left without.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and the Blind Man at Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third and fullest of the passion predictions, and the only one that explicitly grounds the events in Scripture: “everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.” What is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan; it is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before.

Every item can be traced. Isaiah's Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6); he was despised and rejected (Isa. 53:3-5). The psalmist is mocked and surrounded (Ps. 22:7-8). And “delivered over to the Gentiles” is new: the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

Notice how much of the list concerns humiliation rather than pain — mocked, shamefully treated, spat on — and Luke will record every one of them happening.

Then the incomprehension, stated three times in one verse so the reader cannot soften it. Jesus has given six specific things in plain language with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him three years took in nothing.

And the juxtaposition that follows is deliberate and devastating. The disciples, who have eyes, cannot see what he has just told them plainly. A blind beggar outside Jericho, working from one sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right — and “Son of David” is a messianic title, the first time in this Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud.

The crowd tells him to be silent, using the same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the babies two dozen verses earlier. And the people doing it are “those who were in front” — the ones nearest to Jesus.

He cries out all the more, and the widow at the top of the chapter would have recognised him exactly.
verseByVerse.theology:
A reader with three Gospels open will stop at v.35, and the difficulty is worth facing because sceptics have made a good deal of it. Luke has the healing “as he drew near to Jericho” and then has Jesus entering the town (19:1); Matthew and Mark both have it as he was going out (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew reports two blind men where the others report one, and only Mark supplies a name.

The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives a name and a father's name — “Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus” — which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask.

The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart: the ancient city standing as a ruin on its old mound, and the splendid new town Herod the Great had built to the south with his winter palace, with the road running between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there produce exactly these.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's threefold statement that the disciples understood nothing is a mercy to the reader as well as astonishing. These are the men who would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this stupid, and nobody who had merely persuaded himself of a resurrection afterwards would write down that he had been told in advance and had not understood a word.

And there is something here for anyone who has read a passage repeatedly and got nothing from it. They heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity; it arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45).

“And Jesus stopped” is worth the whole paragraph. He is on the last stretch to Jerusalem, has just described in detail what is waiting there, and the entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for a beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

“What do you want me to do for you?” is on the face of it unnecessary — anybody could name the need. But being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. And the mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

He was not told to follow, and he followed. The first thing he does with working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And taking the twelve, he said to them.

He takes them aside. What follows is not for the crowd, and it is the third and fullest of these announcements (cf. 9:22; 9:44).

See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.

Two things before the details.

We are going up. Jerusalem sits high, and pilgrims always went up to it; but the word carries more here, because Luke has had his face set that way since 9:51. This is the last stretch.

And the framing is prophetic. Not this will happen but everything written will be accomplished — brought to completion.

Which means what is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan. It is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before.

Then the list, and it is the most detailed he has given.

Delivered over to the Gentiles — handed to Rome, which is new information; the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests. Mocked. Shamefully treated. Spit upon. Then flogging, then killing.

Every item can be traced. Isaiah's Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6); he was despised and rejected, and by his wounds we are healed (Isa. 53:3-5). The psalmist is mocked, surrounded, and has his garments divided (Ps. 22:7-8, 18).

Notice how much of the list is about humiliation rather than pain. Mocked, shamefully treated, spat on — three of the six items concern what will be done to his dignity, and Luke will record every one of them happening.

And on the third day he will rise.

And, as always, he does not stop at the death. He has never once announced it without the rising in the same breath.

One thing more is worth registering about the pronouns. Every verb in this list is passive or has somebody else as its subject. He will be delivered, mocked, treated shamefully, spat on, flogged, killed — things done to a man who is not doing anything.

And then the last clause turns: he will rise. Active, and his own. Everything up to the grave happens to him; the thing after it is something he does.

verseByVerse.quote: But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.

Three statements of the same fact in one verse, which is Luke making certain the reader does not soften it.

They understood none of these things — not little, not imperfectly. None.

This saying was hidden from them — and Luke does not say who hid it. He said the same at 9:45 after the second prediction, and he will say something like it of the Emmaus pair whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16).

And they did not grasp what was said.

Why put it three times?

Partly because it is astonishing, and Luke knows it. Jesus has just given a list of six specific things, in plain language, with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him for three years took in nothing.

But there is a second reason, and it is a mercy to the reader.

These are the men who would shortly write and preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this stupid. And nobody who had merely persuaded himself of a resurrection afterwards would remember, and write down, that he had been told in advance and had not understood a word.

They did not see it coming. Luke says so three times in one verse — which means that when they did come to believe, it was not because they had been expecting it.

It is worth asking what was actually blocking them, because it was not stupidity. These men had a settled picture of what Messiah meant, and it had no room in it for a crucifixion. The words went in and found nowhere to lodge.

That is how most misunderstanding of Scripture works. Not a failure to hear the sentence, but a frame that will not accommodate it — and the frame is invisible to the person holding it.

Who hid it from them? Luke’s phrase points to God, as at 9:45 and 24:16: the meaning was withheld until the cross and resurrection would make it plain (24:45). The disciples were also slow because they could not imagine a suffering Messiah.

And there is something for anyone who has read a passage of Scripture repeatedly and got nothing from it. The disciples heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity. It arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45).

verseByVerse.quote: As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him, 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging.

A reader with three Gospels open will stop at that first line, and the difficulty is worth facing squarely because sceptics have made a good deal of it.

Luke says the healing happened as he drew near to Jericho, and then opens the next chapter with Jesus entering the town (19:1) — so on Luke's account the man was healed before Jesus ever got there. Matthew and Mark both say it happened as he was going out of Jericho (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46). On top of that, Matthew reports two blind men where Mark and Luke report one, and only Mark supplies a name.

The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives not just a name but a father's name — Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus — which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask; he had evidently become known in the church, and both he and Luke follow the man who mattered to the tradition, while Matthew, careful of the whole scene, notes there were two.

The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart. The ancient city stood as a ruin on its old mound; Herod the Great had built a splendid new town to the south with his winter palace, and the road ran between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there, or who talked to people who were, produce exactly these.

And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant.

He cannot see, so he asks — and the detail is the point of him. He has to work out from sound alone that something is happening, and he does not let it pass.

They told him, Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.

The crowd's description is accurate and small. Jesus of Nazareth — a place and a name. It is what everybody knew, and the blind man is about to say something better with less information.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 17 miles by road east-north-east of Jerusalem. Mark names the man Bartimaeus; Matthew mentions two men.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he cried out, Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!

He was told Jesus of Nazareth. What comes back is Son of David.

That is a messianic title and it is the first time in Luke's Gospel that anybody has used it of him aloud. Gabriel spoke of the throne of his father David (1:32); the genealogy runs through David; but no human being in this book has looked at Jesus and said it until now.

And it is a blind beggar sitting in the dust outside a town.

Set that against the paragraph immediately before it. Twelve men who could see, who had been given the plainest possible account of what was about to happen, understood none of it. A man who cannot see, working from a sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right.

Luke has put the two side by side and he means it to hurt.

Have mercy on me. Not a diagnosis and not a request for anything specific — the same plea the tax collector made in the temple twenty-five verses ago. He asks for mercy and leaves the content of it to Jesus.

And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent.

The same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the babies (v. 15). The crowd is doing again what the disciples had just been corrected for doing — clearing the road of people with no standing so that the important business can proceed.

And notice who they are: those who were in front. The people nearest to Jesus are the ones telling this man to be quiet.

But he cried out all the more, Son of David, have mercy on me!

He does not lower his voice; he raises it. Nothing about his social position, his blindness or the public rebuke is enough to make him stop, because he has worked out that this is the only chance he is going to get and there is not going to be another crowd.

The widow at the top of the chapter would have recognised him exactly.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, 'What do you want me to do for you?' He said, 'Lord, let me recover my sight.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus stopped.

Three words, and they are worth the whole entry.

He is on the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem. He has just told the Twelve, in detail, what is waiting for him there. There is a crowd around him, a procession moving, and a fixed appointment at the far end of it that everything in this Gospel has been travelling towards since 9:51.

And he stops, because somebody is shouting.

Luke does not decorate it. The entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for a beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

And commanded him to be brought to him.

Note who is now employed on the errand. The crowd that was telling him to be quiet is the crowd that has to go and fetch him — Mark records them saying take heart; get up, he is calling you (Mark 10:49), which must have been a considerable adjustment.

And when he came near, he asked him, What do you want me to do for you?

Which is, on the face of it, an unnecessary question. The man is blind and has been begging by a roadside; anybody could name the need.

So why ask?

Partly because being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. Nobody in that town had put a question to him in a long time.

But mostly because a request has to be made. Jesus will not heal him over his head either. The mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to shut up.

Lord, let me recover my sight.

And he asks. Plainly, without preamble, without qualifying it or hedging it or asking whether it is too much.

It is worth setting that beside the ruler at verse 18, who came asking what he must do. This man asks for what he needs.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.' And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to him, Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.

No touch, no clay, no procedure. One word in Greek and it is done.

And the second half is the phrase Luke keeps for the moments that go past the body: hē pistis sou sesōken se — the same words spoken to the woman weeping at his feet (7:50), to the woman in the crowd (8:48), and to the Samaritan leper who came back (17:19).

The verb is sōzō, and it means both healed and saved. Something has happened here that is more than a pair of eyes.

Your faith. Which is worth examining, because there was not much of it and it was not sophisticated. He had heard a name, shouted a title, refused to be silenced, and asked for the obvious thing.

That is the whole content. No theology, no track record, no promise about what he would do afterwards — and Jesus calls it faith and says it has saved him.

And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him.

He was not told to. There is no instruction here, and Jesus had told others to go home (8:39). This man simply falls in behind the procession, and everybody knows where it is going.

The first thing he does with a pair of working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one to Jerusalem.

Glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

And the chapter that began with a widow being ignored ends with a whole crowd praising God — including the people who had told the man to be quiet.

Here, then, is how the last stage of that journey begins. The Son of Man has set out for a city where he will be handed to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged and killed, and he has told his friends so, and they have not understood a word of it. And on the way he stops for one man nobody wanted him to hear, gives him his eyes, and gains a follower who walks the rest of that road with him.

Nothing in Jerusalem was going to be turned aside. But there was time, on the way to it, for a beggar who would not stop shouting.

18.text: <sup>1</sup> And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. <sup>2</sup> He said, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. <sup>3</sup> And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ <sup>4</sup> For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, <sup>5</sup> yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says. <sup>7</sup> And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” <sup>9</sup> He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’ <sup>13</sup> But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ <sup>14</sup> I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>15</sup> Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. <sup>16</sup> But Jesus called them to him, saying, “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>17</sup> Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>18</sup> And a ruler asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>19</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>20</sup> You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>21</sup> And he said, “All these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>23</sup> But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. <sup>24</sup> Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, “How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup> For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup> Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup> But he said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” <sup>28</sup> And Peter said, “See, we have left our homes and followed you.” <sup>29</sup> And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, <sup>30</sup> who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.” <sup>31</sup> And taking the twelve, he said to them, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. <sup>32</sup> For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. <sup>33</sup> And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” <sup>34</sup> But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said. <sup>35</sup> As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. <sup>36</sup> And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. <sup>37</sup> They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.” <sup>38</sup> And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>39</sup> And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, <sup>41</sup> “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, let me recover my sight.” <sup>42</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.” <sup>43</sup> And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

19.title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the Triumphal Entry
19.overview:
Luke 19 is a chapter of arrivals. Jesus arrives at Jericho and finds Zacchaeus — a chief tax collector who has climbed a tree to see him and who will descend, transformed, to receive salvation in his house. Then Jesus tells the Parable of the Ten Minas — a kingdom parable about accountability and fruitfulness during the time of the absent king. Then Jesus arrives at Jerusalem itself, riding on a colt, welcomed by his disciples with praise, weeping over the city as he approaches it, and then cleansing the temple. The chapter is a compressed journey from private transformation (Zacchaeus) to public confrontation (the temple), with the parable providing the theological framework for understanding the entire sequence.

Zacchaeus is one of Luke's most vivid portraits of salvation. He is a chief tax collector, wealthy, despised, short of stature, and apparently desperate to see Jesus. He runs ahead and climbs a tree — an undignified act for a man of his status. Jesus's response is overwhelming: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” The word dei (must) is a divine necessity — the same word used for the Son of Man's suffering. Salvation has come to this house; the Son of Man has come to seek and to save the lost.

The Triumphal Entry (vv. 28–44) contains one of the most emotionally powerful moments in all of Luke: Jesus weeping over Jerusalem. The parade of praise, the disciples crying out about the king who comes in the name of the Lord — and then Jesus stopping on the descent and weeping, because she did not know “the things that make for peace.” This is not despair; it is the grief of the shepherd for the sheep who will not come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus was passing through Jericho — not stopping. The whole story turns on that clause, and on a man who got in the way of it.

Zacchaeus is described with three details that should make him unsympathetic. He is a chief tax collector — architelōnēs, a word that appears nowhere else in surviving Greek literature and may be Luke's own coinage. It means he held the district contract and had other collectors under him, taking a percentage of each man's takings. And Jericho was no backwater: it sat on the trade route from the east, in a plain famous for balsam and dates, at the crossing into Judea. That customs post was one of the most lucrative in the country.

He is rich, and by this point in Luke that word has weight — a rich man in torment three chapters back (16:19-31), a rich ruler grieving one chapter back (18:23-25), and a camel that will not go through a needle. The disciples had asked, reasonably, “then who can be saved?” The next rich man in this Gospel is up a tree.

And he is small in stature, which the crowd exploits. A short man can usually reach the front of a gathering; a short and thoroughly hated man in the town where he holds the tax contract will find that nobody moves.

So he runs — humiliating for a man of standing, since it meant hitching up the robe — and climbs a fig-mulberry, which is a boy's activity in full view of the street. Dignity is the first thing that goes. It nearly always is.

Then Jesus stops, looks up, and uses his name. Nothing in the story explains how he knew it. He announces rather than asks — “I must stay at your house today” — which is a mercy, because a man in Zacchaeus's position does not issue invitations and had learned not to put himself where he could be refused.

The crowd grumbles, all of them. And Zacchaeus stands and gives away half of everything and repays fourfold, and Jesus says salvation has come to the house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The episode is a case study in sovereign grace. Jesus announces the visit before any repentance has occurred; the restitution follows the encounter and is the fruit of salvation received, not the ground of it. It is the exact pattern of chapter 15 — the shepherd finds the sheep, and the sheep does not find its way home.

A crux has to be faced at v.8, because a good many modern commentators press it. Both verbs are present — “I give,” “I restore” — and a present can describe a habitual practice. On that reading Zacchaeus is not promising but defending himself: I already give half away; the grumbling is unjust.

It is possible and should be rejected, for three reasons drawn from the passage. Luke has told us the man was rich, and a chief tax collector who gave away half his income and repaid fourfold every disputed claim would not have stayed rich for a season. Jesus's reply is “today salvation has come to this house,” which is a strange thing to say to a man who has just proved he was fine all along. And the present is also the ordinary form for a promise made on the spot — I give you my word, or a man at an altar saying I take you.

The numbers are not arbitrary either. Half is far beyond anything the law required, and fourfold is the penalty for the aggravated case, a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Ex. 22:1); ordinary restitution was the sum plus a fifth (Lev. 6:5). He sentences himself at the highest rate on the books.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Son of Abraham” is a deliberate provocation, because it is precisely what the grumblers would have denied. A tax collector had forfeited his place in the popular reckoning, and some rabbinic rulings treated his repentance as practically impossible, since he could never trace everyone he had defrauded. Jesus hands the title back — as he did six chapters earlier to a bent woman nobody had helped in eighteen years, “a daughter of Abraham” (13:16).

And v.10 is the sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel. It answers the grumbling completely: they objected that he had gone in to a sinner's house, and he replies that this is the errand. Not a regrettable necessity, not an exception made for a promising case — the stated purpose of the coming. The verbs are the shepherd's from chapter 15: to seek, and to save.

Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him.

The story is also addressed to the crowd. A man in a congregation has a reputation; everyone knows what he was before — the financial impropriety, the trail of damage. He is welcomed into membership and watched carefully, with a persistent sense that his inclusion is provisional. Those who murmur at Christ's table fellowship with notorious sinners share the theology of the men in this street. He does not.

verseByVerse.quote: He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered Jericho and was passing through.

Note the second clause, because the whole story turns on it. He was not stopping. Jericho was on the pilgrim road up to Jerusalem, some seventeen miles short of the city, and he was walking through it on his way to a cross.

And Luke has just told us what happened on the road into Jericho: a blind man shouted until he was heard, and was healed, and joined the procession (18:35-43). So the crowd coming through Jericho is large, loud, and celebrating.

And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus.

The behold is Luke pointing again, as he does whenever somebody is about to be noticed who would not otherwise have been.

The name is Hebrew — Zakkai, which means pure or righteous. Whatever his parents hoped for when they gave it to him, the town had long since drawn its own conclusions.

He was a chief tax collector and was rich.

Two facts, and both are worse than they look.

Chief tax collector means he did not sit at a booth himself; he held the contract for the district and had other collectors under him, taking a percentage of what each of them took.

And Jericho was not a backwater. It sat on the trade route from the east, in a fertile plain famous for its balsam groves and date palms, at the crossing point into Judea. The customs post there was one of the most lucrative in the country.

And was rich. Luke states it flatly, and by this point in his Gospel that word has weight. Three chapters back a rich man was in torment and a beggar was in Abraham's bosom (16:19-31). One chapter back a rich ruler became very sad, and Jesus said it was easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle (18:23-25).

The disciples had asked, reasonably, then who can be saved? The next rich man in this Gospel is up a tree.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich town on a major trade route. A chief tax collector oversaw other collectors and profited from all of them.

parallels.desc: how difficult for those who have wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was seeking to see who Jesus was.

The verb is continuous — he was seeking, and it is Luke's own word for the thing that will be said about Jesus seven verses later: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Two searches are running in this story and they meet under a tree.

And notice what he wants. Not a healing; he is not ill. Not a favour. He is seeking to see who Jesus was — which is either idle curiosity or something a good deal deeper, and Luke does not say which. What he says is that the man kept trying.

But on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature.

The crowd is the obstacle, and it is worth asking whether it was entirely accidental. A short man can usually work his way to the front of a gathering. A short and thoroughly hated man, in the town where he holds the tax contract, is going to find that the people in front of him do not move.

So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree.

Two undignified actions in one sentence, and in that culture both were genuinely humiliating for a man of his standing.

Grown men of position did not run. It required hitching up the long robe and exposing the legs, and the same detail made the father's run in chapter 15 so shocking. And climbing a tree is worse — it is a boy's activity, and it puts him where the whole street can see him.

The tree is a sycamore in the old sense: not the plane tree of northern Europe but the fig-mulberry, a broad low-branching tree with an easy climb and dense foliage, common along Jordan valley roads.

So the richest and most powerful man in Jericho, in a robe worth more than most of the crowd earned in a year, sprints down the road ahead of a procession and gets up a tree like a child, because there is somebody he has to see.

Dignity is the first thing that goes. It nearly always is.
verseByVerse.note: The sycamore here is the sycamore-fig, a tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.' So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, Zacchaeus.

He knew the name.

Nothing in the story explains how. Nobody is described as telling him; there is no introduction. He walks to a particular tree in a town he is passing through, stops, looks up into the branches, and uses the man's name.

And of all the things that could have happened to Zacchaeus that afternoon, this is the one he had not prepared for. He had climbed up to see; he had not expected to be seen.

Hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.

Three things in one sentence, and each is startling.

Hurry. There is an urgency, and it is on Jesus's side.

I must — dei, the divine-necessity word Luke has been using at every hinge of this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father's house (2:49). It has governed a preaching circuit (4:43), a passion prediction (9:22), and a journey to Jerusalem (13:33). Here it governs an evening in a tax collector's dining room. Whatever list that word belongs to, this is on it.

Today. Luke's sēmeron again, and it will come back four verses later.

Note also that Jesus does not ask. He announces. Zacchaeus is not invited to invite him; he is told, in front of the whole street, that his house is where this is happening.

Which is a mercy, and anyone who has ever been the disreputable one in a room will see why. A man in that position does not issue invitations. He has learned not to put himself where he can be refused, and if Jesus had waited to be asked he would have waited under that tree until dark.

So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.

He obeys both verbs — hurried, came down — and Luke adds the third one himself. He received him joyfully.

Nothing has yet been said about sin, restitution, or the tax contract. All that is coming, and it comes from Zacchaeus. What happens first is that a man who was up a tree is on the ground, and glad.

parallels.desc: I will come in to him and eat with him

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they all grumbled, 'He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.' And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they saw it, they all grumbled.

All of them. Not the Pharisees this time — Luke does not name a party, and the previous grumblers were the scribes and Pharisees (15:2). This is the whole crowd, including the people who had been praising God about a blind man shortly before.

He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.

Accurate on every point, and meant as an indictment.

And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.

He stood — probably rising at the meal, which is the posture of someone making a formal declaration rather than a private confession.

Now the crux, and it must be faced because a good many modern commentators press it. Both verbs are in the present tense: I give, I restore. Greek can use a present for a habitual practice, and on that reading Zacchaeus is not promising anything; he is defending himself. I already give half away, and I already make restitution — the grumbling is unjust.

It is a possible reading, and it should be rejected, for three reasons drawn from the passage itself.

First, Luke has told us the man was rich (v. 2). A chief tax collector who gave away half his income and repaid fourfold every disputed claim would not have stayed rich for a season.

Second, Jesus's reply is today salvation has come to this house — which is a strange thing to say to a man who has just proved he was fine all along.

Third, and decisively, the present is also the ordinary form for a promise made on the spot, the way English says I give you my word or a man at an altar says I take you. That is plainly the sense here.

Did Zacchaeus earn his salvation by giving and repaying? No. Jesus pronounces salvation after the vow, but the vow is the fruit of a heart already changed by Jesus’ welcome, not the price of it (Eph 2:8–10). And must a new believer make restitution for past wrongs? Where it is possible, yes: repentance includes putting right what we have wrongly taken (Exod 22:1; Lev 6:1–5). It is not the ground of forgiveness, but it is how forgiven people behave.

Must every Christian give away half his goods? No. Jesus told the rich ruler to sell everything (18:22) and did not tell Zacchaeus to; Zacchaeus chose this freely. The test for every believer is a loosened grip on money and a generous hand.

And look at the numbers, because they are not arbitrary. Half is far beyond anything the law required. And fourfold is the penalty for the aggravated case — a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Ex. 22:1); ordinary restitution was the sum plus a fifth (Lev. 6:5). He sentences himself at the highest rate on the books.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a thief to repay a stolen sheep fourfold; for ordinary wrongs, the amount plus a fifth.

parallels.desc: restore it in full and add a fifth

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Today salvation has come to this house.

Today — one of Luke's great todays, and they form a spine through the Gospel: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior (2:11); today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:21); this one; and, from a cross, today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43).

And note what is said to have arrived. Not you have been forgiven, though he has. Salvation has come — and it came up the road that morning and is currently sitting at the table.

To this house. Not merely to Zacchaeus. Whatever else that means, the household is included in the reckoning — the wife, the children, the servants, all of whom had been living on the proceeds and are now living in a house where half of it has just been given away.

Since he also is a son of Abraham.

Which is a deliberate provocation, because it is precisely what the grumblers would have denied. In the popular reckoning a tax collector had forfeited his place; he was a traitor living off his own people, and some rabbinic rulings treated his repentance as practically impossible, since he could never trace everyone he had defrauded.

Jesus hands him the title back. And Luke has done this once before, six chapters earlier, for a bent woman nobody had helped in eighteen years — a daughter of Abraham (13:16). It is the same move, and it is aimed at the same people.

For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

Here is the sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel, and Luke has been building to it for eighteen chapters.

It answers the grumbling in verse 7 completely. They objected that he had gone in to a sinner's house; he replies that this is the errand. Not a regrettable necessity, not an exception made for a promising case — the stated purpose of the coming.

And the verbs are the shepherd's from chapter 15: to seek, and to save. There is a search going on. It has been going on the whole time, and it is why he was walking through Jericho at all.

Does salvation has come to this house mean that his family and servants were saved with him? Salvation arrived in his home when Jesus came, and blessing spreads through a believing household. But each person must still believe for himself, as at Philippi, where the jailer’s household heard the word and believed (Acts 16:31–34).

Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us exactly why the parable is given, and there are two reasons: they were near Jerusalem, and they supposed the kingdom was about to appear immediately. Seventeen miles from the city, at Passover, behind a man who raises the dead — every expectation they had was about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

So everything in the parable is arranged to insert a delay where they expected a coronation: a departure, a long absence, an accounting on the return. And the shape is strange as a picture of the Messiah and exactly right — the King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem but in a far country, and comes back. Which is precisely what Luke's second volume describes (Acts 1:9-11).

Ten servants, ten minas — one each. Worth registering, because Matthew's cousin-parable of the talents distributes different amounts according to ability (Matt. 25:15). Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity; where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did. And a mina was about three months' wages — modest, and that is the point.

The subplot of the rebel citizens is borrowed from living memory. In 4 BC Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed; he came back with power and dealt with them. Jericho of all towns would have felt it — Archelaus rebuilt it and had a palace there.

The first two servants are rewarded proportionately and without comparison. The third produces the mina intact, wrapped in a handkerchief, and explains that he was afraid — and his accusation is turned against him. If the master really were what he says, the sensible course would have been the bank.

And the parable ends with the enemies. It is the hardest sentence in Luke.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable teaches two related truths. The kingdom has a “not yet”: the King goes away and returns, and faithful servants must live faithfully in the in-between. And stewardship in the in-between is not optional maintenance — “engage in business” is a commercial verb, and it is not “look after this.”

“Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little” is worth weighing for the disproportion. The master calls the mina — everything the servant had for the whole absence — a trifle, and gives ten cities in return. The exchange rate is absurd, and meant to be.

And notice what the reward is: more responsibility, on an enormously larger scale. Not rest, and not a payment. Which says something about heaven that cuts against the popular picture, since Scripture's images run the other way — “his servants will worship him… they will reign forever and ever” (Rev. 22:3-5).

“To everyone who has, more will be given” is not a celebration of the rich getting richer. It is a description of how entrusted things behave: capacity grows by use and atrophies without it. And note the last clause carefully — “from the one who has not.” The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master's reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for a whole absence is not a possession but an absence dressed up as one.

A reader with Matthew open should also know this is not the parable of the talents, though the two are cousins. Matthew's setting asks what you did with what you were given. Luke's, told on the road up to Jerusalem, asks that and one thing more — whether you wanted the King at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The third servant's fear is not reverence, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey — he was too frightened to act, which is a different thing entirely, and he had been calling it caution for the whole of the absence.

And his accusation is untrue, as the parable has already shown. This is a master who handed money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. The servant constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about.

The word “wicked” lands where a reader might not expect it. He has not stolen the money or wasted it or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth — and there is a category of failure here that comfortable religion rarely counts as sin at all. Nothing bad was done; that is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is condemned. A life that has carefully avoided doing anything wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

Verse 27 should not be hurried past. Two things keep it in place. These are words spoken by a character inside a parable, borrowed wholesale from a tyrant's homecoming, and not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task is to trade. And the horror of the image is the point rather than an embarrassment — Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway, and the tears of vv. 41-44 are fourteen verses off. A judgement described in terms this stark, by a man crying about it, is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable.

Luke, unusually, tells us exactly why — and there are two reasons.

Because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately.

Seventeen miles from the city, at Passover, with a man who raises the dead at the head of the procession and a crowd shouting about a blind man. Every expectation they had was about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

They were also wrong about the timing in a way that would nearly destroy them within the week.

So the parable is corrective, and everything in it is arranged to insert a delay where they were expecting an immediate coronation: a departure, a long absence, an accounting on the return.

A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.

And there is the shape of it. Before there is a kingdom there is a journey, and the throne is granted somewhere else.

It is worth registering how strange that is as a picture of the Messiah, and how exactly it fits. The King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem. He receives it in a far country and comes back — which is, as Luke's second volume will describe it, precisely what happened: a man taken up out of their sight, seated at the right hand of God, and a promise that he will come in the same way (Acts 1:9-11).

The disciples wanted the crown on Friday. What they were going to get was a crucifixion, an ascension, and a wait of unspecified length with work to do in it.

Which is where every Christian since has been standing. The kingdom is real, the King has been enthroned, and he is not here — and the whole question of the Christian life is what a man does with the interval.

And it is worth noticing that Jesus is correcting an error of timing, not of hope. He does not tell them the kingdom is a spiritual metaphor, or that they have misunderstood what a king is. He tells them it is further off than they think and that there is work to do meanwhile.

Both halves of that have been lost in turn by the church. A Christianity that expects nothing has stopped believing there is a return; a Christianity that expects it next Tuesday has generally stopped trading.
verseByVerse.note: Local rulers went to Rome to have their kingdoms confirmed. Herod’s son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, and a Jewish delegation went after him to oppose it.

parallels.desc: will you at this time restore the kingdom?

verseByVerse.quote: Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, Engage in business until I come.

Three details, and each is deliberate.

Ten servants, and ten minas — one each. This is worth registering, because Matthew's cousin-parable of the talents distributes different amounts to different men, according to ability (Matt. 25:15). Here everybody gets exactly the same.

Which changes what the parable is measuring. Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity. Where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did.

A mina was a hundred denarii — about three months' wages for a labourer. Not a fortune, and that too is the point. He does not hand over the estate. He gives each man a modest, manageable sum and goes away.

Engage in business until I come.

The verb is a commercial one — trade with it, put it to work. It is not look after this. And the instruction contains its own deadline: until I come, which is both a promise that he will and a statement that the trading has an end date.

So the servants are left with three things: a sum of money, an instruction to risk it, and a return that is certain but unscheduled.

And that is the situation of the church, stated in a sentence. Every believer has been given something — and the parable's insistence that the amounts were identical is a rebuke to the very common conviction that one has been given nothing worth trading. Ten men, ten minas, no exceptions.

What was not given is instructions. He does not tell them what business to engage in, or set targets, or explain how he will assess them. He gives them the money and goes, and the freedom is real — which means the timid servant's failure in a few verses' time is not a failure to follow orders. It is a failure to believe that the freedom was genuinely given.

There is a particular comfort in the smallness of the sum, and it is easily missed. A mina is not a fortune, and the men receiving it are servants — they are not being handed the estate to run.

Which means that whatever a Christian has been given to trade with, the parable has already described it accurately: modest, ordinary, and entirely adequate for the purpose. Nobody in this story is under-resourced, and nobody is asked to produce something out of nothing.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a mina was about three months’ wages for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, We do not want this man to reign over us.

A second plot enters the parable, and it has nothing to do with the servants and their money.

The detail is not invented, and Jesus's hearers would have known it instantly. In 4 BC, on the death of Herod the Great, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by Caesar — and a delegation of fifty Jews followed him there to argue that he should not be given it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed. He came back with power, and he dealt with those who had opposed him.

Jesus is telling this parable on the road up to Jerusalem, within living memory of the event, in a country that had watched it happen. And Jericho of all places would have felt it: Archelaus rebuilt the town and had a palace there.

Which sharpens what he is doing with it. He is walking towards the city that is about to say exactly this about him — We do not want this man to reign over us — and he says it out loud, in a shape they cannot miss, days before they prove it true.

Note also the wording of the objection. It is not this man is unfit or we prefer another. It is we do not want this man to reign over us. The issue is not his credentials but his rule, and that has always been the issue.

When he returned, having received the kingdom.

Their delegation failed. That is the first thing the verse says, and it is said without comment: the objection was lodged, considered, and overruled somewhere far away, and the kingdom was granted anyway.

He ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.

And the first thing he does on arriving with a kingdom is not to deal with the rebels. It is to send for his own servants and ask what they did with what he left them.

parallels.desc: we have no king but Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.

Note whose mina it is. Not I have made ten — your mina has made ten. The servant reports a result without claiming it, and there is no trace of a man presenting his own achievement.

The return is extraordinary. A thousand per cent, on three months' wages, in an unspecified but evidently long absence. Whatever he did, he did it well.

Well done, good servant!

It is the first thing the returning king says to anybody in the parable. Before any assessment of the estate, before the rebels are dealt with, the man who traded faithfully hears his master say good.

Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.

And now the disproportion, which is the whole point of the verse.

A very little. That is the master's description of the mina — three months' wages, and everything the servant had to work with for the entire absence. He calls it a trifle.

Set that against what is given in return: authority over ten cities. Not ten minas, not a hundred. Cities, with people in them, in the kingdom he has just been granted.

The exchange rate is absurd, and it is meant to be. Whatever any Christian is trading with in this life — and it may look and feel like very little indeed — the parable insists on calling it small precisely in order to make the reward look impossible.

And notice what the reward actually is. Not rest, and not a payment. It is more responsibility, on an enormously larger scale. The faithful servant's prize is a bigger job in the King's administration.

Which says something about heaven that is worth having, because the popular picture is largely of rest. Scripture's images run the other way: his servants will worship him… they will reign forever and ever (Rev. 22:3-5). Whatever the life to come is, it is not retirement, and the training for it is going on now, in something the King calls very little.

verseByVerse.quote: And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the second came, saying, Lord, your mina has made five minas. And he said to him, And you are to be over five cities.

Two verses, and it would be easy to read them as a repetition. They are not, and what they add is one of the kindest things in the parable.

The second man has produced exactly half what the first produced. Same starting sum, same length of absence, same instruction — and half the result.

And there is no rebuke of any kind. Not a word about why he did not do better, no comparison with his colleague, no suggestion that five is disappointing.

What he gets is five cities: a reward proportioned exactly to the return, and every bit as real.

Which is worth sitting with by anyone who has ever measured his own Christian usefulness against somebody else's and gone quiet. There is a man in this parable who did half as well as the man standing next to him, and the King's response is to put him over five cities.

It should be said, though, that the master's reply to the second man is noticeably shorter. He gets the reward and not the commendation — no well done is recorded. Some readers press that; it is probably better not to. Luke is compressing, as he does everywhere, and the parable's contrast is not between the ten and the five. It is between both of them and the man with the handkerchief.

What the two together establish is the principle: the King rewards what was actually done, at the rate it was done, without grading on a curve.

And the arithmetic has one further implication that the third servant is about to discover. Five minas earned five cities. One mina, kept safe and returned intact, earns nothing at all — because nothing at all is what it produced.

There is one more thing in these two verses, and it is easy to walk past because so little happens in them. The second servant came. He had a smaller result than the man in front of him and he came anyway, and said out loud in front of the whole court exactly what he had produced.

That takes something. And it is the opposite of what the third servant will do in the next verse, which is to arrive with an explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then another came, saying, Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief.

He has it. That is the first thing, and it is what he thinks will save him. Nothing has been lost, nothing spent, nothing risked. He can put the coin on the table exactly as he received it.

The handkerchief is a soudarion — a cloth for wiping the face, and the same word used of the cloth over the face of Lazarus in the tomb (John 11:44). He wrapped the money in a rag and put it somewhere.

And note the difference from the others. They reported what the mina had made. He reports where he put it.

For I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.

Now the reason, and he offers it as an explanation. It is in fact an accusation.

Severe is austēros — the root of the English austere, used of unripe fruit and of a man with no give in him. And the two charges that follow describe a profiteer: someone who collects where he has not invested and harvests fields he never planted.

So this servant's defence is that his master is grasping and unfair, and that his own inactivity was a rational response.

Two things about that are worth naming, because the type is common and rarely recognises itself.

The first is that his fear is not reverence, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey.
