He was too frightened to act, which is a different thing entirely, and he has been calling it caution for the whole of the master's absence.

The second is that the accusation is untrue, and the parable has already shown it. This is a master who handed out money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. Whatever he is, he is not a man who takes what he did not deposit.

The servant has constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about.
verseByVerse.note: A handkerchief was not a safe place for money; burying it was safer.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant!

The master does not argue the description. He does not say I am not severe. He takes the servant's own account of him and turns it round.

You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow?

The logic is plain: very well — suppose I am exactly what you say.

Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?

And there is the trap closing.

Banking existed and paid interest; the money-changers took deposits, and there was nothing exotic about it. It required no skill, no judgement, and no courage. A man could walk in, hand the mina over, and walk out.

So the servant's own premise convicts him. If the master really were a hard man who reaped where he had not sown, the sensible response would have been to make certain he got something. The one course of action his stated fear cannot possibly justify is doing absolutely nothing.

Which exposes the fear as a cover story. He did not act on his belief about the master, because it was never the reason. It was the excuse he had ready.

And the word wicked lands where a reader might not expect it. He has not stolen the money, or wasted it, or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth — and there is a category of failure here that comfortable religion very rarely counts as sin at all.

Is the third servant a believer who loses reward, or an unbeliever who is lost? He belongs to the household outwardly, but his picture of the master as harsh shows that he never knew him (cf. Matt 25:24–30, where he is cast into outer darkness). Faithfulness is not the ground of salvation; it is the fruit of knowing a gracious master. The servant who buries his gift shows he does not.

Nothing bad was done. That is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is being condemned. The servant was not asked to avoid loss. He was asked to trade, and he did not, and a life that has carefully avoided doing anything wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.

The bystanders object — Lord, he has ten minas! — which is the natural response and the one most readers share. Why give more to the man who already has most?

I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

The principle sounds harsh until it is read as what it is: not a rule about distributing rewards, but a description of how entrusted things actually behave.

The saying has appeared before in this Gospel, attached to hearing (8:18), and the mechanism is the same. Capacity grows by use. A man who trades finds he can trade more, because the trading itself made him a better trader. And a man who hides away what he was given loses even the ability to use it — not by confiscation but by atrophy.

Every musician, every craftsman, every preacher knows this without being taught it. Nothing is more perishable than an unexercised gift.

And notice the last clause carefully: from the one who has not. The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master's reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for the whole of an absence is not a possession at all — it is an absence dressed up as one. He has nothing, because he has done nothing with it, and the removal of the coin is simply the paperwork catching up.

There is a hard word in this for a certain kind of Christian caution, and it is worth stating plainly. The instinct to protect — to hold what one has been given, to take no risk with it, to be able to produce it intact at the end — feels like faithfulness and is its opposite.

The mina was never in danger of being lost. It was in danger of doing nothing, and that is the only danger the parable takes seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.

It is the hardest sentence in Luke, and it should not be hurried past. Readers recoil, and some have quoted the line as though Jesus were commanding violence against opponents.

Two things keep it in its place.

First, these are words spoken by a character inside a parable, not an instruction issued to disciples. The king in the story is doing what such kings did, and the picture has been borrowed wholesale from Archelaus, whose reprisals after Rome confirmed him were remembered with horror. Nobody in that crowd would have heard it as a policy for them to carry out. Not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task, from first to last, is to trade with what they were given.

Second, the horror of the image is the point rather than an embarrassment to be explained away. Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway — and he is doing it while on the road to weep over the city that is refusing him. The tears of vv. 41-44 are fourteen verses off. Both belong to the same person, within a few days of each other.

A judgement described in terms this stark, by a man who is crying about it, is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

And there is a structural point that a reader with Matthew open should have. This is not the parable of the talents (Matt. 25:14-30), though the two are cousins. There the sums are enormous and unequal and there are no rebel citizens; here every servant gets the same modest mina and the throne itself is contested.

Jesus taught constantly and on the road, and a teacher reworks his material for the moment he is in. Matthew's setting asks what you did with what you were given. Luke's, told on the road up to Jerusalem a few days before the crowd shouted for his execution, asks that and one thing more — whether you wanted the King at all.

parallels.desc: kiss the Son, lest he be angry

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Triumphal Entry and Jesus Weeping over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes on ahead, leading — and “going up” is exact: Jericho lies 800 feet below sea level, Jerusalem 2,500 above, so the seventeen miles climb over three thousand feet through desert.

The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had said the LORD's feet would stand on it (Zech. 14:4), and from that ridge a king approaching Jerusalem first sees the city laid out below.

The instructions about the colt are startlingly specific, and Luke will not settle whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge. What it establishes is that nothing about the next hour is improvised. And “on which no one has ever yet sat” is not about comfort: an animal never worked was the requirement for sacred use — the cart that carried the ark (1 Sam. 6:7), the red heifer (Num. 19:2).

He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy: “humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zech. 9:9). A king entering a capital rode a horse, and a horse was the animal of war.

The cloaks on the road are a coronation gesture, not enthusiasm — when Jehu was proclaimed king the officers put their garments under him on the steps and blew the trumpet (2 Kgs. 9:13). And a cloak was a poor man's blanket and often his most valuable possession, so protected in law that a creditor could not keep one overnight (Ex. 22:26-27).

Luke alone specifies who is shouting: “the whole multitude of his disciples.” And the reason is backward-looking — “for all the mighty works that they had seen.”

Then, at the point on the descent where the whole city comes into view at once, he weeps aloud.
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' shout alters Psalm 118:26. The psalm reads “blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” — the greeting pilgrims received at the festivals. They insert one word: “blessed is the King who comes.” That is not a liturgical greeting any more but a public claim, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem — which is exactly why the Pharisees object. And it echoes what Jesus said at 13:35: they would not see him again until they said it.

“Peace in heaven and glory in the highest” closes a circle Luke opened in chapter 2. The angels sang “glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (2:14); the disciples sing it back with the terms reversed. Which is exact, and not sentimental. There will be no peace on earth this week — there will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution. What is settled in heaven is another matter, and it is being accomplished by the very week that is about to look like total defeat.

“If these were silent, the very stones would cry out” has roots in Habakkuk, where the stone cries out from the wall against injustice (Hab. 2:11) — stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced. And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice: he is looking at magnificent stonework, and within four verses will say not one of those stones will be left on another.

The prophecy of vv.43-44 was fulfilled with precision. In AD 70 Titus built a wall of circumvallation right round the city — some four and a half miles, thrown up in three days — to stop anyone getting out or supplies getting in. Josephus, who was there, describes it. The temple was burned and then dismantled, and the great platform stones were levered off the walls into the street below, where they are still lying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's verb for the weeping is not the quiet one. Greek has two words: one for silent tears, used of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), and this one — eklausen, to wail aloud, the word used of the mourners at Jairus's house (8:52) and of Peter after the cock crowed (22:62). So the sound coming from the middle of that procession is a man sobbing audibly, and the singing does not appear to have stopped.

And the sentence he speaks breaks off unfinished in Greek — an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it. “Even you” is emphatic and heartbreaking: of all the cities on earth, this one did not know the things that make for peace.

A pastor preaching this every Palm Sunday finds it tempting to stop at the shouting. The passage insists on including the tears. Palm Sunday is not unambiguously triumphant; it is triumphant and heartbroken at once.

“Visitation” is episkopē — God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used in the Gospel's first chapter: “he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68). The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. And the word cuts both ways, because a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue: the same coming that saves those who know it for what it is condemns those who do not — not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying, 'Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

Went on ahead — in front of them, leading. Nobody is dragging him up that road.

And going up is geographically exact as well as customary: Jericho lies about 800 feet below sea level and Jerusalem some 2,500 feet above it, so the seventeen miles are a climb of over three thousand feet through desert.

When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples.

The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had prophesied that the LORD would come and his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zech. 14:4), and it was from that hill that a king approaching Jerusalem would first see the city and the temple laid out below him.

Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat.

The instructions are startlingly specific — the village, the animal, its condition, and what to say if challenged. Luke does not tell us whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge, and the text will not settle it. What it does establish is that nothing about the next hour is improvised.

And on which no one has ever yet sat is not a note about comfort. An animal never worked was the requirement for sacred use — the cart that carried the ark was drawn by cows that had never been yoked (1 Sam. 6:7), and the red heifer had to be one on which a yoke has never come (Num. 19:2). This colt is being set apart.

If anyone asks you, Why are you untying it? you shall say this: The Lord has need of it.

Which is either a password arranged in advance or a claim of extraordinary boldness, and either way it is the only explanation offered.

Note also what he is choosing. A king entering a capital rode a horse; a horse was the animal of war. Zechariah had described the alternative: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zech. 9:9).

He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, 'Why are you untying the colt?' And they said, 'The Lord has need of it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them.

Luke is careful to record it, and the phrasing is deliberate: just as he had told them. Every detail checked out.

That verification matters more than it looks. The disciples have been told a great deal in recent chapters that they did not understand and could not test — that he must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Here is a small prediction they could walk into a village and check within the hour, and it was exact.

And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, Why are you untying the colt?

So the challenge came, precisely as he said it would — and the fact that Luke bothers to record it tells us he thought the fulfilment worth pointing at.

Note the word owners, plural. This is somebody's animal, and they are standing right there, watching two strangers untie it.

And they said, The Lord has need of it.

Six words, and the owners let it go.

What are we to make of that? The most likely explanation is the simplest: Jesus was known in that area — Bethany was Martha and Mary's village, and he had been staying there — and an arrangement had been made, or the phrase was recognised.

But do not lose what the sentence says while explaining how it worked. The Lord has need of it. The one through whom every colt in Judea was made, who owns the cattle on a thousand hills, sends two men to ask for the loan of a donkey.

He came into the world in a borrowed stable, rode into his capital on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room, and was buried in a borrowed grave. He owned nothing, and everything he used was lent to him by people who did not know what they were lending it for.

Which is worth registering by anyone who has ever wondered whether what they have is of any use to God. The answer this passage gives is that he asks for ordinary things, from ordinary people, at short notice, and that the only reason ever given is that he needs them.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.

The cloaks go on first, over the animal's back, because there is no saddle. And then they set Jesus on it — the disciples lift him up.

It is a small domestic detail and it is the last quiet moment before everything becomes public.

And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.

Now the gesture changes meaning entirely, because this one has a precedent that every Jew would have recognised.

When Jehu was proclaimed king in the north, the officers every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, Jehu is king (2 Kgs. 9:13). Cloaks under the feet of a man is not enthusiasm. It is a coronation.

And consider what a cloak was to a poor Galilean. It was his outer garment, his blanket at night, and often the most valuable thing he owned — so valuable that the law forbade a creditor to keep one overnight in pledge, for that is his only covering (Ex. 22:26-27).

They are laying the most expensive things they possess in the dust of a road so that a donkey can walk over them.

Which is a fair picture of worship, and it is worth noticing what makes it worship rather than waste. Nothing is achieved by putting a coat under a colt. The road was passable; the animal was not troubled by stones. The gesture is pure declaration — a way of saying, with the only material available, this man is the King and nothing I own is too good to be walked on by him.

Nobody in that procession got anything back except a dirty cloak.

And there is a further thing in the gesture that only shows up on the way back down. Within the week, other men will take his clothes off him and gamble for them at the foot of a cross (23:34).

On the road into the city his own people threw down everything they had so that he could pass over it. On the road out, the last garment he owned was taken from him and divided up by strangers.

Of everyone in that procession, the only one who fully understood where it was going was the man on the donkey.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was drawing near — already on the way down the Mount of Olives — the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice.

Luke fixes the exact spot, and anyone who has stood there will know why.

The road from Bethany crosses the shoulder of the Mount of Olives, and at a particular point on the descent the whole city comes into view at once — the Kidron valley below, the wall opposite, and the temple platform filling the eye, its stonework and gold catching the light. It is one of the great sights of the ancient world and it arrives suddenly.

That is where the shouting starts.

And note who is shouting. The whole multitude of his disciples — Luke is specific, and he is the only evangelist who is. Matthew and Mark have the crowds; Luke says it was his own followers. Whatever the pilgrim crowd made of it, this is not a spontaneous public demonstration. It is the people who have been with him.

For all the mighty works that they had seen.

And there is the reason, and it is worth pausing on because it is entirely backward-looking. They are not praising him for what they expect on Friday. They are praising God for what they have already watched him do — and they have watched a great deal.

Luke's readers can supply the list, because they have just read it. A dead girl sitting up. A legion evicted. Five loaves and twelve baskets. A leper who came back. A blind man at the gate of that very morning's town, still with them in the procession and presumably shouting louder than anybody.

These men have three years of evidence and they are using it.

Which is the only honest ground for praise there has ever been. Not a mood, and not an expectation of what God is about to do next. A memory of what he has actually done, recited out loud — and it is available on the days when nothing whatever is happening.

They were wrong about the week ahead. They were not wrong about him, and the reasons they gave were sound.
verseByVerse.note: The road from the Mount of Olives descends into the Kidron Valley, with the city and temple in full view.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!

The line is Psalm 118:26, and it was one of the best-known sentences in Israel's worship. Psalm 118 closed the Hallel, sung at the great festivals, and pilgrims arriving at Jerusalem were greeted with those exact words by the priests. Every person on that road had said it a hundred times.

But they have altered it, and the alteration is the whole point. The psalm reads blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. Luke's disciples insert one word: blessed is the King who comes.

That is not a liturgical greeting any more. It is a claim about the man on the donkey, made in public, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem — and it is precisely why the Pharisees will object in the next verse.

Note also that this is very nearly the sentence Jesus himself said they would not see him again until they said (13:35). The condition he named is echoed on the road, six chapters later, by his own disciples.

Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!

And here Luke closes a circle he opened in his second chapter.

Over a field outside Bethlehem the angels had sung glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). Now human voices sing it back — with the terms reversed. The angels said peace on earth; the disciples say peace in heaven.

Which is exact, and it is not sentimental. There will be no peace on earth this week. There will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution, and the man they are singing about will be dead inside five days.

What is settled in heaven is another matter. The reconciliation is being accomplished, and it is being accomplished by the very week that is about to look like total defeat.

So the song is right and the singers do not know how right. They think they are welcoming a king to a coronation. They are walking beside him to an altar, singing the anthem of a peace that will be made in blood on Friday afternoon — and it will hold for ever.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
glory in the highest, peace on earth

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, rebuke your disciples.' He answered, 'I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, Teacher, rebuke your disciples.

It is the last time the Pharisees appear in Luke's Gospel, and their final recorded words are a request to stop the worship.

Their concern may have been genuine. A messianic acclamation at Passover, with Roman troops reinforced in the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple and a governor in town precisely because festivals produced riots, was a dangerous thing to be shouting. Men had died for less. It is entirely possible that some of them were trying to prevent a massacre.

But notice the address: Teacher. They will not use the word his disciples have just used. The disciples said King; the Pharisees say Teacher — and the whole dispute is contained in the gap between those two nouns.

And notice what they ask for. Not that he deny the claim. Rebuke your disciples — silence them. It is enough for their purposes if nobody says it out loud.

He answered, I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.

The refusal is absolute and the reason is not tactical.

He does not say the disciples are entitled to their opinion, or that he cannot control a crowd. He says that if these voices stop, the created order will take over — which is a claim that the praise is not optional, and not generated by enthusiasm, but owed.

The image has roots. Habakkuk, denouncing a man who builds his house by injustice, says the stone will cry out from the wall (Hab. 2:11) — stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced.

And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice, a verse before he weeps. He is looking at a city of magnificent stonework, and within four verses he will say that not one of those stones will be left on another (v. 44).

The stones will cry out. In forty years' time they will be lying in a heap in the valley, and they will be saying something after all.

parallels.desc: the stone will cry out from the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, 'Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it.

The shouting is still going on. He is on a donkey, surrounded by people singing that he is the King, at the summit of the only public acclaim he ever received — and he is crying.

So the sound coming from the middle of that procession is a man weeping, and the singing does not appear to have stopped.

He has lamented over this city before, in the hen-and-chicks saying of 13:34; now the lament becomes tears. He has been carrying this the whole way.

Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!

The sentence breaks off. In Greek it is unfinished — an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it.

Even you. The pronoun is emphatic and it is heartbreaking. Of all the cities on earth, this one. The city of David, the place of the temple, the address to which every prophet was sent.

The things that make for peace — and Jerusalem, of all places, did not know the things that make for peace.

But now they are hidden from your eyes.

And there is the tragedy stated exactly. Not they were never offered. Hidden — now, at this point, after everything.

Who hid these things from their eyes? Luke’s phrase points to God, who hides in judgment what people have refused to see (cf. 10:21; Isa 6:9–10; Rom 11:7–10). Yet Jerusalem’s refusal was its own, and Jesus weeps over it. Divine hardening and human responsibility stand together, and so do God’s judgment and Christ’s tears.

He is weeping because he can see what is coming and it is too late to stop it, and because it did not have to be this way. Whatever else is true about the God of the Bible, he is not indifferent to the ruin of people who would not have him. He goes to the cross for them with his face wet.

parallels.desc: that I might weep day and night

verseByVerse.quote: For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side.

The prophecy is specific in a way that is worth reading slowly, because within one generation every clause of it happened.

In AD 70, Titus besieged Jerusalem. When the defenders held out and the siege dragged on, he built exactly what this verse describes — a wall of circumvallation right round the city, some four and a half miles of it, thrown up in three days, to stop anyone getting out or supplies getting in. Josephus, who was there, describes it in detail. The famine inside was appalling.

And tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you.

The verb can mean to dash to the ground, and it is used in the Greek Old Testament of infants killed in a captured city (Ps. 137:9; Hos. 13:16). The horror is not softened.

And they will not leave one stone upon another in you.

The temple was burned and then dismantled. The great platform stones were levered off the walls and pushed into the street below, and they are still lying there — visible today, piled at the foot of the southern wall where they fell, with the paving cracked under them.

He said it four verses after saying the stones would cry out.

Because you did not know the time of your visitation.

Here is the cause, and it is the only one given.

Visitation is God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used in his song at the beginning of this Gospel: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68).

The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. God came to Jerusalem, on a donkey, weeping, and the city did not recognise the day.

And that word visitation cuts both ways in Scripture, because a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue. The same coming that saves the people who know it for what it is condemns the people who do not — not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused.
verseByVerse.note: The Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, building a siege wall round it, and destroyed the city and temple. A “visitation” is God coming in mercy or judgment.

parallels.desc: I will encircle you with towers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–48 — The Cleansing of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's account is the briefest of the four — one clause for the action, no overturned tables, no whip of cords. He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words.

The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate: pilgrims from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed foreign coinage changed into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both. What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place — and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

The two quotations are not equally weighted. The first is Isaiah 56:7, and the full verse matters: “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it.

The second is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah's temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety — “the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” — while cheating and oppressing outside it. It ended by announcing that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it. So Jesus, two verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

And note the exact charge. Not “you have made it a market.” A den of robbers is not where robbery happens; it is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards.

Then he stays. Having cleared the court he takes up residence in it, teaching daily — which is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cleansing is a prophetic act, not a reform. Jesus is not trying to improve the temple's efficiency; he is enacting in symbol what he has just prophesied in words. The combination of texts is deliberate: Isaiah 56:7 describes the eschatological temple as a house of prayer for all nations, and Jeremiah 7:11 the corrupt pre-exilic temple. You were called to be one; you have become the other.

“A den of robbers” names a use religion has never stopped being put to — a system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible. That is what Jeremiah's hearers were doing with the first temple, and it is the charge here.

The closing two verses describe the strangest week in history in a single sentence. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him — not because he is hiding but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave. Luke's phrase is worth having: the people were “hanging on his words,” suspended from him.

What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:6). Which settles something about how this ends. The authorities did not overpower him, and Luke says so plainly.
verseByVerse.examples:
A church becomes known primarily for its events, its café, its networking and its programmes — all good things in themselves, which have gradually crowded out sustained corporate prayer. The cleansing is not a template for expelling coffee shops from church lobbies; it is a question every community of faith must ask about its primary purpose and what has displaced it.

And the specific displacement here is worth naming, because it was not frivolous. Everything in that court served the sacrificial system. The animals were for worship; the money-changing existed so that the temple tax could be paid in the right coin. This was religion crowding out prayer, not entertainment crowding out religion — which is much harder to see from the inside and a great deal more common.

It also matters where it happened. Of all the spaces on that platform, the trade had colonised the only one open to Gentiles — so the practical effect of a thoroughly religious arrangement was that the people furthest from God found the door blocked by the machinery of worship.

That is a question worth putting to any congregation. Not whether the activity is legitimate, but whether a stranger walking in could find room to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them, 'It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold.

Luke's account is the briefest of the four — one clause for the action, and no mention of overturned tables or a whip of cords. He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words.

The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate. Pilgrims arriving from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed to change foreign coinage into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both.

What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place, and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

It is written, My house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.

Two quotations, and the second is much sharper than the first.

The first is Isaiah 56:7, and Luke's readers should hear what the verse actually says in full: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it.

The second is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah's temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety — the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD — while cheating and oppressing outside it. And it ended with the announcement that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it.

So Jesus, two verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

And note the exact charge. Not you have made it a market. A den of robbers is not where robbery happens; it is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards. The accusation is that the temple has become a hiding place — a religious system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible.

John records a cleansing of the temple at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–17). The more likely reading is that there were two cleansings: they come at different Passovers, Jesus says different words, and the trade would have returned. Nor does this passage forbid every sale in a church building; the offence was that commerce had crowded out prayer in the one court open to the nations. And it was the Messiah acting with authority over his Father’s house, not a pattern for Christians to use force.

Which is a use religion has never stopped being put to.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was teaching daily in the temple.

Having driven out the sellers, he stays. This is not a raid. He cleared the court and then took up residence in it, teaching every day for the rest of the week.

That is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester. He has just called it my house.

The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him.

Three groups, and between them they are the entire leadership of the nation — the temple establishment, the legal experts, and the leading laymen. Luke names them together, and they kept on seeking.

Note that the object is not to answer him or to discredit him. To destroy him. The decision has been taken; only the method is outstanding.

But they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

And here is the strangest week in history, described in one sentence.

The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him — not because he is hiding, but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave.

The phrase Luke chooses is worth having: the people were hanging on his words — literally hanging out of themselves, suspended from him, the picture of a crowd leaning in.

So for several days the two things run alongside each other. He teaches; they plot; nothing can be done. And what finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:6).

Which is worth noticing as the chapter closes, because it settles something about how this ends. The authorities did not overpower him. They could not, and Luke says so plainly.

He walked into that city on a colt he had sent for, cleared the temple, and taught in it daily under the eyes of men who wanted him dead and could do nothing about it — until the hour came that he had been walking towards since chapter nine, and he let them have him.

19.text: <sup>1</sup> He entered Jericho and was passing through. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. <sup>3</sup> And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. <sup>4</sup> So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way. <sup>5</sup> And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” <sup>6</sup> So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. <sup>7</sup> And when they saw it, they all grumbled, “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” <sup>8</sup> And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. <sup>10</sup> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” <sup>11</sup> As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. <sup>12</sup> He said therefore, “A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. <sup>13</sup> Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ <sup>14</sup> But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ <sup>15</sup> When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. <sup>16</sup> The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ <sup>17</sup> And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ <sup>18</sup> And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ <sup>20</sup> Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; <sup>21</sup> for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ <sup>22</sup> He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? <sup>23</sup> Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’ <sup>24</sup> And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ <sup>25</sup> And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ <sup>26</sup> ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>27</sup> But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’” <sup>28</sup> And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. <sup>29</sup> When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, <sup>30</sup> saying, “Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. <sup>31</sup> If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” <sup>32</sup> So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. <sup>33</sup> And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” <sup>34</sup> And they said, “The Lord has need of it.” <sup>35</sup> And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. <sup>36</sup> And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. <sup>37</sup> As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, <sup>38</sup> saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” <sup>39</sup> And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” <sup>40</sup> He answered, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” <sup>41</sup> And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. <sup>43</sup> For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side <sup>44</sup> and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” <sup>45</sup> And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, <sup>46</sup> saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>47</sup> And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, <sup>48</sup> but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

20.title: Authority, Parables, and Traps in the Temple
20.overview:
Luke 20 records a sustained series of confrontations between Jesus and the religious authorities in the temple precincts during what we call Holy Week. Three major challenges are mounted: the question of authority (by what right does Jesus act?), the parable of the wicked tenants (Jesus's own counter-attack in story form), and a series of trick questions — the tribute to Caesar, the Sadducees' resurrection riddle, and the question about David's son. Each challenge is designed to trap Jesus; each is turned back on its questioners.

The chapter is a masterclass in Jesus's handling of religious and political hostility. He does not evade, capitulate, or compromise. He answers each question in a way that exposes the questioner's bad faith, defends the truth, and advances his own mission. The parable of the wicked tenants is the most sustained theological statement: it is a compressed history of Israel's relationship with God, a prophecy of Jesus's rejection and death, and an announcement of the judgment that will fall on those who reject the cornerstone.

The chapter closes with Jesus warning about the scribes — those who love the long robes and the best seats and the deferential greetings, who devour widows' houses and for a pretence make long prayers. The contrast with the genuine piety of the widow in 21:1–4 is deliberate and damning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chief priests, scribes and elders — between them, the Sanhedrin — approach Jesus while he is teaching in the temple and ask by what authority he does “these things.” The phrase is left unspecified and everyone knows what it means: he had ridden in as a king a few days earlier and then cleared the traders out of the temple court, and stayed.

The question is not unreasonable in itself. The temple was under their jurisdiction, and a man who takes public action in a place you are responsible for can properly be asked who authorised it. But the trap is well made and both jaws are shut: claim human authority and they can produce the records showing he has none; claim divine authority and they have a charge of blasphemy.

And notice the presumption underneath it. Nobody enquires whether the temple needed cleansing, or whether the trade had displaced the prayer it existed to serve. The question is entirely about credentials — which is the standard refuge of an institution that does not want to discuss the substance.

Jesus answers with a question, which was normal rabbinic practice and is not evasion. It is precision, because the two questions are the same question: John's ministry raised the identical issue, and they had never answered it. And the connection runs deeper — John had pointed at Jesus, so if John's baptism was from heaven, the man John pointed at needs no further credentials.

Which makes this more generous than a debating manoeuvre. He is giving a hostile delegation a genuine route to the truth that does not require them to capitulate in public.

They will not take it, and the reason is stated out loud by themselves. Luke lets us hear the huddle, and there is no question about truth in it anywhere — only about consequences. So they answer that they do not know, which is a lie, and Jesus declines to tell them what they have just refused to work out.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's authority is not an administrative question but the central question of the Gospels. By what right does he cleanse the temple, teach, heal, forgive sins? The answer they are trying to avoid is divine right — the right of the Son sent by the Father.

Their counter-question strategy is itself an answer: those who cannot acknowledge John's prophetic authority cannot acknowledge the one John announced. Unwillingness to face the truth is not an epistemic failure but a moral one.

And the principle behind the refusal in v.8 runs right through Scripture. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have — “to the one who has, more will be given” (8:18), and the reverse holds. A man who will not act on what he knows is not helped by being told more.

There is also a price the council paid that is easy to miss. These are the official teachers of Israel, and they have just declared publicly, in the temple, that they cannot tell whether a major prophetic movement was from God. Whatever they saved by that answer, they paid for it with the only thing their office was for. A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The deliberation in vv.5-6 is worth reading twice for what is absent from it. Not one clause considers what John's baptism actually was. The entire discussion is about what happens to us if we say this or that.

The manoeuvre survives in every institution including the church, and it never feels like dishonesty from the inside. It feels like responsibility. There is always a reason why the honest answer would be unhelpful just now, and a man can spend a whole career calculating the reception of his answers without noticing that he has stopped asking whether they are true.

The test is simple and uncomfortable. When a hard question arrives, is the first thing that moves in you an assessment of what is true, or an assessment of what it will cost?

And v.8 bears on a common modern situation. There are people who genuinely do not know and are asking, and Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience — the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross. And there are people whose questions are a way of not arriving anywhere. The tell is not the difficulty of the question but what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or simply replaced by the next question. Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him, 'Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel.

That is where he is when they come for him — standing in the temple court, in the middle of a sentence, teaching. Luke has told us he was doing this daily (19:47), and the phrase preaching the gospel is his own addition: whatever else was going on in Jerusalem that week, the man at the centre of it was announcing good news.

The chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up.

Three groups, and between them they are the Sanhedrin — the temple establishment, the legal experts, and the leading laymen. This is not an individual objection. It is a delegation.

Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.

Two questions, and the second is the real one.

These things is left unspecified and everyone knows what it means. He had ridden into the city as a king a few days earlier, and then walked into the temple — their temple, the building they administered — and thrown out the traders. And he had stayed.

So the question is not unreasonable. The temple was under their jurisdiction. Somebody who takes public action in a place you are responsible for can properly be asked who authorised it, and if a stranger did the same in any institution today the same question would follow within the hour.

But look at the shape of the trap, because it is well made and both jaws are shut.

If he claims human authority — a rabbi's ordination, a licence, a sponsor — they can produce the records and show he has none. If he claims divine authority, they have a charge of blasphemy and a case to take to the Sanhedrin.

There is no third answer available, which is why the question was asked.

And notice the presumption underneath it. They are not asking whether what he did was right. Nobody enquires whether the temple needed cleansing, or whether the trade in the Court of the Gentiles had displaced the prayer it existed to serve. The question is entirely about credentials — which is the standard refuge of an institution that does not want to discuss the substance.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, 'I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?

He answers a question with a question, which was an entirely normal move in rabbinic debate and is not evasion. It is precision.

Because the two questions are the same question. John's whole ministry raised the identical issue: a man with no priestly appointment and no institutional backing, baptising in the Jordan, calling the nation to repent — by what authority? They had faced it once already and had never given an answer.

From heaven or from man. The alternatives are exhaustive and there is no third option, which is the point. A prophetic ministry is either God's or it is not, and every person in Israel had already made a private judgement about John.

And the connection runs deeper than a debating parallel. John had said who Jesus was — he who is mightier than I is coming (3:16) — and the answer to their question about authority had been publicly given at the Jordan by the voice from heaven. If John's baptism was from heaven, then the man John pointed at needs no further credentials.

So this is not a clever deflection. It is Jesus offering them the answer, and offering it in the one form they could have accepted without losing face — by working it out themselves.

Which is worth registering, because he has been accused of merely outmanoeuvring them here. He is doing something more generous than that. He is giving a hostile delegation a genuine route to the truth that does not require them to capitulate in public.

They will not take it.

And the reason they will not is about to be stated out loud, in their own words, by themselves — which is the most damaging thing in the passage and none of it is his doing.

There is one further thing in the counter-question worth registering, because it tells you what Jesus thought was actually wrong with them.

He does not ask them a question about himself. He asks them a question about a matter they had already had years to settle, on which the evidence had been public and the whole nation had formed a view.

Which locates the problem exactly. Their difficulty was never a shortage of data about Jesus of Nazareth. It was what they had already done with the last man God sent.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, 'If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they discussed it with one another.

Luke lets us hear the huddle, and it is the most revealing paragraph in the chapter. Whether he had it from somebody who was standing close enough or from a later member of the council who became a believer, we are given the conversation.

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why did you not believe him?

They see the trap instantly, and note what it consists of. Not a logical difficulty — a personal exposure. If John was from God, then their failure to receive him is a public fact requiring explanation.

But if we say, From man, all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.

And the second option is worse. John had been dead for some time and the popular verdict on him had hardened; to deny him publicly, in a temple court full of Passover pilgrims, would have been physically dangerous.

Now read the whole deliberation again and notice what is missing from it.

There is no question about the truth. Not one clause in either half considers what John's baptism actually was. The entire discussion is about consequences: what happens to us if we say this, and what happens to us if we say that.

These are the religious leaders of the people of God, standing in the temple, weighing a question about a prophet — and truth is not a factor in the deliberation.

Which is worth naming, because the manoeuvre survives in every institution including the church, and it never feels like dishonesty from the inside. It feels like responsibility. There is always a reason why the honest answer would be unhelpful just now, and a man can spend an entire career calculating the reception of his answers and never once notice that he has stopped asking whether they are true.

The test is simple and uncomfortable. When a hard question arrives, is the first thing that moves in you an assessment of what is true, or an assessment of what it will cost?

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they answered that they did not know where it came from.

It is a lie, and everybody present knows it.

They knew exactly what they thought about John; they had been thinking it for years, and had just said it out loud to each other. What they have done is take refuge in an agnosticism they do not hold — which is the safest position available, because it commits to nothing and cannot be attacked.

And there is something worth noticing about the price of it. These are the official teachers of Israel, and they have just declared publicly, in the temple, that they are unable to tell whether a major prophetic movement was from God or not. Whatever they saved by that answer, they paid for it with the only thing their office was for.

A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.

And Jesus said to them, Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

The refusal is not petulance and it is not a debating victory being enjoyed.

He had made them an offer in verse 4 and it was a real one: answer the question about John honestly and you will have the answer to your own. They declined, and the declining was not for want of information.

Which is the principle underneath, and it runs right through Scripture. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have. To the one who has, more will be given (8:18) — and the reverse holds. A man who will not act on what he knows is not helped by being told more.

And this bears on a very common modern situation. There are people who genuinely do not know and are asking, and Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience — the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross, the disciples themselves, who ask badly and are answered anyway.

And there are people whose questions are a way of not arriving anywhere. The tell is not the difficulty of the question but what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or whether it is simply replaced by the next question.

Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He turns from the delegation to the people and tells a story about the delegation, in their hearing — and they understand every word of it (v.19).

The opening line is a quotation. Isaiah's song of the vineyard ends with its own interpretation stated flatly: “for the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:1-7). So the identifications come attached, from a passage everyone knew.

And the arrangement is entirely ordinary — absentee landlords letting estates to tenant farmers for a share of the crop were common in Galilee. But hold on to what it means: the tenants did not plant the vineyard, clear the ground, or build the winepress. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms.

The escalation is exact: beaten; beaten and treated shamefully, which in that culture was the worse injury; then wounded and thrown out. And running alongside it is the stranger thing — a landlord who keeps sending. Any man with sense would have gone to law after the first assault. He sends a second, and a third, because he keeps wanting the relationship rather than the redress.

The servants are the prophets, and the compression is the point: “the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers… but they kept mocking the messengers of God” (2 Chr. 36:15-16). The men hearing this were standing in a building where some of it had happened.

Then the son — “my beloved son,” the phrase from heaven at the Jordan (3:22). And the tenants' reasoning, said aloud among themselves, is the oldest reasoning there is: remove the owner's representative and the property is ours.

Luke has the order deliberately: thrown out of the vineyard, and then killed. Jesus was crucified outside the wall (Heb. 13:12), and he is telling this three days before it happens, with the geography included.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is one of the most explicit statements in Luke of Jesus's divine sonship. The son is not one more servant in a long series but the heir — the beloved son, whose rejection is categorically different from the rejection of the prophets.

“Perhaps they will respect him” puzzles thoughtful readers and has been pressed into service to prove something it does not prove. Does it mean God did not know? Some have read it so. But the same Scripture says the Son was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has already told his disciples three times how this would end.

The perhaps is spoken from the owner's side of the story — the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of divine ignorance. Its point is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last was the owner's own beloved son. God knew exactly what they would do and sent the Son anyway — which is not a father caught out, but a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was never knocked upon.

The verdict — the vineyard given to others — must not be misused. It is not a statement that God has finished with the Jewish people; Paul asks exactly that question after the resurrection and answers it flatly, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Rom. 11:1). The tenants are the leadership, and Luke names the men Jesus was looking at in verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples:
Psalm 118:22 is quoted from the same psalm the disciples had been shouting a few days earlier on the road down the Mount of Olives — verse 26 of it (19:38). He quotes their processional hymn back to the authorities, four verses earlier.

And the image is precise. The cornerstone sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so everything built after it is squared by it; and a builder examining stones on site rejects the ones that will not do. So the picture is of professionals doing their job — men whose whole competence is judging stone, whose professional judgement was that this one would not do. Then the turn: it has become the cornerstone. Their verdict was simply overruled.

Verse 18 turns the image twice, drawing on Isaiah's stone of stumbling (Isa. 8:14-15) and Daniel's stone that grinds a statue to powder (Dan. 2:34-35). To fall on the stone is to trip over it and be broken — bad, and survivable, since broken things can be mended. When the stone falls on a man, it crushes him to dust. The stone cannot be avoided: it can be built on, tripped over, or fallen under, and nobody in this passage walks past it.

And the parable is fulfilled in the hearing of the parable. They grasped it immediately — which answers a question people often put to Scripture, why God does not simply tell people plainly what they are doing. He did, and it produced a decision to do it sooner.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to tell the people this parable: 'A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he began to tell the people this parable.

Note who he turns to. Not the delegation — the people. The council has just refused to answer him, so he tells the crowd a story about them, in their hearing, and they will understand every word of it (v. 19).

A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while.

The opening line is a quotation, and every literate Jew in that court would have heard it.

Isaiah's song of the vineyard begins: my beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones and planted it with choice vines — and it ends with the interpretation stated flatly: for the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa. 5:1-7).

So the identifications are not something a commentator has to supply. The parable comes with them attached, from a passage everyone knew.

And the arrangement described is entirely ordinary. Absentee landlords letting out estates to tenant farmers for a share of the crop were common in Galilee, and the resentment such arrangements generated was real. The listeners would have had no difficulty picturing it.

But hold on to what the arrangement means, because the parable turns on it. The tenants did not plant the vineyard. They did not clear the ground or build the winepress. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms.

When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard.

Some of the fruit. Not the harvest — the owner's share, which was the agreement.

But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

Which is not a rent dispute. Nobody argues about the percentage or pleads a bad season. They assault the man and send him back with nothing, and that is a declaration: we are not paying, and we are not discussing it.
verseByVerse.note: The vineyard is Isaiah’s picture of Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.

Two things run in parallel through these verses, and both are extraordinary.

The first is the escalation. Beaten. Beaten and treated shamefully — Luke's word means dishonoured, publicly humiliated, and in that culture the shame was the worse injury. Then wounded and thrown out: physical damage this time, and an expulsion.

Each envoy is worse treated than the last, and the tenants are growing bolder because nothing has happened to them.

The second is the sending. Three times, into a situation that is visibly getting more dangerous, the owner sends another man.

And that is the strange part. A landlord with any sense would have gone to law after the first assault; he had every legal remedy and the resources to use them. Instead he sends a second servant to men who have just beaten the first, and then a third.

This is the patience of God set out as a plot, and it is not admirable in a normal landlord. It is unaccountable. He keeps sending because he keeps wanting the relationship rather than the redress.

The servants are the prophets, and the compression is the point — the whole tragic history of Israel and the men God sent to it, put into three sentences. The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers… but they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets (2 Chr. 36:15-16). Jeremiah in a cistern. Zechariah stoned in this very courtyard. And Jesus has already said it in so many words: Jerusalem is the city that kills the prophets (13:34).

Which means the men listening to this parable were standing in a building where some of it had happened, hearing their own history read back to them in the third person.

And there is something in the tenants' behaviour that explains a great deal about religious opposition generally. They do not argue with the owner. There is no letter disputing the terms, no counter-claim, no attempt to renegotiate the share.

They simply will not have anyone come from him. The messenger is attacked before the message is heard, every time — because the message is not the problem. The ownership is.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the owner of the vineyard said, What shall I do?

The question is not helplessness; it is deliberation made audible. The owner has exhausted the ordinary options and is deciding.

I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.

Every word of that has been chosen.

My beloved son is ton huion mou ton agapēton — the exact phrase spoken from heaven at the Jordan, you are my beloved Son (3:22), and, in some manuscripts, from the cloud on the mountain (9:35). There is no possibility that Luke's readers, or the men in the courtyard, are meant to miss it.

And the logic is a father's rather than a landlord's. He has run out of servants worth risking; he will send the one person left, and the one person he cannot replace.

Now the phrase that puzzles thoughtful readers and has been pressed into service to prove something it does not prove: perhaps they will respect him. Does that mean God did not know? Was heaven hoping for an outcome it could not foresee, and disappointed on Good Friday?

Some have read it exactly so. But the same Scripture that records this parable says the Son was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has already told his disciples three times, in detail, how this would end. He is not guessing.

The perhaps is spoken from the owner's side of the story — the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of divine ignorance. Its point is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last one was the owner's own beloved son, and that their rejection was therefore without a shred of excuse.

God knew exactly what they would do and sent the Son anyway. That is not a father caught out. It is a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was never knocked upon.

This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.

And there is the reasoning, said aloud among themselves, and it is the oldest reasoning there is. Remove the owner's representative and the property is ours. It is what the serpent offered in a garden, and it has never once worked.

verseByVerse.quote: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.' When they heard this, they said, 'Surely not!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

Note the order, because Luke has it deliberately: out first, and then killed. Mark has the order the other way round, and Luke's arrangement matches what was about to happen.

Jesus was crucified outside the city wall, and the writer to the Hebrews makes the point explicitly: Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:12).

He is telling this in the temple, three days before it happens, with the geography included.

What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?

He asks the crowd for the verdict. In Matthew's telling the hearers supply the answer themselves and condemn themselves out of their own mouths; here Jesus gives it, and the effect is the same.

He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.

Two clauses, and both landed within a generation.

The destruction came in AD 70, in the terms he had wept over in the previous chapter (19:41-44). And the vineyard given to others is the thing that would have been most offensive of all: the tenancy transferred, the covenant privileges passing to people who were not in the room.

It should be said plainly what that does and does not mean, because this parable has been misused. It is not a statement that God has finished with the Jewish people; Paul, writing after the resurrection, asks exactly that question and answers it flatly — has God rejected his people? By no means! (Rom. 11:1). The tenants in the parable are the leadership, not the nation; the men Jesus is looking at while he tells it are named in verse 19.

When they heard this, they said, Surely not!

The crowd's reaction is horror, and Luke's phrase is an emphatic wish that it should not be so.

They have understood it. That is what the exclamation means. They can see where the story is pointing, and the thought of the vineyard being taken away is unbearable — and within days a crowd in this city will call for the death of the son and get it.

verseByVerse.quote: But he looked directly at them and said, 'What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he looked directly at them.

Luke stops the narrative for a look. The verb means to fix the eyes on somebody — the same word used of Jesus turning and looking at Peter in the courtyard after the cock crowed (22:61).

The parable was told to the people (v. 9). The look is for the men who came with the question.

What then is this that is written: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone?

The quotation is Psalm 118:22, and the choice of psalm is not accidental. It is the same psalm the disciples had been shouting on the road down the Mount of Olives a few days earlier — blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord is verse 26 of it (19:38).

He is quoting the crowd's processional hymn back to the authorities, four verses earlier in the same psalm.

And the image is precise. The cornerstone is the stone that sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so that everything built after it is squared by it. A builder examining stones on site rejects the ones that will not do.

So the picture is of professionals doing their job. Men whose whole competence is judging stone look at this one, assess it, and throw it on the discard pile as unfit.

Which is exactly what was happening in that courtyard. The chief priests and scribes were the builders — the men trained and appointed to recognise what God was doing and to build the nation accordingly. They examined the stone, and their professional judgement was that it would not do.

And then the turn: it has become the cornerstone. Not somebody else used it. It was taken up and set at the corner by an authority above the builders, and their verdict was simply overruled.

The early church seized on this verse and could not let it go. Peter quotes it to the Sanhedrin itself (Acts 4:11) and again in his letter (1 Pet. 2:7). It became the standard text for what the resurrection did to Friday's verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.

The image turns, and it turns twice.

The stone has just been the foundation. Now it is a thing that can be tripped over, and a thing that can fall on you — and the two halves describe two quite different disasters.

Both come from the prophets. Isaiah had said the LORD of hosts would be a sanctuary and a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, over which many would stumble and fall and be broken (Isa. 8:14-15). And Daniel had seen a stone cut out by no human hand, striking a great statue and grinding it to powder, becoming a mountain that filled the whole earth (Dan. 2:34-35, 44-45).

So the same stone is foundation, obstacle, and instrument of judgement — and which of the three it turns out to be is determined entirely by what a man does when he meets it.

Note the difference between the two halves. To fall on the stone is to stumble over it; the man is walking along and does not see it, and he is broken. That is bad and it is survivable — broken things can be mended, and Scripture is full of people whose first encounter with Christ knocked them off their feet.
