The second is not survivable. When the stone falls on a man, the verb Luke uses means to winnow, to reduce to dust and blow away. Nothing is left to repair.

Which sets out the alternatives with unusual clarity. This stone cannot be avoided. It can be built on, tripped over, or fallen under, and there is no fourth option — nobody in this passage walks past it.

And the men listening had already stumbled. That was Friday's verdict, and it broke them. What the sentence holds out, terribly, is that a stumble is not yet the end — but that there is a day coming when the stone is no longer lying in the road.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them.

They understood it. Luke says so plainly, and it settles something about the parables in general: they are not a code that only insiders can break. The men who came off worst in this one grasped it immediately.

At that very hour — not later, after deliberation. They wanted him seized on the spot.

And there is the whole tragedy of the passage in one sentence. They have just heard a story in which tenants kill the owner's son, and been told it is about them — and their response is to try to arrest the son.

The parable is being fulfilled in the hearing of the parable. Nothing he said made the slightest difference except to accelerate it.

Which is worth pausing on, because it answers a question people often put to Scripture: why does God not simply tell people plainly what they are doing? He did. There is no gentler or clearer way to say you are about to kill me and you will be judged for it than the story he had just told, and it produced a decision to do it sooner.

But they feared the people.

Luke has now said this three times in two chapters — they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words (19:48); the fear of stoning in verse 6; and here.

The most powerful men in Jerusalem cannot touch a man standing in the open in their own building, because of a crowd.

And note what that means about the fear that is actually running the council. Not the fear of God, which would have stopped them entirely, and not the fear of being wrong. The fear of the people — of a mob, of a riot, of losing position. It has governed every decision they have made in this chapter, and it will govern the one they finally take, which is to arrange the arrest at night, away from the crowd (22:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — The Question about Tribute to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change. Spies are men planted, and they “pretended to be sincere” — actors playing devout enquirers. Luke gives the object before the question: a capital charge Rome will act on, because Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

The flattery is a trap in itself. If he is a man who “shows no partiality,” he cannot now give a diplomatic answer — they have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question. And the terrible thing is that every word of the compliment is true. They have described him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is only possible for people who know exactly who he is and have decided against him anyway.

The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, levied since Judea became a Roman province in AD 6 — and it had provoked an armed revolt at the time. Say yes and he endorses the occupation before a Passover crowd of patriots; say no and there are witnesses ready to report a man inciting tax refusal, which is exactly the charge they will eventually bring (23:2).

He asks for a coin, and does not have one — the man they are trying to trap on taxation has to borrow the currency from his accusers. And somebody produces one immediately, in the temple. The denarius bore the head of Tiberius with an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, and Pontifex Maximus on the reverse: a portrait, which offended the second commandment, and a claim of divinity in writing.

“Caesar's” is the only possible answer and it concedes the whole question. The trap has been sprung without a word of doctrine, and it took one question about a coin.
verseByVerse.theology:
The verb in v.25 is not give but render — pay what is owed. It is the word for settling a debt, not making a donation, which quietly answers the first half: if the coin is Caesar's, handing it over is returning property.

But the weight falls on the second clause. He has just established the principle by which ownership is determined — whose likeness and inscription does it bear? So the question the second half silently asks is: what bears the image of God? And every person listening knew the answer from the first page of their Scriptures (Gen. 1:27).

The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

Two things follow, and the church has often held one without the other. The civil authority is legitimate — Jesus does not tell them to stop paying, and Paul develops it at length (Rom. 13:1-7). And the civil authority is bounded: Caesar gets what has his image on it and nothing more, so the moment he asks for worship, conscience, or the ultimate allegiance of a life, he is asking for property that is not his.

The “two kingdoms” principle drawn from these verses has been foundational for Reformed political theology. But the passage presses beyond institutional analysis to the personal: if you bear God's image, you belong to God — completely, with no reservation, because the image is not stamped on part of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian facing a regulation he considers unjust can think clearly from this. There is a legitimate sphere of civil authority, and there is an authority that is absolute. The question is not whether to comply with any government but whether the specific demand crosses into what belongs exclusively to God.

Note also what the borrowed coin exposes. The men who came to catch him on faithfulness to God were carrying Caesar's portrait and Caesar's divine title in their purses, in the temple courts, and one of them had it out in seconds. Whatever the question was really about, it was not scruple.

And “marveling at his answer” is a surprising word for men who came to destroy him. It is possible to admire the truth and remain entirely unmoved by it — Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8-9). There is a way of appreciating the quality of an answer that functions as a substitute for obeying it, and it is common among people who take religion seriously enough to enjoy a good argument about it.

Which is a hard lesson for anyone who assumes a sufficiently good answer will settle a matter. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed on Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him, 'Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere.

The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change.

Watched is the word for lying in wait; spies is enkathetous, men suborned and planted. And pretended to be sincere is literally that they were pretending themselves to be righteous — actors playing devout enquirers.

Luke tells us the object before we hear the question: so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. This is no longer about winning an argument in the temple. They want a capital charge that Rome will act on, and Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God.

The flattery is thick, and it is a trap in itself. They are not merely being pleasant; they are building a fence. If he is a man who shows no partiality, he cannot now give a diplomatic answer — they have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question.

And the terrible thing about the compliment is that every word of it is true. He does speak rightly, he does show no partiality, he does teach the way of God. They have described him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is possible only for people who know exactly who he is and have decided against him anyway.

Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?

The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, levied on every adult in Judea since it became a Roman province in AD 6 — and it had provoked an armed revolt at the time under Judas the Galilean.

So the question is live and dangerous. Say yes, and he endorses the occupation in front of a Passover crowd of patriots. Say no, and there are witnesses standing there ready to report a man inciting tax refusal, which is precisely the charge they will eventually bring (23:2).
verseByVerse.note: The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason before the governor.

parallels.desc: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, 'Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?' They said, 'Caesar's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he perceived their craftiness.

Craftiness — the quality Paul ties to the serpent in Eden (2 Cor. 11:3), whom Genesis calls more crafty than any other beast of the field (Gen. 3:1). He is not taken in for a moment.

Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?

He does not answer. He asks for a coin — and there is something in that request that is easy to miss.

He asks them for one. The man they are trying to trap on the subject of taxation has the currency produced by his accusers, which tells you a good deal about the relative interest each party had in Caesar's money.

And somebody produces one immediately. In the temple.

That matters more than it looks. The denarius was a silver coin bearing the head of Tiberius, and around the head an inscription: Ti Caesar Divi Aug F Augustus — Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus — with Pontifex Maximus, high priest, on the reverse. It was a portrait, which offended the second commandment, and it carried a claim of divinity in writing.

The men who had come to catch him on a point of faithfulness to God were carrying it in their purses, in the temple courts, and one of them had it out in seconds.

They said, Caesar's.

Which is the only possible answer, and it concedes the whole question. They have just testified, in public, that they are in Caesar's economy and using his money — and a man who accepts a currency has accepted the authority that mints it.

The trap has been sprung without a word of doctrine, and it took one question about a coin.

And note what he has done with the flattery. They said he showed no partiality; he has just declined to flatter them, and made them say the awkward thing themselves.

There is also a lesson in the method that is worth having, because Christians in hostile conversations reach for the wrong tool almost every time.

He does not answer the question as posed. He does not weigh the arguments for and against Roman taxation, or explain his political position, or find a form of words careful enough to survive being quoted.

He asks for an object and asks what is written on it. The answer comes out of their own pockets and their own mouths, and by the time they have given it the argument is over — and nothing has been conceded and nobody has been insulted.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and his titles.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.

The verb is not give but render — apodote, give back, pay what is owed. It is the word for settling a debt, not making a donation.

Which quietly answers the first half of the question. If the coin is Caesar's, handing it over is not collaboration. It is returning property.

But the sentence does not stop there, and the second half is where the weight falls.

And to God the things that are God's.

He has just established the principle by which ownership is determined: whose likeness and inscription does it bear? Caesar's image is on the coin, so the coin goes to Caesar.

So the question the second clause silently asks is: what bears the image of God?

And every person listening knew the answer, because it is on the first page of their Scriptures. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him (Gen. 1:27).

The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

Which makes this a far larger answer than the tax question deserved. Caesar may have the metal; he has a genuine claim, and it is limited to things with his face on them. God's claim is on the person — and it is not a portion of the person, because the image is not stamped on part of a man.

Two things follow, and the church has often held one without the other.

The civil authority is legitimate. Jesus does not tell them to stop paying, and Paul will develop it at length (Rom. 13:1-7). Taxes are owed, and paying them is not idolatry.

And the civil authority is bounded. Caesar gets what has his image on it and nothing more, which means that the moment he asks for what belongs to God — worship, conscience, the ultimate allegiance of a life — he is asking for property that is not his, and the answer is no.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent.

Three things in one sentence, and each is worth having.

In the presence of the people. Luke keeps saying it. The crowd is the reason nothing can be done, and it is the reason the question had to be public — they needed witnesses to a seditious answer, and instead they have witnesses to a devastating one.

They were not able… to catch him. Catch is a hunting word: to take hold of, to seize. It is the third failed attempt in this chapter.

But marveling at his answer.

And that is the surprising word. These men came to destroy him. They had rehearsed the flattery and planted the spies and framed a question with no safe answer — and when the answer came, something in them responded to it.

It is possible to admire the truth and remain entirely unmoved by it. Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8-9). Agrippa asked Paul whether he meant to make him a Christian in so short a time (Acts 26:28). There is a way of appreciating the quality of an answer that functions as a substitute for obeying it, and it is common among people who take religion seriously enough to enjoy a good argument about it.

They became silent.

Not persuaded. Silenced. And the silence is not repentance; it is the end of a line of attack, and they will send the Sadducees in next.

It is worth setting this beside verse 7, where the same men had said we do not know. Twice now this delegation has been reduced to saying nothing — once by choosing not to answer, and once by having nothing left to say.

And there is a hard lesson in the pairing for anybody who assumes that a sufficiently good answer will settle the matter. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed on Friday.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–47 — Sadducees on Resurrection, the Son of David, and Scribal Warning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sadducees were the aristocratic party — the chief priestly families and wealthy landowners who ran the temple and managed the relationship with Rome. They accepted the five books of Moses and treated the rest as secondary, and from that drew the conclusions Acts states fully: “the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit” (Acts 23:8). Which limits the field for Jesus: he cannot answer from Daniel 12 or Isaiah 26, and will have to find the resurrection in Moses.

Their riddle rests on a good law. Deuteronomy 25:5-10 provided that if a married man died childless his brother should marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man's name and inherit his portion — so no family line or allotted land in Israel would be extinguished. It is the law behind Boaz and Ruth, and it was designed to protect a widow from destitution.

They turn it into a joke. Seven brothers, one after another, each obeying Moses, each dying childless. And notice what the story does to the woman: she is unnamed, unnumbered, given no words, and exists purely as contested property. The question at the end is not “what became of her?” but “whose will she be?”

The argument is a reductio, and it rests on one assumption the Sadducees have never noticed they are making — that the age to come is this age carried on, the same arrangements made permanent. So the answer is not a solution to the puzzle. Jesus dismantles the premise and the puzzle goes with it.

He then proves the doctrine on their own ground, from the burning bush; the scribes commend him; and nobody dares ask anything further. Which leaves him free to ask his own question, about Psalm 110 — and to close with a warning about the men who had been asking all day.
verseByVerse.theology:
“They cannot die anymore” is the reason marriage does not continue. Marriage in this age carries the future of the race: where people die, people must be born. Remove death and the mechanism for replacing the dead is no longer needed — the way scaffolding is no longer needed. And “equal to angels” does not mean disembodied; the resurrection is precisely of the body, and Luke's own last chapter has the risen Christ eating fish to prove it (24:41-43). The comparison is specifically to deathlessness, and Jesus says so in the same breath.

The argument from Exodus 3:6 turns on a tense. God does not say “I was the God of Abraham” but “I am” — four hundred years after Abraham was buried. And to be somebody's God is covenant language: to have bound yourself to a person and promised him a future. So if God is still Abraham's God, then either the covenant is with a handful of dust, which is no covenant at all, or Abraham is alive.

Note what the argument does not rest on. Not the immortality of the soul, which is a Greek idea and appears nowhere in the reasoning. It rests entirely on the character of God: he does not enter a binding relationship with a man and then let death end it, because that would make him unfaithful. The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us but something in him — which is why the last clause is one of the great sentences of Scripture: “for all live to him.”

Psalm 110:1 became the most quoted Old Testament text in the New (Acts 2:34-35; 1 Cor. 15:25; Heb. 1:13; 10:12-13). In that world honour ran upward — a man addressed his forebears as “my lord,” never the reverse — so a psalm in which David calls his own descendant “my Lord” is upside down, unless the descendant is more than a descendant.
verseByVerse.examples:
All of the resurrection teaching is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking. She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, reads “neither marry nor are given in marriage,” and hears the one thing she was most afraid of.

For marriage was never the destination. Paul says the whole thing was pointing somewhere: “this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Eph. 5:31-32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city. What waits at the end of this age is a wedding (Rev. 19:6-9) — and marriage is not carried into it because it was too little, not too much. It was the picture; that is the reality.

The chapter closes with predation rather than vanity. Long robes and good seats are appetite; devouring widows' houses is theft — and the two halves of v.47 belong together, because the long prayers are not a separate failing but the instrument. The reputation for piety is what gets a man access to a widow's confidence and her accounts. The prayer is the cover.

Which is a word for anybody holding spiritual standing over others. It is possible to use the things of God to get things from people, and Scripture reserves its severest language for it. And Luke sets the next scene immediately: a widow at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1-4).

verseByVerse.quote: There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, 'Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection.

The third delegation of the day, and Luke supplies the label a reader needs.

The Sadducees were the aristocratic party — the chief priestly families and the wealthy landowners, the men who ran the temple and managed the relationship with Rome. They were fewer than the Pharisees and far more powerful, and they were theologically conservative in a particular way: they accepted the authority of the five books of Moses and treated the rest as secondary.

From that they drew the conclusions Luke gives here and Acts states more fully — the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8). Their argument was that these doctrines are not in the Pentateuch and are therefore later inventions.

Which matters for what follows, because it limits the field. Jesus cannot answer them from Daniel 12 or Isaiah 26, both of which teach the resurrection plainly. He will have to find it in Moses, and he does.

Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.

The law they cite is real, and worth understanding before the riddle is built on it.

Deuteronomy 25:5-10 provides that if a married man dies childless, his brother should marry the widow, and the first son of that marriage would carry the dead man's name and inherit his portion. The purpose was twofold: to stop a family line being extinguished in Israel, and to keep a piece of the promised land in the family that had been allotted it.

It is the law behind the book of Ruth, where Boaz acts as redeemer for Naomi's line.

So it is a good law, and a compassionate one — designed to protect a widow with no son from destitution and a dead man's name from disappearing.

And it is about to be turned into a joke.

Which is worth noticing on its own, because it is a recognisable use of Scripture. The Sadducees are not misquoting Moses; every word of their citation is accurate, and they open with Teacher and the proper formula.

What they are doing is using a true text to make a doctrine they dislike look ridiculous — and the technique is available to anybody with a Bible and a grievance. A passage is quoted correctly, pushed to an extreme its author never envisaged, and the resulting absurdity is laid at the door of the belief rather than the method.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were seven brothers.

The case is constructed, not reported. Nobody is claiming this happened; it is a thought experiment, and the number seven is chosen because it is the number of completeness and because it makes the situation maximally absurd.

The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died.

Luke compresses what Matthew and Mark spell out, and the effect is a kind of grim comedy: seven brothers, one after another, each obeying Moses, each dying childless.

Notice, though, what the story does to the woman. She is the one person in it who is not named, not numbered, and given no words. She exists in the riddle purely as a piece of contested property — the thing seven men had a claim on — and the question at the end is not what became of her? but whose wife will the woman be?

That is worth registering before Jesus answers, because it tells you something about the men asking. They have taken a law given to protect a widow and used it to construct a puzzle in which the widow is an object.

In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.

And there is the question, with its final clause driving the point home.

The argument underneath is a reductio: if the resurrection were true, and Moses' law were true, you would end up with an insoluble situation in the age to come — therefore the resurrection cannot be true.

It is a good argument and it rests entirely on one assumption, which is never stated because the Sadducees have never noticed they are making it. They assume the age to come is this age carried on: the same arrangements, the same institutions, the same questions, only permanent.

Which is why the answer will not be a solution to the puzzle. Jesus is not going to tell them which brother gets her. He is going to dismantle the premise, and the puzzle will go with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage.

He begins by naming a category the Sadducees did not have. This age and that age — two orders of existence, and marriage belongs to the first.

But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore.

And there is the reason, in four words: they cannot die anymore.

Marriage in this age carries the future of the race. Where people die, people must be born, and the institution that provides for that is marriage. Remove death and the mechanism for replacing the dead becomes unnecessary — not abolished by decree, but no longer needed, the way scaffolding is no longer needed.

Because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.

Equal to angels does not mean disembodied — the resurrection is precisely of the body, and Luke's own last chapter will have the risen Christ eating fish to prove it (24:41-43). The comparison is specifically to deathlessness, and Jesus says so in the same breath.

All of which is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking.

She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, and she reads neither marry nor are given in marriage and hears the one thing she was most afraid of: that she will not have him again. So let the verse be read to her properly, because it does not say that.

Look carefully at what ends. Jesus says the institution ends — the marrying, the giving in marriage, the arrangement by which this age replaces its dead. He does not say the people end, and he does not say the love ends. You will not know your husband less there; you will know him better than you ever managed here, without the tiredness and the half-attention that got between you every day of the forty years.

For marriage was never the destination. Paul says the whole thing was pointing somewhere: a man leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife, and this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31-32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city.

Who are those who are considered worthy? Worthiness here is a verdict God gives, not a merit earned (cf. 2 Thess 1:5, 11). Jesus is speaking of the resurrection to life of God’s people; elsewhere he says that all the dead will rise, some to life and some to judgment (John 5:28–29).

And what waits at the end of this age is a wedding — the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:6-9). Marriage is not carried into it because it was too little, not too much. It was the picture. That is the reality.

verseByVerse.quote: But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush.

Having dismantled the riddle, he now proves the doctrine — and he does it on their ground.

They accepted Moses. Very well: Moses.

Where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.

The reference is Exodus 3:6, at the burning bush, and it was one of the best-known sentences in the Pentateuch. God introduces himself to Moses by naming his relationship to three men who had been dead for centuries.

Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.

The argument turns on a tense, and it is worth setting out slowly because it is easy to under-read.

God does not say I was the God of Abraham. He says I am — present tense, four hundred years after Abraham was buried at Machpelah.

Now, what does it mean to be somebody's God? It is covenant language, and it means to have bound yourself to a person: to be his shield and his very great reward, to have promised him a future. That is what God said to Abraham (Gen. 15:1; 17:7).

So if God is still Abraham's God, then either the covenant is with a handful of dust — which is no covenant at all — or Abraham is alive.

And note what the argument rests on. Not the immortality of the soul, which is a Greek idea and appears nowhere in the reasoning. Not the resilience of the human spirit. It rests entirely on the character of God: he does not enter into a binding relationship with a man and then let death end it, because that would make him unfaithful.

The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us. It is something in him.

For all live to him proves the resurrection from God’s faithfulness to his covenant. It also implies that those who have died in the Lord are alive to God now, as other texts say plainly (23:43; Phil 1:23; 2 Cor 5:8). They await the resurrection of the body, but they are with him.

Which is why the last clause is one of the great sentences of Scripture: for all live to him. Whatever the state of the dead in Christ, they are not gone from God's side of it. Nobody who belonged to him has ever been lost track of, and the graves of the patriarchs did not interrupt a single conversation.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes answered, 'Teacher, you have spoken well.' For they no longer dared to ask him any question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of the scribes answered, Teacher, you have spoken well.

An unexpected moment, and Luke alone records it.

These are scribes — and most scribes were Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection and had been arguing with the Sadducees about it for generations. They have just watched a rival party demolished on a doctrine they hold, and they cannot help themselves.

You have spoken well. It is genuine, as far as it goes, and it is worth noticing what it is. Not you are the Christ. Not even we will follow you. It is the approval of men who agreed with the conclusion.

They came to this chapter to destroy him, and here they are commending him — because on this particular point he was on their side.

Which is a familiar thing, and it is not the same as faith. It is entirely possible to be delighted by a preacher who demolishes a position you already disliked, and to walk out having received nothing at all. The test of whether a man is listening to Christ is not whether he applauds when Christ attacks somebody else.

And these particular scribes are back within two chapters, seeking how to put him to death (22:2).

For they no longer dared to ask him any question.

Luke closes the day's interrogation with a verdict, and it covers all three delegations.

The chief priests came with a question about authority and ended by saying we do not know. The spies came about the tribute and became silent. The Sadducees came with the seven brothers and are not recorded as replying at all.

Three attacks, each carefully prepared by men who did this professionally, and after the third nobody would risk a fourth.

They have run out of questions. What is left is the arrest, and it will happen at night, with a bribe, away from the crowd — because that is the only method remaining to men who have been beaten in the open.

Which settles something about the trial that is coming, and it is worth having before Luke gets there.

Nobody in Jerusalem defeated Jesus in argument. Three organised attempts were made by the best-qualified men in the country, on their own ground, at a time of their choosing, and all three collapsed in public — and Luke, who was not there and got this from witnesses, records the details of each failure.

What finally happened to him on Friday did not happen because the case against him was strong.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'How can they say that the Christ is David's son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them, How can they say that the Christ is David's son?

Now he asks. Three delegations have questioned him and failed; he has one question of his own, and it is about who he is.

Note first that he is not denying the premise. That the Messiah would be a descendant of David was not a rabbinic guess but a promise — I will raise up your offspring after you… and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam. 7:12-13); there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isa. 11:1). Luke's own Gospel opened with Gabriel promising the throne of his father David (1:32), and a blind beggar had been shouting Son of David at him outside Jericho two chapters ago (18:38).

So the question is not whether the Christ is David's son. It is whether that is the whole of it.

For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.

The quotation is Psalm 110:1, and it was universally taken to be David's and about the Messiah.

In the Hebrew the two words are different. The first is the covenant name of God, which English Bibles print as LORD in small capitals; the second is adoni, “my lord,” an ordinary word for a master or superior. So it reads: the LORD said to my lord. And in the Greek that Luke's readers had, both come out as kyrios, which is why the English needs the capitals to keep them apart.

Sit at my right hand. An invitation to share the throne of God, extended to a figure who is not God the Father — and the position is not honorary. The right hand is where the authority is exercised.

This verse became the most quoted Old Testament text in the entire New Testament. It is in Peter's sermon at Pentecost, in Paul, and repeatedly in Hebrews (Acts 2:34-35; 1 Cor. 15:25; Heb. 1:13; 10:12-13). The early church could not stop returning to it, and this is where they learned to.

And note where he has gone for it. Not to a prophecy about a suffering servant, and not to anything obscure. Psalm 110 was a coronation psalm that every scribe in the courtyard could recite, and he is asking them a question about a text they had known since childhood.

The material for recognising him had been in their hands the whole time. What was missing was not information.

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.’ David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I make your enemies your footstool.

The image is from the ancient world's iconography of conquest — a victorious king with his feet on the necks of the defeated, and Egyptian and Assyrian reliefs show it literally. Joshua had the commanders of Israel put their feet on the necks of five kings (Josh. 10:24).

And the word until should not be read as a limit on the reign. The sitting does not stop when the enemies are subdued; what stops is the interval in which they are still standing.

David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?

And there is the question, and the whole weight of it rests on a social fact so obvious that nobody in that courtyard needed it explained.

In that world, honour ran upward. A son honoured his father; a descendant honoured his ancestor. A man addressed his forebears as my lord and never the reverse, and the further back the ancestor, the greater the honour due. David was the greatest king Israel ever had, and every Jew traced honour towards him.

So a psalm in which David calls his own descendant my Lord is upside down. It cannot happen — unless the descendant is something more than a descendant.

Jesus does not supply the answer. He leaves the question standing, and Luke records no reply.

But the answer is not obscure, and every reader of this Gospel has had it since chapter one. The Messiah is David's son and David's Lord because he is both: descended from David according to the flesh, and the eternal Son who was there before David and made him. Paul states it in exactly those two halves — descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Rom. 1:3-4).

Which is why the question was asked at all. The scribes had a Messiah who was David's son and nothing more — a king, a deliverer, a national restorer. Their expectation was true and it was too small, and a man with an expectation that is true and too small will reject the reality when it arrives, because it does not fit.

He was standing in front of them, and the psalm they recited was about him.
verseByVerse.note: A conquered king’s neck could be used as a footstool — a picture of total victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, 'Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples.

Luke marks the audience carefully, and the arrangement is deliberate. The words are addressed to his disciples and spoken in the hearing of all the people — a warning given to one group in front of another, so that both hear it.

Beware of the scribes.

The verb is the one for watching out for a danger. And it is worth registering how startling the sentence is: the scribes were the Bible teachers, the men who copied and studied and expounded the Scriptures, and the ordinary person's assumption was that they were the most reliable guides available.

He tells the crowd to be careful of them.

Who like to walk around in long robes.

Four marks follow, and they are all about being seen.

The long robes were the full-length garment worn by men of distinction. And the phrase is walk around in them: not wearing one to a function but promenading, which is a small and perfectly recognisable vanity.

And love greetings in the marketplaces. The public respect due to a teacher, paid in the open square where it could be observed. Note the verb again — not receive greetings, which they could not help, but love them.

And the best seats in the synagogues. The bench at the front, facing the congregation, near the scroll chest — a seat that makes a man visible for the whole service.

And the places of honor at feasts. The couches nearest the host, exactly what Jesus had watched the guests scrambling for at a Pharisee's dinner (14:7).

Not one of these is a sin in itself. Somebody has to sit at the front; robes and greetings are not wicked. What is diagnosed, four times over, is an appetite — and the appetite is for being looked at while being religious.

Which is a hazard of the office and not of the men. Any position in which a person is watched being godly carries it, and it does not announce itself. It feels like enjoying one's work.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers.

The register changes completely. Long robes and good seats are vanity; this is predation.

How did scribes devour widows' houses? Scripture does not say, and the mechanisms available in that world were several. Scribes were forbidden to charge for teaching the law and were therefore dependent on the hospitality and gifts of the devout, of whom widows were a notably generous class. A scribe might be appointed to manage a widow's estate and take a fee from it. He might accept board and lodging from a woman who could not afford it. He might simply encourage a level of giving that ruined her.

What all of these have in common is that none is illegal. They are the abuse of religious standing to extract money from people who trusted the standing — and the victims are chosen with care.

Widows in that society had no earning power, no legal protection worth the name, and nobody to complain to. God's law had singled them out for special protection precisely for that reason: you shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child… my wrath will burn (Ex. 22:22-24), and the prophets returned to it constantly.

These are the men entrusted with teaching that law.

And for a pretense make long prayers.

And the two halves belong together, which is the horror of the verse. The long prayers are not a separate failing; they are the instrument. The reputation for piety is what gets a man access to a widow's confidence and her accounts.

The prayer is the cover for the theft.

They will receive the greater condemnation.

Greater than whom? Than others — and the principle has been running through this Gospel since chapter twelve: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (12:48). The sentence is heavier because the position was higher and the trust was greater.

Which is a word for anybody who holds any kind of spiritual standing over other people. It is possible to use the things of God to get things from people, and Scripture reserves its severest language for it.

And Luke sets the next scene immediately: a widow, at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1-4).

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

20.text: <sup>1</sup> One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up <sup>2</sup> and said to him, “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.” <sup>3</sup> He answered them, “I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, <sup>4</sup> was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?” <sup>5</sup> And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ <sup>6</sup> But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” <sup>7</sup> So they answered that they did not know where it came from. <sup>8</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” <sup>9</sup> And he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. <sup>10</sup> When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>11</sup> And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>12</sup> And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out. <sup>13</sup> Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ <sup>14</sup> But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’ <sup>15</sup> And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? <sup>16</sup> He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “Surely not!” <sup>17</sup> But he looked directly at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? <sup>18</sup> Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>19</sup> The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people. <sup>20</sup> So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. <sup>21</sup> So they asked him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. <sup>22</sup> Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” <sup>23</sup> But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?” They said, “Caesar's.” <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.” <sup>26</sup> And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent. <sup>27</sup> There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, <sup>28</sup> and they asked him a question, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>29</sup> Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. <sup>30</sup> And the second <sup>31</sup> and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. <sup>32</sup> Afterward the woman also died. <sup>33</sup> In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, <sup>35</sup> but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, <sup>36</sup> for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. <sup>37</sup> But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. <sup>38</sup> Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.” <sup>39</sup> Then some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” <sup>40</sup> For they no longer dared to ask him any question. <sup>41</sup> But he said to them, “How can they say that the Christ is David's son? <sup>42</sup> For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>43</sup> until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>44</sup> David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?” <sup>45</sup> And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, <sup>46</sup> “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>47</sup> who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.”

21.title: The Widow's Offering and the Olivet Discourse
21.overview:
Luke 21 opens with a scene that provides the perfect contrast to the scribes condemned at the end of chapter 20: a widow who puts into the temple treasury two small copper coins — “everything she had to live on.” Then, as Jesus leaves the temple and a disciple admires its magnificent stones, he delivers the Olivet Discourse — his most extended eschatological teaching, covering the destruction of Jerusalem, the sufferings of the disciples, the fall of the city, and the coming of the Son of Man.

The Olivet Discourse in Luke (parallel to Matthew 24 and Mark 13) is notable for several features. Luke emphasises the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 more explicitly than the other Gospels, and the discourse includes several passages that apply specifically to that historical event. At the same time, the coming of the Son of Man in glory transcends any single historical event — it is the final, universal, unmistakable arrival of the Kingdom in its fullness.

The chapter closes with a pattern that defines the final days of Jesus's ministry: he teaches in the temple by day; the people come early to hear him; at night he goes out to the Mount of Olives. This is the rhythm of the last week — teaching, opposition, and solitary prayer, all moving toward the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 20 ended with Jesus warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. Chapter 21 opens with a widow whose house has been devoured, giving away the last of it. Luke has put the two paragraphs side by side on purpose.

Jesus is sitting in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-mouthed chests stood against the wall, built so that a coin rang all the way down. He looks up and watches the rich putting in their gifts — nothing is said against them, and nothing should be read in. Then he sees a poor widow put in two lepta, the smallest coin minted, together worth about a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage.

His verdict is that she has put in more than all of them, and the reason he gives is arithmetical: they gave out of their abundance, their overflow, what they would not miss; she gave out of her poverty, and she gave all she had to live on. The measure is not the size of the gift but the size of what remains.

There is a real difficulty in the sequence, and it is worth facing rather than smoothing over. Jesus has just condemned the men who run this temple, and five verses later he will say the building is coming down to the last stone. Is he praising a woman for handing her last coin to a doomed and corrupt institution? Some read the passage as a lament rather than a commendation. But his own words settle it — this poor widow has put in more than all of them is praise, not mourning. He is not endorsing the temple. He is telling us what God saw at the treasury.

Which is the comfort in it for every believer who has given, served and poured out small resources inside a church that was flawed, or failing, or would not outlast them. The worth of the gift was never in the soundness of the institution that received it.
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the divine valuation of giving, and it runs on a different ledger from ours. The rich men’s gifts are not condemned; they are revalued. What looked large is revealed to be cheap, and what looked negligible is revealed to be everything, because heaven measures the cost to the giver and not the benefit to the fund.

Behind that lies a deeper principle: God does not need our money. The temple did not stand or fall on the widow’s two coins, and the kingdom does not advance on donations. What God seeks in giving is the giver — which is why proportion tells the truth about a heart and totals do not.

And the scene is a small portrait of the cross, days before it. She gave her whole livelihood; he was about to give his whole life. She trusted God for the next meal with nothing left in reserve; he would go into the dark with nothing held back either. Complete self-giving is not a heroic exception in the kingdom of God. It is the shape of the King.
verseByVerse.examples:
The test in v. 1 is easy to run and hard to survive. Think of the last thing you gave to God’s work, and ask not how much it was but what you went without because of it. If nothing in the month changed, the answer has already been given.

A church announces the total of a giving campaign with celebration — a large figure, mostly from prosperous members. The pastor privately knows the costliest single gift came from a widow on a fixed income who gave her entire discretionary fund for the month. He has to decide whether the celebration names the total or the sacrifice, and this passage tells him which one heaven has already recorded.

And for anyone whose giving is small: she is remembered in every language on earth two thousand years later, and the names of the wealthy donors that morning are gone without trace — because the Lord noticed, and said so. Nothing done for him is unwitnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box.

Picture where he is sitting. The Court of the Women, the large paved outer court that ordinary Israelites could enter, and ranged around its walls thirteen collection chests. They were shaped like trumpets — narrow at the mouth, widening below — so that a coin dropped in did not fall silently. It rang, and rang all the way down. A small gift made a small sound. A handful of silver made a noise the whole court could hear.

So the temple treasury was, by its own architecture, a public address system for generosity. And the rich are walking past it, and it is ringing.

Luke says Jesus looked up. He had been sitting, doing something else — teaching, most likely, since he had been teaching in that temple every day of that week (v. 37). The lifting of his eyes is deliberate. He is not glancing about; he stops what he is doing to watch what people put in.

That is the first thing in the paragraph, and it is worth stopping on before the widow arrives, because it is the fact that gives the whole scene its weight. The offering is observed. Not audited — observed. There is Someone at the treasury whose interest is not in the total.

Nothing is said against the rich men, and nothing should be read into the passage that Luke does not put there. Their gifts were real, and the temple ran on them. Jesus does not call them hypocrites, does not accuse them of showing off, does not say a word to them at all. He simply watches, and the reckoning he is about to make will not be a rebuke of their giving. It will be a revaluation of it.

And that is the more searching thing. It is easy to guard yourself against the charge of hypocrisy; you know when you are performing. It is much harder to discover that a gift you made in perfectly good faith was, on the ledger that finally matters, worth almost nothing — not because your motive was rotten, but because it cost you nothing to make.

Here is the test, and it takes about ten seconds. Think of the last thing you gave to God's work. Now ask, not how much it was, but what you went without because of it. If nothing changed — if the direct debit leaves and the month proceeds exactly as it would otherwise have proceeded — then you have just been told what heaven saw when your coin rang in the trumpet.

The Lord does not look at what a man gives. He looks at what a man has left (cf. 1 Sam. 16:7; 2 Cor. 8:12).
verseByVerse.note: The offering box was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women.

verseByVerse.quote: and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.

Two lepta — the ESV margin at 12:59 names the lepton as a Jewish bronze or copper coin. It was the smallest coin minted in that world; two of them together came to about a sixty-fourth of a day's wage for a labouring man. In a trumpet-mouthed chest built to broadcast generosity, they would have made almost no sound at all. A tap, and then nothing.

And Luke says he saw her. That is the second time in two verses that the verb is one of sight, and it is the hinge of the paragraph.

Consider what had to be true for that sentence to be written. In a crowded court, on the loudest week of the religious year, with the wealth of Jerusalem filing past a row of collection chests, the eye of the Son of God rested on a woman nobody was looking at, holding a sum nobody would have counted, and it stayed there.

She is a widow, which in that economy is a precise description of destitution, not merely of bereavement. No husband, and therefore no wage; no legal standing to speak of; no pension, no benefits office, no way of earning beyond gleaning and charity. The law had commanded Israel to care for her (Deut. 14:29; 24:19), and Jesus had said one chapter earlier what the religious establishment actually did with women like her: it devoured their houses (20:47). She is the wronged party in the very institution she is about to fund.

And she gives. She does not stand at the back and watch. She walks up to the chest, in the same queue as the men with the silver, and puts in everything.

Israel had seen this before, though nobody in that court made the connection. A widow at Zarephath with a handful of flour and a little oil, gathering sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son before they died, and a prophet asking her for it first (1 Kings 17:12–16). She gave, and the jar did not run dry. God has a long-standing habit of putting the last of somebody's food into the story and then not letting the story end there.

Here, then, is the thing to see, and it has nothing to do with what the reader should now go and do. The Lord of glory, days from the cross, with the weight of the world's sin already pressing on him, is watching a poor woman drop two thin coins into a box. He is not too preoccupied. He is not too exalted. He notices, and he will speak about it, and because he spoke about it she is known in every language on earth two thousand years later while the names of the wealthy donors that morning are gone without trace.

That is the eye that is on his people. Nothing done for him is unwitnessed, and nothing witnessed by him is small.
verseByVerse.note: Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The economy of the kingdom runs on a different ledger entirely. The Greek word behind abundance is perisseuontos — their overflow, what was extra, what they would not miss. The widow gives from her husterēma — her lack, her deficit, the thing she cannot spare. By heaven's arithmetic she has given more than all the wealthy donors combined, because the measure is not amount but proportion, not size of gift but size of trust. She gave all she had to live on. It is an act of utter abandonment to God's provision — and she who gives everything foreshadows him who will give everything on Golgotha.

One difficulty is worth facing, because the very arrangement of Luke's text raises it. Only a few verses earlier Jesus condemned the scribes who devour widows' houses (20:47); a few verses later he says the temple whose treasury she is filling will be torn down to the last stone (21:6). So a thoughtful reader stops: is Jesus really praising a woman for handing her last coin to a corrupt institution he has just denounced and is about to consign to rubble? Some have concluded he is not praising her at all but lamenting her — mourning a religious system that has taught a penniless widow to give away her final means of living. It is an honest reading, and the sequence that suggests it is not accidental.

But it founders on Jesus's own verdict, which is not a lament: this poor widow has put in more than all of them. That is commendation, plainly, and it settles what is being commended. He is not endorsing the temple, and he is not saying her coins repaired anything — within a generation the whole apparatus would be ash. He is telling us what God saw at that treasury: not the sums, but a heart holding nothing back. The worth of her gift was never in the soundness of the institution that received it; it was in the trust of the one who gave it, and that God receives even when the building it was dropped into is under sentence.

Does Jesus mean that every believer should give away everything? No. He commends her trust and her gift; he does not command everyone to give away all they live on. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has (2 Cor 8:12), and a believer must provide for his own household (1 Tim 5:8). And no church may press the poor to give beyond their means; Jesus has just condemned those who devour widows’ houses (20:47).

Which is a mercy for every believer who has ever given, and served, and poured out their small resources inside a church that was flawed, or failing, or would not outlast them. The temple did not deserve her two coins. God received them as if they were the wealth of the world — because, measured on his ledger, they were.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–19 — The Temple, the Signs, and the Cost of Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Someone admires the temple — the noble stones and the offerings fixed to its walls — and it was worth admiring: white limestone blocks over forty feet long, a gold-plated front that Josephus says a man could not look at in the morning sun, a golden vine over the entrance with clusters the height of a man. Jesus replies that not one stone will be left on another. In the year 70 Titus besieged the city, the temple burned, and soldiers levered the stones apart to get at the gold that had run molten into the joints.

The disciples ask the natural question — when, and what sign? He never answers it. What he gives instead is a series of instructions for living in the meantime.

First, do not be led astray: many will come claiming to be the one, and many more will announce that the time is at hand. Second, when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified — these things must happen, and the end will not be at once. Third, the ordinary catastrophes of history — nation against nation, earthquake, famine, pestilence, terrors from heaven — are the weather of this long age, not the signal that it is over.

Then the turn that dominates the section: but before all this. Before any of the cosmic disturbances, the disciples themselves will be seized, delivered to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors. Luke’s second volume then records every item happening in order — Acts 4:3, 9:2, 5:18, 24, 25, 26.

And that, Jesus says, is their opportunity to bear witness. They are not to rehearse a defence; he will give them a mouth and wisdom their adversaries cannot withstand — a promise Luke shows kept, in the same vocabulary, when Stephen’s opponents could not withstand the wisdom with which he spoke (Acts 6:10).

The cost is named without softening: betrayal by parents, brothers, relatives and friends; some put to death; hatred from all for his name’s sake. And then, two verses after saying some of them will be killed, he says not a hair of their heads will perish, and that by endurance they will gain their lives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apparent contradiction between v. 16 and v. 18 is the theological centre of the section, and it is not a contradiction. Not a hair of your head is a Hebrew idiom for total preservation, and Jesus has already used it in this Gospel in exactly this setting (12:7). What enemies can do to a believer is real and can be final in every visible respect, and it cannot reach the person himself. Stephen was stoned, and not a hair of his head perished.

This is providence applied to persecution. The disciple is not promised safety; he is promised supply — words when words are needed — and security that no execution can touch. Endurance is remaining under. It is not gritted teeth or heroic reserves; it is staying at the post today, on grace that arrives daily and never in advance.

Note also the qualifier attached twice to the suffering: for my name’s sake. Not every kind of unpopularity a Christian achieves is covered by these promises. The test is whether the hostility would disappear if the name of Christ were subtracted from the situation.
verseByVerse.examples:
A believer in a country where conversion is punishable by imprisonment reads vv. 12–19 and finds that Jesus does not promise he will avoid arrest. He explicitly promises the opposite, and then promises something more reliable than safety: words at the moment they are needed, and a life that cannot finally be taken.

For readers who will never see a courtroom, the principle needs no handcuffs. The awkward silence after you said where you were on Sunday, the promotion that went elsewhere, the family meal that went quiet — those feel like loss and are being counted as testimony, because a watching colleague learns more from what your faith costs you than from anything you could say when it was free.

Verse 15 also answers a common anxiety that has nothing to do with persecution: the dread of the question at work, the thirty seconds at the kitchen table, the lying awake afterwards composing what you should have said. Settle it therefore in your minds is a phrase about laying something down. The rehearsal was never the preparation; it was the anxiety.

And for those whose faith has cost them a family: it was foreseen, it was foretold, and the one who foretold it had brothers who did not believe in him either. The promise attached to it in this Gospel is not replacement but enlargement — many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life (18:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings.

They were not being foolish. The temple Herod built was one of the wonders of the ancient world, and everyone who saw it said so. Josephus, who had stood in it, describes stones of white limestone so large that the joints were invisible from a distance, so that the whole platform looked as though it had been cut from a single block. Some of the foundation stones still in place today are over forty feet long and weigh several hundred tons. Nobody has ever fully explained how they were moved.

The front was plated with gold, and Josephus says that when the morning sun struck it a man had to look away, and that from a distance the building looked like a mountain covered in snow. Over the entrance hung a golden vine with clusters of grapes said to be the height of a man, given by worshippers who had them added, cluster by cluster, as offerings. That is what Luke means by noble stones and offerings: not just the masonry, but the accumulated gifts of generations fixed to the walls.

It had been under construction for around forty-six years by the first Passover of his ministry (John 2:20), and it was still not finished. It would be completed in the early sixties. Within a few years of completion it would be gone.

So this is admiration of exactly the kind any of us would have felt. It is not idolatry. It is a group of Galilean men, in from the country, standing in the most impressive building they have ever seen, saying what people say.

And that is precisely why the exchange is worth pausing over, because the thing being admired was genuinely magnificent, genuinely God-ordained, and genuinely doomed — and the men admiring it had no way of telling from the stonework which of those three was about to matter.

Jeremiah had met the same instinct six hundred years earlier and named it exactly. Stand in the gate, God told him, and say to the people who come to worship: do not trust in deceptive words, chanting the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD (Jer. 7:4). They were not chanting a lie. It was the temple of the LORD. They were resting on a building instead of on the One who had asked for it, which is a different sin and much harder to see in yourself.

Try it on the nearest object. Think of the church you attend, or the denomination you trust, or the institution whose survival you quietly assume — the one that has been there longer than you have and will, you take for granted, be there after you. Now ask what would remain of your faith if it were not. That question is not cynicism. It is the question Jesus is about to force on the men standing next to him, and he forces it because he loves them and because in forty years they will need to have been asked it already.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with gleaming white stone and gifts displayed by donors.

verseByVerse.quote: 'As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.

It is hard to overstate how violent this sentence would have sounded in that courtyard. This was not merely the national monument; it was the one place on earth where sacrifice could lawfully be offered, where sin was dealt with, where God had put his name. To say the temple would fall was to say that the entire machinery of Israel's approach to God was coming to an end. Men had been executed for saying less. Jeremiah was nearly lynched for it (Jer. 26:8–11), and a version of this saying would be produced at Jesus's own trial as a capital charge (Mark 14:58).

The fulfilment came in the year 70. Titus besieged Jerusalem through the spring and summer; the city fell in August; the temple burned. Josephus, who was present in the Roman camp, says the fire was not part of the plan and that Titus tried to stop it, and that when the gold plating ran molten into the joints of the masonry the soldiers levered the stones apart to get at it. That is how a building of that size comes down to nothing: not by bombardment, but by greed, one block at a time.

The Western Wall that pilgrims visit today is not a survival of the temple. It is a section of the retaining wall of the platform the temple stood on. Of the sanctuary itself, exactly what Jesus said is what is there: nothing.

Some scholars conclude from the precision of this that Luke must have written after the event and shaped the saying to fit. It is an argument worth meeting rather than dodging. But it runs into an awkward fact in Luke's own second volume: Acts ends with Paul alive under house arrest in Rome, and says nothing whatever about the fall of Jerusalem, the death of Paul, or the death of James — the three events that would have been impossible for a Christian historian writing after 70 to leave out of a book about the church's first thirty years. The simplest reading of the two volumes is that they were finished before the thing they never mention had happened.

And there is a plainer objection to the theory. The prediction is not vague enough to be a lucky guess and not detailed enough to be a report. A writer inventing prophecy after the fact tends to include the fire, and Jesus does not mention fire.

What he does say is worth hearing as the men in the courtyard heard it. He looks at the most permanent thing in their world and puts a date on it. Everything they could see, weigh and lean on had a term, and he knew what it was.

He will say the counterpart to this twenty-seven verses later: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (v. 33). Between those two sentences the whole discourse is held. The visible is perishable and the spoken word of Christ is not, which is the exact reverse of how the world grades reality (cf. Isa. 40:8).
verseByVerse.note: The Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, 'Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?' And he said, 'See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?

Two questions, and both of them are about timing. When, and how will we know it is close. It is the most natural response in the world, and it is what any of us would have asked.

Notice what he does not do. He does not answer it. Not here, and in Luke's account not anywhere — there is no date in this chapter, and no formula for calculating one. What he gives instead is a series of instructions about how to live in the meantime, and the very first of them is a warning about people who will answer the question he has just declined to answer.

See that you are not led astray.

The verb is planaō, from which we get the word planet — the wandering star, the light that does not keep its place among the fixed ones. To be led astray is not to be argued out of the faith by an opponent. It is to drift off station while still believing you are travelling in a straight line.

For many will come in my name, saying, I am he! and, The time is at hand! Do not go after them.

Two claims, and they are different. The first is a claim about a person: someone stands up and says he is the one. The second is a claim about a clock: someone announces that the hour has arrived. A great many people who would never dream of making the first claim make the second one every decade, and Jesus puts them in the same warning.

He has reason to. The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of announced dates, and the wreckage is always made of people. Farms sold, savings given away, children taken out of school, and then the morning after, when the sun came up as usual and the believer had to walk back into a town that had watched the whole thing. Every one of those movements was led by someone quoting this very chapter.

So how does an ordinary Christian, who is not a scholar and cannot assess the arguments, avoid being led astray? Jesus gives the test in the sentence itself, and it is beautifully simple. It is not a doctrinal test; it is a directional one. Do not go after them. Watch where the teaching is taking the people who follow it. Teaching from God drives a man back to ordinary obedience — his work, his family, his prayers, his neighbour. Teaching that leads astray always ends with a following gathered around a teacher, doing something exceptional at his direction, on a timetable he supplies.

The mark of the false is not that it is frightening. It is that it makes you dependent on a man who claims to know something Christ declined to tell you (cf. Acts 1:7; 1 John 4:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.

Take the verbs in order, because the pastoral care in this verse is entirely in the sequence.

When you hear. Not when you suffer — when you hear. Jesus is speaking about the effect on the soul of news from elsewhere: the report of a war in a country you will never visit, the account of an uprising among people you have never met. He knew, twenty centuries before the phone on the bedside table, that a man can be destroyed by events that are not happening to him.

Do not be terrified. Not ordinary fear, but being startled out of your senses, the panic of a flushed bird, the mind scattering. He is not forbidding grief. He is not forbidding concern; the man who reads of a famine and feels nothing has a harder problem than anxiety. He is forbidding the specific state in which fear has taken over the controls.

For these things must first take place. The word must is dei, and it is one of Luke's favourite words for the settled purpose of God — the same word he uses of Christ's own suffering: the Son of Man must suffer many things (9:22). That is a startling thing to put under a paragraph about wars. It means that the wars are inside the plan, not outside it. Not caused by God in the way that good is caused by him, but not loose either.

But the end will not be at once. And this is the sentence that does the actual work, because it removes the thing that makes catastrophic news unbearable. What crushes a person watching the world convulse is not the convulsion; it is the conclusion drawn from it — that this is the beginning of the end, that history is unravelling, that there is nothing after this. Jesus flatly denies the inference. Wars are not the end. They are the weather of a long age, and he says so in advance so that nobody has to work it out during the storm.

Here is the practical shape of that, for a reader who genuinely cannot stop. The instruction is not to look away. It is to refuse the interpretation. When the headline arrives, the question is not is this the end — he has told you it is not — but the far smaller and more answerable one: what does love require of me today, in this street, with this news in my head. Pray for the people in it. Give if you can. Then do your work.

The world's foundations are not shaking. They are being carried, by hands that were about to be nailed down for the carrying (cf. Ps. 46:1–3; Heb. 1:3).
