verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.

Four categories, and between them they cover everything that can go wrong on a planet. War, which men cause. Earthquake, which nobody causes. Famine and plague, which are usually both — a failed harvest made lethal by somebody's decision about who eats. And then the sky.

The main point is easy to miss because the list is so vivid, so it is worth stating flatly before anything else. Jesus is not giving signs of the end here. He has just said the opposite in v. 9: these things must happen, and the end will not be at once. He is describing the ordinary content of the long age between his ascension and his return — and he is describing it in advance so that his people will not misread it when it arrives.

That reading is confirmed by the words themselves. Not one item on the list is unprecedented. Israel had known all four within living memory. There had been earthquakes in Judea, and a famine in the reign of Claudius that Luke himself records (Acts 11:28), and war was the normal condition of the eastern Mediterranean. He is not predicting new kinds of trouble. He is naming the old kinds and telling his disciples what they mean, which is: less than you will be tempted to think.

Because the temptation is enormous, and every generation has yielded to it. The plague years of the fourteenth century, when a third of Europe died, produced a certainty that the end had come. So did the wars of the twentieth. So does whatever is on the news this month. And each time, the calculation has the same two effects: it makes the sufferer feel that the universe is finally paying attention to his agony, and it makes the onlooker useless, because a man watching the last act does not plant trees.

Jesus takes the interpretation away, and he does it as a kindness.

Look at what is left once he has. The disaster is still real; he does not minimise a single item. But it is no longer a message. It does not mean God has abandoned the world, and it does not mean the clock has run out. It means the world is what he said it was — a good creation under a curse, groaning (Rom. 8:22), not yet delivered, and not forgotten either.

And there is a mercy in the phrase in various places that is easy to walk past. The suffering is distributed, not universal. That is why the church has always been able to answer it — because when the famine is in one place, the harvest is in another, and the collection can be taken and carried, which is exactly what the Antioch believers did in Acts 11:29 when they heard. The geography of trouble is the opportunity of the body of Christ.

So: expect these things, do not read them, and send help (cf. Rom. 8:20–22; Acts 11:27–30).

verseByVerse.quote: But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness.

Two words carry this paragraph, and the first is before.

Everything in the preceding list — the wars, the earthquakes, the famines, the signs — is pushed back behind something nearer. Before the cosmos does anything, the police will. The disciple's experience of the last age does not begin with a sign in the sky; it begins with a hand on his arm.

And Luke, alone among the Gospel writers, then went and wrote the sequel. Every item on this list happens in Acts, in order. Hands laid on them: Acts 4:3. Delivered to the synagogues: Acts 9:2. Prisons: Acts 5:18, 12:4, 16:23. Before governors: Felix and Festus, Acts 24 and 25. Before kings: Agrippa, Acts 26. The Gospel makes the prediction and the Acts of the Apostles ticks it off item by item. It is one of the quiet pleasures of reading Luke's two volumes together.

The second word is the one that turns the paragraph over. Opportunity.

The Greek is apobēsetai eis martyrion — it will turn out, it will result, in testimony. The verb is the one used of a thing landing somewhere other than where it appeared to be heading. And martyrion is witness, from which we get the word martyr, though at this point in the language it still means simply the evidence a witness gives.

So consider what has just been said about an arrest. Not that God will bring good out of it afterwards, though he will. Not that it will be endurable, though it will. That the arrest is the appointment. The dock is the pulpit. There is no other way for a fisherman from Galilee to get twenty uninterrupted minutes in front of a Roman governor, and the Spirit has booked it.

Paul saw it exactly so, and said so from prison in words that read like a commentary on this verse: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Phil. 1:12). The whole imperial guard heard it. He would never have reached them any other way.

Now bring this down to a reader who will never see a courtroom. The principle does not require handcuffs; it requires only that following Christ has cost you something in front of other people. The awkward silence when you said where you were on Sunday. The promotion that went elsewhere. The family meal that went quiet. Those moments feel like loss, and they are being counted as testimony — because a watching colleague learns more from what your faith costs you than from anything you could have said when it was free.

What the world takes from a Christian, it takes in public. That is the whole point (cf. Acts 4:13; Phil. 1:12–14).

verseByVerse.quote: Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.

Take the crux first, because it is a real one and a reader is entitled to have it dealt with plainly. Does this verse forbid preparation? Should a preacher stop writing sermons and a Bible study leader stop doing the reading, and simply open his mouth and trust?

No, and the reason is in the vocabulary. The verb is promeletan, and it is a technical word from the law courts: to rehearse a defence speech in advance. That is its home. Jesus is not talking about study, or preparation, or thinking hard about Scripture — all of which he commends everywhere else, and all of which Luke's own heroes do constantly. He is talking about the specific practice of a defendant drafting his testimony before a hearing.

Paul settles it by example. This is the man who reasoned in the synagogues for three Sabbaths from the Scriptures (Acts 17:2), who quoted Greek poets in Athens, who asks Timothy to bring the books and above all the parchments (2 Tim. 4:13) — and who also, standing before Agrippa, plainly received something he had not written. Preparation and this promise are not rivals. One is the ordinary work; the other is the extraordinary supply at the moment when the ordinary work has been taken away from you.

I will give you a mouth and wisdom.

Two gifts, and they are not the same. Wisdom is what to say. A mouth is the ability to say it — which is the part most people actually lack. Plenty of Christians know exactly what the truth is and cannot get it past their teeth when it matters.

Then watch what Luke does with this promise later, because the echo is deliberate and verbatim. Here: none of your adversaries will be able to withstand. In Acts 6:10, of Stephen before the synagogue of the Freedmen: they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. Same verb, same claim, kept in the same book by the same author. Luke wants his reader to see the promise land.

And now the pastoral point, because the anxiety this verse addresses is one of the most common in the Christian life and it is rarely about courtrooms. It is the man who dreads the question at work. The mother whose adult child asks something at the kitchen table and she has thirty seconds. The believer who lay awake afterwards composing what he should have said.

The command to such a person is not try harder. It is settle it therefore in your minds — a phrase about laying something down, deciding it in advance and ceasing to carry it. The rehearsal is not the preparation. It is the anxiety.

He has never yet sent a witness into a room and failed to arrive himself (cf. Exod. 4:11–12; Acts 6:10).

parallels.desc: they could not withstand the wisdom of Stephen

verseByVerse.quote: You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. You will be hated by all for my name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. You will be hated by all for my name's sake.

He will not soften it, and the list is arranged so that it cannot be softened. Parents. Brothers. Relatives. Friends. It moves outward from the innermost circle a human being has, and the innermost is named first.

Delivered up means to hand over — to place a person into the power of someone who intends them harm. So the sentence is not describing an argument at Christmas. It is describing the moment a father tells the authorities where his son is.

Then some of you they will put to death. Not all. Some. He does not say which, and there is a terrible tenderness in that, because he is speaking to his disciples and he knows the answer for each of them. James would be first, killed with the sword by Herod within about a dozen years (Acts 12:2). John would die old.

And then hated by all. This is the hardest phrase in the two verses, because hatred from strangers can be borne by anyone with a clear conscience; hatred that is universal cannot, since it removes the last suspicion that the fault might lie with the people doing the hating.

But notice the ground of it, stated twice in six verses so that it cannot be missed: for my name's sake. That qualifier is doing protective work. Jesus is not blessing every kind of unpopularity a Christian can achieve. It is entirely possible to be disliked for being rude, or superior, or strange, or for having opinions that have nothing to do with him, and a man who is suffering that has not been promised anything here. The test is simple and searching: subtract the name of Christ from your situation, and see whether the hostility goes with it.

Now, for the reader for whom this is not theory. Some who read this verse have a chair at the table that has been empty for years. There are believers whose conversion cost them their mother, and who have written letters that were never answered, and who read even by parents and know exactly what it weighs.

Two things are true for them, and both are in Luke. The first is that Jesus said this would happen, which means the silence at the other end of the phone is not evidence that God has abandoned the family or that a mistake was made. It was foreseen and it was foretold and it was foretold by someone whose own brothers did not believe in him.

The second is the promise he attached to it in this same Gospel: there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life (18:29–30). The family is not replaced. It is enlarged, in the church now, and restored in the end.

He did not ask of them anything he had not already accepted himself (cf. Mic. 7:6; John 7:5).

verseByVerse.quote: But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.

This is the sharpest apparent contradiction in the chapter, and it sits two verses after its own opposite. In v. 16 he said some of you they will put to death. In v. 18 he says not a hair of your head will perish. Both sentences are his, both are addressed to the same men in the same breath, and a reader who does not stop here has not been paying attention.

The resolution is not that one of them is exaggeration. It is that they are measured on different scales, and the second one is the true measure.

Not a hair of your head is an established Hebrew idiom for absolute preservation, used when a life is under sentence and God intervenes (1 Sam. 14:45; 2 Sam. 14:11; Acts 27:34, again in Luke's own writing). It is a way of saying: down to the last and smallest detail, nothing of you is lost. Jesus has used it once already in this Gospel, and the setting there is decisive — the very hairs of your head are all numbered; fear not, you are of more value than many sparrows (12:7). That saying, too, comes in a passage about being dragged before the authorities and killed.

So the promise is not that the body is safe. It is that the person is. What can be done to a Christian by his enemies is real, and it can be final in every visible respect, and it cannot reach the man himself. Stephen was stoned to death, and not a hair of his head perished; that is the plain sense of it, and Luke wrote both sentences.

Then by your endurance you will gain your lives.

The word is hypomonē, and the picture inside it is not gritted teeth. It is a compound: hypo, under, and menō, to remain. To remain under. It is the word for the load-bearing beam that is still there in the morning, and for the soldier who has not left his post, and it is the word the writer to the Hebrews uses for running the race set before us (Heb. 12:1).

Which answers the fear that this verse actually raises in most Christians, which is not the fear of martyrdom. It is the quieter one: I do not think I have it in me to last. Not thirty more years. Not through what is coming.

You are not asked to last thirty years. Endurance is not a quantity of strength held in reserve; it is remaining under, today. Nobody is given the grace for a decade at once. The saints who endured to the end did it the way anyone does — the next morning, and then the one after that, on grace that arrived daily and never in advance (cf. Lam. 3:22–23; 2 Cor. 12:9).

Does salvation, then, depend on my endurance? Endurance is the evidence and fruit of God’s keeping, not the ground of salvation. he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil 1:6), and no one will snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28). The call to endure is real, and God uses it to keep his people enduring.

And the tense of the promise is worth hearing exactly: you will gain your lives. Not keep, not retain — gain. The thing that is handed over in the losing is handed back larger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Fall of the City and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Where Matthew and Mark speak of the abomination of desolation and add let the reader understand, Luke gives his Gentile readers the plain meaning: armies around Jerusalem. Then three commands, all of them counter-intuitive — flee Judea, leave the city, and do not go in. Under a normal siege the countryside empties into the walls. Jesus tells them to do the opposite, and the history bears him out: the horror of that siege was concentrated inside. Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church, warned beforehand, withdrew to Pella across the Jordan.

He then names what is happening theologically. These are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written — covenant language, and a quotation. Isaiah 61:2 speaks of the year of the LORD’s favour and the day of vengeance of our God, and that is the passage Jesus read at Nazareth in 4:19, where he stopped mid-sentence and left the vengeance unread. Here he finishes it.

And in the same breath he grieves: Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days. The judgment is deserved and it is agonising, and the one announcing it had already wept over this city (19:41).

Verse 24 adds the clause found only in Luke: Jerusalem trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Readings of that phrase differ, but every reading rests on the same word. Gentile dominion is real, permitted, and bounded.

Then the scene widens from a city to a world. Signs in sun and moon and stars; nations in perplexity, with no way through; people fainting with fear at what is coming — strength leaving the body over an event that has not yet happened.

Against that backdrop, one figure: the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory — Daniel 7:13. And one instruction to his people, and it is physical: straighten up, and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the destruction of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) relates to the coming of the Son of Man (vv. 25–28) is one of the most discussed questions in the Gospels. Three approaches are held by serious readers: that both refer to the events of that generation; that both refer to the final end; or that the fall of Jerusalem is a real judgment which is also a pattern and foretaste of the last one. The third fits the language best — vv. 25–28 are cosmic in scope, and v. 28 is addressed to disciples of every generation — and it has the advantage of taking both halves seriously.

Luke’s own contribution to the question is v. 24, and it is decisive: he alone writes an interval of unspecified length into the discourse, between the trampling of the city and the appearing of the Son of Man. The reader who takes that clause seriously will not be troubled by the objection that Jesus predicted a return that did not come.

The cloud in v. 27 is not weather. In the Old Testament the cloud is where God is — the pillar in the wilderness, the glory filling the tabernacle. And they will see anchors the Christian hope in something public: he was seen born, seen killed, seen ascending, and will be seen returning. The dominion Daniel saw handed over was always going to be handed to a crucified man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 21 raises an honest question: is fleeing not simply cowardice? Jesus says no, and it helps to have a Lord who will say so. Paul was let down the wall in a basket and thought no less of himself. Flight is cowardice only when it abandons a post you were given, and nobody was given the post of dying inside those walls. For anyone facing a collapse they cannot prevent — a business, a church, a marriage — faithfulness sometimes means staying and sometimes means going, and the Lord does not leave his people without direction.

Verse 23 answers a question people really carry: does God take satisfaction in judgment? The answer stands in the temple court with tears not yet dry, grieving in advance for infants not yet conceived — and within the week the wrath he is describing falls on him.

Verses 25–26 describe the commonest suffering in a comfortable country: not disaster, but dread. The mortgage that has not failed, the scan that has not come back, and the strength going out of the body over a thing that has not happened. Jesus does not scold it; he names it with medical precision, and then tells his own people to lift their heads — the one thing no frightened person ever thinks to do.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it.

Matthew and Mark, at this point in the discourse, have Jesus speak of the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not, and add the aside let the reader understand (Mark 13:14). Luke, writing for a Gentile readership who would not catch a Daniel allusion, gives the plain meaning instead: armies around the city. It is a good illustration of how the Gospel writers work — the same words of the same Lord, rendered by one for readers who know Daniel and by another for readers who do not.

Then three commands, and they are startlingly ordinary. Get out of Judea. Get out of the city. Do not go back in.

The third is the strangest and the most revealing. Under any normal siege, the countryside empties into the walled city, because that is where the walls are. Jerusalem's defences were formidable and its people knew it. Jesus tells them to do the exact opposite of the sensible thing, and history records why: those who went in did not come out. Josephus puts the death toll at over a million, which is certainly too high, but every account agrees that the horror of that siege was concentrated inside the walls, where famine and factional slaughter did more than the Romans.

And the church heard him. The historian Eusebius records that before the war reached its height the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by an oracle given to their leaders, left the city and settled at Pella across the Jordan. The tradition has been questioned, but nothing better explains what plainly happened: a movement whose entire leadership and headquarters were in Jerusalem in the year 60 was not destroyed when Jerusalem was.

Now the harder question, because a thoughtful reader will feel it. Is this not simply running away? Should the disciples not have stayed and prayed for the city, and died with it if necessary?

Jesus says no, and it is worth having a Lord who will say so. There is a time to stand and a time to go, and the difference is not measured by how brave it feels. Paul was let down the Damascus wall in a basket (Acts 9:25) and thought no less of himself for it. What determines the answer is not courage but calling: flight from danger is cowardice only when it is flight from a post you were given. Nobody was given the post of dying inside those walls.

And there is a wider comfort in it for anyone facing a collapse they cannot prevent — a business, a marriage, a church. Faithfulness sometimes means staying and sometimes means leaving, and the Lord does not leave his people without direction as to which. He told these ones in advance, forty years in advance, and the ones who took him seriously lived (cf. Gen. 19:17; Prov. 22:3).
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, as the Romans did in AD 66–70; Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation.”

verseByVerse.quote: for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.

Two things are said here that a modern reader instinctively wants to separate, and Luke has bolted them together.

The first is that this is judgment. Days of vengeance is not Roman policy described from the outside; it is covenant language, and it is quoting. Isaiah 61:2 speaks of the year of the LORD's favour and the day of vengeance of our God — and that is the very passage Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth in Luke 4:19, where he stopped reading mid-sentence, closed the book, and sat down, having announced the favour and left the vengeance unread. Seventeen chapters later he finishes the sentence. The same voice that opened his ministry by proclaiming the acceptable year now names the day.

The second is that this is grief. Alas for women who are pregnant. The word is ouai, which is sometimes translated woe and is often heard as a threat. It is not a threat here. It is the sound a man makes over something unbearable, and it is aimed at the least culpable people in the city — a woman eight months pregnant, a mother with a baby at the breast, on the day the ladders go up.

So the same paragraph says that the judgment is deserved and that it is agonising. Both. And the one who says the first is weeping while he says it, which we know because Luke has already shown him doing it — riding towards this city with the crowd shouting, and stopping, and crying over it: would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace (19:41–42).

That combination is not a tension to be resolved. It is the character of God, and it is nowhere better displayed than here. He does not judge reluctantly in the sense of judging half-heartedly, and he does not judge coldly. Ezekiel had heard him say it plainly: I have no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezek. 18:32).

Which is the thing to take away, because the question underneath this passage is one people really carry. Does God enjoy this? Is there, somewhere behind the wrath, a satisfaction in the suffering of the guilty and the collateral suffering of the innocent among them?

The answer is standing in the temple court with tears not yet dry, describing a siege forty years off, and grieving in advance for infants not yet conceived. And within the week the wrath he is describing will fall, in its fullness, on him — so that the mothers and the children and every sinner in that city who would turn to him might not have to bear it at all.

There is no vengeance in Scripture that God has not first been willing to absorb himself (cf. Isa. 53:5; Rom. 5:9).

parallels.desc: the days of punishment have come

verseByVerse.quote: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

The first half of the verse is history, and it happened. Sword, captivity, dispersion, and a city under foreign occupation for the next nineteen centuries.

The second half is a clause that has generated more discussion than almost any other sentence in Luke, and it deserves careful handling, because Christians who love the Bible equally read it in different ways.

Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

Start with what every reading agrees on, because it is the main point and it is often lost in the argument. The word is until. Gentile dominion over Jerusalem is real, it is permitted, and it is bounded. God has written an end date into the sentence that describes the trampling. No empire in that city — Roman, Byzantine, Persian, Arab, Crusader, Ottoman, British — has ever held it on any terms but a lease.

Beyond that, readings differ. Many Reformed interpreters take the phrase to mean the age of Gentile ingathering: the period, running from the fall of Jerusalem to the return of Christ, in which the gospel goes to the nations. On this reading the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled when the last of the nations has been gathered in.

Many others, including teachers a good number of readers will have been fed by, such as John MacArthur, understand the phrase as a defined period of Gentile political domination of Jerusalem, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar and ending when God resumes his particular dealings with national Israel. Their instinct is a sound one and it should be said plainly: they are trying to let the word until mean something, and to take seriously that God has not finished with the people to whom he made the promises.

The two readings are closer than the debate suggests, and the reason is Paul. In Romans 11:25 he says that a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in — the same structure, the same until, the same two peoples. Whatever else it establishes, that verse settles the direction: the hardening is temporary, the Gentile season has a term, and God's purposes for Israel are not cancelled but deferred. On that, both readings stand together.

The first reading is the more likely. It fits Luke's own flow, where Acts carries the gospel out to the nations, and Romans 11:25 itself measures the term by the ingathering of the Gentiles, not by who governs a city.

What the verse will not bear is a calendar. It gives a boundary without a date, deliberately, and every attempt to convert it into arithmetic has expired.

And the pastoral force of it is available to a reader who has no view at all on the question. Look at what the sentence does to the trampling. It does not deny it, or explain it away, or promise that it will not hurt. It puts a horizon behind it. The occupying power is standing on ground it does not own, on a clock it did not set, and the word until is God's, not theirs.

That is true of every trampling. There is no oppression in this world that Scripture describes without a terminus (cf. Rom. 11:25–26; Rev. 11:2).

parallels.desc: the nations have come into your inheritance
until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in

verseByVerse.quote: 'And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

The camera pulls back. Up to this point the discourse has been about a city; now it is about the world, and the language changes to match.

Sun, moon, stars, the shaking of the heavens, the roaring sea — every image here is lifted from the prophets, and they used it in a settled way. Isaiah says the stars will not give their light and the sun will be dark at its rising — and he is describing the fall of Babylon (Isa. 13:10). Ezekiel covers the heavens and darkens the stars — over Egypt (Ezek. 32:7). Joel has the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood, which Peter then quotes at Pentecost and applies to that morning (Joel 2:31; Acts 2:20).

So the honest thing to say is that this language, in the Bible's own usage, is the language of God arriving in judgment and of an old order ending — and that it is used both of historical catastrophes and of the last day. Whether the sun will literally go out is not something this passage settles, and a reader should not be told it does. What it plainly announces is that the created order itself will register the coming of its Maker, and that the registering will be terrifying.

Then Luke does something the other two do not. He turns from the sky to the faces.

Distress of nations in perplexity. The word for perplexity is aporia — literally no way through. It is the state of a man who has run out of options, not of ideas.

People fainting with fear and with foreboding. The verb is apopsychō, which is used of a body giving out — the strength simply leaving. And foreboding is prosdokia, expectation: not fear of what is happening, but fear of what is coming. Luke, who was a physician, describes a world in which the anticipation is doing more damage than the event.

Which is worth naming, because it is the commonest form of suffering in a prosperous country. Many people who are perfectly safe today are exhausted by tomorrow. The mortgage that has not yet failed, the scan that has not yet come back, the collapse that has not yet arrived — and the strength going out of the body over a thing that has not happened.

Jesus does not scold this. He describes it, accurately, with medical precision, forty years before the siege and two thousand before the diagnosis. He knows what dread does to a person.

And then, in the very next sentence, he tells his own people what to do with their heads — which is the one thing nobody dreading anything ever thinks to do (cf. Isa. 13:9–10; Joel 2:30–31).
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.

The picture is Daniel 7:13. There the prophet watches in a night vision as one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven, is brought before the Ancient of Days, and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away and shall not be destroyed. It is the one place in the Old Testament where a human figure is brought into the presence of God and given what belongs to God alone, and it is where Jesus got the title he used of himself more than any other.

The cloud is not weather. In the Old Testament the cloud is where God is: the pillar in the wilderness, the cloud that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exod. 40:35), the glory that settled on the temple so that the priests could not stand to minister. To come in a cloud is to come in the visible presence of God.

And they will see. This is the fixed point of the Christian hope and the reason it can never be reduced to an inner experience. He was seen when he was born; he was seen when he was killed; he was seen going up (Acts 1:9, in a cloud); and he will be seen coming back. The gospel is not finally a set of ideas. It is a report about a Man, and the report ends with him visible.

Hold the picture as Daniel drew it. A figure like a son of man, brought before the throne, and every people and nation and language given into his hands — and it is the same figure who is standing in a temple courtyard, tired, days from being flogged, describing what is coming to men who will run away from him before the week is out. The dominion in Daniel's vision was never a reward for a career. It was always going to be handed to a crucified man, because that is who he is.

Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.

Two commands, and they are physical. Straighten up — the word is used of a bent body being made erect, and Luke has used it once before, of the woman bent double for eighteen years who could not stand up straight until Jesus touched her (13:11–13). Raise your heads — lift the chin, which is what nobody under threat ever does. Fear curls a person up. It is the oldest posture there is.

So while the world is fainting at what is coming, the Christian is told to do the opposite of the natural thing with his own body, and told why: because the very events that terrify everyone else are, for him, the sound of the door opening.

Your redemption — apolytrōsis, the price paid to bring a slave out. It is personal, it is possessive, and the verb is present tense: it is drawing near, now, while the shaking is going on.

Is this the Second Coming, or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some read the coming of the Son of Man as his vindication shown in the temple’s fall, since in Daniel 7 he comes to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom. The more likely reading is that here the far horizon breaks through: the signs in sun, moon and stars, the distress of nations, and the redemption drawing near (v. 28) go beyond anything that happened in AD 70. The fall of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) was a foretaste; this is the final return.

The world sees the end of everything. The church sees him (cf. Dan. 7:13–14; Rom. 8:23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–38 — The Fig Tree, the Weight on the Heart, and the Daily Rhythm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable is deliberately ordinary. Trees come into leaf, and everybody knows summer is near; nobody consults an expert about it. Luke adds a phrase the others do not — and all the trees — which quietly rules out reading the fig tree as a coded symbol requiring decipherment. The signs are meant to be legible from your own doorstep. And note what the application says is near: not the end, not the judgment, but the kingdom of God.

Then the most debated sentence in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Taken with v. 24, Luke’s structure is straightforward — the things the disciples asked about in v. 7 all happened within forty years, and v. 24’s interval of Gentile times stands between that and the Son of Man’s appearing. And the ground under everything is v. 33: heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not. The visible is the perishable thing; his speech is not.

Then, after the cosmos, the kitchen. Watch yourselves — not the sky. Three weights are named, running from the obvious to the invisible: dissipation, the heaviness of the morning after; drunkenness, the night that produced it; and the cares of this life. The third is not a sin in the ordinary sense, which is exactly why it is the deadliest. Nobody will ever be rebuked for it.

The verb is physical — weighed down, like a ship low in the water or eyes too heavy to stay open, as the disciples' were on the mountain (9:32). An overloaded heart does not become wicked. It becomes slow. And a trap works on one principle: the animal is looking at something else.

The remedy is not detachment but prayer: stay awake at all times, praying for strength to escape and to stand before the Son of Man. That is the entire practical conclusion of the discourse.

Then Luke closes with a timetable. Teaching in the temple by day, sleeping on Olivet by night, and the people coming early to hear him. The mount that had seen his tears (19:41) would see his agony (22:39), his arrest, and his ascension (Acts 1:12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Watchfulness in the New Testament is not scanning the news for prophetic fulfilment. It is the settled attention of people who know that today is lived under eternity. That is why Jesus ends a discourse about the end of the world with two verbs — stay awake, pray — and no preparations, no place to go, no date.

The phrase at all times rules out the pattern every generation falls into: intense watchfulness when the news is bad, and none when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness; it is nerves.

And to stand before the Son of Man is courtroom language. The Psalms ask it directly: if you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, who could stand (Ps. 130:3)? The answer of this verse is that the strength to stand is not mustered but asked for, and asked of the very one before whom we shall stand. He is not the examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. Jude puts the ground plainly: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
A test for v. 34, and it is uncomfortable because it is easy to run. Count the hours of the last week spent turning over a practical worry — money, a diagnosis, a difficult colleague. Then count the minutes spent thinking about the return of Christ. The ratio is the answer.

None of this is a call to care less about your family or your work. It is a diagnosis: what will finally leave a Christian unready for glory is very unlikely to be a scandal. It will be a diary.

And vv. 37–38 give the pattern for anyone overwhelmed by what is coming — not a technique but a rhythm. This man has just announced the fall of the temple, the arrest of his friends, the shaking of the heavens and his own return in glory, and he knows he will be crucified within the week. What he does with the days that remain is teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again. No frenzy, no last campaign, no scramble to secure the movement. Work in the day, withdraw at night, be found where the people who need you can find you, and do the next ordinary faithful thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.

Three verses, and there is a small phrase in the first that is entirely Luke's and worth noticing: and all the trees. Matthew and Mark have only the fig tree; Luke adds the rest of the orchard.

It is a useful addition, because the fig tree is sometimes read as a coded symbol for the nation of Israel, and a whole system of date-calculation has been built on that reading. The symbolism is not baseless — Hosea 9:10 and Jeremiah 24 do use figs of Israel — but Luke's and all the trees makes it clear that the point here is not botanical symbolism. It is simply that trees come into leaf before summer, and everybody knows it. If the fig tree were a coded reference, adding all the trees would ruin the code.

What Jesus is appealing to, then, is the most ordinary competence a person has. Nobody needs training to know that summer is coming. You do not consult an expert; you look at a branch. The knowledge is immediate, unanxious and available to a child.

And that, he says, is how the signs are meant to work. Not as a cipher for the initiated, but as a season a Christian can read from his own doorstep.

Notice also what the fig tree does not tell you. It gives no date. Nobody has ever looked at a bud and said summer begins on the fourteenth. It tells you the direction of travel and the nearness of the thing, and it refuses to tell you more — which is precisely the amount of information Jesus has been giving all through this chapter, and precisely the amount that produces watchfulness rather than arithmetic.

Then the application, and there is a change in it that is easy to read past. You know that the kingdom of God is near. Not the end is near. Not the judgment. The kingdom.

That is a deliberate word. Everything in this discourse has been dark — armies, betrayal, famine, dread, a city under sentence — and the thing all of it announces is the reign of God arriving in its fullness. The signs are not the symptoms of a world dying. They are the leaves on the branch.

Which supplies a test worth running on your own reaction to the news. When you read of the world convulsing, is the emotion dread or expectancy? Both are possible responses to the same headline, and the difference between them is not temperament. It is whether you believe the thing on the far side of the shaking is a ruin or a King.

Winter is not the last season. It has never once been the last season (cf. Song 2:11–12; Rom. 13:11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This generation — if taken naturally, it refers to the generation alive at Jesus's speaking, and much of what he describes (the siege of Jerusalem, the dispersion) was indeed fulfilled within forty years. But the grounding claim is the permanence of his word: heaven and earth, which seem so solid, are actually the perishable things. Jesus's words are the imperishable ones. It is one of the most audacious claims Jesus ever made — ranking his own words above the visible cosmos. The one who speaks this is either deluded or divine.

But the phrase deserves more than that guarded much of what he describes, because the part it leaves out is the part sceptics press. Jesus has just spoken of the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory (v. 27), and then says this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. If all includes the return, the objection writes itself: that generation did pass away, and he did not come. It is the standard charge that Jesus was a failed apocalyptic prophet, and it should be answered rather than stepped around.

The answer, in Luke, is sitting eight verses earlier, and it is Luke's own contribution to this puzzle. Where Matthew and Mark keep the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the age tightly braided, Luke pulls them apart and names the gap: Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (v. 24). That clause is an interval of unspecified length, written into the discourse by Jesus himself, standing between the city's fall and the Son of Man's appearing.

Luke's structure therefore reads straightforwardly. The all that must take place is what the disciples actually asked about in v. 7 — the stones thrown down, the siege, the armies, the captivity — and every one of them happened inside forty years, exactly as he said. Then comes an age of unknown duration in which the gospel goes to the nations. Then the end. Jesus was not mistaken by a single day; the reader who takes v. 24 seriously will never feel the force of the objection in the first place.

Which also disposes of the opposite error, and it is the commoner one in our own time. Because v. 24 sets a limit on Gentile dominion, and v. 32 attaches a generation to the fulfilment, people have repeatedly bolted the two together to calculate a date — a political event in Jerusalem is declared the fulfilment of the times of the Gentiles, a generation is priced at forty years, and the arithmetic is published.

Did Jesus promise to return within that generation? Some take this generation to mean the Jewish people, who will last until the end, or the generation alive when the final signs appear. But elsewhere in Luke it means Jesus’ contemporaries (7:31; 11:29–32). The more likely reading is that all refers to the things Jesus has said would come before the end, culminating in Jerusalem’s fall, which that generation saw. The day of the final coming itself no one knows (Mark 13:32).

Every such attempt so far has expired quietly, and it was doomed before it began. Luke does not even record the saying about the day and the hour that Matthew and Mark preserve at this point in the discourse; what he gives instead is an ending that is a command rather than a calculation — stay awake at all times, praying (v. 36) — and then, in his second volume, the risen Christ declining the question outright when the apostles put it to him one last time: it is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7). A man who has worked out the date does not need to stay awake. That is precisely why we are not given it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.

After the cosmos, the kitchen. The whole discourse has been building through wars and sieges and the shaking of the heavens, and now Jesus names the three things that will actually cost his disciples their readiness, and not one of them is on the news.

Watch yourselves. Not the sky. Not the headlines. Yourselves.

Three weights are named, and the order matters because it runs from the obvious to the invisible. Dissipation is kraipalē, an old medical word for the heaviness in the head the morning after — the hangover, precisely. Drunkenness is the night before that produced it. Both are the sins a congregation expects to hear about, and both are named in about four words.

Then the third: the cares of this life — daily living, not the great questions but the small ones. Bills, rotas, the boiler, the appointment, the form that has to go back by Friday.

And that one is not a sin at all in the ordinary sense. That is what makes it the deadliest item on the list. Nobody will ever be rebuked for it. No elder will visit. It does not show. A man can be entirely sober, faithful to his wife, honest in business, in church every Sunday, and be so comprehensively occupied with things that will not exist in a hundred years that the return of Jesus Christ is, in practice, no part of how he thinks about Thursday.

The verb is precise and physical: weighed down. Think of a ship low in the water, or of eyes too heavy to stay open — as Peter and those with him were heavy with sleep on the mountain while Jesus prayed (9:32). Notice what happens to a heart with too much on it. It does not become wicked. It becomes slow.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable because it is easy to run. Think back over the last week and count the hours you spent turning over a practical worry — the money, the diagnosis, the difficult person at work. Now count the minutes you spent thinking about the return of Christ. The ratio is your answer, and almost nobody likes it.

Then the image: like a trap. A snare works on exactly one principle. It is not that the animal is stupid; it is that the animal is looking at something else. It is head-down, occupied, entirely absorbed in a perfectly reasonable activity — and that is when the cord closes.

None of this is a call to care less about your family or your work. The remedy is in the next verse and it is not detachment; it is prayer. But the diagnosis has to be heard first, and it is this: what will finally make a Christian unready for glory is very unlikely to be a scandal. It will be a diary (cf. Luke 8:14; 1 Pet. 5:8).

parallels.desc: like a thief in the night

verseByVerse.quote: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.

This is the conclusion of the entire discourse. Everything — the falling stones, the wars, the arrests, the trampled city, the shaken heavens — funnels into one sentence with two verbs in it: stay awake, and pray.

It is worth registering how little else there is. No preparations to make, no place to go, no list of signs to monitor, no date to mark. The Lord who has just described the end of the world tells his followers to remain alert and to talk to God about it. That is the whole programme.

At all times is not decoration. It rules out the thing every generation of Christians does instead, which is to become intensely watchful when the news is bad and forget entirely when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness; it is nerves.

Now the crux, because there is one here and readers deserve it dealt with straight. Strength to escape all these things. Many Christians have been taught to hear in that phrase the promise of a removal — that the church will be taken out before the worst arrives. Others read the escape as coming safely through rather than being spared. The people who hold these views are not careless readers; they are trying to give full weight to the word escape, which is a real word and does mean escape.

What the verse itself supplies is this. The escape is asked for in prayer, not announced as automatic; it is coupled with strength, which is language for endurance rather than absence; and it is paired with a second outcome, to stand before the Son of Man, which is plainly the final scene and not an earlier one. Whatever a reader concludes about the timing, the verse gives him something to do about it, and what it gives him is prayer.

And the second half is where the weight really falls, because to stand is legal language. It is what a man does when the case is called and his name is read. The Psalms ask the question directly: if you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, who could stand (Ps. 130:3)?

Which raises the fear that this verse leaves in many sincere hearts. Will I be able to stand? Have I watched enough, prayed enough, endured enough?

Read the verse again and see where the strength comes from. It is not mustered; it is asked for. The prayer is not that we might be strong but that we might have strength given, and the one being asked is the one before whom we shall stand. He is not the examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. He is the one supplying the answer to his own examination.

Is strength to escape a promise of rapture before the tribulation? The more likely reading is that it means being kept faithful through what is coming, so as to stand before the Son of Man at the end, not being removed beforehand. Jesus has just said his followers will be persecuted and some put to death (vv. 12–16), and promised that by their endurance they will gain their lives (v. 19).

No one has ever stood before the Son of Man on his own record. Jude ends his letter with the only ground there is: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). The standing is his doing (cf. Ps. 130:3–4; Jude 24).

verseByVerse.quote: And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

Luke ends the greatest prophetic discourse in his Gospel with a timetable, and it is one of the most quietly astonishing paragraphs in the book.

Consider what has just been said, and by whom. This man has announced the destruction of the temple he is standing in, the siege of the city he is standing in, the arrest and death of the friends standing next to him, the shaking of the heavens, and his own return in the glory of God. He knows, to the day, that within a week he will be flogged, mocked and crucified. He knows which of the men around him will betray him and which will deny him.

And what he does with the days that remain is: teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again.

There is no frenzy in him. No last campaign, no attempt to gather a following while there is time, no scramble to write things down or secure the movement. He teaches, which is what he had been doing for three years, and he is available to whoever turns up — and Luke says all the people came, early, to hear him. On the last ordinary mornings of his life the crowds were still getting up before dawn and he was still there.

He had said it himself: foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (9:58). In the last week of his life it was still true, and the mountain he slept on was the one he had wept over the city from (19:41), the one where his sweat would fall like drops of blood on Thursday (22:39, 44), the one where the arrest would happen, and the one from which he would ascend (Acts 1:12).

Here, then, is the pattern for anyone who has ever been overwhelmed by what is coming. Not a technique — a rhythm. Work in the day. Withdraw at night. Be found in the morning where the people who need you can find you. Do the next ordinary faithful thing. That is what perfect knowledge of a terrible future looked like when it was worked out in an actual week by an actual man.

And it looked like peace. Not the peace of someone who does not know what is coming, but of someone who knows exactly and is not afraid of it, because the Father who holds the whole of it is his Father and has never once been late.

He is teaching in the temple he has just condemned, sleeping on the hill where he will be arrested, and there is no tremor in him anywhere. That is the Lord of the Olivet Discourse. He did not merely predict the shaking of heaven and earth; he slept under those heavens, on that earth, days before the worst of it fell on him, and rose early to teach whoever came.
verseByVerse.note: Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside it.

parallels.desc: as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives

21.text: <sup>1</sup> Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box, <sup>2</sup> and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. <sup>3</sup> And he said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. <sup>4</sup> For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.” <sup>5</sup> And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said, <sup>6</sup> “As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>7</sup> And they asked him, “Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?” <sup>8</sup> And he said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them. <sup>9</sup> And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.” <sup>10</sup> Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. <sup>11</sup> There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven. <sup>12</sup> But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. <sup>13</sup> This will be your opportunity to bear witness. <sup>14</sup> Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, <sup>15</sup> for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. <sup>16</sup> You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. <sup>17</sup> You will be hated by all for my name's sake. <sup>18</sup> But not a hair of your head will perish. <sup>19</sup> By your endurance you will gain your lives. <sup>20</sup> “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. <sup>21</sup> Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it, <sup>22</sup> for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. <sup>23</sup> Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. <sup>24</sup> They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. <sup>25</sup> “And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, <sup>26</sup> people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>27</sup> And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. <sup>28</sup> Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” <sup>29</sup> And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. <sup>30</sup> As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. <sup>31</sup> So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. <sup>32</sup> Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. <sup>33</sup> Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>34</sup> “But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. <sup>35</sup> For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. <sup>36</sup> But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.” <sup>37</sup> And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. <sup>38</sup> And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

22.title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and the Arrest
22.overview:
Luke 22 covers the most theologically concentrated night in human history. It begins with Judas's betrayal agreement and the preparation of the Passover meal, moves through the institution of the Lord's Supper, includes a remarkable dispute among the disciples about greatness, records Jesus's prediction of Peter's denial and his commissioning of Peter to strengthen the brothers, narrates the agony in Gethsemane, and ends with the arrest, Peter's denial, and Jesus before the Sanhedrin.

Luke's account of the Last Supper has several distinctive features: he records two cups (v. 17 and v. 20), emphasises the kingdom dimension of the meal (“I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”), and includes the unique account of the disciples' dispute about greatness followed immediately by Jesus's teaching about servant leadership. The contrast between the disciples' argument about rank and Jesus washing their feet (in John) — and more immediately, serving them with his body and blood — could not be sharper.

The Gethsemane account in Luke is distinctive for the appearance of an angel strengthening Jesus (v. 43) and for the detail that “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (v. 44) — a possible description of hematidrosis, a rare condition in which extreme distress causes capillaries to rupture into the sweat glands. Luke the physician may be noting what he understood as a medical phenomenon of extreme psychological anguish. The cup Jesus prays about is not merely the physical suffering of crucifixion but the cup of God's wrath that he will drink on behalf of sinners.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Conspiracy, Preparation, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke lays two sentences on top of each other and makes the reader hold both. The Passover — the feast of the lamb whose blood turned the destroyer aside in Egypt — draws near; and in that week the chief priests are looking for a way to kill the Lamb of God. Their reasoning is entirely practical: they feared the people. A crowd-control problem, being managed during a busy festival, by men who had no idea what they were aiming at and hit it exactly.

Then the most disturbing sentence in the chapter: Satan entered into Judas — who was of the number of the twelve. Luke offers no psychology. But his next sentence makes the responsibility plain: Judas went, conferred, agreed a figure, consented, and began looking for a moment without a crowd. Every verb is his. Matthew gives the price, and it is the compensation the law set for a slave killed by an ox, and the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah.

The preparation is handled the way the colt was handled in chapter 19 — two disciples sent, a sign described in advance, everything found just as he said. A man carrying a water jar would stand out in that crowd, since water-carrying was women's work. Whether Jesus had arranged it quietly or knew it prophetically, the effect is the same: nothing about this night is happening to him.

At the table he says he has earnestly desired this meal, and then looks past his suffering to a Passover still owing in the kingdom of God. He takes the Passover cup and the unleavened bread, both of them fifteen centuries old, and fills them with himself: this is my body, which is given for you; this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. Jeremiah's promise, unfulfilled for six hundred years, is claimed at a supper table.

And then, only after the bread and the cup have been handed round, the betrayer is named — his hand on the same table. The Son of Man goes as it has been determined, and woe to the man by whom he is betrayed. Both, in one breath, unreconciled.

The disciples begin questioning one another, and not one of them looks at Judas.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper is memorial, proclamation and anticipation at once. Memorial: do this in remembrance of me — remembrance of the kind Passover itself was, never bare recollection but an act that brought a past deliverance into the present of the people keeping it (cf. Exod. 12:14). Proclamation: you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Cor. 11:26). Anticipation: he will not eat or drink it again until the kingdom of God comes, so every communion table is an unfinished meal.

Four views are held on what happens at that table. Rome teaches transubstantiation — the substance becomes the body and blood while the appearances remain. Luther held the body is present in, with and under the elements. Zwingli held the elements purely symbolic, the Supper a remembrance and a pledge. The Reformed position, with Calvin and the Westminster standards, is that the bread remains bread and Christ is nonetheless truly given: by his Spirit the believer really feeds on Christ, not with the teeth but by faith. The strongest argument for it is that his body was in front of them, unbroken, when he said the words — and he habitually spoke this way: I am the door, I am the vine.

Note the two words in both sayings: for you — on behalf of, in the place of. Substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before he was substituted.

And vv. 21–22 set divine determination and human guilt side by side without reconciling them. This is the settled pattern of Scripture — Joseph's you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, and Peter's delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 3 frightens some believers, who wonder whether they could be handed over like Judas. The fear is itself the answer. Judas is never recorded as afraid of what he was becoming; he was calm, he negotiated, he ate the supper, he came with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at the thought of betraying Christ is not being handed over — it is being held. And the man in this chapter who did deny his Lord out loud, three times, was being prayed for while he did it.

Verses 4–6 supply a test that needs no theological training. Every part of that transaction required the absence of a crowd. Is there any part of what you are arranging that has been arranged so that it happens where you will not be seen?

Verse 20 answers the fear that keeps some believers away from the table — that they are not good enough to come. The cup does not commemorate anyone's fitness. It was poured out for a table that contained a traitor, a denier, and ten men who would run before morning.

And v. 23 is quietly searching. When a sin is named from a pulpit, notice who comes to mind first. The eleven looked inward before they looked around, and they were right to. When Judas asked it, he already knew the answer (Matt. 26:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.

Two sentences, and Luke has laid one on top of the other so that you cannot read the second without the first.

Passover was the feast of the lamb. Every family in Israel that could afford one brought a year-old male without blemish to the temple, and on the fourteenth of the month, between the afternoon and the evening, it was killed. Josephus, who had reason to know, reckoned the number slaughtered in a single Passover in the hundreds of thousands. The city smelled of it. And the whole ritual existed to keep one night alive in the national memory: the night in Egypt when the blood went on the doorposts and the destroyer passed over the houses that had it.

That is the week the chief priests choose to kill the Lamb of God.

They do not know that is what they are doing. That is the point of putting the two sentences together. They think they are managing a political problem, and their reasoning is entirely practical — they feared the people. Not God. The people. The whole calculation is about crowd control during a festival week when the city's population multiplied several times over and Rome was watching.

Notice how small it is. The men entrusted with the worship of Israel are conspiring against the salvation of Israel, and the thing governing their deliberations is a public-order risk assessment.

And behind them, unseen by any of them, a purpose is running to time. Peter would say it publicly seven weeks later: this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Both halves of that sentence are true at once. Their scheming was genuinely theirs, freely chosen and fully culpable — and it was the appointed means by which the Lamb was brought to the appointed feast on the appointed day.

This is worth holding on to when your own circumstances look like they are being decided by people with small motives. Very often they are. A department is restructured because someone wanted a title. A church divides because two men could not back down. The motives are as petty as they look, and naming them honestly is not cynicism.

But the reach of those motives is not what it appears. The chief priests set the date of Jesus's death for reasons of crowd management, and the date they set was the day the lambs died, which was the day the Scriptures had been pointing at for fifteen hundred years. They chose freely and they hit the target exactly, and they had no idea they were aiming (cf. Exod. 12:5–7; Acts 2:23).
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; the two names were used together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve.

Luke says it without preamble and without explanation, and it is the most disturbing sentence in the chapter.

He does not tell us why Judas did it. The other Gospels give hints — John says he was a thief and helped himself to the money bag (John 12:6) — and preachers have supplied a hundred theories about disappointed political hopes. Luke supplies none of them. He names a spiritual event: the enemy of God entered a man who had been walking beside Jesus for three years.

And then he adds the clause that makes it unbearable: who was of the number of the twelve. Not a hanger-on. Not a stranger. One of the twelve, chosen after a night of prayer (6:12–16), sent out with authority to preach and to heal (9:1–2), who had come back and told Jesus all they had done (9:10). Whatever else this verse teaches, it teaches that proximity to Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.

Now the question that has to be faced, because a reader will not get past it otherwise: if Satan entered him, was Judas responsible?

Luke's own next sentence answers it. Satan entered him, and then he went away and conferred — he walked to the meeting, he opened the negotiation, he named his terms, he took the money. Every verb belongs to Judas. Scripture never once treats him as a man who was overpowered. Jesus calls the betrayal a woe upon the man who commits it (v. 22), which would be monstrous if the man were a puppet.

The plainest way to put it is this. Satan does not manufacture desires in a man that were not there. He finds them, feeds them and hands the man the opportunity. What entered Judas found a door already unlocked, and Judas had been the one turning the key, quietly, for a long time — a coin here, a resentment there, a growing private conviction that he understood things better than his master did.

Which brings the verse to where a Christian reader most needs it, because some who read it are frightened by it. There are believers who wonder whether they might be a Judas — whether they could be taken over like that, whether the sin they cannot shake is the beginning of it.

The fear itself is the answer, and it should be said plainly. Judas is never once recorded as being afraid of what he was becoming. He was calm; he negotiated; he ate the supper; he came to the garden with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at the thought of betraying Christ is not a conscience being handed over — it is a conscience being held. And the man in this very chapter who did deny his Lord, out loud, three times, was being prayed for while he did it (v. 32), and was fully restored.

Judas went out to a meeting. Peter went out and wept. The difference between them is not the size of the sin (cf. John 13:2; 2 Cor. 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.

Read it slowly, because Luke has written it as a sequence of ordinary business, and the flatness is deliberate.

He went. He conferred. They were glad. They agreed a figure. He consented. He began looking for a window.

There is no drama anywhere in it. No struggle recorded, no hesitation, no dark night of the soul. It reads like the minutes of a meeting, which is exactly what it was, and that is far more frightening than if Luke had given us a scene of tormented decision. The worst thing ever done by a human being was arranged administratively.

The officers are the temple police — the Levitical guard who kept order in the precincts and could make an arrest. So the negotiation is not a conspiracy of shadowy figures; it is a meeting between the religious executive and the head of security, with an informant, about an operational difficulty.

And they were glad. Luke will not let that pass. These are the men who had been unable to touch Jesus because of the crowds, and now the solution has walked in the door by itself, wearing the face of one of his own friends. Their gladness is a small and squalid emotion, and it is recorded so that we can see what the leadership of Israel had become: relieved, at a problem solved.

Matthew tells us the figure — thirty pieces of silver (Matt. 26:15), which is not an arbitrary sum. It is the compensation set in the law of Moses for a slave gored by an ox (Exod. 21:32), and it is the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah's strange prophecy, the money God calls the lordly price at which I was priced by them (Zech. 11:12–13). That is the valuation placed on the Son of God by the guardians of his own house: the going rate for a dead slave.

And then the last phrase, which is the tell: in the absence of a crowd. Both parties want the same thing — darkness. The priests want it because their power cannot survive daylight, and Judas wants it because betrayal cannot be done in front of witnesses.

Sin has a settled preference and this is it. Not one thing in this transaction could have been done at noon in the temple court. That is worth turning on yourself, because it is one of the few tests of conduct that is genuinely reliable and takes no theological training to apply: is there any part of this I am arranging so that it happens where I will not be seen?

Whatever needs the absence of a crowd usually needs it for a reason (cf. John 3:20; Eph. 5:11–13).
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the captains of the temple police. Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, 'Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.

Three words in the first sentence carry more weight than they seem to: had to be. The Greek is edei, from dei — it was necessary, it must. Luke uses this word all through his Gospel for the fixed purposes of God. The Son of Man must suffer many things (9:22). It was necessary that the Christ should suffer and enter into his glory (24:26). Here it is used of the lamb.

Luke almost certainly means only that the law required it on that day, and that is the plain sense. But he has chosen the word he uses for divine necessity, and he has used it about a lamb being killed, on the day the true Lamb would be killed, in a chapter about a death he keeps calling determined. Luke does not do this by accident.

Then the practical arrangement, and there is a tenderness in it worth noticing. Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.

Peter and John are sent — the two who will be at the centre of everything that follows in Luke's second volume, standing together in the temple in Acts 3, before the Sanhedrin in Acts 4, sent to Samaria in Acts 8. Their partnership begins here, running an errand.

And what an errand it is.
