Preparing a Passover meant work: securing the room, buying the lamb, taking it to the temple court to be killed in the afternoon rush, catching the blood, carrying the carcass back, roasting it whole on a pomegranate spit, buying and grinding the bitter herbs, mixing the fruit paste, arranging the unleavened bread and the wine. It was a whole afternoon of ordinary labour, and Jesus asked his two closest friends to do it on the last day of his life.

He could have dispensed with it. He knew what the evening was. He knew what the following afternoon was. A man with hours to live might reasonably conclude that the details of a meal no longer mattered.

Instead the last day proceeds like the others, with an errand given and jobs to do, and two men walking into the city with a list. There is a whole doctrine of vocation sitting in that, and it will comfort anyone who has ever felt that their own tasks are too small to be part of anything. Peter and John spent the afternoon before the Lord's Supper buying groceries.

Was this a Passover meal? Luke, with Matthew and Mark, says so plainly. John seems to put the Passover a day later (John 18:28; 19:14). The more likely explanation is that John’s “Passover” there means the meals of the festival week, and “Preparation” the Friday before the Sabbath of Passover week. The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus is the true Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7).

That we may eat it. Not that you may eat it. He includes himself in the meal he is about to become, and he is looking forward to it — as the next paragraph will say outright (cf. Exod. 12:6; Luke 9:22).
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, 'Where will you have us prepare it?' He said to them, 'Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him, Where will you have us prepare it? He said to them, Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters.

Their question is entirely reasonable and slightly anxious. Jerusalem at Passover was overwhelmed. Estimates of the festival population run from a hundred thousand to several times that, in a city normally holding perhaps forty thousand. Rooms were impossible. Custom held that no householder in Jerusalem could charge for Passover lodging, which meant that space went early and went to the connected. Two Galileans arriving on the afternoon of the fourteenth with no arrangement would have been in serious difficulty.

So: where.

And the answer is a sign that will pick itself out of a crowd of thousands. A man carrying a jar of water will meet you.

Water-carrying was women's work. It was done in the morning and the evening, by the women of the household, and the sight of a man with a water jar on his shoulder in that city would have been as conspicuous as it is now for someone to walk down a street carrying a stepladder. Men carried wineskins. Women carried water jars. In a crowd of tens of thousands, one man with a jar is findable.

Which raises the question every reader asks here, and it is worth answering rather than leaving as atmosphere. Had Jesus arranged this beforehand, or did he know it prophetically?

Luke does not say, and both are entirely possible. The parallel is the colt in 19:29–34, where the same pattern occurs — two disciples sent, a specific sign described, a password given, and everything found exactly as told. Jesus may well have made quiet arrangements; a man who knew the city was full of people wanting to arrest him had good reason to keep the location of his last evening out of Judas's hands until the last possible hour, and that in itself explains the code.

What Luke is certainly saying is the thing both explanations agree on. Nothing about this night is happening to Jesus. He is arranging it.

That matters enormously for how the next twenty-four hours are read. Everything from here to the tomb will look like a man being carried along by other people's decisions — arrested, tried, condemned, executed. Luke opens the sequence by showing you a man who knows what a stranger will be carrying on his shoulder tomorrow afternoon.

He is not being taken. He is going (cf. John 10:18; Luke 19:29–34).
verseByVerse.note: Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And tell the master of the house, The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.

The message is a phrase, not an explanation: the Teacher says to you. No name is given. Whoever this householder was, he needed only that much, which tells you the arrangement was already understood between them, and that there was at least one man in Jerusalem that week who counted it an honour to be trusted with something and asked no further questions.

He is never named. He appears for one sentence in the history of the world and disappears, and the room he lent has been remembered for two thousand years.

A large upper room furnished. Furnished — spread, laid out: carpets down, the low couches arranged around three sides of the table in the Roman fashion, cushions in place. The room was ready. Somebody had already done the work.

So consider what this unnamed man gave, and what came of it. A room. Not a sermon, not a miracle, not a martyrdom. A furnished upper room, put at somebody's disposal for an evening — and in that room the Lord's Supper was instituted, the meal the church has kept in every century and on every continent since. It is not a large thing to lend a room. It was the room.

Which is the encouragement for every believer whose contribution to the kingdom is logistical. Someone opens the building. Someone sets out the chairs. Someone drives the elderly member who cannot get there otherwise. None of it preaches, and none of it will be mentioned. The householder of the upper room had no idea what he was providing space for, and that is the ordinary condition of Christian service: you are almost never told what your small provision is for.

Where I may eat the Passover with my disciples. The last thing to notice is the possessive. On the eve of the night when every one of them will fail him — one betraying, one denying, the rest scattering — he calls them my disciples.

He knows exactly what they are going to do. He has already told Peter what he will do. And the room is booked for them, the meal is being prepared for them, and they are still his (cf. John 13:1; Luke 19:30–34).
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

A single short sentence, and Luke uses the same construction he used of the colt: they went, and found it just as he had told them (19:32). He is building a pattern in his reader's mind on purpose, and the pattern is about to be tested to destruction.

Because what has been said so far is easy to trust. A room, a signal, a stranger with a jar — the words of Jesus proved reliable in a small domestic matter, and two men walked back up the hill with the meal ready and the details confirmed.

Within hours the same two men will hear him say things that are impossible to receive. That one of them will betray him. That Peter will deny him before dawn. That he himself will be numbered with criminals. And by the following afternoon they will be looking at a body.

Luke puts just as he had told them here, at the start of the night, because it is the last easy verification any of them will get. Everything afterwards has to be believed in the dark.

That is not a small point of technique; it is the ordinary shape of a Christian life. There is usually a stretch early on where the promises are checkable — a prayer answered plainly, a provision arriving at the right hour, a door opening exactly as you had asked. And then a season comes in which nothing is confirmable at all, and the only thing you have is that the same voice was accurate before.

Here is the test, and it can be run today. Think of one thing God has actually done for you that you could not have arranged — the sort of thing you have told other people about. Now consider what it would mean if the person who did that is the same person who has said nothing at all about the situation you are currently in. It does not make the silence pleasant. It makes it survivable, because the silence of a proven friend is a different thing from the silence of a stranger.

And notice the last clause, which is where the disciples' part actually lies: and they prepared the Passover. He told them where. They did the work. Foreknowledge in this Gospel never once replaces obedience; it directs it.

They found it as he said, and then they went and roasted a lamb — not knowing that they were laying a table for the end of the world's long night (cf. Luke 19:32; John 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.

Fourteen words, and one of them is loaded.

The hour. In one sense it simply means the appointed time for the Passover meal, which began after sunset. But this is the Gospel in which Jesus has been walking towards something with his face set (9:51), and it is the chapter in which he will say to the arresting party, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (v. 53). John's Gospel makes the theme explicit — his hour had not yet come, his hour had not yet come, and then at last it had. Luke says it more quietly. The hour came, and he sat down to dinner.

He reclined at table. This is worth picturing correctly, because most people carry a painting in their heads instead. They were not sitting upright on chairs behind a long table. They were lying on their left sides on low couches arranged around three sides of a low table, propped on the left elbow, feet away from the food, eating with the right hand. It is why John could be leaning back against Jesus (John 13:23), and why a person could reach the feet of a guest without crawling under anything.

Reclining had its own meaning. Free men reclined; slaves stood and served. At the Passover in particular, the posture was deliberate: you eat this meal lying down, at ease, because you are no longer slaves in Egypt. The whole night was a rehearsal of freedom.

So look at the tableau Luke has framed. The hour has come — the hour he has been moving towards since the first page — and what he does with it is lie down among his friends in the posture of a free man at a feast of deliverance, on the last evening of his life, with the man who has already sold him lying somewhere along the same table.

And the apostles with him. All of them. Luke has told us in v. 3 what one of them has done, and he places him here without comment, reclining with the rest.

There is no scene in the Gospels of Jesus being unable to eat. He is going to be flogged before this time tomorrow, and he is at table, at peace, keeping the feast. Whatever composure is, this is what it looks like when it is real: not the absence of dread — the garden will show you the dread — but the refusal to let dread eat the hours that are still good (cf. John 13:1; Ps. 23:5).
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.

The English is polite. The Greek is not.

Epithumia epethumēsa — literally with desire I have desired. It is a Hebrew way of speaking that doubles the word to intensify it, the same construction used in the Greek Old Testament for the strongest longings recorded there. Laban, accusing Jacob after his flight: you longed greatly for your father's house (Gen. 31:30). It is the language of aching for something.

And the object of the longing is this: an evening with eleven ordinary men and one traitor, in a borrowed room, eating roast lamb.

Stop there before moving on, because the sentence is easy to admire and hard to take personally. He is not saying he was resigned to the meal. He is not saying he was glad of some company on a hard night. He is saying he had ached for it — that of everything available to the Son of God in the last hours of his earthly life, the thing he had set his heart on was being at a table with them.

These are the men who will, before morning, argue about rank, fall asleep on him twice, draw a sword he did not want, deny him and run. He knows all of it. The longing is not based on a misreading of their quality.

Then, immediately, the shadow: before I suffer. The word is pathein, and it is the same root as the church's old name for these events, the Passion. He is not merely aware that suffering is coming. He is dating the meal by it.

And then, having named the suffering, he looks straight past it: I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.

That is a startling thing to say at that table. It assumes there is a far side. It treats the cross not as the end of the story but as the passage through which the story reaches its own feast — the wedding supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9), the mountain feast of rich food that Isaiah saw, where the covering that is cast over all peoples is swallowed up and God wipes away tears from all faces (Isa. 25:6–8).

So every communion table since has faced two ways. It looks back to a death, and it is also, on his own word, an unfinished meal. He said he would not eat it again until then — which means there is a Passover still owing, and he intends to be at it (cf. Isa. 25:6–8; Rev. 19:9).

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, 'Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.

Readers sometimes stumble here because Luke has a cup before the bread, and then another cup after it (v. 20), and it looks like a muddle or a duplication.

It is neither, once you know the shape of the meal. The Passover was structured around four cups, spaced through the liturgy, each with its own place: the cup of sanctification at the opening, the cup of deliverance after the telling of the Exodus story, the cup of blessing after the meal, and the cup of praise at the end with the singing of the psalms. Luke, writing for people who may never have seen a Passover, simply records what happened in order. The cup here belongs to the earlier part of the evening. The cup in v. 20 is the one after supper — almost certainly the cup of blessing, the third.

Which means Jesus did not invent a new ceremony out of nothing. He took a cup that already had fifteen centuries of meaning attached to it and filled it with himself.

Take this, and divide it among yourselves. There is a small thing here that the church has argued over and that is worth saying plainly: he did not drink it and pass it, he gave it to be shared out. The Supper is corporate at its root. Nobody at that table received it alone.

Then the vow: from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.

He is fasting. Having said in the previous breath how deeply he had longed for this meal, he now announces that he is setting the cup down and will not lift it again until the kingdom has come. And in fact the next thing offered to him to drink will be sour wine, held up by mocking soldiers at the cross (23:36).

The abstinence is not asceticism. It is the vow of a man with unfinished business. He will not sit down to the feast until his people can sit down with him, and there is a death between here and there.

So the cup he pushes away at this table is the measure of the cup he accepts in the garden. He declines the wine of the feast in order to drink the cup of wrath, and he does it so that when the kingdom comes there will be somebody there to drink with.

The King fasts, so that his people may eat (cf. Matt. 26:29; Rev. 19:9).
verseByVerse.note: The Passover meal included several cups of wine; Luke mentions a cup before the bread and another after supper.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.

At this point in the Passover the host lifted the unleavened bread and said the ancient words: this is the bread of affliction which our fathers ate in the land of Egypt. Every man at that table had heard them every year of his life and knew what came next.

Jesus says something else. This is my body.

Four words that have divided the church for five hundred years, so let them be handled honestly, because the reader is entitled to know what the argument is about and which view is taken here.

Rome teaches transubstantiation: at the priest's word the substance of the bread becomes the actual body of Christ, though every observable property of bread remains. Luther rejected that but insisted the body is genuinely present in, with and under the bread. Others, following Zwingli, hold that the bread simply signifies the body and the Supper is a memorial and a pledge. The Reformed position, held here with Calvin and the Westminster divines, is that the bread remains bread and Christ is truly given — that by his Spirit the believer really does feed on Christ, not with the teeth but by faith, so that the Supper is neither a re-sacrifice nor a bare reminder but a real communion with a living Saviour.

The plainest argument for that reading is standing at the table holding the loaf. His body was in front of them, unbroken, when he said it — which settles what kind of sentence it is. He spoke as he always spoke: I am the door, I am the vine, I am the good shepherd.

Then given for you. The preposition is hyper: on behalf of, in the place of. Not merely for your benefit, but in your stead. This is substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before, in the plainest words he ever used about his own death.

And then a command, and it is a rite he instituted himself: do this in remembrance of me. The word is anamnēsis, and in the Old Testament it is never a private effort of memory. It is a public act that brings the past event into the present of the people doing it. The Passover was not a history lesson; each generation ate it as though it had come out of Egypt itself.

So he takes the oldest memorial of the covenant, puts himself where the lamb had been, and hands it to men who have not the faintest idea yet what they are holding — and the church has been holding it ever since. He broke it before anyone broke him. He gave it before anyone took him. Nothing about that night was extracted from him (cf. 1 Cor. 11:23–26; John 6:53–56).

verseByVerse.quote: And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, 'This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

For a table of Jewish men, the word blood in connection with a cup was not merely solemn. It was very close to unthinkable. The law forbade the consumption of blood absolutely, on the ground that the life is in the blood and God had given it for atonement on the altar (Lev. 17:11–14). Blood belonged on the altar, not in the mouth.

Which is exactly why the words work. He is not inviting them to drink blood; he is telling them what the cup means, and the meaning is atonement.

The new covenant. This is a quotation, and every man there would have caught it. Jeremiah, six centuries earlier, in the ruin of everything: behold, the days are coming when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel — not like the covenant I made with their fathers, which they broke. This one will be different in three ways. The law will be written on the heart rather than on stone. Every member will know God personally, from the least to the greatest. And the ground of it will be forgiveness: I will remember their sin no more (Jer. 31:31–34).

That promise had stood unfulfilled for six hundred years. Israel had come home from exile, rebuilt the temple, resumed the sacrifices — and no one had seen a new covenant. Now a man at a supper table lifts a cup and says: here it is, and it is in my blood.

Every covenant in Scripture is ratified with blood. Noah's with sacrifice, Abraham's with divided animals, Sinai's with Moses throwing blood on the people and saying behold the blood of the covenant (Exod. 24:8). The pattern never varies, because a covenant is a bond made at the cost of life. What is new here is not the mechanism but the victim. God is not asking for a bull.

Poured out for you. Hours in advance, and the same for you as the bread: in your place.

This is the answer, incidentally, to the fear that keeps some believers from the table — that they are not good enough to come. The cup does not commemorate their fitness. It commemorates the death that made them fit, and it is offered by the one who was pouring it out for a table that included a traitor, a denier and ten men who would run.

Some ESV readers will see a note that a few manuscripts omit the rest of v. 19 and v. 20. The longer text has overwhelming support, and the same words are found independently in Paul (1 Cor 11:23–25) and in Matthew and Mark. No doctrine rests on Luke’s wording alone.

Who may come to the Lord’s Table? Those who belong to Christ: baptized believers who trust him and are willing to turn from sin. Paul tells each to examine himself and then eat (1 Cor 11:28). It is not a reward for being good enough; it is for sinners who need Christ. But it is not for unbelievers, nor for those living in unrepentant sin under the church’s discipline.

The law said the life is in the blood and the blood is given to make atonement. He said: here is mine, and now it is yours (cf. Jer. 31:31–34; Heb. 9:22).

verseByVerse.quote: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!

Note where Luke has put this. Matthew and Mark have the announcement of the betrayal before the bread and the cup. Luke puts it after. The order is almost certainly deliberate, and the effect is devastating: Judas has just been handed the bread and the cup along with everyone else.

The hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. Not among you — on the table. In that culture the shared dish was the sign of covenant friendship; to eat with a man was to pledge yourself to him. David had felt this exact wound and written it down: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9).

Then the two halves of the hardest sentence in the chapter.

The Son of Man goes as it has been determined. Marked out, fixed, appointed. The cross is not a catastrophe that overtook the plan; it is the plan. Nothing that happens between here and the tomb is an accident, an unlucky turn, or an escape that failed.

But woe to that man by whom he is betrayed. And the betrayal, though it fulfils a determined purpose, remains entirely the betrayer's own, and the guilt of it is his.

Two things are asserted in one breath which the human mind cannot fit together, and Jesus makes no attempt to reconcile them. That is worth registering, because it is the settled pattern of Scripture rather than an isolated puzzle: the same combination appears in Joseph's you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20), and in Peter's Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:23).

And there is a pastoral use for it, which is where most readers actually need it. People who have been badly wronged live between two temptations. One is to conclude that the wrong was outside God's reach, which makes the world random and God small. The other is to conclude that because God had a purpose in it, the person who did it was not really guilty — a piece of false comfort that leaves the victim unable even to name what happened.

This verse refuses both. God's purpose stood, and the man who did it is answerable. You are permitted to say that what was done to you was wicked, and that God was not absent from it, and you are not required to make those two sentences into one.

Did Judas receive the bread and cup? Matthew and Mark put the warning about the betrayer before the Supper, and John has Judas leave after the morsel (John 13:30). Luke often arranges events by subject, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the cup was shared. Either way, he sat at the table with Jesus and betrayed him.

Joseph said both to his brothers' faces and then wept and fed them (cf. Gen. 50:20; Acts 2:23).

parallels.desc: according to the definite plan of God

verseByVerse.quote: And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.

A short verse, easily skipped, and it is one of the most searching sentences at that table.

Consider what did not happen. Nobody looked at Judas. Eleven men, three years in his company, sharing every meal and every road and every night on a hillside — and when a betrayer is announced, not one of them can identify him. Matthew adds that they each asked, Is it I? (Matt. 26:22).

Two things follow from that, and both are worth having.

The first is about Judas. Whatever he was, he was not obvious. He had not been drifting visibly, or arguing, or absenting himself. He was so entirely unsuspected that the natural assumption of every other man in the room was that the traitor was more likely to be himself. That should end, permanently, the comfortable idea that serious spiritual defection announces itself in advance. It does not. It is generally invisible until it is complete, including to the person concerned.

The second is about the eleven. Their instinct was to look inward before looking around, and it was a sound instinct — the last sound instinct several of them would show that night. They had heard him say things all evening that they had not fully understood, but they had grasped this much: if the Lord says one of us is capable of it, I had better start with myself.

That is the exact opposite of the reflex most of us have, which is to run the accusation across everyone we know and stop just short of our own door. And it explains why Paul, writing about this very table, tells the Corinthians to examine themselves before eating (1 Cor. 11:28) — not to examine each other, which is what that church was busy doing.

Here is the practical form of it. When you hear a sermon that names a sin, notice who comes to mind first. If it is reliably someone else — a spouse, a colleague, a member of the congregation who really does need to hear it — that is worth knowing about yourself, because the eleven at that table did the reverse and they were right to.

And there is comfort in it too, for the reader whose own heart frightens him. The men who asked is it I in fear were not the ones who did it. Judas asked it knowing the answer (Matt. 26:25; cf. 1 Cor. 11:28; Ps. 139:23–24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–38 — Greatness, Sifting, and the Turning Season
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The bread has been broken and the betrayal announced, and in that room an argument breaks out about rank. It was a love of winning, and they had done it before (9:46). It is not a failure peculiar to them: a congregation can have a moving communion service and a dispute about who was asked to serve at it in the car park afterwards.

Jesus describes the world they know. Gentile kings play the lord, and those in authority are called benefactors — a formal honorific, voted by cities and inscribed on stone, claimed by rulers who had done real good and intended it remembered. So the mechanism of worldly power is not brute force. It is force that has arranged to be thanked.

But not so with you. He does not abolish leadership — he distinguishes the greatest from the rest in the same sentence in which he redefines them. The greatest becomes as the youngest, who in that world ran the errands and was interruptible. And then: I am among you as the one who serves, said while reclining at his own table, having handed round the bread himself.

Then he satisfies the ambition he has just corrected. You are those who have stayed with me in my trials — said to men who will scatter within hours, and said accurately, because three years of staying is not cancelled by one night of failure. He assigns them a kingdom on the same terms his Father used with him: a table to eat at, and thrones.

To Peter, by his old name and doubled: Satan demanded to have you — the plural you, the whole barn — that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, singular, that your faith may not fail. Not that the sifting be cancelled, nor the fall prevented, but that the faith itself hold. And the commission comes before the failure, with when and not if: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

Peter contradicts him and is told the number and the deadline. Then the season turns: the disciples who once went out with no moneybag and lacked nothing are told to take the bag, and the sword saying arrives — which the next two verses immediately defuse.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 32 is the doctrine of perseverance in one sentence, and it is not a claim about the strength of Christians. Peter's faith survived because Christ was praying, and he prays still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25). The scene behind Satan's demand is Job 1 — the accuser must ask, is given a limit, and cannot exceed it.

The teaching on greatness in vv. 25–27 is not a management philosophy but the application of the incarnation to the question of authority. The one holding the basin is the eternal Son by whom all things were made, and within a day the serving goes further than a towel. Authority in the kingdom is real and it exists for those under it.

Verses 35–38 must be read as a unit or they will be abused. Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 — numbered with the transgressors — which is precisely why the swords must go: a man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one. Two swords for a band of disciples facing an armed detachment is absurd for a fight, and it is enough is not a quartermaster approving the arsenal but a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong. Both the crusading reading and the absolute-pacifist reading are more than the passage will carry.
verseByVerse.examples:
A test for anyone who leads anything, and it is sharper than asking whether you serve, since everyone believes they serve. When did you last do something for your church that carried no credit whatever, that nobody would notice was done, and that could not be mentioned afterwards without losing the point? That is the youngest man's work, and Jesus took it.

Verse 28 is one of the most reassuring things in the Gospel about how Christ assesses a life. He is not scoring the worst night. He looks at eleven men hours from failing him completely and says: you stayed.

Verses 33–34 are for anyone who has made God a promise they did not keep — the resolve after a hospital ward, the change that lasted eleven days. Peter's sincerity was real, his self-confidence was misplaced, his failure was total, and none of it surprised Jesus or altered anything he had decided about the man. Being told in advance is what made restoration possible: the denial could only ever mean he knew, and prayed for me anyway.

And v. 35 is worth answering out loud, as the disciples had to. Not has life been easy, but the narrower question: has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the same word they used.

verseByVerse.quote: A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them, 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them, The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.

The placing is almost unbearable and Luke means it to be. The bread has been broken. The cup has been passed. The betrayal has been announced. And in that room, minutes later, an argument breaks out about rank.

The word is philoneikia — literally a love of winning. Not a disagreement they fell into but an appetite they indulged, and it had been running for some time: they had argued about this before (9:46), and had been told then, with a child set in front of them.

It is worth resisting the urge to be shocked at them, because the honest response is recognition. This is what human beings are like, including converted ones, including in the presence of the holiest thing that has ever happened. A church can have a genuinely moving communion service and a dispute about who was asked to serve at it in the car park afterwards. The two things do not feel connected from the inside. They were not connected in the disciples' minds either, which is exactly the problem.

Jesus does not shame them. He describes a world they know.

The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them. They play the lord, they exercise mastery. And then the sharper observation: those in authority over them are called benefactors.

Benefactor — euergetēs — was not a compliment paid spontaneously. It was a formal honorific, voted by cities, inscribed on stone, and claimed by rulers who had done something for the public and intended everyone to remember it. Several of the Ptolemies took it as an official title. It was a brand.

So Jesus has named the exact mechanism by which worldly power sustains itself, and it is not brute force. It is force that has arranged to be thanked. The men who dominate are the men publicly known for their generosity, and the generosity is real, and it is also the instrument of the domination.

That is a very modern observation, and it lands closer to home than the word kings suggests. The tell is not whether a person does good. It is whether the doing of good has been arranged so that it is seen, credited and remembered — whether the title is coming back.

He is about to say what the alternative is. But he begins by making sure they can see the water they are swimming in (cf. Luke 9:46–48; 3 John 9).
verseByVerse.note: “Benefactor” was an official title that rulers loved to claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.

But not so with you. Five words, and they carve the church out of the world. Whatever else the Christian community is, it is to be the one place on earth where the usual arithmetic of status does not operate.

Notice what he does not say. He does not abolish leadership. He distinguishes the greatest from the rest and the leader from those led, in the same sentence in which he redefines them. The New Testament is full of appointed elders and real authority. What is forbidden is not office; it is what office is used for.

Let the greatest among you become as the youngest. In that world the youngest at a gathering was not merely the least honoured; he was the one who ran the errands. He fetched. He was interruptible. Everybody's needs came before his own plans for the evening.

And then Jesus asks a question with an obvious answer and gives the obvious answer himself, which is a way of making sure nobody escapes into cleverness. Who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Everyone in the room knew: the man lying down. That is not a trick question and he does not pretend otherwise. In every society that has ever existed, the served outrank the servers.

But I am among you as the one who serves.

He says it while reclining, at his own table, having personally handled the bread and the cup and put them into the hands of men who had just been arguing about precedence. On the same evening, John tells us, he got up, took a towel, and washed their feet — including the feet of the man who had already been paid to betray him.

This is where the passage stops being about management and becomes about God. The one speaking is not a good leader modelling humility to inspire imitation. He is the eternal Son, by whom all things were made, holding a basin. And within a day the serving will go further than a towel: the hands that poured the water will be nailed through, and the same word — serve — will be used of the Son of Man who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

Here is a test for anyone who leads anything. Not do I serve — everyone believes they serve. Ask instead: when did I last do something for this church that carried no credit whatever, that nobody would notice was done, and that I could not mention afterwards without it losing the point? That is the youngest man's work, and Jesus took it (cf. John 13:4–5; Mark 10:45).

verseByVerse.quote: 'You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom,
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom.

Having corrected their ambition, he now satisfies it — which is not what anyone expects, and it tells you something important about how Jesus handles wrong desires. He does not tell them to want less. He tells them they have been wanting the right thing in the wrong shape.

You are those who have stayed with me in my trials.

Read that in the light of what is about to happen and it becomes almost incredible. Within hours they will fall asleep on him, and then scatter into the dark. One of them will deny three times that he ever knew him. And on the evening before all of it, Jesus looks around the table and says: you stayed.

He is not being sentimental, and he is not unaware. He is describing three years accurately. They did stay. Through the hostility in the synagogues, the accusations of collusion with demons, the plots, the crowds falling away when the teaching got hard (John 6:66), the long homeless walk to Jerusalem — they were there. The failure that is coming is real and he has already named it, and it does not cancel what preceded it.

This is one of the most reassuring things in the Gospel about how Christ assesses a life. He is not scoring the worst night. He sees the whole thing, and he counts the staying.

And I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom.

The verb is diatithemai — the word used for making a will, disposing of an estate. It is the verb behind the noun covenant. He is bequeathing. A man about to die is settling his affairs, and what he has to leave is a kingdom.

And the chain of it is the astonishing part: as my Father assigned to me. The kingdom passes from the Father to the Son and from the Son to these eleven men, on identical terms, by the same verb. Whatever the disciples were arguing about ten minutes earlier, this is larger, and they are not being fobbed off with a consolation.

Which recasts the whole dispute about greatness. They were fighting over a portion of something that was already being left to all of them in full. That is nearly always the shape of status-hunger in the church: a scramble for a slice, conducted by heirs (cf. Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:12).

parallels.desc: he himself has suffered when tempted
if we endure, we will also reign

verseByVerse.quote: that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

Two pictures, and the church has generally been much happier with the first than the second.

Eat and drink at my table. He has just told them he will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes (v. 18), and now he says what the resumption looks like. The meal is not over; it is adjourned. The same table, the same host, the same men — and this time nobody is arguing about seats, and nobody leaves in the dark.

Take that concretely, because heaven is usually left vague and should not be. It is not a sensation, and it is not a choir practice that never ends. It is, in his own image, a table: food, drink, faces, conversation, and the person you most want to be near presiding over it. Everyone who has ever sat at a long meal with people they love and felt the evening going too fast has been given a small, accurate sample of it.

Then the second picture: and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

The word judging here carries the sense it has in the book of Judges — to govern, to rule, to put right — rather than merely to pass sentence. This is not a promise of a courtroom rota. It is authority: the twelve, who represent the renewed people of God, given real governance in the world to come. Paul says the same thing in passing to a church that was suing itself, as though everybody already knew it: do you not know that the saints will judge the world (1 Cor. 6:2)?

Which means the future is not passive. Christians are not going to be looked after for ever; they are going to be trusted with something. Jesus has said it before in this Gospel in the parable of the minas: well done, good servant, you shall have authority over ten cities (19:17). The reward for faithfulness is more responsibility, given by a Master who will not have to take it back.

And notice who is being handed it. Not a shortlist of the impressive. Eleven provincial men, mostly uneducated, who had spent the last few minutes squabbling about precedence and would spend the next few hours failing comprehensively.

What are these thrones? Premillennial Christians see a future earthly reign over a restored Israel. Matthew places it in the new world (Matt 19:28), the renewed creation. The more likely reading is that the apostles share in Christ’s rule over his people, the true Israel, which begins now through their word and will be complete in the new creation.

He knew what they were. He set a table for them anyway, and he wrote thrones into the will (cf. 1 Cor. 6:2–3; Rev. 3:21).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

The doubled name is how Scripture speaks when something enormous is about to be said to one person: Abraham, Abraham; Moses, Moses; Martha, Martha; Saul, Saul. It is the sound of a hand on the shoulder.

And notice which name. Not Peter, the rock — the name Jesus gave him. Simon, the name he was born with. He is being addressed as the man he still is.

Satan demanded to have you — asked formally, demanded a person be handed over. There is only one other place in Scripture where this happens in the open, and it is the first chapters of Job — where the accuser appears before God, asks for a man, is granted a limit, and cannot exceed it by a hair. That is the scene behind this sentence. Satan does not have free access to God's people; he has to ask.

The you here is plural in the Greek — he demanded to have all of you. The you in I have prayed for you is singular. Satan asked for the whole barn; Jesus names one man.

That he might sift you like wheat. Sifting is violent — the grain thrown and shaken until what is not grain is separated out. It is worth saying what Satan's aim was: not to shake the chaff out of Peter but to demonstrate that Peter was chaff. The intended verdict was that there was nothing there.

But I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail.

Sit with what he did not pray. He did not pray that Peter would be spared the sifting; the sifting comes. He did not pray that Peter would not fall; Peter falls within hours, three times. He prayed for the one thing underneath all of it: that the faith itself would not give out — that the man would go down and not stay down.

This is the doctrine of perseverance in one sentence, and it is not a claim about the strength of Christians. Peter's faith did not survive because Peter was strong. It survived because Jesus was praying, and he is praying still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25).

Then the commission, given before the failure and with a word that is not if: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers. The restoration is settled before the fall has happened, and so is the job afterwards. The man who is about to be the worst failure in the room is being appointed to hold up everyone else — and he will be able to, because a man who has been carried back knows the way.

Does strengthen your brothers make Peter the head of the church? The commission is personal and pastoral: Peter, restored after his fall, would strengthen the others, as he did in Acts and in his letters. Nothing speaks of an office passed to successors, and Paul later rebuked Peter to his face (Gal 2:11–14).

Every believer's endurance rests on the same thing Peter's did, and it is not their grip on Christ. It is his prayer for them (cf. Job 1:6–12; Heb. 7:25).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the first “you” is plural — Satan asked for all of them — while in verse 32 it is singular: Jesus prayed for Peter. Sifting shook wheat in a sieve to separate it.

parallels.desc: Satan asks leave to test Job
shake Israel as one shakes with a sieve

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, 'Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.' Jesus said, 'I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death. Jesus said, I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.

Peter is not lying, and that is what makes this so useful.

He means it entirely. In a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed detachment on Jesus's behalf, which is not the act of a coward, and he will follow into the high priest's courtyard when the others have gone. His love is real and his courage is real. What he does not have is any accurate knowledge of himself.

And notice what he has just done. Jesus has said I have prayed for you and when you have turned again — that is, you are going to fall — and Peter's response is to contradict him. He heard a warning and answered with a résumé.

Then the reply, and it is exact. This day. Three times. Before the rooster crows. No hedging, no you might. Jesus does not say Peter is weak in general; he tells him the number and the deadline.

Why say it at all? It cannot be to prevent the denial, because it does not. It cannot be to humiliate him, because Jesus has just promised to restore him. The reason is in the word he uses in the previous breath — when you have turned again. If Peter had denied Christ without warning, the collapse would have been total: he would have concluded that Jesus had misjudged him, that his discipleship had been a mistake from the start, that there was nothing to go back to. Judas made an inference of that kind and it killed him.

Because he was told in advance, the denial could only ever mean one thing: he knew. He knew, and he prayed for me anyway, and he told me I would come back.

Which is the thing to carry away, for anyone who has ever made God a promise they did not keep — the giving-up promised on a hospital ward, the resolve after a conviction that lasted eleven days. The pattern is nearly always the same: sincerity, self-confidence, collapse, and then the conviction that the whole thing was a sham.

Peter's case says otherwise. His sincerity was real, his confidence was misplaced, his failure was total, and none of it took Jesus by surprise or altered anything he had decided about the man.

Mark says the rooster would crow twice (Mark 14:30). Luke gives the general warning, before the cock-crow; Mark, from Peter’s own memory, gives the precise form. There is no contradiction.

He knew what Peter would do before Peter did it, and had already prayed for him, and had already given him his next assignment. That is the Christ people are actually dealing with (cf. Ps. 103:14; 2 Tim. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?' They said, 'Nothing.' He said to them, 'But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything? They said, Nothing. He said to them, But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.

He begins with a question about the past, and he makes them answer it out loud.

The reference is to the missions of chapters 9 and 10, when he had sent them out deliberately unprovisioned — no bag, no money, no spare sandals — into a countryside that received them. And he asks: did you lack anything? Their answer is one word. Nothing.

It is a good question to be made to answer, and it is worth answering yourself before reading on. Not has life been easy, but the narrower and more testable one: has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the same word the disciples used, and are surprised by it.

But now. Something has changed, and the change is not in God's care but in the world's welcome.

The season of open doors is closing. Israel is about to crucify her Messiah, and the men at this table will go out into a world that will treat them accordingly — the arrests and courtrooms he described in the previous chapter. So the instructions are reversed: take the bag, take the money, and if you have no sword, sell your cloak.

That last clause is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and the honest thing is to say what it plainly means before saying what it does not. In that world a cloak was a man's most necessary possession — his coat by day and his blanket by night, so basic that the law forbade keeping it overnight as collateral because he had nothing else to sleep under (Exod. 22:26–27). To sell the cloak for a sword is to say: the danger ahead is now greater than the cold.

It is a picture of how sharply the conditions are about to alter, put in the most arresting terms available. And it is not a licence for the disciples to arm themselves, as the next two verses will show beyond argument.

But the pastoral point stands on its own. The man who provisioned them so completely in the easy season is the same one preparing them for the hard one, and he does not pretend the second is like the first. There are seasons in a Christian life when the doors open and the provision arrives unasked, and seasons when it is cold and hostile and every step is uphill. The same Lord governs both, and he tells his people in advance when the weather is about to turn (cf. Luke 10:4; Phil. 4:11–13).
verseByVerse.note: The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance, as verses 38 and 51 show.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.' And they said, 'Look, Lord, here are two swords.' And he said to them, 'It is enough.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: And he was numbered with the transgressors. For what is written about me has its fulfillment. And they said, Look, Lord, here are two swords. And he said to them, It is enough.

He quotes Isaiah 53:12, the last line of the Servant Song, and it is the lens through which he is reading his own arrest. He will be taken like a criminal, tried as a criminal, and killed between two of them — numbered with the transgressors, counted in the same column, entered on the same list.

That is the reason the swords must go. A man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one.

Then the exchange, which has puzzled readers for centuries and been pulled in two opposite directions, so the tension deserves naming plainly. Jesus says let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one (v. 36); a few hours later, when a disciple actually swings one, he says no more of this and heals the wound (v. 51). Buy a sword, then put it away — which is it?

Down the centuries the church has misread it both ways. Some have taken the earlier verse as a divine licence for the sword, and built crusades and holy wars on it. Others have taken the later verse as an absolute ban on any force whatever, in any hands, for any cause. The passage will not carry either load.

The key is a detail easy to miss. They answer, Lord, here are two swords, and he says, it is enough. Two swords for twelve men about to be surrounded by an armed detachment is not enough for a fight. It is absurd for a fight, and Jesus knows it.

That is the point. It is enough is not a quartermaster approving the arsenal; it is a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong — the weary enough of this of a man whose friends have heard sword and reached for iron when he meant the coming cold of a world that will no longer feed and shelter them. He was telling them the friendly season was over; they thought he was mustering a militia.

And when the iron did come out in the garden, he stopped it with a word and mended the only casualty of the night with a touch. The single sword-stroke of the whole Passion was struck by a disciple, against Christ's will, and Jesus reversed it. That is the last word Luke gives on swords in the kingdom.

Underneath the misunderstanding, though, hear what he actually said about himself. The Servant of Isaiah 53 is the one who was despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions, and who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many. Jesus reads that chapter and finds his own name in it — and goes out to the garden to make it true (cf. Isa. 53:12; 2 Cor. 5:21).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes to the Mount of Olives as was his custom — which is why Judas knew where to look, and why he had a path to walk on the worst night of his life. The habit was already worn smooth. And his instruction to the disciples is not that they pray for him but that they pray for themselves: pray that you may not enter into temptation, the petition from the prayer he taught them.

A stone's throw away he kneels, which was not the customary posture, and prays Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. The cup is not a general image of suffering. In the prophets it is fixed: the cup of the wrath of God, which the wicked drain to the dregs (Ps. 75:8; Jer. 25:15; Isa. 51:17).

Luke adds two details the others do not: an angel strengthening him, and sweat like great drops of blood. Both verses carry a note in modern Bibles — some manuscripts omit them, as the ESV margin says — because the manuscript evidence is genuinely divided — including the real possibility that early scribes removed them because a Christ who trembled embarrassed them.

He finds the disciples asleep, and Luke alone says why: for sorrow. They were not indifferent; grief of that weight shuts a body down. He wakes them without rebuke and gives them the smallest possible next action: rise and pray.

Then, while he is still speaking, the torches. Judas leads them and comes to kiss him, and Jesus names it to his face — using his name, in a question, which is a door held open to the last second. A disciple strikes and takes an ear, and Jesus stops his own arrest to heal a member of the arresting party.

To the officials who came out at night with clubs, he points out that he had been in their temple every day that week and they had not touched him. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness — real authority, genuinely theirs, and lasting exactly an hour.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not my will, but yours, be done is the perfect alignment of a human will with the divine, and it required agony to reach — which is what makes it obedience rather than indifference. Both wills are real: he genuinely did not want the cup. Gethsemane is the counterpart of Eden. In one garden a man said my will, not yours and the world broke; in another the second Adam said it the other way round.

The unanswered request is itself doctrine. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful of that cup, there was no other way for sinners to be saved. The silence after if you are willing is the measure of what the cross was for.

Verse 51 is the last healing before the cross and it is performed on an enemy, unasked, by the prisoner. He had said love your enemies and do good to those who hate you (6:27), and here he does it with his own disciple's blade still wet.

And this is your hour, and the power of darkness concedes two things and withholds a third. The hour is genuinely theirs; the authority is real and belongs to darkness. What is withheld is any suggestion that it is more than an hour. Luke has used that clock before — the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 39 is for anyone who has tried to pray in an emergency and found nothing there. The crisis is a terrible time to begin; what carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden, and paths are made in the ordinary weeks when nothing is wrong.

Verse 42 settles a question many carry: is if you are willing a failure of faith? A woman facing a diagnosis, told that Christian prayer should always be confident and specific, wonders whether her honest conditional is weakness. The Son of God prayed exactly that prayer, in those words, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is the highest thing faith ever does.

Verse 44 ends another argument — the idea that visible distress proves weak faith. The sinless Son, in perfect communion with his Father and doing exactly his will, was in such distress that his body gave way under it.

And vv. 45–46 name one of the least-discussed experiences in the Christian life: the point at which grief makes prayer impossible. Bereavement, depression, exhaustion after months of caring — and the believer finds the one thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do, with the accusation following that a real Christian would be praying. Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through worse, and he wakes them gently and tells them to pray. They were kept that night, and it was not by their own watchfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them, 'Pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them, Pray that you may not enter into temptation.

As was his custom. Luke has already told us this was the pattern of the week — teaching in the temple by day, lodging on Olivet by night (21:37). It is a small phrase with two large consequences.

The first is that Judas knew where to find him. John says so explicitly: Judas knew the place, because Jesus often met there with his disciples (John 18:2). Jesus goes, on the one night when his habits are lethal, to the one place his betrayer would look. He is not hiding.

The second is about prayer, and it is the more useful of the two for most readers. The worst night of his life did not send him somewhere new. He went where he always went. The habit was already in place, worn smooth by years of use, and when the crisis came he did not have to invent a practice; he had only to keep one.

That is worth weighing by anyone who has tried to pray in an emergency and found nothing there. The hour of crisis is a terrible time to begin. What carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden — and the paths are made in the ordinary weeks when nothing is wrong and prayer feels unnecessary.

Then the instruction, and it is not what he might have asked for. Pray that you may not enter into temptation.

He does not ask them to pray for him. He is about to enter the deepest agony any human being has known, and what he asks of his friends is that they pray for themselves.

The words are lifted straight out of the prayer he taught them: lead us not into temptation (11:4). Temptation here is testing as well as enticement, and the request is not for an easy life. It is a prayer to be kept from the situation in which faith is put under a pressure it cannot bear — a plea born of self-distrust, which is precisely what these men lack and precisely what the next hour will prove they needed.

And note what he does not tell them to do. Not stay alert for Judas. Not arm yourselves. Not watch the path. The danger closing in on that garden was real and armed, and the only defence he issued was prayer.

Does God lead us into temptation? God tempts no one to sin (Jas 1:13), but he does bring his people into testing. The prayer asks to be kept from falling when the test comes; and God promises that he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability (1 Cor 10:13).

He is walking into the worst hour in history, and his last instruction before he kneels is a warning for their sakes (cf. Luke 11:4; 1 Cor. 10:12–13).

verseByVerse.quote: And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying, 'Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying, Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.

A stone's throw — near enough to be seen, far enough to be alone. Luke measures the distance, which is the kind of detail a man includes when he has spoken to someone who was there.

And knelt down. The customary posture for Jewish prayer was standing. Kneeling was for extremity. In Matthew and Mark he is on his face on the ground.

Father. Whatever else is about to be said, it begins there, and the address never wavers.

Then: remove this cup from me. And the cup has to be identified correctly, because everything depends on it. In the prophets the cup is a fixed image, and it is not an image of pain in general. It is the cup of the wrath of God: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it to the dregs (Ps. 75:8); take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jer. 25:15); the cup of staggering (Isa. 51:17).

So what makes him shake is not the nails. Thousands of men were crucified in that province and many faced it with composure; there were Maccabean martyrs who went to worse deaths singing. If Jesus were merely facing execution he would be less brave than his own martyrs, which is absurd. What is in front of him is the cup — the undiluted judgment of God against every sin ever committed, to be drunk by the only man who never deserved a drop of it.

If you are willing. He does not presume. He asks, and the asking is real: if there is another way, let there be another way. There was not, and the silence that followed that request is the measure of what the cross was for. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful of it, there was no other way for you to be saved.

Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.

Two wills are in that sentence, and both are real. He genuinely did not want it. That is not a flaw in his obedience; it is what makes it obedience rather than indifference.

And for the reader praying an if you are willing prayer over something they are terrified of — a diagnosis, a marriage, a child — this settles the question of whether such a prayer is weak faith. The Son of God prayed it, in those words, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is not a failure of faith. It is the highest thing faith ever does.

In a garden a man once said my will, not yours, and the world broke. In another garden the second Adam knelt in the dark and said the sentence the other way round, and the world began to be mended (cf. Ps. 75:8; Rom. 5:19).
verseByVerse.note: A stone’s throw is a short distance. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.

The Father does not remove the cup. He sends someone to help his Son drink it.

Take that in before anything else, because it is the pattern of answered prayer through the whole of Scripture and it is what most people actually need to know about their own unanswered ones. God rarely removes the furnace. He goes into it. The angel does not come to rescue Jesus from the cross; the angel comes so that he can get to it.

And notice what it says about the Son in his humanity: he needed strengthening. Not metaphorically. The one who made the angel is being ministered to by it.

Now, a reader looking at this verse in a modern Bible will see something and should be told what it is. Verses 43 and 44 are usually printed with a note that some manuscripts do not have them, as the ESV margin says. The evidence really is divided — the two verses are absent from several of the oldest copies of Luke, including one of the great fourth-century codices, and present in many others, some of which mark them with a scribal sign meaning the copyist knew there was a question. This is not the situation of the longer ending of Mark, where the case runs mostly one way. Here it is close.

Two explanations are held by careful people. Either the verses were written by Luke and some scribes cut them, or they preserve a true early memory that was later written in. The first has more force than it may sound. We know from the writings of the first few centuries that a Jesus who sweated and shook and needed an angel embarrassed some readers, who thought it made the Son look weak, and there is evidence of copies being tidied in exactly that direction. A scribe who removed these lines would have thought he was defending Christ's dignity. He was removing the proof of his humanity.

How then should they be read? Read them, and rest nothing on them that rests nowhere else. Nothing in them is unique to them. The agony in the garden is in Matthew and Mark without these verses. Angels attending Jesus after a great trial is already in the record (Matt. 4:11). And a Christ who prays in anguish is not a fragile idea propped up by two disputed lines — it is the settled teaching of the New Testament: in the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Heb. 5:7).

Whether Luke's own pen wrote these two sentences or an early hand preserved them, what they describe is true, and the church has never had a Saviour who suffered at a comfortable distance (cf. Matt. 4:11; Heb. 5:7).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44.

verseByVerse.quote: And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

The word is agōnia, and it does not mean misery. It comes from the arena — the agōn was the contest, and agōnia was the state of a man at the point of maximum exertion in it. This is not despair. It is struggle, at the limit of what a body can do.

And look at what the agony produced: he prayed more earnestly. That is the reverse of the usual direction. Under that kind of pressure the human instinct is to stop praying, because prayer requires an attention that terror takes away. He went the other way. The worse it got, the harder he prayed.

Then the detail that only the physician records. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

Careful readers have long noticed the word like, and it is possible Luke means only that the sweat fell in heavy drops, the way blood falls. But there is a rare documented condition, hematidrosis, in which extreme distress ruptures the small vessels around the sweat glands so that blood is released with the sweat. Cases are recorded in men under sentence of death. Luke was a doctor, and if he saw or was told of something of that kind, he described it exactly as a doctor would.

Either way, the point is not clinical. The point is that it went that far.

And it is worth naming what this means for anyone who has ever felt ashamed of how badly they were coping. There is a strain of Christian teaching that treats visible distress as evidence of weak faith — that a believer facing something terrible ought to be calm, and that fear is failure. This verse ends that argument. The sinless Son of God, in perfect communion with his Father, doing exactly the Father's will, was in such distress that his body gave way under it.

He is therefore not a Saviour who is puzzled by human dread. He has been further into it than anyone reading this will ever go, and he went in freely, and he did not come out of it until he had drunk the whole cup.

There is blood on the ground of that garden before a single Roman has laid a hand on him. He had not yet been arrested, tried, flogged or nailed, and the giving had already started (cf. Heb. 5:7–8; Heb. 12:3–4).
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, describes the extreme anguish; “like great drops of blood” may be a comparison or describe a rare medical condition.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them, 'Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them, Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.

Matthew and Mark record that the disciples slept. Luke alone tells us why: for sorrow — from grief.

That is a physician's observation and it is a kindness. They were not bored, and they were not indifferent. They had spent an evening being told that one of them was a traitor, that their leader was going to die, that Peter would deny him — and grief of that weight does something to a body. It does not keep you awake. It shuts you down. Anyone who has sat with the bereaved knows the heaviness that comes over people in the days after a death, the sleep that is not rest.

Luke says the men who failed Jesus in the garden failed him because they were grieving over him, and he wants his reader to know it.

Which makes what Jesus says next remarkable for what is not in it. Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray. There is no rebuke in those words — Mark records a sharper line to Peter, but Luke gives us this — and there is no discussion of their failure at all. Just: get up, and pray, because the thing I warned you about is coming up the path.

Now bring this to where it belongs, because it names one of the most common and least-discussed experiences in the Christian life: the point at which grief makes prayer impossible. Bereavement, depression, a marriage coming apart, exhaustion after months of caring for someone — and the believer finds that the very thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do. He opens the Bible and reads the same paragraph four times. He kneels and falls asleep. And then, on top of the sorrow, comes the accusation: a real Christian would be praying.

Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through something immeasurably worse, and his response is to wake them gently and tell them to pray — not to inform them that they have forfeited anything.

And note the instruction itself. He does not say feel better or stop grieving. He says rise and pray, which is the smallest possible next action, and the only one available.

There is one more thing here, and it is the heart of the paragraph. He had asked them to pray for themselves and they could not manage it — so he had been praying, a stone's throw away, for them. The disciples were kept that night, and it was not by their own watchfulness (cf. Ps. 121:3–4; John 17:15).

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him, 'Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him, Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?

While he was still speaking. The warning and the danger arrive in the same breath. He was mid-sentence telling them to pray, and the torches were already coming up the hill.

And Luke, who has already told us in v. 3 who this man was, says it again here as though it still cannot be believed: the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He is at the front. He is not being brought along as a witness; he is guiding an armed party to a place only an insider knew.

Then the kiss. In that world it was not a small gesture and not a private one — it was the standard greeting of a disciple to his rabbi, an act of honour and affection performed in public.

So the sign agreed with the arresting party was the gesture of love. He could have pointed. He could have said the name. He chose the one movement in the whole repertoire of human behaviour that means I am yours, and used it as a marker for a squad of temple police.

Which is why this is the definitive picture of what sin does when it is finished. It does not merely break things; it takes what is good and makes it the instrument. Worship offered to be seen. Truth told to wound. Affection used as a lever. The kiss of a disciple, turned into a target sight.

Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?

Note that he uses his name. This is the last recorded word of Jesus to Judas, and it is not a curse. It is a question, and it is his name — the same name he had spoken on the mountain when he chose him (6:13-16).

Some read it as a rebuke. It is better read as what it plainly is: a last door, held open. He puts to Judas the thing Judas is actually doing, in words, at the moment of doing it, and the question hangs there waiting for an answer. This is how the Lord deals with a man walking into ruin — not by ambush, but by naming it to his face while there is still a second in which to stop.

He does not stop. And the one who asked the question goes with them, and dies within the day for men exactly like the one who kissed him (cf. Ps. 55:12–14; Rom. 5:8).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, 'Lord, shall we strike with the sword?' And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, 'No more of this!' And he touched his ear and healed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, shall we strike with the sword? And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, No more of this! And he touched his ear and healed him.

They ask the question and then do not wait for the answer, which is the whole trouble with them in one line. Lord, shall we strike? — and before the reply comes, a sword is out and a man is bleeding.

John names them both: Peter with the sword, and the victim Malchus, a servant of the high priest (John 18:10). Peter was a fisherman, not a swordsman, and the detail that he took an ear rather than a head suggests a wild stroke aimed higher that the man ducked. It is a serious wound and it is also, in the circumstances, suicidal: eleven Galileans and two swords against an armed detachment.

No more of this! Four words, and they are the last command Jesus gives before he is bound.

Consider what he is stopping. Not an enemy — a friend. Not an act of cowardice — an act of reckless courage performed out of love for him. Peter is the only man there willing to die for Jesus at that moment, and Jesus tells him to stop.

Because the kingdom does not come that way, and never has. He would say it under interrogation the next morning: if my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36).
