The one thing he would not permit in his own defence was the thing his followers have most often reached for since.

And then the sentence that is easy to read past and is one of the most extraordinary in the Gospels. And he touched his ear and healed him.

He is minutes from being bound and led away. Torches are in his face, weapons are drawn, and his own men are about to run. And in the middle of it he stops his arrest, in order to repair the injury his disciple has done to one of the men who came to take him.

Malchus went to work that night to arrest a man and came home whole. The last miracle of healing before the cross was performed on a member of the arresting party, by the prisoner, without being asked.

That is who he is when everything is against him. Not merely non-retaliating — actively mending. Enemies at the gate, and the Son of God is doing good to the man in front of him because he is the man in front of him.

He said love your enemies and do good to those who hate you (6:27), and then he did it with a servant's blood on his own disciple's blade (cf. Luke 6:27–29; 1 Pet. 2:23).
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, records that Jesus healed the ear. John names the servant Malchus and the swordsman Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, 'Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.

He speaks to the officials, not to the muscle. Luke names them: the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders — the leadership itself has come out to the garden at night. They wanted to see it done.

A robber here is not a pickpocket but a brigand or an insurgent — a man with a weapon and a hillside. So the question is precise: have you come out equipped for an armed rebel?

And then the fact that convicts them without a word of accusation. When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me.

He was there every day of that week, in the open, in their own building, teaching in front of thousands. If he were a danger to public order, that was the moment. They chose the olive grove, at night, with a paid informant and a mob carrying clubs — and the choice tells you everything about who believed his own case would survive daylight.

Then the sentence, and it is one of the darkest things Jesus ever said: But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.

Two things are conceded and one is withheld. He concedes the hour — this is genuinely theirs, and what follows is not a divine puppet show in which the participants are only pretending to arrest him. And he concedes the power: exousia, real authority, and it belongs to darkness, and it is operating.

What he withholds is any suggestion that this is more than an hour. Luke has used that clock before — the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13), and here is the time. It gets an hour. That is the lease.

Which is worth having when the darkness is at its most convincing, because it usually looks permanent from inside. It looked permanent to the eleven men running down that hillside, and by Sunday morning it was over.

He is being arrested, and he is the only one present who knows what time it is. The men with the torches thought they had taken him. They had been given an hour, by him, and they used it exactly as he said they would (cf. Luke 4:13; Col. 1:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–71 — The Denial and the Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter follows at a distance — more than anyone else managed, and still far enough to be nobody. In the courtyard a fire is kindled and he sits down among the men who arrested his Lord. It was cold, and there is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm; but this is how a fall actually happens. He did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm.

The accuser is a servant girl, the person of least standing in that yard, and her charge is about as mild as an accusation can be: this man also was with him. Peter answers, Woman, I do not know him — denying not a fact but a person.

Luke keeps the clock running: a little later, then an interval of about an hour. This is not a moment of panic; Peter had an hour to get up and leave. And the denials deteriorate — first the person, then the fellowship (I am not), then the subject itself (I do not know what you are talking about). The third accuser has evidence nobody can argue with: his accent. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

Then the rooster, mid-sentence — the most ordinary sound in the world, and enough, because it had been named in advance. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. It was not a look of contempt; a man looked at with contempt remembers the contempt, and Peter remembered the saying of the Lord — which included I have prayed for you and when you have turned again. He went out and wept bitterly.

Inside, the guards fill the night with a game: blindfold him, strike him, and demand he name the hand. While they demand a prophecy, three of his prophecies are being fulfilled in that building.

At daybreak the council reconvenes to give the night's work a lawful appearance, and asks its one question. He declines to perform — if I tell you, you will not believe — and then makes a claim larger than the question: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God. They ask if he is the Son of God. He affirms it, and they need nothing further.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's fall and Judas's ruin are the two halves of the same night, and the difference between them is the most important distinction in the chapter. Both men were sorry. Matthew says Judas was seized with remorse and threw the money back; then he hanged himself. Peter wept and lived. Paul named the difference exactly: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The test is not the intensity of the grief but its direction.

Verse 69 is one of the most explicit claims of identity in the Synoptic Gospels, and it welds two Scriptures together: Psalm 110:1, the Lord seated at God's right hand, and Daniel 7:13, the Son of Man receiving an everlasting dominion. The right hand is not geography but authority, and the sitting means the work is finished — under the old covenant the priests stood, because it never was (Heb. 10:11–12). And the timing is the audacity: from now on, said with his hands tied.

The council's reaction disposes of the notion that Jesus never claimed divinity and the church invented it. His enemies, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion and put it to him, and he affirmed it in the recognised idiom of assent. They convicted him under exactly the right law. They got one thing wrong, and it was the identity of the defendant.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 54 gives a better test than a resolution. Not would I deny Christ under pressure — everyone answers no, and Peter answered no out loud a few hours earlier. Ask instead: where do I habitually sit, whose fire am I warming myself at, and what have I already agreed, without saying so, never to bring up there? The distance always comes before the denial.

A Christian leader fails publicly — not a considered defection but a collapse of nerve under social pressure — and concludes he has forfeited his calling. Peter is the specific answer. The man who denied Jesus three times within earshot of him was restored, commissioned, and preaching Christ in that same city within seven weeks. The look did not end his ministry; it began it.

Verses 63–65 describe the commonest kind of cruelty, which has nothing ideological in it: a man who was available and could not retaliate, and it passed the time. He could have named every man in that room and the day of each one's death. He said nothing, and the power that made the hands striking his face was restrained by nothing but his own will to be struck.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.

Two details, and Luke has placed them with care.

Peter was following at a distance. The phrase deserves both halves. He was following, which is more than most of the others managed. Whatever is about to happen to him, it happens to the bravest man there.

And he was at a distance — far off. Close enough to see, far enough to be nobody. It is the precise position of a man who cannot bear to leave and cannot afford to be counted.

Most Christians recognise that distance, because most have stood at it. Not apostasy, and not confession either. The conversation where you did not lie about your faith but did not mention it. The invitation you declined without saying why. Following, and following at a distance, and telling yourself that the following is the important part.

Then the fire. Luke says they kindled it in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, and Peter sat down among them.

It was cold — John notes it (John 18:18) — and there is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm. But look at the picture. Inside the house his Lord is being interrogated. Outside in the yard Peter is sitting shoulder to shoulder with the men who brought him there, faces lit by the same fire, waiting to see what happens.

This is how the fall actually occurs, and it is worth naming because it almost never happens the way people expect. Peter did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm. He drifted to the safest available place, sat down with people whose questions he had no intention of answering honestly, and the denial came out of his mouth an hour later as the natural consequence of where he was sitting.

Nobody plans the third denial. They choose the fire.

Which gives a test more useful than a resolution. Not would I deny Christ under pressure — everyone answers no, and Peter answered no out loud a few hours earlier. Ask instead: where do I habitually sit? Whose fire am I warming myself at, and what have I already agreed, without saying so, not to bring up there?

The distance always comes before the denial (cf. Ps. 1:1; 1 Cor. 15:33).
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, 'This man also was with him.' But he denied it, saying, 'Woman, I do not know him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, This man also was with him. But he denied it, saying, Woman, I do not know him.

Luke has arranged the details so that the reader cannot miss how small the pressure was.

The accuser is a servant girl — a young female slave. In that courtyard she was the person with the least standing of anyone present. She commanded nothing, could arrest no one, and her word carried no legal weight whatever.

Seeing him as he sat in the light. He had put himself where the fire was, and the fire showed his face. He was recognised because he was warm.

And looking closely at him. She stares. That is all. There is no interrogation, no threat, no soldier.

And her charge is about as mild as an accusation can be: this man also was with him. Not he is one of the ringleaders. Not he drew a sword in the garden, which was true and would have been dangerous. Merely: he was with him.

Against which stood the promise made a few hours earlier, in a lit room, with bread in his hand: Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.

What he actually says is Woman, I do not know him.

Not I was not there — which would have been a lie about a fact. He denies the person. Three years of it: the boat, the storm, the mountain, the loaves, you are the Christ of God — and the sentence that comes out is that he does not know who the man is.

Here is what this passage is for, and it should be said without softening and without despair. The gap between what Peter sincerely intended and what Peter did was total, and the force required to open that gap was one stare from a slave girl.

Which is the reason self-confidence is not a Christian virtue and never has been. It was not that Peter overestimated his love; his love was real. He overestimated what love can do on its own in a cold yard at night when nobody is watching who matters.

And it is the reason the previous instruction was pray that you may not enter into temptation (v. 40). He did not pray. He slept, and then he sat down at the fire, and then a girl looked at him (cf. Prov. 28:26; 1 Cor. 10:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And a little later someone else saw him and said, 'You also are one of them.' But Peter said, 'Man, I am not.' And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, 'Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.' But Peter said, 'Man, I do not know what you are talking about.' And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a little later someone else saw him and said, You also are one of them. But Peter said, Man, I am not. And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean. But Peter said, Man, I do not know what you are talking about. And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

Luke keeps the clock running, and the times are the point. A little later. Then an interval of about an hour. This is not a moment of panic. It is a long, cold, deteriorating night, and Peter had an hour to get up and walk out and did not.

Watch the denials themselves, because each one is worse than the last and the movement is instructive.

The first denied the person: I do not know him. The second denies the fellowship: Man, I am not — I am not one of them, I have no part in that group. The third denies the subject altogether: I do not know what you are talking about. He has gone from disowning his Lord, to disowning the church, to pretending the whole matter is unintelligible to him.

Sin does not stay the size it started. The second lie exists to protect the first, and the third to protect the second, and each one costs less to tell than the one before.

The third accuser has evidence, and it is the sort nobody can deny for long: he too is a Galilean. Matthew adds that his accent gave him away (Matt. 26:73). Galilean speech was mocked in Jerusalem — country pronunciation, swallowed consonants. Peter could control what he said. He could not control how it sounded. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

Then: and immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

He is mid-sentence. Luke does not even let him finish. The lie is still in the air when the sound comes across the courtyard, and it is the most ordinary sound in the world — the sound that had woken him a thousand mornings on the lake.

That is worth pausing on. God did not send an earthquake or a voice from heaven to stop Peter. He used a bird doing at dawn precisely what birds do at dawn, and it was enough, because it had been named in advance.

The Gospels differ in who accused Peter: a servant girl, another girl, a man, the bystanders. In a crowded courtyard several people likely spoke at each turn, and each writer records the voices he chose. All four agree on the threefold denial and the rooster.

The Lord had said this day, and three times, and before the rooster crows, and every element of it happened exactly as spoken, in a yard where nobody was watching but the one who had said it (cf. Matt. 26:73; Num. 23:19).
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.' And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times. And he went out and wept bitterly.

Only Luke records the look, and it may be the most affecting sentence in his Gospel.

How it happened is not explained. Most likely the interrogation was in a room off the courtyard, or Jesus was being moved across it between hearings, and the timing put him within sight of the fire at the instant the rooster sounded. Luke does not fill the gap. He simply says: the Lord turned, and looked at Peter.

Everything depends on what was in that look, and the text tells us by what it produced. It did not produce despair, and it did not produce self-justification. It produced memory — and Peter remembered the saying of the Lord — and then tears.

So it was not a look of contempt. A man who has been looked at with contempt does not remember a promise; he remembers the contempt. What Peter remembered was words — including, we may be certain, the ones that came just before the prediction: I have prayed for you, and when you have turned again.

Which means the look said something like: I told you. And I knew. And nothing between us has changed.

Notice also that Jesus does not speak. He is bound, mocked and about to be beaten, and he has no opportunity to cross a courtyard and put a hand on his friend's shoulder. All he has is a turn of the head. It was enough.

And he went out and wept bitterly.

Now the distinction the reader most needs from this verse, because it is the one that decides everything. Judas also felt the weight of what he had done, and Matthew says he was seized with remorse and threw the money into the temple (Matt. 27:3–5), and then he went and hanged himself. Peter wept and lived. Both men were sorry. Only one of them was sorry towards God.

Paul named the difference exactly: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The test is not the intensity of the grief but its direction — whether the man turns towards the one he has wronged, or away.

Peter went out into the dark and wept, and within seven weeks was preaching Christ to thousands in the city that had killed him. The look did not end his ministry. It began it (cf. 2 Cor. 7:10; John 21:15–17).
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, 'Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?' And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, Prophesy! Who is it that struck you? And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.

These are not the Sanhedrin and not the Romans. They are the guards — the men holding him overnight, with hours to fill and a prisoner nobody would ask about.

They kept asking. This was not a moment of violence but a game, and the game had a rule. Blindfold him, hit him, and demand that he name the hand.

It is worth stating plainly what kind of cruelty this is, because it is the commonest kind. There is nothing ideological in it. These men had no theological objection to Jesus; most of them probably had no idea what he was accused of. He was simply available, and unable to retaliate, and it passed the time.

And the mockery aims at the one thing they had heard about him — that he was a prophet. So the sport is to prove he is not, by a test he cannot pass without playing along.

Which is where the irony becomes almost unbearable, and Luke has built the whole chapter so that his reader sees it. In the very hours that these men are demanding a prophecy, three of his prophecies are being fulfilled in that building. Judas has betrayed him with a kiss, exactly as foretold. Peter has denied him three times before the rooster, exactly as foretold — Luke has just told us so, a verse earlier. And the Son of Man is being numbered with the transgressors, as he said from Isaiah at the table.

They blindfold the only man in the room who can see anything, and then ask him to prove he can see.

And he does not answer. That is the thing to hold. He could have named every man in that room, their fathers, their homes and the day of their deaths. He says nothing. Isaiah had written it seven hundred years earlier: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

Consider what is being held back. Not merely a retort — legions (Matt. 26:53). The power that made the hands striking his face was under perfect control, restrained by nothing but his own settled will to be struck.

Blindfolded, bleeding, taunted by men whose names he knew, the Lord of glory took it in silence, for them and for us (cf. Isa. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, 'If you are the Christ, tell us.' But he said to them, 'If I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, If you are the Christ, tell us. But he said to them, If I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.

When day came. The daylight session is not an accident of scheduling; it is a repair. Jewish legal tradition held that capital cases could not be tried at night, and required that a verdict of death be reached only on a second day. The proceedings of that night had value for the prosecution but none in law, so at first light the council reconvenes to give the outcome a lawful appearance.

That is the shape of the thing to notice. This is not a mob. It is a formal body, following a procedure, producing a record — and the procedure has been arranged around a verdict decided days before (v. 2). The most respectable machinery in Israel is being operated correctly in order to kill the Son of God.

Then the question: If you are the Christ, tell us.

It sounds like an inquiry and it is not one. Luke records nothing before it — no charge read, no evidence presented (Matthew and Mark tell how the false witnesses failed to agree). The council does not want information; it wants a sentence it can take to Pilate.

And Jesus says so, in two clauses that are entirely without bitterness and quite unanswerable. If I tell you, you will not believe. That is not a guess; it is a description of a settled state. They had seen a man born blind receive sight, a paralytic walk, and Lazarus come out of a tomb, and their response had been to plan another death (John 11:53). A further sentence from him was not going to move anything.

And if I ask you, you will not answer. This is a direct reference to what had already happened. He had asked them a question in that same temple earlier that week — was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? — and they had refused to answer it (20:1–8). They had form.

So he declines to perform. He will not supply an answer to men who have already demonstrated that answers make no difference to them, and there is a solemn warning in that for anyone who treats the claims of Christ as a debate to be prolonged rather than a matter to be settled.

But he does not stay silent, and what he says next is not a defence. It is a claim so large that the council will need nothing else (cf. Luke 20:1–8; John 8:45–47).
verseByVerse.note: A night hearing had no legal standing; the council met formally at daybreak.

verseByVerse.quote: But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.

He has just told them that answering their question is pointless. Then he answers it, and gives them far more than they asked for.

Two Scriptures are folded into one sentence, and every man in that room would have heard both. Seated at the right hand is Psalm 110:1 — the LORD says to my Lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool — a psalm the scribes read as messianic and could not fully explain, as Jesus had shown them earlier that week (20:41–44). The Son of Man is Daniel 7:13, the figure who comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away.

Put together, they make a claim no mere Messiah could make. Israel expected a deliverer. Israel did not expect a man to sit down on God's own throne.

The right hand is not about geography. It is the position of the one who exercises the king's authority, and to be seated there is to have the business settled. Under the old covenant the priests stood, day after day, offering the same sacrifices that could never take away sins — there were no chairs in the tabernacle, because the work was never finished. The letter to the Hebrews makes the point precisely: when Christ had offered a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb. 10:11–12).

And the timing is the audacity of it. From now on. Not after some future vindication — from this moment, in this room, with his hands tied and his face bruised and a death sentence being drafted.

They think they are trying him. He tells them the throne is already occupied and the enthronement begins tonight.

Which is where the reader should simply stop and look at him. The council of Israel is sitting in judgment on a bound provincial, and the bound provincial is the one Daniel saw coming with the clouds, to whom all peoples and nations and languages are given, whose dominion is everlasting and shall not pass away. He is not on his way to the throne by way of the cross despite it. The road to that seat runs through Golgotha, and he is walking it on purpose.

He said it standing before men who would kill him for it, and it was true when he said it, and he has not left that throne since (cf. Ps. 110:1; Heb. 10:11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: So they all said, 'Are you the Son of God, then?' And he said to them, 'You say that I am.' Then they said, 'What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they all said, Are you the Son of God, then? And he said to them, You say that I am. Then they said, What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.

They heard it. That is the first thing to note, and it disposes of a modern idea that will not survive this paragraph — that Jesus never claimed to be divine and the church invented it later. His enemies, sitting in front of him, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion from what he had just said, and put it to him as a question.

Are you the Son of God, then? The then is doing real work: it means so it follows that. They have understood v. 69 correctly. A man who takes the seat at God's right hand is claiming a relation to God that no creature has.

You say that I am.

English readers sometimes hear evasion in that, and it is not. It is a recognised idiom of affirmation — the equivalent of those are your words, and they are correct. The council's own reaction settles the question beyond argument: if the answer had been a dodge, they could not have said we have heard it ourselves from his own lips. They took it as a yes because it was one.

And there may be more in it. The Greek is egō eimi — I am — the words God gave Moses at the bush for his own name (Exod. 3:14), and the phrase Jesus had used before in a way that made men pick up stones (John 8:58).

What further testimony do we need? The trial ends without proof of any crime, because there was never one. In Luke no witness is called; in Matthew and Mark the false witnesses fail to agree. No act is established. He is condemned for saying, truthfully, who he is.

Which is the deepest irony in Luke's passion narrative, and he lets it stand without comment. The charge is blasphemy — a creature claiming the honour of God. The charge would be entirely just, and the sentence entirely correct, if the man in the dock were anyone else. They convicted him on exactly the right law. They only got one thing wrong, and it was the identity of the defendant.

And so the innocent is condemned by the guilty, on his own true testimony, so that the guilty might one day be acquitted on his.

Who was responsible for Jesus’ death? A small group of leaders handed him over, and Rome executed him; Jew and Gentile together, as the church confessed (Acts 4:27–28). Behind them all stood God’s plan, and the sins of everyone he came to save. It gives no ground for blaming the Jewish people as a whole, and Peter, preaching to Jerusalem, said they had acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17).

He could have said less and lived. He told them the truth about himself, knowing precisely what it would cost, because the truth about himself was the whole reason he had come (cf. Exod. 3:14; 1 Tim. 6:13).

Follow him into the house that he enters <sup>11</sup> and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>12</sup> And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.” <sup>13</sup> And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>14</sup> And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. <sup>16</sup> For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” <sup>17</sup> And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, “Take this, and divide it among yourselves. <sup>18</sup> For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” <sup>19</sup> And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” <sup>20</sup> And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. <sup>21</sup> But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. <sup>22</sup> For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” <sup>23</sup> And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this. <sup>24</sup> A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors. <sup>26</sup> But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. <sup>27</sup> For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves. <sup>28</sup> “You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, <sup>29</sup> and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, <sup>30</sup> that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>31</sup> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, <sup>32</sup> but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” <sup>33</sup> Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” <sup>34</sup> Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.” <sup>35</sup> And he said to them, “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.” <sup>36</sup> He said to them, “But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. <sup>37</sup> For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.” <sup>38</sup> And they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” And he said to them, “It is enough.” <sup>39</sup> And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. <sup>40</sup> And when he came to the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>41</sup> And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” <sup>43</sup> And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. <sup>44</sup> And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. <sup>45</sup> And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, <sup>46</sup> and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>47</sup> While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, <sup>48</sup> but Jesus said to him, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” <sup>49</sup> And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” <sup>50</sup> And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. <sup>51</sup> But Jesus said, “No more of this!” And he touched his ear and healed him. <sup>52</sup> Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? <sup>53</sup> When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” <sup>54</sup> Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. <sup>55</sup> And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. <sup>56</sup> Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, “This man also was with him.” <sup>57</sup> But he denied it, saying, “Woman, I do not know him.” <sup>58</sup> And a little later someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” <sup>59</sup> And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.” <sup>60</sup> But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. <sup>61</sup> And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.” <sup>62</sup> And he went out and wept bitterly. <sup>63</sup> Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. <sup>64</sup> They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>65</sup> And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. <sup>66</sup> When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, <sup>67</sup> “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe, <sup>68</sup> and if I ask you, you will not answer. <sup>69</sup> But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” <sup>70</sup> So they all said, “Are you the Son of God, then?” And he said to them, “You say that I am.” <sup>71</sup> Then they said, “What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.”

23.title: The Trial, the Cross, and the Tomb
23.overview:
Luke 23 is the passion narrative — the most carefully and deliberately structured chapter in the Gospel, in which every detail carries theological weight. Jesus is tried before Pilate, sent to Herod, returned to Pilate, condemned, led to Golgotha, crucified between two criminals, and buried in a borrowed tomb. Through it all, Luke maintains a single consistent emphasis: Jesus is innocent. Pilate declares it three times (vv. 4, 14, 22). Herod finds no crime worthy of death (v. 15). The criminal on the cross confesses it (v. 41). The centurion declares it at his death (v. 47). This is the innocent One dying for the guilty.

Luke's crucifixion account is distinctive in several ways. He records Jesus's prayer for his killers: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (v. 34). He preserves the remarkable conversion of the dying criminal — the most compressed account of salvation in the Gospels: a man with minutes to live, who can offer nothing but a confession and a request, receives from Jesus the promise of paradise this very day. And he records the moment of Jesus's death as a prayer of trust: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” — drawn from Psalm 31:5, later used in Jewish tradition as a prayer before sleep, now spoken by the Son into the Father's hands in the sleep of death.

The chapter ends in mourning and waiting. The women from Galilee follow and see the tomb; they return and prepare spices and ointments; they rest on the Sabbath. The darkness before the dawn of resurrection is total — and in the silence, everything depends on whether the one who said “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” was speaking to Someone who was listening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Trial before Pilate and Herod
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sanhedrin cannot execute — only Rome can — so the charge has to change. In their own chamber they convicted him of blasphemy; before Pilate they produce three fresh charges built for a Roman ear: subversion, tax revolt, and a claim to a throne. The middle one is a flat lie, and they knew it when they said it: they had asked him that very question in the temple and heard him answer render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (20:25). The third is not a lie at all, and it is the one that will kill him.

Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him, hears a qualified affirmation, and reaches the correct verdict at once: I find no guilt in this man. He was not a soft man — Judea had already made him notorious for handling unrest badly — and he had crucified rebels before. He looks at this one and says there is nothing here.

The accusers press, mentioning Galilee as an aggravating detail, and Pilate hears in it an escape route: Galilee is Herod's jurisdiction. It is not a legal necessity; it is a door. Herod is delighted, because he has wanted to see Jesus for a long time (9:9) and is hoping for a sign. He questions him at length and gets nothing — the one occasion in Luke on which Jesus is asked a direct question by a ruler and answers not a word. Herod counts him as nothing, has him arrayed in a bright robe as a joke, and sends him back. And two enemies become friends over him that day, which is the world's unity at its truest: a peace built on a shared contempt.

Pilate then convenes a public assembly and states his finding for the record — not guilty of any charge, and neither did Herod find anything — and follows it, in the same breath, with I will therefore punish and release him. Flogging an innocent man as a concession is the hinge of the chapter, and it fails, as such compromises do.

The crowd asks for Barabbas: an insurrectionist and a murderer, guilty of precisely what Jesus was falsely accused of. Three times Pilate declares the innocence; three times the shouting overrules him. And their voices prevailed. He releases the guilty man and delivers Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke's repeated declarations of innocence are the theological spine of the chapter: Pilate three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod by implication (v. 15), the dying criminal (v. 41), the centurion (v. 47). This is not a deserved death, and the innocence is not a tragic detail — it is the point, because a guilty man dying settles nothing for anybody. Only an innocent one has a life to spare.

The Barabbas exchange is the atonement enacted in the street before it is accomplished on the hill. He is not pardoned and not reviewed; nothing about him changes. He is guilty when he goes into the cell and guilty when he walks out, and he goes free because another man dies in his place that day. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21).

Verses 23–25 must hold two truths at once. These men are entirely guilty — Peter says so to their faces at Pentecost. And behind the crowd stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32) — and Paul can say of the Father's act what Luke says of Pilate's: he was delivered up for our trespasses (Rom. 4:25). Pilate surrendered him to pressure; the Father gave him in love. The same handing over, and the difference is everything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Pilate's sin is not brutality but procedure. He never once says he believes Jesus guilty; he simply never gets round to acting on the fact that he is not. Every institution has that move and most of us have used it — refer it upward, wait for the review, ask for another opinion. The test is simple: is the referral a way of finding the right answer, or a way of not having to act on the answer you already have? Responsibility does not transfer. The man who tried hardest not to be involved has had his name said in the creed every Sunday for eighteen centuries.

Verse 5 is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people, and it alleges no crime — only disturbance. Honesty requires admitting that some of the trouble Christians attract is their own manner and not the gospel, and it is worth asking which before claiming this verse. But when the charge is that a man taught the truth and people were changed, the disturbance is real and the complaint is a compliment.

Herod is the frightening figure here, and not for the reason people assume. He had already had his word from God in John the Baptist and had killed him; what he wanted now was a trick. But the believer who fears that God has gone silent on him is answered by the shape of the case: Herod was not troubled about it. He was very glad. Anxiety about God's silence is itself evidence that he has not gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, 'We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.

They have to come to Pilate because they cannot do it themselves. Rome reserved capital punishment to itself in the provinces, and the Sanhedrin, whatever it had just voted, could not carry out a sentence of death.

Which means the charge has to change, because the one they convicted him on is useless here. In their own chamber the charge was blasphemy — he claimed to be the Son of God (22:70–71). A Roman governor would have thrown that out before lunch; provincial religion was not his business and every province had a god of its own.

So watch what they do with it. Three charges, freshly manufactured, each one designed for a Roman ear.

Misleading our nation — sedition. Forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar — tax revolt. Saying that he himself is Christ, a king — treason.

The middle one is a flat lie and they knew it when they said it. It was they who had come to him in the temple with that exact question, hoping to trap him, and he had answered render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (20:25). They had been standing there. Luke expects his reader to remember, because he recorded it three chapters ago.

And notice what the lie is made of. It is not invention out of nothing; it is his own words turned upside down. He had said pay it; they report that he forbade it. That is how false witness usually works — not fabrication, which is easy to disprove, but a true thing rotated until it points the other way.

The third charge is the interesting one, because it is not false. He is the Christ. He is a king. He had told them so a few hours earlier and it was the reason they wanted him dead. They accuse him of it here in the confidence that Pilate will hear the word king and stop listening.

So the Son of God is brought before the empire on two lies and a truth, and the truth is the one that will kill him.

They came for a man they could not execute and found a wording that would do it for them, and every word of it was chosen by men who knew better (cf. Luke 20:20–25; Ps. 35:11).
verseByVerse.note: The charges are framed for a Roman governor: sedition, tax refusal, and a rival king. The tax charge was false.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pilate asked him, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' And he answered him, 'You have said so.' Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, 'I find no guilt in this man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Pilate asked him, Are you the King of the Jews? And he answered him, You have said so. Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, I find no guilt in this man.

Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him. Sedition and tax revolt are secondary; a claimant to a throne inside a Roman province is a matter for the governor personally.

Are you the King of the Jews?

Note the phrasing, because it is not how a Jew would put it. No Israelite said the Jews when speaking of his own nation; it is an outsider's term. Pilate is asking a political question in political language, and what he means is: are you a pretender to a throne.

You have said so.

The same idiom he used before the council a little earlier — an affirmation, not a dodge. But it is a qualified one, and the qualification is the whole difference between the truth and what Pilate has in mind. Yes, and the word is yours. John's account fills in what Luke compresses: my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). It is a yes with the sword taken out of it.

And Pilate believes him, which is the striking thing. I find no guilt in this man.

He was not a soft man and he was not a fool. Judea had already made him notorious for handling unrest badly — he had marched imperial standards into Jerusalem and provoked a crisis, and had put down a protest over an aqueduct with clubs. He knew what a rebel looked like. He had crucified some. He looks at this one and says there is nothing here.

That verdict is the first of three in this chapter, and it is worth counting them as Luke sets them down, because he is building something. Pilate says it here (v. 4). He says it again in public after Herod (v. 14). He says it a third time under pressure (v. 22). Herod finds nothing (v. 15). A dying criminal says it (v. 41). A Roman officer says it (v. 47).

Six declarations of innocence, from Rome, from Herod's court, from a condemned man, and from the officer commanding the execution — and the execution proceeds.

Nothing about the cross is a miscarriage that God later put right. The innocence is not a tragic detail; it is the point. A guilty man dying would settle nothing for anybody. Only an innocent one has a life to spare (cf. 1 Pet. 3:18; Heb. 4:15).
verseByVerse.note: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, saying, 'He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent, saying, He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.

The verdict was not what they came for, so they change tactics. They were urgent — the word means to insist, to press hard, and the ESV uses the same English again at v. 23, when the pressing turns into shouting.

What they say has been carefully adjusted. Notice the geography: from Galilee even to this place. That is not a description of a teaching itinerary; it is a threat assessment. Galilee was the province that produced insurgents. The name of Judas the Galilean and his revolt was still current in Jerusalem — Luke records a member of that very council naming him in a speech a few years later (Acts 5:37). To tell a Roman governor that a Galilean has been stirring people up all the way to the capital is to say the word rebellion without having to prove it.

And there is one word in the sentence which is not a lie. Teaching. That is exactly what he had been doing, every day of that week, in the temple, in the open, in front of them.

So here is the accusation stripped down: he has been teaching, in public, and people have listened. They cannot produce an act. They can only produce an effect.

Which is worth registering, because it is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people and it has not changed in twenty centuries. Nobody has to allege a crime. It is enough to allege disturbance — that the message is divisive, that it upsets people, that things were calmer before.

Sometimes that charge is fair, and honesty requires saying so. Christians can be needlessly abrasive, and quite a lot of the trouble some believers attract has nothing to do with Christ and everything to do with the manner of the man carrying his name. It is worth asking, before claiming any of this passage, whether the offence being caused is the gospel's or your own.

But when the accusation is what it is here — that a man is teaching the truth and people are being changed by it — the disturbance is real and the complaint is a compliment. He was doing it. Judea was not the same. The rulers were right about the effect and wrong about everything else.

He stirred up the people, and he did it by telling them the truth, and it is still the only thing he has ever been guilty of (cf. Acts 17:6; Luke 12:51).

verseByVerse.quote: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.

The accusers meant Galilee as an aggravating detail. Pilate hears it as an escape route.

Galilee was the territory of Herod Antipas, a client ruler under Rome, and Antipas was in Jerusalem for the festival as the ruling family generally was. So there is a technically defensible administrative argument available: the accused is another jurisdiction's problem.

It is not a legal necessity. The offence, if there were one, was alleged to have occurred in Judea, and Pilate had every authority to try it. He is not applying a rule. He is looking for a door.

And what makes this so recognisable is that the door is entirely procedural. He does not release Jesus, which is what his own verdict required. He does not condemn him, which the evidence would not support. He transfers the file.

That is the characteristic sin of this chapter and it is not brutality. It is the sin of a man who knows exactly what is right, does not want to pay for it, and finds a mechanism that lets him postpone the decision without ever having made a wrong one. There is no point in the whole narrative at which Pilate says I believe this man is guilty. He simply never gets round to acting on the fact that he is not.

Every institution has this move and every one of us has used it. Refer it upward. Wait for the review. Ask for another opinion. It looks like diligence, and it is sometimes genuinely diligence — but the tell is simple, and it is worth applying honestly: is the referral a way of finding the right answer, or a way of not having to act on the answer you already have?

And responsibility does not transfer. Pilate discovered this in the only way that matters. He tried to get the case off his desk on a Friday morning in Jerusalem, and the church has said his name in the creed every Sunday for eighteen centuries: suffered under Pontius Pilate. Of all the men in that story, the one who was trying hardest not to be involved is the one whose name is fixed to it for ever.

He sent the case away and kept the guilt (cf. Jas. 4:17; Prov. 24:11–12).
verseByVerse.note: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and was in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.

Herod Antipas is delighted, and Luke has prepared this moment for a long time.

This is the man who had John the Baptist arrested, kept him in prison, liked listening to him, and then had him beheaded to save face at a birthday party. Luke has already told us that when reports of Jesus reached him, Herod was perplexed, and said John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things? — and he sought to see him (9:9). He got his wish on the last morning of Jesus's life.

He was hoping to see some sign done by him. There is the whole man in one clause. He does not want teaching, and he certainly does not want repentance; he has had that offered and killed the man who offered it. He wants a display. Jesus has been reduced, in the mind of a king, to an entertainment that has finally been secured.

So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.

Not one word. It is the only occasion in Luke's Gospel on which Jesus is asked a direct question by a ruler and says nothing at all — and this from the Christ who answered scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, lawyers, a Samaritan woman, a Roman centurion and a thief.

The silence is not sulking and it is not fear. It is the answer. Herod had already had his word from God, in the person of the greatest prophet born of woman, and had put him in a cell and then in a grave. There was nothing further to be said, and the mercy of God does not perform on request.

Which raises the question the passage exists to raise, and it deserves care because it frightens people. Does God ever stop speaking to a man?

He does, and Scripture says so more than once. But the fear that a sensitive believer carries — that this has happened to him — is answered by the very shape of the case. Herod was not anxious about it. He was very glad. A man who is troubled that God may have gone quiet has, in that trouble, the evidence that he has not.

The tragedy of Herod is not that he never met Jesus. He met him, face to face, and had nothing to ask him but a request for a trick (cf. Luke 9:9; Matt. 12:39).

verseByVerse.quote: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.

The chief priests have followed him across the city. They are not going to let the case out of their sight, and Luke gives them an adverb: vehemently. The word suggests strain — men raising their voices, pressing, working at it.

They have to work at it, because the accused is not helping. There is nothing to answer, so the volume has to do what the evidence cannot.

Then Herod's response, and it is worse than a verdict. He does not condemn him. He finds him ridiculous.

Treated him with contempt. The Greek is exouthenēsas — to count as nothing, to reckon at zero. It is not hatred; hatred at least concedes that its object matters. This is the judgment of a bored man who has been offered a miracle-worker and received a silence, and has decided the whole thing was beneath him.

And so the soldiers get their turn, and then comes the robe.

Arraying him in splendid clothing — bright, shining, gorgeous. A royal robe, thrown over a prisoner as a joke, because he had been accused of claiming a throne. Dress him up and send him back across town in it so that everyone in the street can see the king.

This is the first of the mockeries and every one that follows will have the same shape. The soldiers will offer him sour wine and call him king (v. 37). Pilate will nail a title over his head (v. 38). Matthew records a crown made of thorns and a reed for a sceptre. In every case the mockery consists of treating him as what he actually is.

They put a bright robe on the King of kings in order to laugh, and every thread of it was true. He was a king. He was going to a throne. The road to it went through that courtyard, and he walked back across Jerusalem in the mocking robe without taking it off or saying a word.

The one who counted him as nothing was standing in front of the one by whom all things were made, wearing the crown he had murdered a prophet to protect (cf. Isa. 53:3; Phil. 2:7–9).

parallels.desc: a similar mockery by Pilate’s soldiers

verseByVerse.quote: And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.

A single sentence, easily read as a footnote, and Luke has put it there because he wants it seen.

We are not told the cause of the quarrel. Something in the long friction between a Roman governor and a client ruler sharing a border — jurisdiction, revenue, an insult, an incident. Luke does not care about the cause. He cares about the cure.

What healed it was Jesus. Not his teaching, and not any appeal for peace. Pilate had sent the prisoner over as a courtesy, Herod had sent him back with a joke attached, and the two men found in that exchange something they could share. They discovered they could work together, and what they had in common was that neither of them would take him seriously.

That is a real observation about the world and it has not dated. Contempt is one of the most efficient bonding agents available to human beings. Two people who agree on nothing will warm to each other instantly over a third party they both find absurd, and the friendship will feel genuine while it lasts, because the pleasure is genuine. Office politics runs on it. So does a good deal of family life. So, at certain periods, has a great deal of public discourse.

And Luke, who has read his psalms, knows exactly what he is recording. Peter and John would quote it in prayer a few weeks later, naming both these men: why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed (Ps. 2:1–2; Acts 4:25–27).

The psalm says gathered together, and here is the gathering — a governor and a tetrarch who could not stand each other, reconciled over the body of the Son of God, on the day they killed him.

It is a small, sordid, entirely believable detail, and it is the world's unity at its truest: a peace built on a shared refusal.

They became friends that day, and the price of the friendship was already being carried up a hill outside the city (cf. Ps. 2:1–2; Acts 4:27).

parallels.desc: the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, 'You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.

Pilate convenes a formal assembly and puts his finding on the record, and he does it with unusual care.

Note the structure of the sentence. He restates their charge in their own words — you brought me this man as one who was misleading the people — then states the procedure — after examining him before you — and then delivers the finding: not guilty of any of it.

Before you. He is establishing that the examination was not conducted in a back room. They were present. They heard it. There is no room for anyone afterwards to claim the governor rushed it.

This is a man building a defensible file, and he is doing it because he already suspects he is going to need one.

And that is the tragedy of Pilate in one motion. He is being scrupulous about the record and careless about the man. Everything he does from here is aimed at ensuring that when this goes wrong, it will not be attributable to him — and none of it is aimed at the only thing his own verdict required, which was to open the door and let an innocent man walk out.

He had the authority. That is what makes it damning. A Roman prefect in a province held the power of the sword and answered to the emperor, not to a crowd. Nothing whatever prevented him from dismissing the case except the calculation of what it would cost him.

Which is worth putting to yourself in the smaller currency most of us deal in. There is a difference between not knowing what is right and knowing it and pricing it. Pilate knew. He held a hearing, reached the correct conclusion, announced it publicly — and then began negotiating with people who had no standing to negotiate with him.

The moment a man starts asking what the right thing will cost, the answer has usually already been decided, and the asking is the decision.

He said the words that should have ended it, and then he kept talking (cf. Prov. 29:25; Jas. 4:17).

parallels.desc: I find no guilt in him

verseByVerse.quote: Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.

The first two sentences are the high-water mark of the trial. A second authority has examined him and found nothing; the governor states it aloud; and then, in the plainest words used by anyone that day, nothing deserving death has been done by him.

And then, in the same breath, without any transition at all: I will therefore punish and release him.

Read the two halves against each other, because the joint between them is where the whole chapter turns. The word is therefore. He has established innocence, and the conclusion he draws from innocence is a flogging.

The verb is paideusas, which literally means to discipline or instruct — a chillingly domestic word for what was involved. Roman flogging was not a formality. The lash was weighted, men died under it, and Pilate proposes it here as a concession: something to give the crowd, so that they will accept the release.

There is no version of justice in which this is a defensible sentence, and Pilate knows it. He is not confused about the law. He is bargaining, and what he has put on the table is somebody else's back.

Which names the exact mechanism by which decent men do monstrous things, and it is almost never a single decision to do evil. It is a series of small settlements, each one presented as the reasonable middle course between two extremes. He will not release the prisoner and he will not condemn him; he will do something in between, and the something in between is to have an innocent man beaten.

The compromise fails, as compromises with this kind of pressure always do, and it fails for a reason worth naming. Once Pilate conceded that innocence was not a protection, there was no longer any principle left in the room to stop at. If the man can be flogged though innocent, the argument against crucifying him though innocent is only a matter of degree, and the crowd could do arithmetic.

He offered them half of an innocent man to save the other half, and within ten verses they had all of him (cf. Isa. 53:5; Prov. 17:15).
verseByVerse.note: To “punish” here means a flogging.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all cried out together, 'Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas'— a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all cried out together, Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas — a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.

A reader following in a modern Bible will notice something here and should be told plainly what it is: the text jumps from verse 16 to verse 18, and verse 17 appears only as a note at the foot of the page — Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.

Nothing has been removed from Scripture. The explanation is a matter of history and it is reassuring rather than otherwise. Verse numbers are not inspired; they were added in the sixteenth century, long after the New Testament was written, and they were fitted to the printed Bibles then in use. Since that time far older copies have been found — copies centuries closer to the apostles than anything available to the men who numbered the verses — and in the oldest of them this sentence is not there. It appears in later copies, and it looks very much like a helpful marginal explanation of the Passover custom, added by a scribe so the reader would know why a release was expected, which a subsequent copyist then wrote into the text.

So the translators face a choice, and the honest one is the one they took: leave the number, print the words in the note, and tell the reader exactly what the evidence is. A Bible that quietly renumbered to hide the gap would be a less trustworthy Bible, not a more trustworthy one. What is displayed here is not damage to the text but the care with which it has been kept.

And nothing in the account depends on it. The custom is attested by Matthew, Mark and John independently, and the story runs perfectly without the sentence.

Now the shout itself. Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas.

Luke will not let the reader past the choice without naming what Barabbas was: an insurrectionist and a murderer. Insurrection is exactly what the leadership had charged Jesus with in v. 2 — misleading the nation, subverting Caesar. Pilate is being asked to release the man who had actually done what the innocent man is accused of doing.

The crowd is asked to choose between the guilty man and the innocent one. They pick the guilty one, and the Son goes to the cross that had been prepared for him.

Somewhere in Jerusalem that morning a condemned murderer was let out of a cell without explanation and told he could go home, and another man went to the beam with his name on it. The whole gospel happened to Barabbas before it happened to anybody else (cf. Isa. 53:6; 2 Cor. 5:21).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 17: “Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting, 'Crucify, crucify him!' A third time he said to them, 'Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting, Crucify, crucify him! A third time he said to them, Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.

Luke keeps count deliberately: a third time. Three declarations of innocence from the bench, and three refusals from the floor.

They kept shouting — it did not stop. And what they shout has stopped being an argument. There is no charge in it, no accusation, no reasoning. Two words, repeated: crucify, crucify. A crowd that has reached this state is not being persuaded and cannot be answered, because it is no longer making a case.

Against which Pilate puts a question that ought to have ended everything. Why? What evil has he done?

It is the right question. It is the only question. And nobody answers it — not in Luke, not in Matthew, not in Mark, not in John. The question hangs there in the middle of the loudest morning in Jerusalem's history and no one supplies a reply, because there is not one.

So consider what has actually defeated the governor of Judea. Not evidence, which does not exist. Not law, which is entirely on the other side. Not force, since he commands the only soldiers present. Noise. He is beaten by volume, and he knows it, and he capitulates anyway.

Which is a fact about crowds worth holding on to, because most people will never face a mob and almost everyone will face its smaller relatives. A room in which one view is being expressed loudly and confidently exerts a pressure that has nothing to do with whether the view is true, and the pressure works on people who can see perfectly well that it is not true. That is the whole mechanism, and Pilate is its most famous casualty.

The test, when it comes, is never can I see what is right. Pilate could see it and said so three times. It is whether you can still say it when saying it is expensive and the room has already decided.

He asked the right question and did not wait for an answer, because he had begun to prefer the noise to the silence that would have followed it (cf. Exod. 23:2; Gal. 1:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.

And their voices prevailed.

Four words, and they are among the bleakest in the Gospel. Not the evidence prevailed. Not the law, not the truth, not the verdict that had been given three times by the only man with authority to give it. The voices.

Prevailed — overpowered, had the mastery. Here the mastery belongs to a crowd.

Then: Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. A demand, a request, a petition. Luke's phrasing is almost administrative, and the flatness is the point. A judicial murder is being processed as a granted application.

Two things need saying, and they must be held together or the passage will be misread.

The first is that these men are entirely guilty. Not one of them is excused by anything that follows. Peter would say so to their faces at Pentecost — you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23) — and he was not being rhetorical.

The second is that behind the crowd, behind Judas's price and the council's hatred and Pilate's cowardice, stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32). And Paul's verb there is the same verb Luke uses of Pilate in the next breath — paradidōmi, to hand over, to deliver up.

Pilate handed him over to a mob. The Father handed him over for us. The identical act, and the difference is everything: one was a surrender to pressure, the other was love with nothing forced about it at all.

Which is where a reader may take comfort who has been handed over by someone — abandoned to a situation by a person who had the power to stop it and would not pay the cost. That is exactly what happened here, to him, and he did not merely permit it. He was being given, at the same moment, by a Father who had never wanted anything less and gave him anyway (cf. Acts 2:23; Rom. 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.

Luke has already told us who Barabbas was. He tells us again, in the same sentence as the release, and he uses the same two words: insurrection, murder. He wants no reader to reach the end of the trial without knowing precisely who walked out of that building alive.

Picture it, because it happened to a real man on a real morning. A condemned prisoner is lying in a cell in Jerusalem waiting to be crucified, and there is no doubt about his sentence or his guilt. He hears a crowd outside and cannot make out the words. Then a door is unlocked, and a soldier tells him he is free to go, and he walks out into the daylight past a beam being carried in the other direction.

He is not pardoned. That is the thing to be exact about. Nobody has said he is innocent, nobody has reviewed his case, and nothing about him has changed. He is guilty of insurrection and murder when he goes in and guilty of insurrection and murder when he comes out, and he goes free because another man is going to die in his place on that particular day.

There is no better picture of it anywhere in Scripture, and it happens in the street before it happens on the hill.

Which is the sentence the New Testament will spend the rest of its length unpacking: he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him (2 Cor. 5:21). Christ died for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).

And then the last clause, which Luke has placed at the very end where it will be felt: but he delivered Jesus over to their will.

Not to justice. Not to a sentence. To their will — to whatever they wanted, which is the most complete abandonment a court can perform. The governor stops governing. From this point, until a centurion speaks at the end of the chapter, no authority in Jerusalem stands between the Son of God and whatever men feel like doing to him.

Does this passage blame the Jewish people as a whole? No. Luke names the actors: a handful of leaders, a crowd stirred up by them, Pilate and his soldiers. Jesus himself, his apostles and the first thousands of believers were Jews. The charge of collective or inherited guilt, used to justify hatred of Jews, has no ground here.

Every Christian who has ever understood the gospel has understood it by finding himself in this verse. Not among the crowd, though we would have shouted with them. In the cell — guilty, sentenced, unchanged, and inexplicably outside in the sunlight, because they took somebody else instead (cf. 2 Cor. 5:21; 1 Pet. 3:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — The Way of the Cross and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Simon of Cyrene is seized out of the crowd — coming in from the country, with plans for the day, compelled by a soldier as any provincial could be. Luke says he carried it behind Jesus, which is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship in 9:23. He did not volunteer. He is the only human being who ever carried the cross of Christ, and Mark's readers in Rome evidently knew his sons by name.

Women follow, mourning and wailing, and Jesus turns round on the way to his own execution to speak to them about their future: do not weep for me, but for yourselves and your children. What is coming to Jerusalem will be so terrible that barrenness — the standard image of shame in that world — will be called a blessing, and people will ask the mountains to fall on them (Hos. 10:8). Then the proverb: if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

At the place called The Skull he is crucified between two criminals, one on his right and one on his left — the arrangement two disciples had once requested for themselves (Mark 10:37), and the fulfilment of numbered with the transgressors (22:37). Luke records the execution in four words and describes none of it.

The first word from the cross is a prayer for the men driving the nails: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, while the squad gambled for his clothes exactly as Psalm 22:18 had said they would.

Three groups mock, and all three say the same thing: the rulers (let him save himself), the soldiers (if you are the King of the Jews — the wilderness temptation in its original form), and one of the criminals. Above his head Pilate's notice states the only charge ever proved against him: that he is the King of the Jews.

And the other criminal turns. He fears God, agrees with his own sentence, declares Jesus innocent, and asks only to be remembered. He is told he will be accompanied — today you will be with me in paradise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do raises the question of how far ignorance mitigates. It is real and partial: they knew they were killing a man, not that they were killing the Author of life. The plea is not an acquittal — if it acquitted them no forgiveness would be needed — but a ground on which to ask. And Luke shows the prayer answered in his own second volume: Peter tells that same city you acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and three thousand are forgiven in a day.

The mockery of v. 35 states the atonement with perfect accuracy and no understanding. He could not save himself and save others; not for lack of power, since legions were available for the asking, but because the two were mutually exclusive.
