To come down would leave the work undone and everyone he came for still under sentence. He saved others; himself he did not save.

The dying criminal answers works-based salvation and deathbed scepticism at once. He cannot be baptised, cannot make restitution, cannot demonstrate any fruit, and has no time in which to try. He brings a verdict on himself, a recognition of who Jesus is, and a request. And the reply exceeds it at every point: not someday but today; not somewhere but with me. There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 26 is one of the most useful in the chapter, because most crosses in a Christian life are not chosen. People speak of taking up a cross as a decision, and sometimes it is — but the diagnosis was not chosen, nor the redundancy, nor the decade of caring for a parent. It was laid on. Simon is not recorded as willing, and he may have resented every step, and he is the man who walked closest behind the Son of God.

Verses 27–28 correct the commonest sentiment attached to the cross: a devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, dwelling on the physical agony, producing much sympathy and no repentance. He declines it on the road. And grief that fastens on someone else's situation can be a way of not looking at your own — it is far easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face one's own household.

Verses 39–40 demolish the assumption that suffering makes people better. Two men, identical pain, identical distance from Jesus and from death, and Matthew says both began by reviling him. One changed. Proximity to Christ saved neither of them; one of them looked at him.

And v. 43 is for anyone who thinks it is too late — the man in a hospice, raised near the church and never committed, wanting to know whether there is time. There was no baptism, no restitution, no probation, no changed life, because there was no life left in which to change. There was a confession and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.

A condemned man carried the crossbeam himself — not the upright, which stood permanently at the execution ground, but the patibulum, a beam of perhaps thirty or forty kilograms lashed across the shoulders. That a stranger had to carry it suggests what the flogging had already done to him.

So a soldier looks along the crowd for someone to take it, and the man he picks is a stranger. Coming in from the country — arriving, on his way somewhere, with plans for the day. Cyrene was in North Africa, in what is now Libya, and had a large Jewish community; Simon may well have come a great distance for this Passover. A Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry a load, and did.

He had no say in it whatever. He did not volunteer, he was not asked, and he had no idea who the man in front of him was.

Then Luke chooses his words with great care: to carry it behind Jesus. Behind him. That is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship in this same Gospel: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (9:23). Luke has recorded the metaphor; now, on the road, he shows a man doing it literally, and doing it against his will.

Which is where this verse becomes one of the most useful in the chapter, because most of the crosses in a Christian life are not chosen. People speak of taking up a cross as though it were a decision, and sometimes it is. But the illness was not chosen. The child's diagnosis was not chosen. The redundancy, the parent who needs care for a decade, the marriage that became a long endurance — none of that was volunteered for. It was laid on.

Simon says nothing in the Gospels. He is not recorded as willing, and he may have resented every step. And he is the only human being who ever carried the cross of Christ.

Mark, writing later, adds a detail that reads like a signature: Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), which means that when Mark's readers in Rome heard the name they knew the family. Something happened to that household. The man pressed into service that morning did not stay a bystander.

He set out for a festival and was handed a load he had not asked for, and it turned out to be the nearest any man has ever walked behind the Son of God (cf. Luke 9:23; Mark 15:21).
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said, Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.

Something must be said first about the walk itself, because it is easy to picture and hard to hold. He has been awake all night. He has been beaten by the temple guard, mocked by Herod's soldiers, and flogged by Roman ones. He is walking through his own capital city carrying nothing now, because a stranger has the beam, towards a place where he will be nailed down.

And he turns round to speak to a group of women, about their future.

They are mourning and lamenting — the words describe formal, audible grief, beating the breast and wailing. Some of it may have been professional; it was a recognised practice at executions. But there is no hint that Jesus thinks it insincere, and he does not rebuke them for it.

He redirects it. Do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.

Not because his suffering is not worth weeping over. Because theirs is nearer than they think, and because pity is not what he needs from anyone.

That is worth sitting with, since it corrects the commonest sentiment attached to the cross. There is a kind of devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus — a Good Friday emotion that dwells on the physical agony and produces a good deal of sympathy and no repentance at all. He declines it here, on the road, in the middle of it. He did not go to Golgotha to be pitied.

And the pastoral point in the redirection is sharper than it looks. Grief that fastens on someone else's situation can be a way of not looking at your own. It is far easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face the state of one's own household, and the tears are real either way, and only one of them costs anything.

These women wept for a man being executed. Within forty years their city would be under siege and their children in it, and the thing that would bring that about was happening in front of them, and they had not seen it.

He is on the way to be crucified, and what occupies him is what will become of the women crying at the roadside and the children holding their hands. Even the last mile is spent on somebody else (cf. Luke 19:41–44; John 11:35).

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For behold, the days are coming when they will say, Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed! Then they will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us.

To understand how terrible the first sentence is, you have to know what childlessness meant in that world.

It was the standard image of grief and shame. Sarah, Rachel, Hannah — the Old Testament is full of women weeping over it, and Elizabeth, at the start of this very Gospel, says of her pregnancy that the Lord had taken away her reproach among people (1:25). To be barren was, in the plain speech of the culture, a misfortune everyone could see.

Jesus says a day is coming when women will be congratulated on it.

That is not a statement about the value of children. It is a measurement, and it is the most precise measurement of horror available in that language: a day so bad that the worst thing that could happen to a woman will look like an escape. What is being described is a siege, and specifically the siege of the year 70, when the mothers inside those walls watched what happened to their children before it happened to them.

He is not saying it with satisfaction. He wept over this city on the way in (19:41), and he is weeping over it on the way out.

Then the second image, and it is a quotation. They will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us. That is Hosea 10:8, spoken over the northern kingdom on the eve of its destruction. It is the cry of people who would rather be crushed than face what is coming — and John heard it again, at the end of all things, from the kings and the great and the slave and the free, hiding in the rocks from the face of him who is seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb (Rev. 6:16).

Which tells you what the fear in that sentence really is. Being buried under a mountain is not the thing they are fleeing. It is the alternative they prefer.

And it is worth saying plainly what that means, because it is the reason the cross exists. There is a day coming when men will find the presence of God unbearable, and the terror of it is not that he is cruel but that he is holy and they are not.

He was walking towards a hill to make sure the people crying by that road would never have to say those words (cf. Hos. 10:8; Rev. 6:16).

parallels.desc: they shall say to the mountains, “Cover us”

verseByVerse.quote: For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

It has the sound of a proverb, and it probably was one. Green wood is living wood, full of sap; it resists a fire and has to be forced to burn. Dry wood is dead, and it goes up at a spark.

So the question is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and it is a form of reasoning the rabbis used constantly: if this is what happens in the unlikely case, what will happen in the likely one?

The application is not stated, which is why readers have taken it two ways, and both are worth having.

The first reads the green wood as Jesus himself. If Rome and the temple authorities between them will do this to a man who is entirely innocent — the living wood, the one who gave no cause at all — what will they do when the city is full of genuine insurgents and the case against it is real? The answer came in forty years, and Jerusalem burned.

The second reading goes deeper and does not exclude the first. If the judgment of God falls like this on the green wood — on the one man in history who never deserved a stroke of it — what will it be when it falls on the dry? That is not a comparison anyone can make comfortably. What is happening on that hill is the wrath of God against sin, absorbed by a substitute, and even so it produced three hours of darkness and a cry that has never stopped echoing.

Which supplies the answer to a question people raise honestly and often: is the judgment of God not out of all proportion? Would a loving God really deal with sin so severely?

Look at what he was prepared to do to his own Son rather than overlook it. Nobody who has understood Calvary can go on thinking that God takes sin lightly or that he deals with it cheaply. The cross is not evidence that judgment is mild. It is the fullest evidence available of how serious it is — and, in the same act, the reason a sinner need never face it.

He is being led out to be burned as the green wood, so that the dry might be spared the fire (cf. Ezek. 20:47; 1 Pet. 4:17–18).
verseByVerse.note: A proverb: if this is done to the innocent (green wood), what will happen to the guilty (dry wood, ready to burn)?

parallels.desc: every green tree and every dry tree

verseByVerse.quote: Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

Note how little Luke says about the crucifixion itself. There they crucified him. Four words. No description of the nails, no account of the pain, nothing of what the Gospel writers could easily have supplied and every one of them declined to.

They were writing for a world that knew exactly what crucifixion was and had seen it. Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty, and said the very word should be kept away from the ears of Roman citizens. It was designed for slaves and rebels, and its purpose was not death, which could be achieved faster, but public degradation over a period of hours. Every reader of Luke's Gospel could fill in the detail unaided, and Luke's restraint is a kind of reverence.

What he does record is the company. Two others, who were criminals — and then, so it cannot be missed, one on his right and one on his left.

That is exactly the arrangement two of his disciples had once asked for. Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory (Mark 10:37). They had no idea what they were requesting. When the places either side of him were finally filled, they were filled by convicted criminals on crosses.

And a chapter earlier he had quoted the reason from Isaiah: he was numbered with the transgressors (22:37; Isa. 53:12). Here is the numbering, carried out by a Roman work detail who thought they were simply executing three men that morning. He is not placed near them. He is placed among them, in the middle, in the central position, the place one would give a ringleader.

The place that is called The Skull. Luke gives the meaning rather than the Aramaic name, for readers who would not know that Golgotha means this. Nobody now knows why it was called that.

What was in the middle of that row was not a criminal among criminals. It was the Lord of glory, put in the worst place on the hill by men who were guessing, and it was the right place, because he had come to stand exactly where the guiltiest stands (cf. Isa. 53:12; Mark 10:37).
verseByVerse.note: Luke uses the Greek name, “The Skull”; the Aramaic is Golgotha.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' And they cast lots to divide his garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. And they cast lots to divide his garments.

The first word from the cross in Luke is a prayer, and it is a prayer for the men holding the hammer.

Father. He is still calling him that. Nothing that these men are doing to him has changed one syllable of how he addresses God.

Forgive them, for they know not what they do. The ignorance is real and it is partial. They knew they were killing a man; they did not know they were killing the Author of life (Acts 3:15). That is not offered as an acquittal — if it acquitted them, no forgiveness would be needed — but as a ground on which to plead. It is the intercession of a High Priest, begun before he is dead, on behalf of people who have not asked and are not sorry.

Then the flat sentence about the soldiers gambling for his clothes. The condemned man's garments were the perquisite of the execution squad; this was routine, a small bonus at the end of a shift. And it is Psalm 22:18 happening in front of them, word for word: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.

This sentence too carries a footnote in most modern Bibles: some manuscripts do not have it. The same honesty applies as at Gethsemane. It is missing from several early copies and present in many others, and scholars have long noticed how odd its absence is, since no evangelist is more preoccupied with forgiveness than Luke. One suggestion is that a later scribe, looking back on the destruction of Jerusalem, concluded that the prayer had gone unanswered and quietly let it fall. If so, he stopped reading too soon.

Because Luke wrote a second volume, and in it he tells you what became of this prayer. Peter stands up in that same city, before some of the same people, and says you crucified and killed him — and then, I know that you acted in ignorance (Acts 2:23; 3:17), which is precisely the ground Jesus pleaded here. Three thousand of them are forgiven in a day. And Stephen, dying under the stones, prays it again (Acts 7:60); he had heard where it came from.

Nailed to a piece of wood by men who were dividing his clothes before he was dead, the Son of God spent his first breath asking his Father to let them off (cf. Ps. 22:18; Acts 3:17).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer “Father, forgive them.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, 'He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!

Luke separates two groups, and the distinction will matter by the end of the chapter.

The people stood by, watching. No mockery is attributed to them. They are silent, and they will go home beating their breasts (v. 48). It is the rulers who scoff.

And what they say is true. That is the extraordinary thing about it. He saved others — they are not disputing it. These are men who had watched a paralytic get up, a leper cleaned, a widow's son sit up on his bier, and they concede all of it in the middle of a taunt, as an agreed fact not worth arguing about. Their case against him was never that the works had not happened.

Then the sneer: let him save himself.

They think they have found the flaw. A saviour who cannot get himself off a cross is no saviour, and the logic feels unanswerable, and it will be repeated by the soldiers in two verses and by one of the criminals in four. It is the settled assumption of the whole hill: real power rescues itself.

And it is exactly wrong, and the reason is one of the most important things in this Gospel. He could not save himself and save others. Not because the power was lacking — he told Peter in the garden that legions were available for the asking — but because the two things were mutually exclusive. To come down would be to leave the work undone and every person he came for still under sentence.

So the mockery states the gospel with perfect accuracy and no understanding whatever. He saved others; himself he did not save. That is not a taunt. It is the doctrine of the atonement, put into words by his enemies, at the foot of the cross, on the day it was accomplished.

They gave him a title too, without meaning it: the Christ of God, his Chosen One. That is Isaiah's word for the Servant — behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (Isa. 42:1). They were quoting the Father's own delight in his Son back at him as an insult.

He heard them say it and stayed where he was, and every hour he stayed was a decision, and the decision was for them (cf. Isa. 42:1; Ps. 22:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, 'If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!

A different group, a different reason, the same sentence.

The rulers mocked him theologically; they cared what he claimed. The soldiers have no theology in this at all. They are an execution detail, they have done this many times, and this is how they pass the afternoon.

Sour wine was the cheap, vinegary ration wine that soldiers drank, thin and sharp. Offering it to a crucified man was a joke about hospitality: here you are, your majesty, a drink. Whether it ever reached his lips Luke does not say. And this too is Psalm 22 territory, and Psalm 69: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink (Ps. 69:21).

If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself.

That opening word should stop a reader who has been reading Luke from the beginning. If you are. It has been said to him before, twice, in the wilderness, by a voice that knew perfectly well the answer: if you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread; if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here (4:3, 9).

Luke closed that scene with a sentence he clearly intended his reader to keep: the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13). This is that time. The temptation in the wilderness and the temptation at Golgotha are the same temptation, put in the same grammatical form: prove it by using your power on your own behalf.

And the answer is the same both times: he will not use his power for himself. In the wilderness he answered with Scripture; on the cross he answers with silence.

Which is worth carrying into ordinary life, because the shape of that temptation is universal even when the stakes are small. If you really were what you claim to be, you would not be in this position. It is what a Christian hears in a hospital corridor, in a marriage that has gone cold, in the fourth month of looking for work. If God loved you, this would not be happening.

The Son of God heard it at the beginning of his ministry and at the end of his life, and both times he declined to prove anything, and he was never once not the Son of God while he was being told he might not be (cf. Luke 4:3–13; Ps. 69:21).
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

verseByVerse.quote: There was also an inscription over him, 'This is the King of the Jews.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was also an inscription over him, This is the King of the Jews.

The titulus was standard Roman practice: a board carrying the charge, either hung round the condemned man's neck on the walk or fixed above him at the site, so that everyone who passed knew what he was dying for and thought twice.

So this is a legal document. It states the crime. And the crime, as recorded by the Roman government, is that he is the King of the Jews.

Which means the only formal charge ever proved against Jesus of Nazareth is that he is who he said he is.

Pilate wrote it, and he wrote it as a sneer — not at Jesus so much as at the men who had forced his hand. John records the sequel: the chief priests objected, and asked him to change it to this man said, I am King of the Jews, and Pilate refused with the flattest sentence he ever spoke: what I have written I have written (John 19:21–22). He had lost every round of that morning. He won this one, and it was the only thing he got right.

John also tells us it was written in three languages — Hebrew, Latin and Greek: the tongue of revelation, the tongue of government, the tongue of the world's commerce and thought. Every category of person in that crowded festival city could read it in his own words.

And there is a note that should be made about the wording, because a careful reader comparing Gospels will spot it. Matthew has this is Jesus the King of the Jews; Mark has the King of the Jews; John has Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. This is what happens when four witnesses report a sign in three languages: each gives the substance, and the substance is identical in every one. It is the ordinary variation of honest testimony, and a set of accounts that agreed word for word would be more suspicious, not less.

Above his head, in the three great languages of the earth, the government of Rome published the truth about him without meaning to, refused to withdraw it, and left it there until he died (cf. John 19:19–22; Rev. 19:16).

verseByVerse.quote: One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, 'Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!' But the other rebuked him, saying, 'Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us! But the other rebuked him, saying, Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?

Two men, the same distance from Jesus, the same distance from death, in identical pain, hearing identical words. And they go opposite ways.

That is the whole point of the paragraph, and it demolishes something people believe without examining it: the idea that suffering makes people better, or that a man facing death will naturally turn to God. These two were nailed up on the same morning by the same soldiers for the same kind of crime. Suffering did not soften one of them. Matthew tells us that at the start both were reviling him (Matt. 27:44), so the difference between them emerged during those hours, on the wood.

Look at what the first man wants. Save yourself and us. He has repeated the rulers' sneer and added a request to it — and the request is entirely about his circumstances. Get me down. He is not asking for mercy; he is asking for rescue, and there is no sign that he has any interest in Jesus beyond what Jesus might be able to do about the nails.

That is a real form of religion and it is very common. It appears in hospital wards and in financial crises, and it is perfectly sincere at the time. It wants God to change the situation. It has no view at all about God.

Then the second man, and his first recorded words are not about Jesus and not about himself. Do you not fear God?

There it is — the beginning of everything. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Prov. 9:10), and here is a dying criminal, hours from the end, with no religious education anyone knows of, arriving at the one thought that no amount of pain had produced in the man on the other side.

And note what he says next: since you are under the same sentence of condemnation. He is not lecturing from above. He includes himself. The whole rebuke rests on we are both getting what we deserve, which is a thing almost nobody says about themselves.

Two men were crucified beside the Saviour of the world, close enough to touch him. Proximity saved neither of them. One of them looked at him (cf. Prov. 9:10; Rom. 3:18).
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first.

verseByVerse.quote: And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.' And he said, 'Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong. And he said, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.

What this man says in two sentences is a more exact statement of the gospel than most Christians could manage on a good day, and he is dying while he says it.

We indeed justly. He does not minimise, excuse, blame his upbringing or plead circumstances. He says the sentence is right. Whatever he had done, he agrees with the court.

But this man has done nothing wrong. One more voice for the innocence, and this one from a man who has nothing to gain by saying it — the fifth declaration in the chapter and the only one made by someone who was dying at the time.

Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.

Consider what he is looking at while he says it. Not a miracle-worker with crowds around him. A man nailed to a beam a few feet away, bleeding, mocked by everyone present, visibly dying, with a Roman notice above his head calling him a king as a joke.

And he calls him by his name — Jesus, with no title; others who used the name added one, Jesus, Master (17:13), Jesus, Son of David (18:38) — and asks to be included in a kingdom that not one visible thing on that hill supports the existence of.

That is faith with everything stripped off it. He has no Bible, no baptism, no church, no time, and no capacity to do a single good work; he cannot even come down and be useful. He has nothing to bring except an honest verdict on himself and a conviction about who the man beside him is.

And notice how modest the request is. Not save me, not give me a place. Just: remember me. Do not let me be forgotten when you come into what is yours.

Which is worth measuring against how many Christians pray — carefully, apologetically, working out in advance whether they have the standing to ask. This man had no standing whatever, and asked anyway, and the whole New Testament doctrine of grace is standing behind him: while we were still weak, at the right time, Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6).

Everyone else on that hill was talking about him. One man, guilty and condemned and out of time, talked to him (cf. Rom. 5:6–8; Ps. 51:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him, Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

He asked to be remembered. He is told he will be accompanied.

Take the answer in its three parts, because each one gives more than was requested.

Today. Not at the resurrection, not after some interval of waiting, not once something further has been done about him. Before the sun goes down on the worst day of his life, this man will be somewhere else entirely. There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one: the same day, straight through, from a Roman cross to paradise.

You will be with me. That is the heart of it. Paradise is not described, and it does not need to be. Paul says the same thing when he thinks about his own death — his desire is to depart and be with Christ, which is far better (Phil. 1:23) — and again, away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:8). Whatever else heaven contains, its content is a person, and the man who has him has everything in it.

Paradise. The word is Persian in origin and means a walled garden, a royal park. The Greek Old Testament uses it of Eden, and Revelation places the tree of life in the paradise of God (Rev. 2:7). So the last promise Jesus makes before he dies is that the garden is open again, and he says it to a criminal.

You may meet an alternative punctuation of this verse, since some who deny that the dead go consciously to be with Christ move the comma: truly I say to you today, you will be with me in paradise — making today describe when Jesus spoke rather than when the man would arrive. The Greek carries no punctuation, so the question is fair. But truly I say to you is a fixed formula on Jesus's lips, used scores of times across the Gospels, and not once does it take a trailing today. It would be a pointless thing to say in any case; the man could hardly have supposed he was being answered on some other day. Read it as it stands.

And read it to anyone who thinks it is too late. A man raised near the church but never committed, dying in a hospice, wanting to know whether there is time — this verse is the answer, and it is unqualified. There was no baptism, no restitution, no probation, no evidence of a changed life, because there was no life left in which to change. There was a confession, a recognition, and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb, and his soul went to the Father: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (v. 46). That is why he could promise the thief today. The creed’s “descended into hell” has been read in different ways; the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) understands it as the anguish he suffered on the cross, and others as his remaining under the power of death until the third day. It does not mean he went to suffer further after saying It is finished.

In Luke's account the last person Jesus speaks to before he commits his spirit to the Father is a convicted criminal, and he speaks to him about a garden (cf. Phil. 1:23; 2 Cor. 5:8).
verseByVerse.note: “Paradise” is a Persian word for a walled garden, used for the dwelling of God’s people after death.

parallels.desc: the tree of life in the paradise of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–56 — The Death of Jesus and the Burial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From noon until three the land goes dark — not an eclipse, which is impossible at Passover full moon and never lasts three hours, and Luke names no mechanism, only that the sun's light failed. The Old Testament supplies the meaning: I will make the sun go down at noon (Amos 8:9), and the three-day darkness over Egypt, the plague just before the night the firstborn died. This is the sign of judgment, falling this time on one man.

And the temple curtain tears — a woven hanging some sixty feet high, guarding the room nobody entered but the high priest, once a year, with blood. Matthew and Mark record the direction: from top to bottom, where no hand could reach.

Then, with a loud voice — which is not how crucified men died — Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. It is Psalm 31:5, which later Jewish tradition used as a prayer before sleep, with one word added: Father. And he breathes his last.

The centurion praises God and says certainly this man was innocent. The crowds who came for a spectacle go home beating their breasts — the gesture of the justified tax collector in 18:13. And his acquaintances and the women from Galilee stand at a distance, watching, having been there through all of it.

Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented to the verdict and who was waiting for the kingdom of God, goes to Pilate and asks for the body — a request that publicly identifies him with a man executed for treason. He takes it down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a rock-cut tomb where no one had ever been laid.

It is the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath is beginning. The women see the tomb and how the body was laid, go home and prepare spices against the clock — and then, with the jars ready by the door, rest according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.theology:
The darkness is judgment language, not grief. The blow that fell on Egypt and was promised on Israel falls here on the Lamb, in the middle of the day, in the dark, so that it need not fall on anyone else.

The tearing of the veil is the architecture of the atonement. For fifteen centuries the message of that room was not yet, and not you. Hebrews states the consequence exactly: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20). It was torn from the top and has never been mended.

A reader who knows Matthew and Mark will notice that Luke has no cry of dereliction. He has not softened the death. No Gospel records the horror more directly — the agony, and the sweat like blood and the strengthening angel that are Luke's alone. He shows the abandonment in Gethsemane and chooses trust for the last moment, and both are true. Stephen would die with almost the same words on his lips (Acts 7:59).

And the burial is not an appendix. Paul lists it among the four facts of first importance — died, was buried, was raised, appeared (1 Cor. 15:3–5) — because it proves he was dead and supplies the address at which he stopped being dead. A rock-cut tomb with one entrance, previously unused, its location known to a named councillor and to the women watching. Isaiah had written it: and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 47 rewards a reader who compares Gospels. Mark's centurion says truly this man was the Son of God; Luke's says certainly this man was innocent. A man watching an execution says more than one sentence, and each writer keeps the one that serves his account. Luke is building a case for a Roman reader who will shortly read a second volume full of Christians before magistrates: the founder of this movement was examined by every competent authority, pronounced innocent by all of them, and executed anyway.

Verse 49 is for anyone whose service to Christ has been the kind nobody records. The women who had followed him from Galilee had been funding the ministry out of their own means (8:2–3). The twelve are gone; the women are still on the hillside. They see him die, they see where he is buried and how, and they are the first human beings on earth to hear that he is alive — and in that world their testimony would not have been admitted in a court.

Verse 54 leaves a gap that the church has never quite known what to do with, and a great deal of Christian life is lived in it: not the crisis and not the deliverance, but the flat interval afterwards when nothing whatever is moving and prayers appear to land nowhere. Nothing here suggests that gap means abandonment. The most decisive work in history had just been finished, and from the outside on the Saturday it looked exactly like defeat.

And vv. 55–56 describe faithfulness with no feeling left in it. The spices are made up, the tomb is a walk away, every instinct says go — and the commandment says rest, so they rest a whole day with the jars by the door. Anyone who has kept turning up, praying with nothing in it, holding the line in the dark, is standing where those women stood, and should notice how their Saturday ended.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.

The sixth hour is noon and the ninth is three in the afternoon. So this is not evening coming on early. It is darkness at the brightest part of the day, for three hours.

It was not an eclipse, and it is worth saying so, because the suggestion is sometimes made and it will not work. Passover falls at full moon, and a solar eclipse is impossible at full moon; besides, no total eclipse lasts more than a few minutes. Luke says only the sun's light failed, and leaves the mechanism alone.

What he does not leave alone is the meaning, because the Old Testament had already supplied it. Amos, prophesying judgment: I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9). And Egypt had three days of a darkness that could be felt (Exod. 10:21–22) — the plague immediately before the Passover lamb.

So the sign is not grief. It is judgment, and the reason for the darkness is the reason the sky went black over Egypt: God is dealing with sin. Only this time the blow does not fall on a nation. It falls on one man, in the middle of the day, in the dark.

Then the second sign, and it happens across the city, where nobody at Golgotha can see it.

The curtain of the temple was torn in two. Later Jewish tradition describes the veil as an enormous woven hanging, a handbreadth thick and many cubits high. Behind it was the Most Holy Place, and behind it nobody went — one man, one day a year, with blood, and not without trembling (Lev. 16; Heb. 9:7). The whole architecture of Israel's worship was a statement that the way in was closed.

Matthew and Mark note the direction of the tear: from top to bottom. Nobody could reach the top. That is not vandalism and it is not an earthquake's doing; it is a verdict, and it was passed from above.

The letter to the Hebrews spells out what it meant, and there is nothing left to add to it: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

For fifteen centuries the message of that room was: not yet, and not you. In one afternoon, while the sky was dark and a man was dying outside the walls, God tore it from the top and left it hanging open, and it has never been mended (cf. Amos 8:9; Heb. 10:19–20).
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!' And having said this he breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! And having said this he breathed his last.

With a loud voice. That is not how crucified men died. Death on a cross came by exhaustion and suffocation, and the end was a fading, not a shout. Every observer on that hill would have known the difference, and one of them is about to say so.

And the words are a quotation. Psalm 31:5 — into your hand I commit my spirit — which later Jewish tradition came to use as a prayer before sleep — the last thing said before the dark.

He added one word to it. The psalm says into your hand I commit my spirit. He says Father.

Now, a reader who knows Matthew and Mark will notice something missing, and it should be faced rather than passed over. In those Gospels the cry from the cross is my God, my God, why have you forsaken me — and Luke does not have it. Has he softened the death?

He has not, and the answer is in what he has already given. No Gospel records the horror of that night more directly than Luke's: the agony in the garden, and the sweat like blood and the angel sent to strengthen him, which are his alone. Luke has shown the abandonment; he shows it in Gethsemane. What he chooses for the last moment is the other true thing about it, and both are needed. The cry of dereliction tells you what the cross cost. This word tells you how it ended.

Because it ended in trust. After the darkness, after whatever passed in those three hours that no writer describes, the last sentence out of his mouth is the one a child says to a father he is certain of.

Commit is paratithemai — to deposit, to place something valuable into safe keeping. It is not resignation. It is a man handing something over to someone he trusts, on purpose.

And Stephen, dying, would say almost the same words, addressed to Jesus (Acts 7:59), because that is what the first Christians did with this sentence: they took it as the pattern for how to die.

He was not overcome. He called out, in a strong voice, at the moment of his choosing, in the words of a child going to sleep — and then he gave up his spirit, which nobody was able to take from him (cf. Ps. 31:5; John 10:18).
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition used Psalm 31:5 as an evening prayer.

parallels.desc: into your hand I commit my spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, 'Certainly this man was innocent!' And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, Certainly this man was innocent! And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.

The first voice after the death belongs to the officer in charge of killing him.

A centurion commanded around eighty men and had generally served for years to get there. This one had run executions before; it was routine duty for the garrison. He is the last man on that hill who could be moved by sentiment, and Luke says he praised God.

Certainly this man was innocent. The Greek is dikaios — righteous, or innocent, depending on the setting. A reader coming from Mark will notice he says something different there: truly this man was the Son of God (Mark 15:39). A man watching an execution says more than one sentence, and each writer has kept the one that serves his account.

But Luke's choice is not arbitrary, and it is the key to his whole passion narrative. Count the verdicts. Pilate, three times (vv. 4, 14, 22). Herod, by implication (v. 15). The dying criminal (v. 41). And now the officer commanding the execution squad — the last voice, and a Gentile one.

Luke is building a case, and building it for a Roman reader. Theophilus is about to read a second volume in which Christians are dragged before magistrates in city after city and the charges keep collapsing. So Luke establishes at the outset that the founder of this movement was examined by every competent authority, pronounced innocent by all of them, and executed anyway. That is not a smaller confession than Mark's. It is the same verdict from the other side: Mark tells you who he was, and Luke tells you what Rome could not find in him.

Then the crowd. They came for a spectacle — a viewing, a show — and they go home beating their breasts.

That gesture has appeared once before in this Gospel, and it is worth remembering where. A tax collector, standing far off, who would not lift his eyes to heaven, beat his breast and said God, be merciful to me, a sinner — and Luke says that man went home justified (18:13–14).

They came to watch a man die and went home striking their chests, and some of them would be in Jerusalem seven weeks later when Peter stood up and told them whose death they had watched (cf. Luke 18:13–14; Acts 2:37).
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers but in practice about eighty. Beating the breast was a sign of grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.

At a distance. Luke used that phrase of Peter in the high priest's courtyard (22:54), and he uses it again here of everyone who loved him.

They are there. That has to be said first, because it is more than can be claimed for most of the men: after the arrest the apostles scattered, and Luke does not put a single one of them at the foot of the cross by name. Whoever these acquaintances are, they came, and they stayed until it was over, and they watched a man they loved die slowly over hours without being able to do anything at all.

And they stood at a distance, which is where soldiers keep the friends of a condemned man, and where grief itself often stands.

Then the second group, and Luke names their qualification: the women who had followed him from Galilee.

He has told us about them before, and it is one of the least-noticed sentences in his Gospel. Mary called Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod's household manager, Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means (8:2–3). They had been travelling with him for the length of the ministry, and they had been paying for it.

They are still there. The twelve are gone, the crowds have gone home beating their breasts, the rulers have said their piece and left — and the women who came down from Galilee are standing on a hillside outside Jerusalem watching the end of everything they had given three years to.

Luke is quietly building something, and the payoff is a few verses away and again at dawn on Sunday. They see him die. They see where he is buried, and how (v. 55). They come back with the spices. The unbroken chain of witness that runs from the cross to the empty tomb is held, in this Gospel, entirely by women — whose testimony, in that world, carried no weight in a court at all.

Which is a word for anyone whose service to Christ has been the kind nobody records. They funded a ministry, walked its roads, buried its founder, and were the first human beings on earth to hear that he was alive (cf. Luke 8:2–3; Ps. 38:11).

parallels.desc: my friends stand aloof from my plague

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.

Luke introduces him carefully, the way you introduce a witness whose credentials matter.

A member of the council — of the Sanhedrin, the body that had condemned Jesus a few hours earlier. So the man who is about to take the body down belonged to the body that condemned Jesus.

Who had not consented to their decision and action. Luke goes out of his way to clear him, and the phrasing is precise: not the decision only, but the action. He had not gone along with it.

Which raises the honest question, and the passage does not hide from it. Where was the dissent when it might have mattered? John says Joseph was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). He was a good man who had been keeping his convictions private in a chamber where they would have cost him everything, and by the time he acts, the man he might have defended is dead.

That is worth saying plainly, because the temptation is to flatten Joseph into a hero or dismiss him as a coward, and he is neither. He is the far more recognisable thing: a believer who was afraid, whose silence had a real cost, and who then did the bravest available thing at the moment he had left.

He was looking for the kingdom of God — waiting expectantly, as Simeon had waited for the consolation of Israel at the start of the Gospel (2:25). Joseph belongs to that company — the people in Israel who had not given up, who read the prophets and expected God to act.

And here is what his waiting had come to on that Friday afternoon: the man he had privately hoped was the answer was hanging dead outside the city, and his own council had arranged it.

What he does next is not the act of a man whose hope has survived intact. It is the act of a man doing the last decent thing available to him for someone he had believed in. And it turned out to be the thing that put the tomb, and its location, and its emptiness, permanently on the record (cf. John 19:38; Luke 2:25).
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.

Consider what that request cost him.

Crucified bodies were not usually surrendered. The whole point of the penalty was public and continuing degradation, and Roman practice was to leave the corpse for the birds or throw it into a common pit. To go to the governor and ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to identify yourself, on the record, with the treason. Joseph does it hours after the council he sits on has procured the execution, and he does it in person.

Whatever he had been keeping quiet, he is not keeping it quiet now. This is the most public act of his life, and it is performed for a dead man who cannot know about it.

And then the ordinary, terrible work. He took it down. Somebody had to draw the nails and take the weight of the body as it came free, and Joseph — a wealthy councillor, by Matthew's account — did it, or stood there while it was done, and then wrapped the body in linen with his own hands.

Every clause after that is doing quiet evidential work, and Luke knew exactly what he was writing.

A tomb cut in stone — not a shallow grave that could be disturbed, but a chamber hewn out of rock, with one entrance. Where no one had ever yet been laid — so that on Sunday morning there could be no confusion about whose body was missing, and no possibility that some other occupant was being mistaken for him. And the location known to a named member of the Sanhedrin, and to the women watching from a few yards away, and therefore checkable by anyone in Jerusalem who cared to walk out and look.

The burial is not a sad appendix to the crucifixion. Paul lists it among the four facts he says are of first importance: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared (1 Cor. 15:3–5).

It is there because it is the proof that he was dead, and because it is the address at which he stopped being dead. And Isaiah had put it in writing seven centuries before, in the same breath as the transgressors: and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9).

They laid the Author of life in a borrowed grave, in a hurry, before sundown, and the stone was rolled across a room that would be famous for being empty (cf. Isa. 53:9; 1 Cor. 15:3–4).
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone.

verseByVerse.quote: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.

One short sentence of chronology, and it explains the haste of everything around it.

The day of Preparation was Friday — the day on which everything for the Sabbath had to be done, because from sunset nothing could be. Food cooked, lamps lit, work finished. And the Sabbath was beginning: the first stars, the point at which the new day began by Jewish reckoning.

So Joseph and whoever helped him are working against a clock. There is no time to wash the body properly, no time for the full anointing, no time for anything but linen and stone and a rolled door. The women watching are noting exactly where it is, because they can see it is unfinished and they intend to come back.

And then the sun goes down, and nothing more can be done, and nothing more is done for a day and a half.

That silence is worth staying in rather than hurrying past, because Luke does not hurry past it and the church has never known quite what to do with it. Between the last verse of this chapter and the first verse of the next lies the emptiest space in the Bible. God had become man, and was dead, and was in a grave, and it was the Sabbath, and nobody knew anything.

There is a great deal of Christian life lived in that gap. Not the crisis, and not the deliverance — the flat interval afterwards, when the worst has already happened and nothing whatever is moving, and prayers go up and appear to land nowhere, and the only thing available is to keep the ordinary rules of an ordinary day while your heart is in pieces.

Nothing in this chapter suggests that gap is a sign of abandonment. The most decisive work in the history of the world had just been finished — it is finished, John records him saying — and from the outside, on the Saturday, it looked exactly like defeat.

How is Friday to Sunday “three days”? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day (cf. Esth 4:16 with 5:1), so three days and three nights (Matt 12:40) and on the third day mean the same span. All four Gospels say Jesus died on the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42), and some theories of a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion have arisen only to fit a literal count of hours.

The Sabbath came on, as it did every week, and the Lord of the Sabbath lay still and kept it (cf. Gen. 2:2; Heb. 4:9–10).
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday; the Sabbath began at sundown.

verseByVerse.quote: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

Three verbs, and they are the last three of the chapter: they saw, they prepared, they rested.

They saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Luke is being an historian again. They did not merely know which tomb; they watched the laying out, so that when they came back they would know what had been done and what had not. It is the observation of women who intend to finish a job.

Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. This is Friday evening, in the shrinking minutes before sunset, and they go home and start grinding and mixing.

Stay with what that means, because it is one of the most affecting details in the Gospel. They are preparing to anoint a corpse. They have no expectation whatever of a resurrection — he had told them, more than once, and they had not taken it in, and Luke will say so bluntly in the next chapter when the angels have to remind them. Everything they are doing is the work you do when hope is finished. And they do it beautifully, at speed, with care, for a man who cannot thank them.

Then: on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

Read that as obedience with nothing left to fuel it. The spices are made up and sitting in the house. The tomb is a walk away. Every instinct they have is to go — and the commandment says rest, so they rest, for a whole day, with the jars ready by the door.

Which is where this chapter leaves the reader, and it is exactly the right place. There is a kind of faithfulness that has no feeling in it at all. Nobody is watching. Nothing is being achieved. The obedience produces no comfort and changes nothing, and it is done because it is commanded and God is God.

Anyone who has kept going through a season like that — turning up, praying with nothing in it, holding the line on a Monday in the dark — is standing exactly where these women stood, and should know how their Saturday ended.

Does this mean Christians must keep the Sabbath? These women lived under the old covenant, and Christ had not yet risen. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17; Heb 4:9–10), and that from the next morning, the first day of the week, the church gathered on the day of resurrection.

They rested on the Sabbath with the spices ready, and every one of those jars was wasted, because before they could use them he was up and out and asking a woman why she was crying (cf. Exod. 20:8–10; Luke 24:1–5).

23.text: <sup>1</sup> Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. <sup>2</sup> And they began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” <sup>3</sup> And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>4</sup> Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no guilt in this man.” <sup>5</sup> But they were urgent, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.” <sup>6</sup> When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. <sup>7</sup> And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time. <sup>8</sup> When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. <sup>9</sup> So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. <sup>10</sup> The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. <sup>11</sup> And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate. <sup>12</sup> And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other. <sup>13</sup> Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, <sup>14</sup> and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. <sup>15</sup> Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. <sup>16</sup> I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>18</sup> But they all cried out together, “Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas”— <sup>19</sup> a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. <sup>20</sup> Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, <sup>21</sup> but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!” <sup>22</sup> A third time he said to them, “Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>23</sup> But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. <sup>24</sup> So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. <sup>25</sup> He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will. <sup>26</sup> And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus. <sup>27</sup> And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. <sup>28</sup> But turning to them Jesus said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. <sup>29</sup> For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ <sup>30</sup> Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ <sup>31</sup> For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” <sup>32</sup> Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. <sup>33</sup> And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” And they cast lots to divide his garments. <sup>35</sup> And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!” <sup>36</sup> The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine <sup>37</sup> and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” <sup>38</sup> There was also an inscription over him, “This is the King of the Jews.” <sup>39</sup> One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, “Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!” <sup>40</sup> But the other rebuked him, saying, “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? <sup>41</sup> And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” <sup>42</sup> And he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” <sup>43</sup> And he said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” <sup>44</sup> It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, <sup>45</sup> while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. <sup>46</sup> Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” And having said this he breathed his last. <sup>47</sup> Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, “Certainly this man was innocent!” <sup>48</sup> And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts. <sup>49</sup> And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things. <sup>50</sup> Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, <sup>51</sup> who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God. <sup>52</sup> This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>53</sup> Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid. <sup>54</sup> It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning. <sup>55</sup> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. <sup>56</sup> Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

24.title: Resurrection, Recognition, and Commission
24.overview:
Luke 24 is one of the most carefully constructed chapters in the New Testament. It moves through three episodes — the empty tomb, the road to Emmaus, and the appearance to the disciples in Jerusalem — each building on the last, each advancing the disciples' understanding from confusion to recognition to burning conviction to mission. The chapter does not merely report the resurrection; it shows how the resurrection makes sense of everything that has come before and commissions everything that comes after.

The Emmaus account (vv. 13–35) is Luke's unique contribution to resurrection narrative, and it is one of the most theologically rich passages in the entire Gospel. Two disciples, walking away from Jerusalem in bewilderment, encounter the risen Jesus — who does not reveal himself immediately but walks with them, opens the Scriptures to them, and is recognised only in the breaking of bread. The entire sequence is a model of Christian formation: Scripture opened, heart burning, Jesus recognised in the meal, and immediate return to the community to testify.

The final appearance in Jerusalem includes Jesus's most explicit post-resurrection teaching: that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms has been fulfilled; that repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations; that the disciples are witnesses; and that they must wait in Jerusalem for the power from on high. The chapter — and the Gospel — ends with the ascension and with the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God. Luke's Gospel that began in the temple (Zechariah at the altar of incense, 1:9) ends in the temple. The story is complete — and about to begin again in Acts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The previous chapter ended with jars of spices standing ready while the Sabbath was kept. This one opens with them being carried out at first light. Nobody grinds spices for a man they expect to be alive — which disposes of the theory that the resurrection was something wishful people talked themselves into. These women were carrying embalming materials, and their only practical worry was who would move the stone.

It was already moved. Luke describes no rolling, no earthquake, no angel heaving at it; he simply reports the state of things on arrival. And the stone was not moved to let him out — a body that would enter a locked room that evening needed no doorway. It was moved to let them in.

Then the first fact of the Christian faith, arriving as an absence: they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. Luke uses that full title here for the first time in the Gospel, and writes it over an empty shelf.

Two men in dazzling apparel ask the finest opening question in the New Testament: Why do you seek the living among the dead? It is not a rebuke but a reorientation — they have come to the right place with the wrong category. And the phrasing claims more than he is alive again: the living is a class, a permanent condition.

The remedy the angels give for bewilderment is not new information. It is old information that was not believed: remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee. He had — three times, plainly, with the details (9:22; 9:44; 18:31–33).

They remember, and that is the first act of Easter faith on record: they believe a promise before any appearance at all. Then they run to the eleven — the men who had abandoned him — and hand over the best news in the world, and are told it is an idle tale.

Peter gets up and runs. He sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, which no grave-robber ever left behind, and goes home marvelling — which Luke is careful not to call believing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The resurrection is a bodily event in space and time, and Luke is meticulous about the physical detail — the stone, the body, the cloths — because what is claimed is not the survival of a spirit but the raising of the one who died. Paul builds everything on it: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile; if he has, death is defeated and the future of the universe is different (1 Cor. 15:14–20).

That women are the first witnesses is one of the strongest historical arguments the Gospels contain. In that world a woman's testimony carried little weight in court, and pagan critics would later sneer at a religion resting on it. Every instinct of a forger would put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke names the women, reports that the apostles dismissed them as hysterical, and leaves it standing. Nobody invents a story that embarrasses their own leadership and undermines their own witnesses.

And the angels' remember is the hermeneutical key to the whole chapter. The failure to understand the resurrection is a failure to have believed the word already given. Everything that happened had been announced in advance; the only question was whether those who heard it would take it seriously.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women's walk to the tomb is obedience with no expectation attached. They were not going out to meet a risen Lord; they were going to finish a burial. A great deal of faithful Christian service has exactly that shape, and it does not make it less faithful — it was the people carrying the spices who were first at the empty tomb.

Verses 6–8 supply the most practical test in the chapter. Think of the thing that frightens you most at present, and ask what God has actually said about it in Scripture — not what you feel, but the words. Most Christians discover they know the verse, could quote it, and have not once thought of it since the trouble began. Faith rarely fails for lack of material. It fails for lack of memory.

Verse 11 is for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool. They were right, they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree.

And v. 12 names a real place on the road that is not a disqualification. Peter looked at the strongest evidence anyone had yet seen and went home wondering. Marvelling is not believing — but nobody who ran to the tomb stayed outside it for long.

verseByVerse.quote: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

The chapter before ended with jars of spices standing ready in a house while the Sabbath was kept. This one opens with the jars being carried out of the door.

At early dawn. They went as soon as the law allowed and as soon as there was light enough to see the path. Nobody asked them to. There was no duty here; the burial had been done, hurried but done. This is simply what love does when it has been made to sit still for thirty-six hours.

And every step of that walk was taken in the belief that they were going to a corpse. That is the thing to hold on to, because it disposes of the theory that the resurrection was a story wishful people talked themselves into. Nobody grinds spices for a man they expect to be alive. These women were not primed for a miracle; they were carrying embalming materials, and their only practical worry, Mark tells us, was who would move the stone for them.

And they found the stone rolled away.

Luke does not describe the rolling. He gives no earthquake, no angel heaving at it, none of the drama a storyteller would have supplied. He simply reports the state of things when they arrived: it was open, and it had been done by somebody else, before they got there.

Which is worth noticing, because the stone was not moved to let him out. A body that could enter a locked room later that evening did not need a doorway. It was moved to let them in.

Then the flat, devastating sentence: they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

That is the first fact of the Christian faith and it arrives as an absence. Not a vision, not a voice, not a shining figure — an empty shelf in a rock chamber, and three or four bewildered women holding jars they no longer have any use for.

Note the title Luke chooses at exactly this point: the Lord Jesus. He has not used that full form before in the Gospel. He writes it over the empty place where the corpse was supposed to be.

They had prepared everything necessary for the burial of a dead man and arrived to find the preparation unnecessary, which is what happens to all our careful arrangements when God has already acted (cf. Mark 16:3; 1 Cor. 15:3–4).
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, Why do you seek the living among the dead?

Perplexed — the word Luke used of the nations in perplexity in the Olivet discourse (21:25): no way through. They are standing in an open grave with no explanation available, and Luke says the messengers came while they were in that state, not after they had worked something out.

Two men, in dazzling apparel. Luke calls them men because that is what they looked like, and every reader knows what they were.

And the terror is the ordinary response. Every angelic appearance in this Gospel has begun with a frightened human being — Zechariah at the altar, Mary in Nazareth, shepherds on a hillside — and every one has needed to be calmed before anything could be said. Here the women go face down on the floor of the tomb.

Then the question, and it is the finest opening line in the New Testament.

Why do you seek the living among the dead?

It is not a rebuke, though it is sometimes read as one. It is a reorientation. They have come to the right place with the wrong category. Tombs are where the dead are, and everything about their errand was correct except its central assumption.

And the phrasing carries a claim no other sentence had yet made. Not he is alive again, which would put him back where he was. The living — a description, a class, a permanent condition. He has not returned to life. He has passed into a life that death has no further business with.

Which turns the question outward, and it has been doing its work on readers ever since. There are people who take Jesus of Nazareth seriously as a teacher, an example, a great moral figure of the past, and would be embarrassed to be thought unserious about him — and every one of those categories is a tomb. It is possible to hold him in the highest regard and still be looking for him in the wrong place, among the honoured dead, where he cannot be found because he is not there.

Matthew has one angel, Mark a young man, and Luke and John two; the women and the times differ too. Each Gospel is a selective, independent report, and “one” does not deny “two”. The women seem to have come in more than one group, and Luke himself says some of those who were with us went to the tomb (v. 24). All agree on the empty tomb, the women first, and the message that he had risen.

Two men in dazzling light stand in a grave at first light and ask a question that has never stopped being asked: what are you doing here, looking for him among the dead (cf. Rev. 1:18; Rom. 6:9).

verseByVerse.quote: He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.

Seven words, and everything turns on them. He is not here, but has risen.

The New Testament most often puts it as something done to him — he will be raised (9:22) — because the resurrection is the Father's verdict on the Son. God vindicated him. The tomb was not broken out of; it was opened from the throne.

And then, having announced the greatest news ever delivered to human beings, the messengers do something unexpected. They do not explain it. They tell the women to remember something.

Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee.

He had. Three times in this Gospel, plainly, with the details. The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22). Again after the transfiguration: let these words sink into your ears (9:44). Again on the road to Jerusalem, with the mockery and the spitting named in advance (18:31–33). Luke notes after the second and third that they did not understand, and that the saying was concealed from them.

So the angels' remedy for bewilderment is not new information. It is old information that was not believed when it was given.

That is worth sitting with, because it is the most practical sentence in the chapter. The women are standing in the worst confusion of their lives, and what they are handed is not an explanation of the present but a reminder of a promise made in Galilee, months earlier, on an ordinary afternoon, which they had heard and filed away and not taken seriously.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Think of the thing that is currently frightening you most. Now ask what God has actually said about it in Scripture — not what you feel about it, but the words.
