Most Christians discover in that moment that they know the verse, could quote it, and have not once thought of it since the trouble began.

Faith very rarely fails for lack of material. It fails for lack of memory, which is why God fills his book with commands to remember and gives his people bread and wine and says do this in remembrance of me.

He told them in Galilee, on the road, in the plainest words he had, and they were standing in an empty tomb before it occurred to them that he had meant it (cf. Luke 9:22; 18:31–33).

verseByVerse.quote: And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.

And they remembered his words. Five words, and they are the first act of Easter faith recorded by anyone.

Nothing has been proved to them. They have not seen him; that will come later and to others first. What they have is an empty tomb, a message from two figures they could not identify, and a sentence from Galilee suddenly coming back to them with everything in it that they had missed the first time.

And it is enough. They believe a promise, on the strength of a word they had already been given, before any appearance at all.

Then: returning from the tomb they told.

Notice how short the interval is. There is no reflection, no waiting to see, no discussion of whether they would be believed. They remembered, and they went, and the going was immediate.

And they went to the eleven and to all the rest, which is a phrase worth pausing over. The eleven are not named at the cross. They had slept in the garden, and Peter had denied him in a courtyard, and none of them had come to the tomb. The women had every human reason to nurse a grievance and none of it appears anywhere in the account. They ran to the men who had abandoned him, with the best news in the world, and handed it over.

So the first sermon of the Christian era was preached by women, on a Sunday morning, to a room of disillusioned men who did not want to hear it. Every proclamation since has had roughly the same shape.

And it is worth saying, since a good deal of Christian service goes unrecorded, that Luke has now tracked this group across three chapters without them once being in the foreground. They funded the ministry (8:3). They watched the crucifixion when the men had gone (23:49). They marked the tomb and how the body was laid (23:55). They rested on the Sabbath with the spices ready. They came at dawn.

They had been there for everything, and they were the first to be told, and the first to tell (cf. Luke 8:1–3; John 20:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.

Luke names them, and the naming is deliberate. In a document of this kind, names are checkable. Mary Magdalene, out of whom seven demons had gone. Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager (8:3) — a woman with a position, whose husband worked in the palace of the man who had mocked Jesus two days earlier. Mary the mother of James. These were living people with addresses when Luke wrote.

And then the apostles' reaction, which Luke reports without softening it at all: these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.

The word is lēros. It is a medical term in classical Greek for the babbling of a delirious patient, and it is the only time it appears in the New Testament. The apostles did not simply doubt the report. They dismissed it as the raving of women unhinged by grief.

Two things follow, and both matter.

The first is apologetic, and it is one of the strongest arguments the Gospels contain. If you were inventing a resurrection story in the first century, you would not do this. Under Jewish legal convention a woman's testimony carried little or no weight in court, and the surrounding pagan world was no better — a Greek critic of Christianity would later sneer at the whole religion as resting on the word of a hysterical female. Every instinct of a forger would be to put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke puts it in the hands of women whose report was rejected by the apostles themselves, and he names them.

Nobody makes up a story that embarrasses their own leadership and undermines their own witnesses. This detail is in the account because it happened.

The second is pastoral, and it is for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool. They were right, and they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree. Within the hour some of those same men would be running to a tomb.

The best news in the history of the world was delivered accurately by reliable witnesses and dismissed as nonsense by the men who had heard it predicted three times (cf. 1 Cor. 1:27; Luke 8:2–3).
verseByVerse.note: A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time; no one inventing the story would have made women the first witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened.

Everyone else stayed sitting. Peter ran.

This is the man whose last recorded act was to weep bitterly in a courtyard after denying three times that he had ever met Jesus of Nazareth. He has not been restored yet — that comes later in the day, in a meeting Luke will mention and refuse to describe. He has spent Friday and Saturday with the worst thing he ever did sitting on his chest, and the moment a rumour reaches him that the tomb is open, he is out of the door.

Which tells you something true about repentance that is easy to miss. Peter has every reason to hang back. Shame's instinct is always to withdraw, and if the report were true, he would have to face the man he had disowned. He ran anyway. Real sorrow for sin moves towards Christ, not away from him; that is the whole difference between Peter and Judas, and it is visible here in a pair of running feet.

He saw the linen cloths by themselves. Not disturbed, not gone, not taken. The wrappings lying there without a body in them, in a sealed chamber, with the spices still in them.

That is a detail no grave-robber ever left behind. Anyone stealing a corpse takes it as it lies; nobody unwraps a body in the dark and carries it out naked, leaving the valuable linen behind.

And he went home marveling.

Not believing. Luke is precise, and the honesty is a mercy. Peter looked at the strongest physical evidence any human being had yet seen and walked home wondering, with the thing not yet settled in him.

There is a whole class of people standing exactly there, and they should be told that it is a real place on the road and not a disqualification. Something has begun to move; the old explanations no longer fit; and faith has not yet arrived. Marvelling is not believing. But nobody who ran to the tomb was left standing outside it for long.

John tells the same story at greater length (John 20:3–10; cf. 2 Cor. 7:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the same Sunday, two disciples walk seven miles out of Jerusalem, going over the events again and again the way grief does. Jesus draws near and walks with them, and their eyes are kept from recognising him — deliberately and temporarily, until in v. 31 they are opened.

He asks what they are discussing, and they stop dead in the road, downcast. Cleopas's reply is one of the great ironies in Scripture: are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know what has happened? He is addressing the only person alive who knows what actually took place on that hill, and Jesus does not correct him.

Their summary of him is entirely accurate and completely insufficient: Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet mighty in deed and word, delivered up by our own chief priests, crucified. Every clause is true. The sum of it is a dead prophet and a walk home. And then the saddest tense in any language: we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel — followed by it is now the third day, the very fact that should have sent them running back, offered as the closing argument for despair.

They have the empty tomb, the angelic message and independent corroboration, and they are walking away. So he gives them not more evidence but the key: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interprets in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself — making a foreign language intelligible.

At the village he acts as if he were going farther. He will not force the door. They press him — stay with us, for it is toward evening — and at their table the guest becomes the host: he took the bread, blessed, broke and gave it, the same four actions as on the hillside and in the upper room. Their eyes are opened, they recognise him, and he is gone.

Then, and only then: did not our hearts burn within us? And they rise that same hour and walk the seven miles back in the dark — to find the room already alight with news that the Lord has appeared to Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Necessary — the divine must that governs this Gospel. Their whole difficulty inverts here: they thought the crucifixion was the reason he could not be the Christ, and are told it is the reason they should have known he was. The suffering was never a detour from the plan; it was the plan, and the glory is entered through it rather than after it.

Verse 27 is the hermeneutical claim on which the church has read its Bible ever since. The Old Testament is not religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book with one subject: the seed of the woman, the ram in the thicket, the lamb at the door, the serpent on the pole, the goat driven out, the servant who said nothing, the son of man receiving a kingdom. To read it without him is to miss what it is about.

And the sequence of the afternoon is the pattern the church has followed since: Scripture opened, then bread broken, and Christ known in both. This is not the Lord's Supper — it is an ordinary meal in a private house — but the Reformers' insistence stands: Word and Table belong together, and neither is complete without the other.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 16 describes a real and common condition of the Christian life: he is nearer than at any point you could identify, and you cannot see him, and the not-seeing is preparation rather than abandonment. These men later said their hearts had burned the whole way. At the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger.

Verse 21 is for anyone currently living inside a we had hoped. Their hope was not disappointed; it was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked, on the very day they gave it up, and the redemption they wanted for Israel turned out to be a redemption for the world.

Verses 19–20 describe a position a great many decent people hold: Jesus was remarkable, his teaching profound, his death unjust, the world would be better if people lived as he said. All true, all sincere, and it is a description of a corpse.

And v. 32 answers a question honest Christians carry privately — what do I do when the Bible feels dead? Not try harder, and not a better method. The burning came from a person, and the response is a prayer he grants: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Ps. 119:18). Note also the reverse error: they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is a gift, not a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.

That very day. The same Sunday. The tomb has been found open that morning, the report has been made and dismissed, Peter has been and come back — and two disciples are walking out of the city.

Seven miles is around two hours on foot. They are not fleeing; a man does not flee at walking pace in daylight with a companion. They are simply going home, because it is over.

Consider what that means, since it is the most ordinary and most recognisable thing in the chapter. There has been a catastrophe, and there has been a strange report about it that they do not believe, and the practical question of a Sunday afternoon is what to do next — and the answer is to go back to the village and pick life up again.

Where Emmaus was is not certainly known. Several sites have been proposed and none is secure, which is itself a small argument for the account's honesty: a legend attaches itself to a famous place, and this one is attached to a village nobody can now find.

Two of them — not of the eleven, then, but of the wider company. One is named five verses later; the other never is. It has been suggested that the unnamed one is Cleopas's wife, since they arrive at a shared home and press the stranger to stay, and it is a reasonable guess and no more than that.

And they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.

They are going over it, back and forth. This is what grief does on a long walk: it recounts. They are doing what every family does in the week after a death, turning the events round and round, trying to make a shape out of them that does not hurt so much, and getting nowhere.

Two ordinary disciples, walking away from Jerusalem on the greatest morning in history, discussing a defeat that had not happened. And the risen Christ, with the whole world made new that day and every claim in the universe on his time, was about to spend the afternoon walking seven miles with them (cf. Mal. 3:16; Matt. 18:20).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is about sixty stadia; the location of Emmaus is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.

Jesus himself drew near and went with them.

Luke puts the emphasis on the person: Jesus himself. Not a messenger, not a vision. And the verb for what he does is entirely undramatic — he came alongside and walked with them, which is what any traveller does on a public road when he catches up with people going the same way.

The first act of the risen Lord recorded in this Gospel is to join two disappointed people on a walk and let them talk.

But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.

Their eyes were held. This is not a failure of observation on their part and not a disguise on his; it is deliberate, and it is temporary, and it will be lifted in v. 31 by the same hand.

So the question is why — and the answer is in what the next fifteen verses contain. If he had made himself known at the roadside, there would have been joy, and there would have been no Bible study. They would have had the fact and not the meaning. Instead he keeps his face hidden long enough to walk them through Moses and the Prophets, so that when recognition comes they will understand what they are looking at.

He withheld himself in order to give them more of himself.

Which is worth carrying into the seasons when he seems absent, because this verse describes a real and common condition of the Christian life: he is closer than at any point you can identify, and you cannot see him, and the not-seeing is not abandonment but preparation. These two men later said their hearts had been burning the whole way. At the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger.

The Lord of glory, hours out of the grave, matched his pace to two people who had given up on him, and walked with them for two hours while they explained his death to his face (cf. Gen. 28:16; John 20:14).

parallels.desc: the disciples did not know that it was Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?' And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, 'Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk? And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?

He asks a question he does not need the answer to, which is what he has done throughout this Gospel. Where is your faith? Who touched me? What do you want me to do for you? He is not gathering information. He is opening a door and letting them walk through it in their own words.

And they stood still, looking sad.

That is one of Luke's small masterpieces of observation. The question stops them dead in the road. Grief that has been talking freely between two people cannot always survive being asked about by a third; something in the stranger's enquiry brings the whole weight of it back, and they cannot walk and hold it at the same time.

Looking sad — gloomy, downcast, the look of a man who has stopped expecting anything.

Then Cleopas answers, and his reply is one of the great ironies in Scripture. Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened?

He is addressing the only person in the world who knows what happened. Everyone else in that city, including these two, had watched from outside: the crowd saw an execution, the council saw a problem solved, the soldiers saw a shift completed. One man knew what had actually taken place on that hill, and he was standing in the road being asked whether he had heard the news.

And he does not correct him. He does not say I was there. He asks another question and lets Cleopas go on.

Which is a picture of the patience of Christ worth taking home. He listens to a mistaken account of his own death, from a man who is grieving, without interrupting to put the record straight — because the man needs to say it more than he needs to be corrected, and because everything Cleopas is about to get wrong will be answered properly a few minutes later.

He asked them what they were talking about, and stood in the road, and let two heartbroken people tell him he must be the only man in Jerusalem who had not heard (cf. Luke 8:25; John 21:15).
verseByVerse.note: Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What things?' And they said to him, 'Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, What things? And they said to him, Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.

What things? Two words, and he has them talking.

What follows is a small creed, and it is worth taking seriously as a statement of what these disciples actually believed on Easter afternoon — because everything in it is true, and it is not enough.

Jesus of Nazareth — the right man, correctly identified. A prophet — true; he was, and Moses had said one would come. Mighty in deed and word — true, and in that order, which is how Luke has told the story: the works first and the words interpreting them. Before God and all the people — true; his ministry was public and God attested it.

Then the history, and it is accurate to the last detail. Our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. They do not blame Rome, which would have been the easy account. They say our — our leaders did this — and they use the language Luke used of Pilate: delivered him up (23:25).

So here is a man with the facts entirely straight and no gospel at all. Every clause is correct. And the sum of it is a dead prophet and a walk home.

Which is the state of a great many people who are not hostile to Christianity in the least. Jesus was a remarkable man; his teaching was profound; he was killed unjustly by the religious establishment; the world would be better if people lived as he said. All of that is true, all of it can be held with real respect, and it will not save anybody, because it is a description of a corpse.

Notice the one word missing from their summary. They call him a prophet. They do not call him the Christ — and they are about to be told, by the man walking beside them, that they had it in the Scriptures all along.

The most accurate account of Jesus of Nazareth ever given by an unbeliever was given on that road, and the man it was given to had to spend two hours explaining what it left out (cf. Deut. 18:15; Acts 2:22–23).

parallels.desc: a man attested to you by God

verseByVerse.quote: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.

We had hoped.

There is no sadder tense in any language. Not we hope, which is alive; not we never hoped, which is safe. We had hoped is the tense of a thing that was once real and is now over, and everyone who has ever prayed for something and watched it not happen knows the exact weight of it.

It is worth being clear about what they had hoped for, because it was not a small or foolish thing. The one to redeem Israel — the word is lytrousthai, to ransom, to buy out of slavery, and it is the language Zechariah used in the first chapter of this Gospel when he sang that God had visited and redeemed his people (1:68). They wanted the promises kept. They wanted the occupation ended and the covenant honoured and God to act. They were not wrong to want it.

They were wrong about the shape and the timing, and that is nearly always where hope goes wrong.

Then the second sentence, which is the more remarkable of the two: it is now the third day since these things happened.

They know it is the third day. They say so. He had told them repeatedly that the Son of Man would rise on the third day, and here are two of his disciples reciting the timetable as the reason their hope is finished. The very fact that should have had them running back to the city is offered as the closing argument for despair.

That is what unbelief does with evidence. It does not ignore it. It files it on the wrong side of the ledger.

And here is the thing to see, for anyone who is living inside a we had hoped at the moment. Their hope was not disappointed. It was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked for, on the very day they gave it up, and the redemption they had wanted for Israel was walking beside them and turned out to be a redemption for the world.

They said we had hoped to the face of the risen Son of God, three days into a rescue so much larger than the one they had prayed for that they could not recognise it while it was happening to them (cf. Luke 1:68; Eph. 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.

Read what they have and then read where they are going, because the gap between the two is the point of the paragraph.

They have the empty tomb, reported by named witnesses of their own company. They have the announcement of angels. They have independent corroboration — some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said. Three separate strands, all pointing one way.

And they are walking to Emmaus.

The tell is in the phrase a vision of angels. The women had seen angels, but what mattered was the message they were given: he is alive. In this retelling the sight survives and the message is held at arm's length — and once a report is filed under that heading it requires nothing of anybody.

And then the closing clause, which is where the whole account collapses for them: but him they did not see.

That is honest, and it is the sticking point. They will not go beyond the evidence, which is in one sense creditable. But notice what it means: they have decided in advance what would count. Only a sighting will do. The empty tomb is a puzzle, the angelic word is a rumour, and the promise from Galilee has not entered the conversation at all.

Which is why the answer he is about to give them is not what anyone would expect. He does not say look at me. He could have. Instead he spends two hours in the Old Testament — because their problem was never a shortage of evidence, and giving them more of the same kind would have left the real defect untouched.

Facts do not interpret themselves. Two men had every piece of the resurrection in their possession by Sunday lunchtime and used them to build a case for going home.

They were carrying the news of the empty tomb in their own mouths, walking in the wrong direction, and the answer to it was matching their stride (cf. Luke 16:31; John 20:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?

It sounds severe in English and it is gentler in Greek. Foolish is anoētoi — literally un-minded, not stupid but not thinking; people who have the material and have not put it together. And slow of heart is not a word for wickedness. It is the word you would use of someone who takes a long time to be persuaded of something he already half knows.

Note also what he does not correct. He does not say slow of heart to believe the report of the women, or slow to believe the empty tomb. He says to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Their failure is not that they doubted the evidence of that morning. It is that they had a Bible.

Then the question that reframes everything: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?

Necessary — it must be. Luke has used the idea all through his Gospel for the fixed purposes of God, and here it is applied to the one event these men had decided was the end of the story.

Consider how completely that inverts their position. They think the crucifixion is the reason he cannot be the Christ. He tells them the crucifixion is the reason they should have known he was.

Their difficulty was that they had read the Scriptures selectively, and so has almost everyone. The glory was easy to find — a throne, a kingdom, an everlasting dominion — and the suffering was on the same pages and had been left unread: the servant despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions, led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isa. 53); the man of Psalm 22 with his hands and feet pierced, his garments divided; the shepherd struck. It was all there. Nobody had wanted it.

And enter into his glory is not a consolation offered after the suffering. It is a destination reached through it. The word is one of movement, of going in by a door — and the door was a cross.

Which answers the question a suffering Christian most often asks, though it does not remove the pain: whether the hard road is a detour from God's plan or part of it. If it was necessary for the Christ, it is not evidence of a mistake in anyone else's case either.

He had been raised from the dead that morning, and the first thing he did with his risen voice was open the Scriptures to two people who had stopped believing them (cf. Isa. 53:3–5; 1 Pet. 1:11).

parallels.desc: it was necessary for the Christ to suffer

verseByVerse.quote: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

Every preacher who has ever read this verse has wished for a transcript. There is none, and Luke plainly does not think one is needed, because the whole New Testament is written by men who had this lesson or were taught by those who did.

Beginning with Moses. So he started at Genesis. The seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head and be struck in the doing of it (Gen. 3:15). A ram caught in a thicket on the mountain where God would provide, dying in the place of a son (Gen. 22). A lamb slaughtered and its blood on the doorposts so that death would pass over the house (Exod. 12). A bronze serpent lifted on a pole, so that anyone dying of the bite could look and live (Num. 21). A tabernacle with a veil and a mercy seat and blood carried in once a year by one man. A scapegoat driven into the wilderness carrying the sins of the people on its head.

And all the Prophets. A servant pierced for our transgressions, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isa. 53). A shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zech. 13:7). A son of man coming with the clouds to receive a kingdom that shall not pass away (Dan. 7). A new covenant, written on the heart, with sins remembered no more (Jer. 31).

And the word Luke uses for what he did with all this is diermēneusen — he interpreted, he translated. It is the word for making a foreign language intelligible. The Scriptures were not new to these men; they had heard them read every Sabbath of their lives. What they had never had was the key.

That is the claim being made here, and it is enormous: the Old Testament is not a collection of religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book, with one subject, and the subject is walking down a road to Emmaus explaining himself.

He is the ram in the thicket and the lamb at the door and the serpent on the pole and the goat driven out and the servant who said nothing. Every altar in Israel had been pointing at him for fifteen hundred years, and on the afternoon of the third day he went through them one at a time (cf. John 5:39; 1 Pet. 1:10–11).
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and all the Prophets” means the whole Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying, 'Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.' So he went in to stay with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying, Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent. So he went in to stay with them.

He acted as if he were going farther.

Readers sometimes find this uncomfortable, as though it were a pretence unworthy of him. It is not. He is a traveller on a road who has reached the point where his companions turn off, and the courteous thing — the only thing that leaves them free — is to keep walking unless he is asked.

He will not force the door. That is the whole of it. He had joined them uninvited on the road and given them two hours they will never forget, and at the gate of the village he leaves the next move to them.

And they make it. They urged him strongly — pressed him, constrained him; they took hold of him, in the ordinary way of eastern hospitality, and would not let him go on.

Their reason is entirely practical. It is toward evening and the day is now far spent. The roads were not safe after dark and a stranger should not be walking them alone. They are not asking for more teaching; they think they are doing a kindness to a man who has nowhere to sleep.

So the invitation that changed their lives was, on the face of it, ordinary courtesy to a fellow traveller. They had no idea what they were asking for. That is worth remembering by anyone who thinks the great moments of the Christian life announce themselves in advance.

But notice what had been happening underneath. Something in those two hours had made them unwilling to let this man walk away, and they would tell each other later what it was: their hearts had been burning. They could not have named it at the gate. They only knew they did not want the conversation to end.

And the sentence at the end of the verse has been the prayer of Christians ever since, for exactly the reason they first said it — because the day is far spent and the light is going. Stay with us.

He went as far as the door and would not go in until he was wanted, and the moment he was asked he came in and sat down and stayed (cf. Rev. 3:20; Gen. 18:3).
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight.

Look at who is doing what. It is their house. They invited him in as a guest, and at the table he takes the bread, and he blesses it, and he breaks it, and he gives it to them.

The guest has become the host. That happens wherever he is welcomed, and it is never announced.

Four actions, and Luke has recorded them twice before: he took, he blessed or gave thanks, he broke, he gave. Once on a hillside with five thousand men sitting on the grass (9:16). Once in an upper room, three nights ago, with a cup and a new covenant (22:19).

Whether these two had been in that upper room, we are not told. What is certain is that they had seen those hands do this before, and that the hands were now marked.

And their eyes were opened. The reverse of v. 16, and the same hand behind it. He had held their sight; now he releases it. Recognition, from first to last in this account, is a gift and not an achievement.

And he vanished from their sight. The instant they see him, he is gone.

Which has struck readers as cruel, and is the opposite. He does not leave them with nothing; he leaves them with everything they now need and no longer requires them to have him visible in the room. Something has been permanently established at that table, and the way they behave in the next verse proves it — they do not sit down and grieve his going. They get up and run.

And there is a settled Christian instinct here that is right, so long as it is not pressed into a doctrine the passage does not carry. This is not the Lord's Supper; it is an ordinary meal in a private house. But the pattern the church has followed ever since is the pattern of this afternoon: the Scriptures opened, and then bread broken, and Christ known in both. Word and Table belong together, as the Reformers insisted, and neither is complete without the other.

He had walked seven miles and preached the whole Old Testament to them, and it was when he broke the bread that they saw who had been beside them all day (cf. Luke 9:16; 22:19).

parallels.desc: he took bread and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: They said to each other, 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to each other, Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?

They say it afterwards, which is the first thing to notice. Nobody said at the time my heart is burning. It was only when they knew who he was that they understood what had been happening to them for the last two hours.

That is very often the shape of it. A Christian looks back on a stretch of road — a season of reading, a conversation, a hard year — and sees that God was doing something in him that he was entirely unaware of while it was going on.

Our hearts burn within us — a fire kindling. And in the Bible the heart is not the seat of the emotions as against the mind; it is the whole inner person — thinking, willing, loving, deciding. So this is not a description of a mood. It is a man saying that something caught light in him.

Then the two clauses that tell you what lit it, and they are worth separating because most people run them together.

While he talked to us on the road — the person. While he opened to us the Scriptures — the book. Neither alone did it. A stranger's company on a walk would not have set a heart burning, and the Scriptures had been read to these men every Sabbath of their lives without producing this. It was Christ, in the Scriptures, opening them.

Which is the answer to a question a great many honest Christians carry privately and are ashamed to ask: what do I do when the Bible feels dead?

The answer this verse gives is not try harder and it is not find a better method. The burning came from a person, and the request that follows from it is a prayer rather than a technique — that the one the book is about would open it. That prayer is entirely in line with what he does elsewhere on this same day: thirteen verses later he opens the minds of the eleven, and Luke uses the identical verb.

It is worth adding, because the reverse error is real, that they had a burning heart and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is not the test; they were warmed for two hours before they understood anything. The fire is a gift, not a verdict.

Two men who had given up on him sat in a house at nightfall and realised they had been on fire since mid-afternoon and had thought it was only a good conversation (cf. Jer. 20:9; Ps. 119:18).

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, 'The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!' Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon! Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.

That same hour. The meal is abandoned. It is dark, they have already walked seven miles that day, the roads are dangerous, and the reason they gave for pressing him to stay — that the day was far spent — applies with equal force to them.

They go anyway, back over the same seven miles they had walked out in despair, in the dark, because there are people in Jerusalem who need to hear this tonight. Nobody had told them to.

And they arrive to a room that is already alight. Before they can say a word, the news is shouted at them: the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon.

Simon. Not Peter, the rock — the old name, the one Jesus used in the upper room when he warned him. Somewhere in that Sunday, between the run to the tomb and this moment, the risen Christ met privately with the man who had denied him three times.

And Luke does not describe it. Neither does anyone else. Paul confirms it happened and names him first among the witnesses — he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve (1 Cor. 15:5) — and that is all the record there is.

It is hard not to feel the tact of that. Whatever passed between those two, it stayed between them. The Gospel writers had every reason to include a scene of Peter's restoration and they left the door shut, and the only trace of it is a room full of people repeating a name.

Which is worth knowing by anyone whose own worst failure has been dealt with quietly, without a public account of it ever being given. The church heard that the Lord had appeared to Simon. It never heard what was said.

Then the Emmaus pair tell their story, and Luke's summary of it is the shape of the whole afternoon: what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.

Two men who had walked away from that room in the morning had come back at night, and the first thing they heard was that the man who had denied him had been found first (cf. 1 Cor. 15:5; John 21:15–17).
verseByVerse.note: Simon is Peter.

parallels.desc: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–53 — Jerusalem, the Commission, and the Ascension
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He arrives mid-sentence into a locked room, and the first word of the risen Christ to the gathered church is peace — spoken to men who had failed him in the garden and the courtyard, by the one who bought it on Friday. Their response is not faith: they think they are seeing a ghost. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was apparitions, not resurrection. Nobody in that room was expecting this.

So he offers evidence, which is a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing. See my hands and my feet — the identification runs through the wounds. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. And then, while they are disbelieving for joy, he asks whether there is anything to eat, and eats a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

Then he sends them back to the book. The Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms is the standard threefold division of the Hebrew Scriptures — the whole Bible they possessed, listed by its own sections. And he opened their minds to understand it: the third opening of the day, after their eyes at the table and the Scriptures on the road, all three by the same hand.

The commission follows, and it is still inside thus it is written: repentance for the forgiveness of sins, in his name, to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem — the city that had just killed him. You are witnesses of these things. And then a command nobody expects at the end of a commission: stay in the city and do nothing until you are clothed with power from on high.

Finally Bethany, and hands lifted in the priestly posture of Leviticus 9:22 — hands with holes in them. He parts from them while he blessed them, in the middle of the blessing, and is carried up.

They worship him — Jewish monotheists, on their faces, before a man they had eaten with in those forty days — and return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 39–43 close off an entire family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, nor a vision granted to grieving friends, nor a cause living on. It is a body, with hands and feet, that can be handled and that eats. A reader who knows 1 Corinthians 15 may feel a difficulty, since Paul calls it a spiritual body — but Paul is describing not what it is made of but what governs it, as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning immaterial. Paul's argument is that ours will be like his, and Luke has just shown his eating fish.

And the wounds are kept. He did not leave the marks in the tomb as an unpleasantness now finished with; the Lamb in John's vision stands in the middle of the throne looking as though it had been slain (Rev. 5:6).

Verse 45 carries a whole doctrine. These men had the text, had heard it since childhood, and had just spent an evening with the risen Christ expounding it — and still needed their minds opened before they could take it in. Understanding Scripture is not finally a matter of intelligence or access (1 Cor. 2:14; Acts 16:14). That is humbling, and it is freeing: the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask the one who opens it.

And the ascension is not the end of the story but the beginning of the reign — seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb. 1:3), exactly as he told the council would begin from that moment (22:69). The disciples' worship of him is the first unambiguous worship of the risen Jesus in this Gospel, given by monotheists, with nobody correcting them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Disbelieved for joy is the commonest form of unbelief among genuine Christians: not doubt that the gospel is true, but the inability to take it personally — believers who can recite justification and cannot quite accept that they are forgiven. Jesus neither rebukes it nor argues with it. He asks for something to eat. Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed.

Beginning from Jerusalem is the measure of the thing announced. Any ordinary movement starts where it is welcome and works back to hostile ground later. The risen Christ orders the reverse: the first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it, carried by men who watched. Three thousand of them took it in a day.

Verse 48 defines what any Christian is actually asked for. Not to have the answers to every question, and not to argue anyone into the kingdom — simply to say what he has seen of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed. And it was entrusted to eleven men who had all failed him within the previous seventy-two hours.

Verse 49 is for anyone in a season of enforced waiting. There is a stillness that is disobedience and a stillness that is obedience, and the difference is not how it feels — both feel like wasting time. These men went nowhere and did nothing, on orders, until the power came. Zeal without the Spirit was what Peter had already shown in the garden with a sword.

And v. 52 speaks to anyone who half wishes he had been there instead of here. These men had the choice between seeing him in the room and having him enthroned with the Spirit about to come, and they went home with great joy.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, 'Peace to you!' But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, Peace to you! But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.

As they were talking about these things. He arrives mid-sentence, into a room where he is being discussed. John adds that the doors were shut for fear of the authorities.

Jesus himself stood among them. There is no entrance described. One moment the room contains a dozen frightened people arguing about reports; the next it contains him.

And the first word of the risen Christ to the assembled church is peace.

It was the ordinary greeting — shalom, said by everyone to everyone. But consider who is saying it and to whom. The last time most of these men saw him, he was being arrested in a garden while they looked on. Peter had denied him. If ever there was a moment for a reckoning, this was it, and what he says is peace to you.

And it is not merely a courtesy, because of where he has just come from. Peace with God through the blood of his cross (Col. 1:20) was purchased on Friday; on Sunday evening the one who bought it walks into a locked room and says the word.

Then the reaction, which Luke reports without any attempt to make his subjects look better: they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.

They have just been shouting that the Lord is risen. He appears, and they conclude they are looking at a ghost.

That is an important detail and not a flattering one, which is why it is worth trusting. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was not resurrection; it was apparitions. Everyone believed in those, and nobody thought they involved a body. So the disciples' instinct here is precisely the instinct of their culture, and it is the opposite of the thing they are about to be forced to accept.

Nobody in that room was expecting a resurrection. They were expecting a haunting, and they were terrified.

He came through a locked door into a room full of men who had abandoned him and were now afraid of him, and the first thing out of his mouth was the word he had bought for them on Friday (cf. John 20:19; Col. 1:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.

He does not scold the doubt. He asks about it, and then he answers it with evidence, which is a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing.

See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself.

Why the hands and the feet? Because that is where the nails went. He is not simply proving that a body is present; he is proving whose. The identification runs through the wounds.

Which is worth stopping on. The resurrection body is glorious, imperishable, no longer subject to death — and it is scarred. He did not leave the marks behind in the tomb as an unpleasantness now finished with. He carried them out, and he carries them still: the Lamb standing in the middle of the throne, John says, looking as though it had been slain (Rev. 5:6). The only man-made things in heaven are the scars of Christ.

Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.

That sentence closes off an entire family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, nor a vision granted to grieving friends, nor a symbol of a cause living on. It is a body, with hands and feet, in a room, that can be handled.

Now, a reader who knows 1 Corinthians 15 may feel a difficulty here, because Paul calls the resurrection body a spiritual body, and that sounds like the opposite of flesh and bones. It is not, and the confusion is worth clearing. Paul is not describing what the body is made of but what it is animated and ruled by — as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning they are immaterial. A spiritual body in Paul's sense is a body wholly governed by the Spirit of God, imperishable and powerful. It is not a ghost. Paul's whole argument in that chapter is that ours will be like his, and Luke has just shown us his eating fish.

So the Christian hope is not the escape of the soul from the body. It is the redemption of the body, and the ground of it is standing in a room in Jerusalem holding out his hands.

He rose with his wounds still on him and showed them to his friends as identification, and they are the only proof of love that has ever been offered by a body that could not die again (cf. 1 Cor. 15:42–44; Rev. 5:6).

parallels.desc: which we have looked upon and touched

verseByVerse.quote: And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, 'Have you anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, Have you anything here to eat? They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.

Disbelieved for joy. It is one of the truest phrases in Scripture, and only a very honest writer would have set it down.

They are no longer frightened; that has passed. What is holding them back now is not doubt of the ordinary kind but the specific paralysis of a person to whom something has been offered that is too good to be believed. Everyone knows the feeling, and it is not the same as scepticism. It is the fear of letting yourself accept a thing in case it turns out not to be so.

And it is the commonest form of unbelief among genuine Christians, which is why the phrase deserves its own paragraph in any commentary. There are believers who can recite the doctrine of justification and cannot quite accept that they personally are forgiven — not because they think the gospel untrue, but because they cannot make themselves take it. That is disbelieving for joy, and Jesus's response to it here is worth studying, because he does not rebuke it and he does not argue with it.

He asks for something to eat.

Have you anything here to eat? It is the most ordinary sentence in the chapter and the most disarming. The Son of God, three days out of a grave, with the powers of the age to come in his body, asks whether there is anything in the house.

They give him a piece of broiled fish — leftovers, plainly, from men who had not been cooking that evening — and he takes it and eats it in front of them.

He did not need it. Nothing suggests the resurrection body requires food; he ate because they needed to watch him do it. A ghost cannot chew. Whatever they were prepared to believe about apparitions, none of it survived a man sitting down with a piece of fish.

And there is something almost unbearably homely in it that ought not to be lost in the argument. Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed.

The Lord of glory ate a scrap of cold fish in a borrowed room to settle the stomachs of eleven men who were too happy to think straight (cf. Acts 10:41; John 21:12–13).

parallels.desc: who ate and drank with him

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.

These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you.

There is a small phrase in that which repays attention: while I was still with you. He is with them at that moment, in the room, eating. So he is marking off a period that has now ended — the years of walking Galilee together — and speaking from the other side of it. A new arrangement has begun, and he says so in passing before anyone has noticed.

And what he does first, in this new arrangement, is exactly what he did on the road: he sends them back to the book.

The Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms. That is not a loose gesture at religious literature. It is the standard threefold division of the Hebrew Scriptures as the Jews arranged them — the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings, here named after their best-known book, the Psalms. In other words: the whole Bible they possessed, listed by its own sections, with nothing left out.

Everything written about him in all three must be fulfilled. There is that word again, dei, which has governed this Gospel from the boy in the temple who must be about his Father's business to the Son of Man who must suffer.

So the claim is total. Not that the Old Testament contains some prophecies which he happened to satisfy, the way a candidate meets criteria — but that the whole of it, in every division, is about him, and that it had to come out this way.

Which settles the question every new Christian eventually asks about the first three-quarters of his Bible: what am I supposed to do with all this? Genealogies, sacrifices, a tabernacle measured in cubits, kings who mostly failed, prophets shouting at a nation that would not listen.

Read it as the setting-up of a story whose ending you already know. It is not a different religion appended to the front of yours. It is the same God, working towards the same person, for two thousand years before he arrived.

Is every Old Testament passage about Christ? The whole Old Testament leads to him: its promises, its patterns and its law find their goal in him. But each passage has its own meaning in its own setting, and that must be read first. Finding Christ is not a matter of hunting for hidden symbols; it is tracing how each part of the story moves toward him.

He had said all this before — that is the point of these are my words — and they had not understood a syllable of it until the man who was crucified stood in front of them saying it again (cf. John 5:46; Acts 3:18).
verseByVerse.note: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (the Writings) are the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.

Nine words, and there is a whole doctrine in them.

The verb is diēnoixen — he opened thoroughly, he unlocked. Luke has used it twice already in this chapter, and the repetition is deliberate: their eyes were opened at the table (v. 31), the Scriptures were opened on the road (v. 32), and now their minds are opened in the room. Three openings in one day, and the same hand performs all three.

So the sequence is worth stating plainly, because it corrects an assumption almost everyone makes without examining it. These men had the text. They had heard it since childhood. They had just spent an evening with the risen Christ expounding it, and two of them had had seven miles of it that afternoon. And they still needed something done to them before they could take it in.

Understanding Scripture is not, finally, a matter of intelligence, education, or access. It is a matter of a closed mind being opened by God, and he does the opening.

Paul says the same thing from the other side: the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned (1 Cor. 2:14). And Luke will show it happening again in his second volume, in almost the same words: the Lord opened Lydia's heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14).

Which has two consequences and they pull in opposite directions, and both are needed.

The first is humbling. Nobody reasons himself into the kingdom by being clever with a text. If you understand the gospel, someone opened your mind, and you did not do it.

The second is enormously freeing, and it is where this verse belongs in a Christian's actual practice. If the opening is his work, then the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask him — which is what generations of believers have done from Psalm 119: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Ps. 119:18). That is not a pious formula. It is a request that this verse says he grants.

He had risen from the dead, walked through a wall, and eaten fish in front of them, and none of it was enough by itself; so he reached into their minds and opened them (cf. 1 Cor. 2:14; Acts 16:14).

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead.

Thus it is written. Everything the risen Christ says about himself in this room is anchored to a text.

He might have argued from what had just happened, and it would have been unanswerable — the wounds, the fish, the locked door. He argues instead from Scripture, which tells you what he intends the church to stand on when the eyewitnesses are gone.

Two things are said to be written, and they are the two halves of the gospel Paul would preach for the next thirty years.

The Christ should suffer. That is the half nobody had wanted. The word Christ means the anointed King, and a suffering King was not what Israel was watching for. It was in the book all the same, in Isaiah's servant and in the psalms of the righteous sufferer, and it had been read past for centuries.

And on the third day rise from the dead. Which raises a fair question: where exactly is that written? No verse in the Old Testament says the Messiah will rise on the third day in so many words.

The apostles answered it two ways, and both are worth knowing. They pointed to particular texts — Peter at Pentecost quotes Psalm 16, you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption, and argues that David died and was buried and his tomb is still here, so he was speaking of another (Acts 2:27–31). Paul does the same at Antioch. And Jonah supplied the pattern of the third day, as Jesus himself had said (Matt. 12:40; cf. Luke 11:29–30).

But the deeper answer is the one this chapter has been making since the road: it is written not in one verse but in the shape of the whole thing. A story that runs from a garden lost to a people redeemed by blood, from exile to return, from a valley of dry bones to an army standing up — that story does not end in a tomb. Resurrection is written across the Old Testament the way a key is written across a piece of music.

He stood in a room in Jerusalem with the marks in his hands and said that the death he had died and the rising he had done were, both of them, in the book all along (cf. Ps. 16:10; Acts 2:24–32).

parallels.desc: on the third day he will raise us up

verseByVerse.quote: and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

Notice where this sentence sits. It is still inside thus it is written. The mission of the church is not an application drawn from the resurrection; it is part of what the Scriptures foretold, on the same footing as the suffering and the rising.

Four things are specified, and between them they define what the church is for.

Repentance for the forgiveness of sins. That is the message, and it is worth being exact about it, because a great deal gets preached in its place. Not moral improvement. Not social respectability. Not a technique for a better life. Repentance — a change of mind that turns the whole person round — and forgiveness, which is the thing a guilty person actually needs and cannot obtain for himself.

In his name. That is the authority and the ground. Not in the name of the church, and not on the strength of anyone's sincerity. Peter would put it flatly: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

To all nations. The scope is the world. And Luke has been signalling this from the beginning of his Gospel — Simeon holding a baby and calling him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32), the genealogy traced back not to Abraham but to Adam (3:38).

And then the last clause, which is the one to stop at. Beginning from Jerusalem.

Jerusalem. The city that had just done it. The place where the crowd had shouted crucify, where the council had condemned him, where the soldiers had blindfolded and beaten him, where the cross had gone up outside the wall seven weeks before Peter would stand up and preach.

Any ordinary movement would begin somewhere else. Start where you are welcome; work back to the hostile ground later, when you are strong. The risen Christ orders the exact opposite: the first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it, and it is offered by men who watched them do it.

That is the measure of the thing being announced. And when Peter did preach there, three thousand of the people of that city and its pilgrims, men Peter charged with the crucifixion, were forgiven in a day (Acts 2:41).

He was crucified in Jerusalem on Friday, and on Sunday he told his friends to take the forgiveness there first (cf. Acts 2:38–41; 1 Tim. 1:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses of these things.

Six words, and the whole church rests on them.

A witness is not an advocate and not a theorist. He is a person who was present and can say what he saw. That is the entire qualification, and it is also the entire limitation: a witness may not embellish and may not speculate, and his usefulness depends absolutely on his having been there.

The word is martyres, and English has taken it and narrowed it, because so many of the men in that room ended up dying for the testimony. But at this moment it means only what it says. You saw it. Say so.

Which is what makes the Christian claim a different kind of claim from most religious claims, and it is worth being clear about the difference. Christianity is not in the first instance a philosophy, or a set of values, or a way of interpreting existence. It is a report — that a particular man, in a particular place, under a named Roman governor, was executed and buried and three days later was alive, and here are the people who watched it.

Paul argued exactly this way, and staked everything on it: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:5–6). That is not the language of a man offering a spirituality. It is the language of a man saying: go and ask them.

Now look at who is being commissioned. These are the men who fell asleep in the garden, denied him in a courtyard, dismissed the women's report as raving, and were standing in that room a few minutes ago convinced they were seeing a ghost. Not one of them has a record to be proud of. Every one of them is about to be sent to the ends of the earth on the strength of what he saw.

And they will not be asked to be impressive. Only truthful.

Which is the whole of what any Christian is asked for. Not to have the answers to every question, and not to argue anyone into the kingdom — simply to say what he has seen of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed.

He entrusted the report of his own resurrection to eleven men who had all failed him inside the previous seventy-two hours, and he has never taken it back (cf. 1 Cor. 15:5–8; Acts 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.

The promise of my Father is the Holy Spirit — what Joel had foretold when God said he would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and what Luke will describe in the second chapter of his second volume.

And clothed with power is a striking image: the verb is the one used for putting on a garment. The power comes from outside and is put on. It is not a capacity discovered within, and it is not the disciples becoming better men. It is something they will wear.

Then the command, and it is not what anyone would expect at the end of a commission. Stay in the city.

He has just told them the message, the authority, the scope and the starting point, and given them their commission as witnesses. And then he tells them to do nothing at all.

Consider how hard that instruction was. They had the greatest news in the world and were forbidden, for the moment, to take it anywhere — and forbidden to leave the one city where every person who wanted them dead was still in office.

Which is worth having on record for anyone in a season of enforced waiting. There is a kind of stillness that is disobedience, and there is a kind that is obedience, and the difference is not how it feels — both feel like wasting time. These men were not idle for those days; Acts says they were praying. But they went nowhere and did nothing, on orders, until the power came.

Zeal without the Spirit was exactly what Peter had shown in the garden with a sword.

A reader who compares Gospels will notice a difficulty here and it should be met, because sceptics have pressed it for a long time. Here Jesus says stay in the city; but the angel at the tomb in Matthew and Mark says he is going ahead of them to Galilee, and Matthew's great commission is given on a Galilean mountain seventy miles north. Stay here, go there — which is it?

Should Christians today wait for the Spirit as the disciples did? No. Their waiting was for one unrepeatable event, the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost. Now every believer receives the Spirit when he believes (Rom 8:9; 1 Cor 12:13; Acts 2:38–39). Some Pentecostal Christians teach a later baptism to be sought; but we are not waiting for the Spirit to come, only asking him to fill us.

The objection only bites if all of this happened on one evening, and it did not. Luke's own second volume says Jesus appeared over forty days (Acts 1:3). Restore that span and the accounts unfold in sequence: appearances in and around Jerusalem on Easter Day and the week after; then Galilee, where Matthew's mountain and John's breakfast on the shore belong; then back to Jerusalem for the last days before Pentecost. Luke compresses the forty days: stay in the city is given on Easter evening and repeated at their end (Acts 1:4), and it governs the last days before Pentecost (cf. Joel 2:28; Acts 1:3–5).
verseByVerse.note: The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.

Bethany, of all places. Two miles from Jerusalem on the far side of Olivet — the village of Martha and Mary and Lazarus, where he had stayed during the last week, where he had wept at a grave and called a dead man out of it. He goes back there to leave.

Lifting up his hands he blessed them. That is the posture of the priest. Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them (Lev. 9:22), and the blessing given to him to speak was: the LORD bless you and keep you, the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Num. 6:24–26). And Luke, who opened this Gospel with a priest named Zechariah going into the sanctuary while the people waited outside for the blessing — and coming out unable to say a word (1:22) — now closes it with a priest whose hands are raised and whose blessing is not silent.

The hands lifted over them had holes in them.

While he blessed them, he parted from them. He did not finish and then go. He went in the middle of the blessing, which is a way of saying that the blessing never stopped. What those men saw last was his hands raised over them, and he is doing it still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25).

And was carried up into heaven. Not vanished, as at Emmaus. Taken up — the Father receiving the Son. This is not an exit from the story but an enthronement: he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb. 1:3), which is exactly what he had told the council would begin from that moment (22:69).

Some older editions left out several short phrases in this chapter, including and was carried up into heaven, because a small group of manuscripts lacks them, and nineteenth-century editors judged the shorter readings original. Then a very early copy of Luke came to light in the twentieth century which contained them, and opinion moved back; that is why the ESV prints them. It is worth noticing the direction of that story. The evidence did not erode the text as it accumulated. It confirmed it.

Did the ascension happen on Easter evening? Luke tells us in Acts that it came forty days later (Acts 1:3, 9). Here he gives the story in brief, without marking the time after v. 49.

He walked them out to a village he loved, raised the hands that had been nailed down, and went home to his Father in the act of blessing them (cf. Num. 6:24–26; Heb. 7:25).
verseByVerse.note: Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven.”

parallels.desc: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed them

verseByVerse.quote: And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.

Three things, and every one of them is impossible without the resurrection.

They worshiped him. The word is prosekynēsan — they fell down before him. These are Jewish men, raised on the first commandment, who had said the Shema every day of their lives: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. There was no category in their religion more absolute than the one forbidding worship to any but God. And they give it, without hesitation and without anyone correcting them, to a man they had eaten with in those forty days.

That is not a doctrine developed over centuries by a church drifting from its roots. It is monotheists on a hillside outside Jerusalem, six weeks after the crucifixion, on their faces.

And returned to Jerusalem with great joy.

Which is the strangest word in the sentence, because he had just left. Every human instinct says this should be a bereavement — they had him back for forty days and now he is gone again. Luke says great joy.

And the reason is that they finally understood where he had gone and what he was doing there. This was not another loss. It was the coronation of the man they loved, and the beginning of everything he had promised. Grief looks at an empty sky. They looked at a throne.

That is worth taking home by anyone who has trouble with the absence of Christ — who reads these accounts and half wishes he had been there instead of here. These men had the choice between having him visible in the room and having him seated at the right hand of God with the Spirit about to come, and they were not sorry.

And were continually in the temple blessing God.

The Gospel began in that temple. An old priest at the altar of incense, a crowd waiting outside, an angel with a promise, and a man who came out mute and could not give the blessing. It ends in the same building, with a company of ordinary people who cannot stop.

Every promise made in the first chapter has been kept. The horn of salvation raised up in the house of David; the dawn from on high visiting those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death; the light for revelation to the Gentiles, held once by an old man who was ready to die. All of it has happened, and the temple that Zechariah left in silence is now full of people blessing God out loud.

The book closes on worship, in the place it opened, and the Christ they are worshipping is alive and will not die again (cf. Luke 1:68–79; Acts 1:12–14).

24.text: <sup>1</sup> But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. <sup>2</sup> And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, <sup>3</sup> but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. <sup>4</sup> While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. <sup>5</sup> And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? <sup>6</sup> He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, <sup>7</sup> that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.” <sup>8</sup> And they remembered his words, <sup>9</sup> and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. <sup>10</sup> Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, <sup>11</sup> but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. <sup>12</sup> But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened. <sup>13</sup> That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup> and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened. <sup>15</sup> While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. <sup>16</sup> But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. <sup>17</sup> And he said to them, “What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?” And they stood still, looking sad. <sup>18</sup> Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to them, “What things?” And they said to him, “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, <sup>20</sup> and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. <sup>21</sup> But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. <sup>22</sup> Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, <sup>23</sup> and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. <sup>24</sup> Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.” <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! <sup>26</sup> Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” <sup>27</sup> And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. <sup>28</sup> So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, <sup>29</sup> but they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” So he went in to stay with them. <sup>30</sup> When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. <sup>31</sup> And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight. <sup>32</sup> They said to each other, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” <sup>33</sup> And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, <sup>34</sup> saying, “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” <sup>35</sup> Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. <sup>36</sup> As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace to you!” <sup>37</sup> But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. <sup>38</sup> And he said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? <sup>39</sup> See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” <sup>40</sup> And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. <sup>41</sup> And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, “Have you anything here to eat?” <sup>42</sup> They gave him a piece of broiled fish, <sup>43</sup> and he took it and ate before them. <sup>44</sup> Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” <sup>45</sup> Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, <sup>46</sup> and said to them, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, <sup>47</sup> and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. <sup>48</sup> You are witnesses of these things. <sup>49</sup> And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” <sup>50</sup> And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. <sup>51</sup> While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. <sup>52</sup> And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, <sup>53</sup> and were continually in the temple blessing God.
